statement: The main cable of the Golden Gate Bridge is about $$2300\;\mathrm{m}$$ long when unstretched. It is made of steel with density $$8\;\mathrm{g\;cm^{-3}}$$ and has a Young's modulus of about $$200\;\mathrm{GPa}.$$ Estimate the amount that the cable would stretch if it were hung vertically under its own weight.

desc: A domino of height $$h = 2 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ thickness $$t = 0.5 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ and width $$w = 1 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ tilts at an angle $$\theta = \pi/6$$, with its top touching a wall and its bottom touching a floor. If the wall is frictionless, find the minimum static coefficient…
statement:
A domino of height $$h = 2 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ thickness $$t = 0.5 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ and width $$w = 1 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ tilts at an angle $$\theta = \pi/6$$, with its top touching a wall and its bottom touching a floor. If the wall is frictionless, find the minimum static coefficient of friction with the floor so that the domino does not slip.

Assume the domino has uniform density.

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: This problem extends the idea of a cylinder as a spring and gives you some practice in…
desc: This problem extends the idea of a cylinder as a spring and gives you some practice in working with formulas that are given in the problem. You should come away "half way" understanding the formulas. That is, you should be able to make some inferences about them needed to solve…
statement:
This problem extends the idea of a cylinder as a spring and gives you some practice in working with formulas that are given in the problem. You should come away "half way" understanding the formulas. That is, you should be able to make some inferences about them needed to solve the problem, but should not expect to understand everything about where the formulas come from. This mode of reasoning about formulas is common in olympiad physics.

**a)** Suppose a cylinder has length $$L_0,$$ radius $$R_0,$$ and Young's modulus $$Y,$$ all when under no stress. If the cylinder is subjected to a uniform tension $$T,$$ it stretches, and its volume may increase from $$V_0 = \pi R_0^2 L_0$$ to $$V(T) = \left(1+\lambda(T)\right) V_0.$$ Assuming the radius stays constant as the cylinder stretches, find $$\lambda(T).$$

**b)** Most cylinders, when stretched, do not maintain constant radius. A more realistic assumption for certain materials is that the volume of the cylinder does not change at all when stretched. Suppose we have such a cylinder and we stretch it so that its length $$L$$ increases: $$ L \to (1+\alpha) L.$$ Then the radius also changes $$ R \to (1+\beta) R.$$

Suppose the change in length is very small, so $$\alpha \ll 1.$$ Find $$\beta$$ as a function of $$\alpha.$$

Your answer should be approximate for finite $$\alpha,$$ but exact in the limit $$\alpha \to 0.$$

**c)** The ratio $$-\dfrac{\beta}{\alpha}$$ is called **Poisson's ratio**. A common symbol for Poisson's ratio is $$ u.$$ What is Poisson's ratio for the material in part (a) of this question? What is it for the material in part (b) of this question?

**d)** The material in part (b), which strongly resists changes to its volume, has a very high **bulk modulus** $$B.$$ The material in part (a) has a very low bulk modulus. One of the following formulas gives Poisson's ratio as a function of bulk modulus and Young's modulus. Which one?

\begin{aligned} u & = \dfrac{3B - Y}{6B} \\ \vspace{2pt} \\ u & = \dfrac{Y - 3B}{3B} \\ \vspace{2pt} \\ u & = \dfrac{3B - Y}{6Y} \\ \vspace{2pt} \\ u & = \dfrac{3Y - B}{6Y} \\ \vspace{2pt} \\ u & = \dfrac{3B - Y}{3B} \end{aligned}

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain

name: A winch is used to haul sand up from the bottom of a dry dock using a crane constructed…
desc: A winch is used to haul sand up from the bottom of a dry dock using a crane constructed from a very light framework of girders. The crane geometry can be seen in the diagram. The crane is fixed to the horizontal dock side at points $$A$$ and $$B.$$ The dimensions of the sides…
statement:
A winch is used to haul sand up from the bottom of a dry dock using a crane constructed from a very light framework of girders. The crane geometry can be seen in the diagram.

The crane is fixed to the horizontal dock side at points $$A$$ and $$B.$$ The dimensions of the sides $$CB, CD,$$ and $$BD$$ are as shown. The girder $$CB$$ is vertical, and the winch is hauling a load of weight $$15 W$$ at constant velocity.

The crane touches the dock only at points $$A$$ and $$B.$$

**a)** Find the magnitude of the force exerted on $$D$$ by the member $$BD.$$

**b)** Find the tension in the member $$CD.$$

**c)** If the force on the crane at $$A$$ by the ground acts vertically downwards and has magnitude $$31W,$$ find the distance $$AB$$ in terms of $$L.$$

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: In Victor Hugo's novel __Les Misérables,__ the main character, Jean Valjean, an escaped…
desc: In Victor Hugo's novel __Les Misérables,__ the main character, Jean Valjean, an escaped prisoner, was noted for his ability to climb up the corner formed by the intersection of two vertical perpendicular walls. Let Valjean's mass be $$m$$ and the coefficient of friction between…
statement:
In Victor Hugo's novel __Les Misérables,__ the main character, Jean Valjean, an escaped prisoner, was noted for his ability to climb up the corner formed by the intersection of two vertical perpendicular walls.

Let Valjean's mass be $$m$$ and the coefficient of friction between him and the walls be $$\mu.$$

**a)** Find the minimum force with which he had to push on the walls while climbing.

**b)** What is the minimum coefficient of static friction required for him to be able to perform such a feat?

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: A soap bubble of mass $$m = 0.01 \;\mathrm{g}$$ has a surface tension $$\gamma = 0.01…
desc: A soap bubble of mass $$m = 0.01 \;\mathrm{g}$$ has a surface tension $$\gamma = 0.01 \;\mathrm{N/m}.$$ The bubble has been inflated through a short thin tube. The bubble is then charged with an electric charge $$Q = 5.4 \times 10^{-8} \;\mathrm{C}.$$ The tube remains open. Find…
statement:
A soap bubble of mass $$m = 0.01 \;\mathrm{g}$$ has a surface tension $$\gamma = 0.01 \;\mathrm{N/m}.$$ The bubble has been inflated through a short thin tube.

The bubble is then charged with an electric charge $$Q = 5.4 \times 10^{-8} \;\mathrm{C}.$$ The tube remains open.

Find the equilibrium radius of the bubble.

**Note:**

Although each week of PhysicsWOOT has a certain focus, many problems call on knowledge from all over physics. (This is why a complete physics course is a prerequisite for PhysicsWOOT.) In this problem, you may need to, for example,

do a calculation to find the capacitance of a sphere relative to infinity.

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain

name: A cylinder of mass $$M$$ has a block of mass $$m$$ sitting inside it. The small block is…
desc: A cylinder of mass $$M$$ has a block of mass $$m$$ sitting inside it. The small block is much smaller than the cylinder. The coefficient of friction between the block and the cylinder is $$\mu.$$ The cylinder sits on an incline of angle $$\theta.$$ It cannot slip on the incline…
statement:
A cylinder of mass $$M$$ has a block of mass $$m$$ sitting inside it. The small block is much smaller than the cylinder. The coefficient of friction between the block and the cylinder is $$\mu.$$

The cylinder sits on an incline of angle $$\theta.$$ It cannot slip on the incline.

What is the greatest angle $$\theta$$ at which the cylinder can be at rest (as a function of $$m, M,$$ and $$\mu)?$$

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: A zero effective length spring (ZLS) is a spring for which the force is proportional to…
desc: A zero effective length spring (ZLS) is a spring for which the force is proportional to the spring's length, $$F = kL$$ for $$L>L_0,$$ where $$L_0$$ is the minimal length of the spring as well as its unstretched length. The figure shows the relation between the force $$F$$ and…
statement:
A zero effective length spring (ZLS) is a spring for which the force is proportional to the spring's length, $$F = kL$$ for $$L>L_0,$$ where $$L_0$$ is the minimal length of the spring as well as its unstretched length. The figure shows the relation between the force $$F$$ and the spring length $$L$$ for a ZLS, where the slope of the line is the spring constant $$k.$$

A ZLS is useful in seismography and allows very accurate measurement of changes in the gravitational acceleration $$g.$$ Here, we shall consider a homogenous ZLS whose weight $$Mg$$ exceeds $$kL_0.$$ We define a corresponding dimensionless ratio, $$\alpha = kL_0/(Mg) < 1$$ to characterize the relative softness of the spring. The toy known as a "slinky" may be (but is not necessarily) such a ZLS.

**a)** Consider a segment of length $$\Delta l$$ of the unstretched ZLS which is then stretched by a force $$F$$ under weightless conditions. What is the new length $$\Delta y$$ of this segment as a function of $$F, \Delta l,$$ and the parameters of the spring?

**b)** For a segment of length $$\Delta l,$$ calculate the work $$\Delta W$$ required to stretch it from its original length to a length $$\Delta y.$$

Throughout part (c), we will denote a point on the spring by its distance $$0 \le l \le L_0$$ from the bottom of the spring when it is unstretched. In particular, for every point on the spring, $$l$$ remains unchanged as the spring stretches.

**c)** Suppose that we hang the spring by its top end, so that it stretches under its own weight. What is the total length $$H$$ of the suspended spring in equilibrium? Express your answer in terms of $$L_0$$ and $$\alpha.$$

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: A car of mass $$M$$ attempts to drive over a road barrier, starting from rest, as shown…
desc: A car of mass $$M$$ attempts to drive over a road barrier, starting from rest, as shown in the figure. The radius of its wheel is $$r = 0.5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ The coefficient of friction between the wheels and the ground is $$\mu = 1.$$ The sketch is drawn using correct proportions…
statement:
A car of mass $$M$$ attempts to drive over a road barrier, starting from rest, as shown in the figure.

The radius of its wheel is $$r = 0.5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ The coefficient of friction between the wheels and the ground is $$\mu = 1.$$ The sketch is drawn using correct proportions. Point $$C$$ marks the position of the car's center of mass.

Assume there is no drag in the non-driving axis (i.e. the wheels rotate without friction).

**a)** Determine the maximal height of the road barrier so that the car can still drive over it assuming the car has front-wheel drive.

**b)** Repeat part (a) assuming the car has rear-wheel drive.

**c)** Suppose the car has all-wheel drive and the road barrier is replaced with a wall. Would it be possible to raise the front of the car by driving slowly against the wall?

(You may need to make measurements on the picture for some subparts of this problem.)

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: The following is a problem based on IPhO, 1990 (Netherlands). However, the analysis…
desc: The following is a problem based on IPhO, 1990 (Netherlands). However, the analysis presented by the Netherlanders was actually incorrect! Here, we'll try to replicate what they thought the right approach was, then see if we can find where they went wrong. If the Earth didn't…
statement:
The following is a problem based on IPhO, 1990 (Netherlands). However, the analysis presented by the Netherlanders was actually incorrect! Here, we'll try to replicate what they thought the right approach was, then see if we can find where they went wrong.

If the Earth didn't rotate, it would be almost a perfect sphere (if we ignore mountains, which are relatively small). However, due to its rotation, the Earth bulges out at the center. Here we will calculate the size of the Earth's equatorial bulge.

Let the distance from the center of the Earth to one of the poles be $$r_p$$ and the distance from the center of the Earth to the equator be $$r_e.$$

The following information is useful: \begin{aligned} \text{mass of Earth} & = 5.97 \times 10^{24} \;\mathrm{kg}\\ \text{radius of Earth} & = 6.37 \times 10^6 \;\mathrm{m} \\ \text{Newton's gravitational constant} & = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{N \cdot m^2 \cdot kg^{-2}} \end{aligned}

**a)** Above pressures of about $$1 \;\mathrm{GPa},$$ rocks and metals cannot hold their solid shape. They can be thought of as essentially liquids at these pressures. Can the rotating Earth be thought of as a liquid?

**b)** In a frame co-rotating with the Earth, the centrifugal force on an object of mass $$m$$ can be thought of as the gradient of a potential energy, $$U(r),$$ where $$r$$ is the distance from the axis of rotation. Find $$U(r).$$

**c)** The Earth's shape should be an equipotential surface in the rotating frame. This means that if we took a small rock of mass $$m$$ at the equator and moved it to a pole, its potential energy wouldn't change.

The rock's gravitational potential energy at the equator is higher than at the pole by approximately $$mgh,$$ where $$h = r_e - r_p.$$ So this must be balanced by the centrifugal potential. Use this to calculate $$r_e - r_p$$ for Earth.

**d)** On Earth, $$r_e - r_p \approx 21 \;\mathrm{km}.$$ Does this agree with the theory derived in part (c)? If not, what is the major source of error in the calculation?

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: Pushing a Block Sideways on an Incline — A block of mass $$m$$ sits on a plane inclined at an angle…
desc: A block of mass $$m$$ sits on a plane inclined at an angle $$\theta.$$ The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $$\mu,$$ with $$\mu > \tan\theta,$$ so the block sits still on its own. A force $$F$$ is now applied to the block, pushing it __sideways__…
statement:
A block of mass $$m$$ sits on a plane inclined at an angle $$\theta.$$ The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $$\mu,$$ with $$\mu > \tan\theta,$$ so the block sits still on its own. A force $$F$$ is now applied to the block, pushing it __sideways__: parallel to the surface of the plane, but perpendicular to the uphill direction. What is the maximum $$F$$ such that the block does not move? (Olympiad convention: when a problem gives a single coefficient of friction, assume the static and kinetic coefficients are equal.)

__(a)__ Assuming the block is not moving, what is the normal force on the block?

__(b)__ Suppose first that $$F = 0.$$ What is the friction force on the block? Careful: the answer is not $$\mu N$$ — the law of static friction is the inequality $$F_{\mathrm{friction}} \le \mu N,$$ so the friction force must be found from the equilibrium condition instead.

__(c)__ Now push with the sideways force $$F,$$ with the block still at rest. The friction force gains a second component, in the plane of the incline, canceling $$F.$$ Find the magnitude of the total friction force in terms of $$m,$$ $$g,$$ $$\theta,$$ and $$F.$$

__(d)__ Use the static friction law to find the maximum force $$F_{\mathrm{max}}$$ in terms of the variables given in the problem.

__(e)__ Test your answer in a special case: what relationship between $$\mu$$ and $$\theta$$ makes $$F_{\mathrm{max}} = 0,$$ and why is that relationship familiar? (Recall: the steepest slope a climber can stand on without slipping satisfies $$\mu = \tan\theta.$$)

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: A Block on a Rotating Platform — A flat horizontal platform rotates at angular frequency $$\omega.$$ A block…
desc: A flat horizontal platform rotates at angular frequency $$\omega.$$ A block sits on the platform a distance $$r$$ from the axis of rotation. What is the minimum coefficient of friction between the block and the platform needed to keep the block from slipping relative to the…
statement:
A flat horizontal platform rotates at angular frequency $$\omega.$$ A block sits on the platform a distance $$r$$ from the axis of rotation. What is the minimum coefficient of friction between the block and the platform needed to keep the block from slipping relative to the platform?

__(a)__ This is not literally a statics problem: the block moves in a circle, so it accelerates. Explain how viewing the situation from a reference frame rotating along with the platform turns it into a statics problem. (In that frame, a __centrifugal force__ of magnitude $$F_c = m\omega^2 r$$ pushes the block directly away from the axis of rotation.)

__(b)__ The centrifugal force is proportional to the block's mass, just as gravity is, so the two can be combined into a single __effective gravity__. Find the angle $$\theta$$ that the effective gravity makes with the vertical.

__(c)__ A block resting on a surface starts to slip when the surface is tilted at angle $$\theta$$ relative to (effective) gravity with $$\tan\theta > \mu.$$ Use this to find $$\mu_{\mathrm{min}}.$$

__(d)__ Re-derive the answer from the inertial (non-rotating) frame, where friction must supply the block's centripetal acceleration.

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: The Shape of a Suspension-Bridge Cable — A suspension bridge consists of a heavy horizontal road with mass…
desc: A suspension bridge consists of a heavy horizontal road with mass per unit length $$\lambda,$$ supported by a cable hanging between two towers. Frequent, closely spaced vertical lines connect the cable to the road. The cable and the vertical lines are massless, so the cable…
statement:
A suspension bridge consists of a heavy horizontal road with mass per unit length $$\lambda,$$ supported by a cable hanging between two towers. Frequent, closely spaced vertical lines connect the cable to the road. The cable and the vertical lines are massless, so the cable supports only the road's weight. Find the shape $$y(x)$$ of the cable.

(The Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco is a famous example of the shape we are after.)

Use the __subsystem__ idea: you may choose any piece of the cable you like, and the forces on that piece must sum to zero. A smart choice starts at the lowest point of the cable, where the cable is horizontal, so the tension there is purely horizontal. Take as your system the piece of cable from the lowest point out to a horizontal distance $$x$$ to the right, whose right end is a height $$y$$ above the low point. The forces on this piece are: a horizontal tension $$T_L$$ pulling left at the low end; a tension at the right end pointing along the cable, with components $$T_{R;x}$$ and $$T_{R;y}$$; and the weight of the section of road beneath the piece, transmitted through the vertical lines.

__(a)__ Balance the horizontal forces on the piece. What does the result tell you about the horizontal component of tension throughout the entire cable?

__(b)__ Balance the vertical forces to find $$T_{R;y}.$$ (The cable itself is massless — what mass does a piece of cable spanning a horizontal distance $$x$$ actually support?)

__(c)__ The tension at the right end must point __along__ the cable. Use this to find an equation for the slope $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$$ in terms of $$\lambda,$$ $$g,$$ $$x,$$ and $$T_L.$$

__(d)__ Integrate to find $$y(x).$$ What is the shape of the cable called?

__(e)__ Keeping the same model but adjusting its parameters, what could engineers change to make the cable's curve flatter?

For more practice, two variations to try on your own: (1) there is no road, and the cable must support its own weight; (2) the cable supports its own weight, but it is a spring of zero rest length rather than a fixed-length cable. Each gives a different shape.

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: Why a Climbing Cam Never Slips — A "spring-loaded camming device," or "friend," is a climbing aid. A climber…
desc: A "spring-loaded camming device," or "friend," is a climbing aid. A climber inserts one into a crack in the rock and anchors the rope to it. The device consists of two cams attached at a common hinge; the cams are free to rotate about the hinge. The cams' spiral shape is…
statement:
A "spring-loaded camming device," or "friend," is a climbing aid. A climber inserts one into a crack in the rock and anchors the rope to it. The device consists of two cams attached at a common hinge; the cams are free to rotate about the hinge. The cams' spiral shape is designed so that, no matter the width of the crack (within a range), the segment from each cam's contact point with the rock to the hinge makes the same fixed angle $$\theta$$ with the horizontal. A load $$W$$ — the climber's weight, or far more during a fall — pulls straight down on the hinge. The cams are massless, and the device's own weight is negligible compared with the load. Find the minimum coefficient of friction $$\mu$$ between rock and cam such that the friend will not slip under __arbitrarily large__ loads $$W.$$

__(a)__ Take a __single cam__ as your system. (The cams rotate freely about the hinge, so each rigid cam must be in equilibrium on its own; analyzing the whole device gives no way to find the horizontal forces.) The forces on one cam are: a friction force $$F_f$$ upward at the contact point, a normal force $$N$$ from the rock (horizontal), and a force $$H$$ from the hinge, about which we know little. By balancing vertical forces on the whole device, show that $$F_f = \dfrac{W}{2}$$ on each cam, so the friction law requires $$\mu \ge \dfrac{W}{2N}.$$ Explain why this alone cannot answer the question.

__(b)__ Bring in torque, taking the hinge as the axis. Why is the hinge a smart choice of axis? Show that the vector sum of the normal force and friction force on the cam must point directly toward the hinge, and use the geometry to find $$\mu_{\mathrm{min}}.$$

__(c)__ The load $$W$$ should drop out of your answer to (b). What does that tell a falling climber about how hard they can afford to jerk on the rope?

__(d)__ If you were unsure how large the friction coefficient with a particular kind of rock was, would you prefer a cam built with a small $$\theta$$ or a large $$\theta$$? What is the tradeoff?

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: An Off-Center Cylinder on a Tilting Ramp — A solid wooden cylinder has radius $$R.$$ A smaller cylindrical…
desc: A solid wooden cylinder has radius $$R.$$ A smaller cylindrical hole of radius $$r,$$ parallel to the axis, is drilled out and filled with a metal cylinder of higher density; the center of the metal cylinder is a distance $$d$$ from the center of the wooden cylinder. The…
statement:
A solid wooden cylinder has radius $$R.$$ A smaller cylindrical hole of radius $$r,$$ parallel to the axis, is drilled out and filled with a metal cylinder of higher density; the center of the metal cylinder is a distance $$d$$ from the center of the wooden cylinder. The cylinder is placed on a ramp whose angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal can be varied. The ramp is first set to $$\theta = 0$$ and the cylinder comes to rest. The ramp (rising up to the right) is then slowly tilted to $$\theta = \theta_f$$; as the ramp tilts, the cylinder rolls without slipping through an angle $$\phi,$$ coming to rest at this angle when $$\theta = \theta_f.$$ Find the distance $$b$$ from the geometric center of the cylinder to the center of mass of the whole (wood plus metal) system, as a function of $$R,$$ $$\theta,$$ and $$\phi.$$ (IPhO 2016, Problem 1, adapted.)

__(a)__ First understand the setup. When the ramp is flat ($$\theta = 0$$), where does the metal cylinder sit relative to the wooden cylinder's center? As the right side of the ramp rises, which way does the cylinder roll — and what force holds the round, freely rolling cylinder in place on the slope?

__(b)__ The net torque on the resting cylinder must be zero. Choose the contact point between the cylinder and the ramp as your axis, and explain why that choice is better than the cylinder's center or the center of mass. Then determine where the center of mass must be relative to the contact point, and derive $$b$$ in terms of $$R,$$ $$\theta,$$ and $$\phi.$$ (Note that after rolling through $$\phi,$$ the line from the geometric center to the center of mass — vertical when $$\theta = 0$$ — makes angle $$\phi$$ with the vertical, while the line from the geometric center to the contact point is perpendicular to the ramp, making angle $$\theta$$ with the vertical.)

__(c)__ Now check the result with energy. At equilibrium, a small displacement causes no first-order change in potential energy. Let the cylinder roll an infinitesimal angle $$\mathrm{d}\phi$$ farther down the incline. The geometric center moves a distance $$R\,\mathrm{d}\phi$$ parallel to the ramp surface; the center of mass also moves relative to the geometric center, along a direction inclined at angle $$\phi$$ to the horizontal. Compute the two height changes and show that the total change in the center of mass's height vanishes precisely when your answer to (b) holds.

__(d)__ A puzzle: a stable equilibrium is a __local minimum__ of potential energy, so any small displacement should raise the center of mass — yet in (c) you found the height change is zero. Resolve the apparent contradiction.

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: The Rope in a Chain of Rhombi — Four long rods and four rods half as long are hinged together to form three…
desc: Four long rods and four rods half as long are hinged together to form three identical rhombi in a vertical chain, as shown: each long rod runs straight through one of the side hinges, forming one side of each of two adjacent rhombi. The top vertex of the chain is hinged to the…
statement:
Four long rods and four rods half as long are hinged together to form three identical rhombi in a vertical chain, as shown: each long rod runs straight through one of the side hinges, forming one side of each of two adjacent rhombi. The top vertex of the chain is hinged to the ceiling, and a mass $$m$$ hangs from the bottom vertex. The bottom vertex is also connected to the hinge directly above it by a massless rope, which spans the lowest rhombus along its vertical diagonal. The rods are massless and rigid. Find the tension $$T$$ in the rope.

The angles between the rods are not given — a hint that chasing forces through every hinge would be a mess, and that an energy (__virtual work__) approach may pay off. Imagine letting the mass descend a small distance $$\mathrm{d}y$$ while the linkage flexes, and demand that the total potential energy not change to first order: $$\mathrm{d}U_{\mathrm{total}} = 0$$ at equilibrium.

__(a)__ When the mass descends by $$\mathrm{d}y,$$ the two hinges joined by the rope separate by some additional distance $$\mathrm{d}s.$$ Explain why this contributes a potential energy change $$\mathrm{d}U_{\mathrm{rope}} = T\,\mathrm{d}s.$$

__(b)__ Let $$\ell$$ be the total distance from the ceiling to the mass. Use the geometry of the chain to relate $$\mathrm{d}s$$ to $$\mathrm{d}y.$$

__(c)__ Set $$\mathrm{d}U_{\mathrm{total}} = 0$$ and solve for $$T.$$ What is remarkable about the answer?

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: Squeezing a Rolled Plastic Film — A thin plastic film is rolled into a cylinder (think of a stiff…
desc: A thin plastic film is rolled into a cylinder (think of a stiff transparency sheet taped into a tube). The elastic energy stored in curved film is $$U = \dfrac{\kappa}{2}\,\dfrac{1}{R_c^2}\,A,$$ where $$\kappa$$ is the film's __bending modulus__, $$R_c$$ is the radius of…
statement:
A thin plastic film is rolled into a cylinder (think of a stiff transparency sheet taped into a tube). The elastic energy stored in curved film is $$U = \dfrac{\kappa}{2}\,\dfrac{1}{R_c^2}\,A,$$ where $$\kappa$$ is the film's __bending modulus__, $$R_c$$ is the radius of curvature, and $$A$$ is the area of the curved surface (the side of the cylinder, excluding its open ends). You are not told where this formula comes from — being handed an unfamiliar formula and asked to reason with it is common in olympiad physics; the principles you need are ones you already know.

The film cylinder, of length $$l$$ in the direction perpendicular to its cross-section, is placed between two horizontal boards on a scale. A weight on the top board presses down on the cylinder with total force $$F,$$ and the cross-section deforms into a "stadium": two half-circles of radius $$R_0$$ connected by straight segments, so the top board sits at height $$2R_0.$$ Find the bending modulus $$\kappa$$ as a function of $$R_0,$$ $$F,$$ and $$l.$$ (Adapted from IPhO 2010.)

The original problem included this photo of the experimental setup:

__(a)__ For film bent into an arc of radius $$R_c,$$ rewrite the energy formula using the side area $$A = 2\pi R_c l$$ of a full cylinder, eliminating $$A.$$ Then consider the stadium shape: how much elastic energy is stored in its flat parts?

__(b)__ The board-film system is in equilibrium, so the total potential energy is stationary: $$\mathrm{d}U_{\mathrm{total}} = 0$$ for a small vertical displacement $$\mathrm{d}y$$ of the top board. Write $$\mathrm{d}U_{\mathrm{gravitational}}$$ for the pressing weight, relate $$\mathrm{d}R_0$$ to $$\mathrm{d}y,$$ write $$\mathrm{d}U_{\mathrm{film}},$$ and solve for $$\kappa.$$

__(c)__ We still don't know exactly what $$\kappa$$ "means" physically — but find its dimensions, and interpret them.

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: The Sea Level Above an Iron Deposit — An iron deposit lies under the ocean floor, where the water depth is…
desc: An iron deposit lies under the ocean floor, where the water depth is $$h = 2\;\mathrm{km}.$$ Model the deposit as a sphere of radius $$r = 1\;\mathrm{km}$$ whose density exceeds that of the surrounding rock by $$\Delta\rho = 1000\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}},$$ and whose top just…
statement:
An iron deposit lies under the ocean floor, where the water depth is $$h = 2\;\mathrm{km}.$$ Model the deposit as a sphere of radius $$r = 1\;\mathrm{km}$$ whose density exceeds that of the surrounding rock by $$\Delta\rho = 1000\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}},$$ and whose top just touches the ocean bottom — so its center is at depth $$r + h.$$ By how much does the water level directly above the iron deposit differ from the average ocean level? Use $$G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$$ and $$g \approx 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ (From Jaan Kalda's mechanics problem collection; this style of problem appears on USAPhO often — the calculation is short, and the challenge is seeing which calculation to do.)

__(a)__ First, no calculation: is the water level directly above the deposit __higher__ or __lower__ than the average sea level? (Many people's first instinct is wrong here — think carefully about what the deposit's gravity does to the surrounding water.)

__(b)__ The ocean is in equilibrium. Explain why its surface must be an __equipotential surface__ — a surface on which the gravitational potential energy per unit mass is the same everywhere. (Hint: imagine pouring a teaspoon of extra water onto the surface midway up the mound above the deposit, and ask which way it would flow.)

__(c)__ Compare two points on the surface: one far from the deposit (define the potential there to be zero) and one directly above it, where the water stands $$\Delta h$$ above the average level. The potential per unit mass at the second point gets a contribution $$g\,\Delta h$$ from rising in Earth's uniform field, plus a contribution from the deposit's extra gravity, $$-\dfrac{G\,\Delta M}{r+h},$$ where $$\Delta M$$ is the deposit's mass __excess__ over ordinary rock (only the excess matters — ordinary rock is already part of the baseline Earth). Write $$\Delta M$$ in terms of $$\Delta\rho$$ and $$r,$$ set the total potential difference to zero, and solve for $$\Delta h$$ symbolically.

__(d)__ Put in the numbers. (Number crunching is part of the game — USAPhO will supply constants like $$G,$$ but you must be quick and accurate with the arithmetic.)

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: From Young's Modulus to Bending Modulus — How hard is it to bend a sheet of material? In this problem you…
desc: How hard is it to bend a sheet of material? In this problem you will derive the __bending modulus__ $$\kappa$$ of a thin sheet — defined so that sheet of side area $$A$$ bent to radius of curvature $$R_c$$ stores elastic energy $$U = \dfrac{\kappa}{2}\,\dfrac{A}{R_c^2}$$ — from…
statement:
How hard is it to bend a sheet of material? In this problem you will derive the __bending modulus__ $$\kappa$$ of a thin sheet — defined so that sheet of side area $$A$$ bent to radius of curvature $$R_c$$ stores elastic energy $$U = \dfrac{\kappa}{2}\,\dfrac{A}{R_c^2}$$ — from the material's __Young's modulus__ $$Y$$ and the sheet's thickness $$d.$$ Recall the key fact about Young's modulus: a beam of natural length $$x$$ and cross-sectional area $$A$$ acts, for small stretches, like a spring with spring constant $$k = \dfrac{AY}{x}.$$

__(a)__ Warm-up: a straight beam of length $$x,$$ depth $$l,$$ and thickness $$d$$ is stretched by $$\Delta x.$$ Find the elastic potential energy stored in the beam.

__(b)__ Now take a thin film of thickness $$d,$$ depth $$l,$$ and Young's modulus $$Y,$$ and bend it into a complete cylinder of radius $$R_c$$ (in terms of the bending modulus, its energy is then $$U = \kappa\pi\,\dfrac{l}{R_c},$$ using side area $$A = 2\pi R_c l$$). Bending stores energy even if the film's overall length is unchanged, because the layers through the thickness cannot all keep their length: if the middle layer keeps its natural length $$2\pi R_c,$$ the outer layers are stretched and the inner layers compressed. By how much is the layer a distance $$r$$ outward from the middle stretched? (For inner layers, $$r < 0,$$ and the "stretch" is negative.)

__(c)__ Treat the material between $$r$$ and $$r + \mathrm{d}r$$ as a thin beam of length $$2\pi R_c,$$ depth $$l,$$ and thickness $$\mathrm{d}r.$$ Write the energy $$\mathrm{d}U$$ stored in this layer, and integrate over $$-\dfrac{d}{2} \le r \le \dfrac{d}{2}$$ to find the total bending energy.

__(d)__ Compare with $$U = \kappa\pi\,\dfrac{l}{R_c}$$ to read off the bending modulus $$\kappa.$$

__(e)__ The IPhO problem this derivation comes from quotes $$\kappa = \dfrac{Yd^3}{12(1-\nu^2)},$$ where $$\nu$$ is the material's __Poisson's ratio__. Our derivation assumed each layer stretches independently of the others; in reality they interact. To get a feel for the missing physics: when you stretch a long cylinder of a typical material, what happens to its radius, and why? (The animation below illustrates the effect.)

__(f)__ Structural beams that must resist bending are usually built as "I-beams," like the one pictured below. Use your result to explain the design: why concentrate the material at the top and bottom, leaving only a thin web in the middle?

lesson: PW201: Static Equilibria, Stress, and Strain
label: PW201
name: Why a Long Balloon Pops Lengthwise — You blow up a long balloon of the kind used to make balloon animals…
desc: You blow up a long balloon of the kind used to make balloon animals. When it bursts, does the tear run __around the circumference__ of the balloon, or __along its length__? Idealize the balloon as a cylinder of radius $$r$$ and length $$l,$$ with the inside pressure exceeding…
statement:
You blow up a long balloon of the kind used to make balloon animals. When it bursts, does the tear run __around the circumference__ of the balloon, or __along its length__? Idealize the balloon as a cylinder of radius $$r$$ and length $$l,$$ with the inside pressure exceeding the outside pressure by $$P$$; ignore gravity and the rounded ends. In a membrane, the relevant stress is the __tension per unit length__ $$T$$: the force transmitted across a cut, per unit length of the cut. Tension across a circumferential cut (tear A in the figure) is called __axial stress__ — you could produce that tear by pulling along the axis. Tension across a lengthwise cut (tear B) is called __hoop stress__.

__(a)__ To find the axial tension $$T_{\mathrm{axial}},$$ take the right half of the balloon as your subsystem. Two forces act on it: the pressure force from the air inside, of magnitude $$P\pi r^2$$ (the pressure difference times the area enclosed by the cut), and the pull of the left half's material across the circumferential cut of length $$2\pi r.$$ Balance them to find $$T_{\mathrm{axial}}.$$

__(b)__ Now slice lengthwise instead, taking the top half of the cylinder as the subsystem. The pressure force pushing the top half up is $$P \cdot 2rl$$ (pressure times the projected area), and the bottom half pulls down across two lengthwise cuts, each of length $$l.$$ Find $$T_{\mathrm{hoop}}.$$

__(c)__ Compare the two tensions. Which way does the balloon pop, and why?

__(d)__ Re-derive both tensions from energy. At equilibrium, a small deformation changes the total energy by zero, so the work done by the pressure, $$P\,\mathrm{d}V,$$ must equal the work done against the membrane tension, $$T\,\mathrm{d}A$$ — giving $$T = P\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}A}.$$ Using $$V = \pi r^2 l$$ and $$A = 2\pi r l$$: for the hoop direction, hold $$l$$ fixed, write $$V$$ as a function of $$A,$$ and differentiate; for the axial direction, hold $$r$$ fixed and repeat.

__(e)__ What does this problem reveal about stress in general — is "the stress" in a material a single number?

label: PW202
name: A stunt elephant in a circus leaps from a platform to land some tens of meters on a…
desc: A stunt elephant in a circus leaps from a platform to land some tens of meters on a mattress below. (The elephant does not reach terminal velocity in this first part of the fall.) Halfway down, the elephant opens a parachute, slowing its descent. **a)** Draw a free body diagram…
statement:
A stunt elephant in a circus leaps from a platform to land some tens of meters on a mattress below. (The elephant does not reach terminal velocity in this first part of the fall.) Halfway down, the elephant opens a parachute, slowing its descent.

**a)** Draw a free body diagram showing the forces acting on the elephant after it has jumped from the platform, but before the parachute has opened. Indicate the relative sizes of the forces acting by the length of the arrows representing the forces.

**b)** Draw a free body diagram showing the forces acting on the elephant after the parachute has opened, but before the elephant touches the mattress, while it is falling at constant speed. Indicate the relative sizes of the forces acting by the length of the arrows representing the forces.

**c)** Draw a free body diagram showing the forces acting on the elephant after the elephant touches the mattress but before it comes to a complete stop. Indicate the relative sizes of the forces acting by the length of the arrows representing the forces.

**d)** Sketch a plot of the net force acting on the elephant as a function of time from the time it jumps from the platform until it comes to rest on the mattress. Label all relevant events on the sketch, such as the time the parachute opens, the time the elephant touches the mattress and the time it comes to a rest.

label: PW202
name: A cyclist travels along a straight road at speed $$v=20.0 \;\mathrm{km/h}$$ on two…
desc: A cyclist travels along a straight road at speed $$v=20.0 \;\mathrm{km/h}$$ on two separate occasions; on Day 1 there is no wind, whereas on Day 2 there is a steady wind blowing at a speed $$w = 40 \;\mathrm{km/h}$$ in a direction perpendicular to the road (i.e. a crosswind)…
statement:
A cyclist travels along a straight road at speed $$v=20.0 \;\mathrm{km/h}$$ on two separate occasions; on Day 1 there is no wind, whereas on Day 2 there is a steady wind blowing at a speed $$w = 40 \;\mathrm{km/h}$$ in a direction perpendicular to the road (i.e. a crosswind). The force on the cyclist due to air resistance is proportional to the square of the speed of the air relative to the cyclist; as a consequence, to maintain the same constant speed on Day 2 as on Day 1, the cyclist has to produce a greater power output.

**a)** Draw diagrams showing the velocities of the cyclist and air in both the road frame and the cyclist's frame of reference, first on Day 1 when there is no wind and then on Day 2 when there is the crosswind.

**b)** What is the speed of the air relative to the cyclist when the steady crosswind is blowing?

**c)** At what angle to straight ahead is the wind speed relative to the cyclist when the steady crosswind is blowing?

**d)** Draw additional diagrams showing the velocity of the cyclist and the force due to air resistance on Day 1 and on Day 2.

**e)** What is the factor by which the cyclist must increase power to maintain a constant speed in the crosswind compared to without the crosswind?

label: PW202
name: A tug boat winch is fitted with friction brakes that slip when the tension in the winch…
desc: A tug boat winch is fitted with friction brakes that slip when the tension in the winch cable reaches $$50 \;\mathrm{kN.}$$ The winch is mounted on a $$4.50 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ tug which is to tow a floating barge of mass $$6.3 \times 10^6 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ The barge is…
statement:
A tug boat winch is fitted with friction brakes that slip when the tension in the winch cable reaches $$50 \;\mathrm{kN.}$$ The winch is mounted on a $$4.50 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{kg}$$ tug which is to tow a floating barge of mass $$6.3 \times 10^6 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

The barge is initially at rest while the tug moves away from it. The speed of the tug at the moment that the cable becomes taut is $$2.5 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ At that moment the winch friction brakes start slipping in order to prevent the cable from breaking. The thrust exerted on the tug by its propeller is $$35 \;\mathrm{kN}.$$ The winch and arrangement might look something like the figures below.

Drag on the tug can be ignored.

**a)** Calculate the time during which the brakes slip.

**b)** Find the common velocity of the tug and barge when the brakes stop slipping.

**c)** What length of cable runs out of the drum of the winch during the time the brakes are slipping?

label: PW202
name: An airplane of mass $$m$$ flies at speed $$v$$ through air of density $$\rho.$$ As viewed…
desc: An airplane of mass $$m$$ flies at speed $$v$$ through air of density $$\rho.$$ As viewed in the airplane's rest frame, air crossing the airplane's wings is deflected downward at an angle $$\theta,$$ which you can assume is small. The speed of the air can be assumed to be…
statement: An airplane of mass $$m$$ flies at speed $$v$$ through air of density $$\rho.$$ As viewed in the airplane's rest frame, air crossing the airplane's wings is deflected downward at an angle $$\theta,$$ which you can assume is small. The speed of the air can be assumed to be constant. Find the volume of air per second which the plane must deflect downward in order to fly at constant altitude. Building on this result, explain why planes designed to fly slowly have very large wings relative to their weight and planes designed to fly quickly can have smaller wings relative to their weight. You can assume the angle $$\theta$$ is similar for all planes (though in reality it varies, even for a single plane).

label: PW202
name: A rocket, total mass $$m_0 = 1.00 \times 10^4 \;\mathrm{kg},$$ is launched vertically…
desc: A rocket, total mass $$m_0 = 1.00 \times 10^4 \;\mathrm{kg},$$ is launched vertically. $$80\%$$ of the mass of the rocket is fuel. At ignition, time $$t = 0,$$ the thrust equals the weight of the rocket. The ejected exhaust gases have a speed of $$v_e = 9.00 \times 10^2…
statement:
A rocket, total mass $$m_0 = 1.00 \times 10^4 \;\mathrm{kg},$$ is launched vertically. $$80\%$$ of the mass of the rocket is fuel.

At ignition, time $$t = 0,$$ the thrust equals the weight of the rocket. The ejected exhaust gases have a speed of $$v_e = 9.00 \times 10^2 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

Air resistance on the rocket can be neglected.

Assuming the rate of fuel consumption and the acceleration due to gravity are constant, calculate:

**a)** the mass, $$\dot{m},$$ of gases ejected per unit time **b)** the acceleration, $$a_e,$$ of the rocket when the fuel is almost exhausted at time $$t_e$$ **c)** the mass, $$m,$$ of the rocket at time $$t,$$ where $$0 \le t \le t_e.$$ **d)** the acceleration, $$a,$$ of the rocket at time $$t,$$ where $$0 \le t \le t_e.$$ **e)** the time at which the rocket hits the ground.

You may use the fact $$\int \ln(u)\mathrm{d}u = u\ln(u) -u + c.$$

**note:** part (e) is a significant difficulty jump over the rest of the problem

name: A box of mass $$m$$ lies at rest on a smooth horizontal table. Two identical springs with…
desc: A box of mass $$m$$ lies at rest on a smooth horizontal table. Two identical springs with the same spring constant $$k$$ are attached to it. The springs are originally at their rest length. The left end of the left spring is attached to a wall. The right end of the right spring…
statement:
A box of mass $$m$$ lies at rest on a smooth horizontal table. Two identical springs with the same spring constant $$k$$ are attached to it. The springs are originally at their rest length.

The left end of the left spring is attached to a wall. The right end of the right spring is slowly pulled to the right at velocity $$v,$$ starting at $$t=0.$$

What is the first time at which the box has velocity $$v?$$

name: **a)** You are holding onto a massless rope which runs over a frictionless pulley which…
desc: **a)** You are holding onto a massless rope which runs over a frictionless pulley which is connected to a bag that sits on the floor. Your mass is $$M$$ and the bag's mass is $$m$$. If the coefficient of friction between the bag and the floor is $$\mu,$$ find your acceleration…
statement:
**a)** You are holding onto a massless rope which runs over a frictionless pulley which is connected to a bag that sits on the floor. Your mass is $$M$$ and the bag's mass is $$m$$. If the coefficient of friction between the bag and the floor is $$\mu,$$ find your acceleration.

**b)** A mass $$M$$ is hanging from a rope which runs over a frictionless pulley and attaches to a mass $$m.$$ The mass $$m$$ sits onto another mass $$m_3$$ which can roll freely back and forth across the ground. (Its wheels have zero mass.) The coefficients of static and kinetic friction between mass $$m$$ and $$m_3$$ are $$\mu.$$ Find the acceleration of all three masses and the tension in the rope at the moment all three masses are stationary.

label: PW202
name: **a)** Consider a solid circular disk of uniform density which has been cut in half. Find…
desc: **a)** Consider a solid circular disk of uniform density which has been cut in half. Find the center of mass of the half-disk via integration. **b)** Read the statement of (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pappus%27s_centroid_theorem#The_second_theorem). (The text uses "centroid"…
statement:
**a)** Consider a solid circular disk of uniform density which has been cut in half. Find the center of mass of the half-disk via integration.

**b)** Read the statement of (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pappus%27s_centroid_theorem#The_second_theorem). (The text uses "centroid" for something that is identical to the center of mass for objects with uniform density.) Use Pappus' theorem and your knowledge of the volume of a sphere to find the center of mass of the half-disk. Your answer should be the same as in part (a).

**c)** Consider a rigid circular pizza of radius $$R$$ and uniform density which has been tossed up in the air and is spinning. Now consider a slice of this pizza whose angle is $$\theta.$$

The center of mass of the slice lies on its symmetry axis, some distance $$r(\theta)$$ from the center of the pizza.

What forces act on this slice? (Ignore gravity.)

The net force on the slice is equal to its mass times the acceleration of its center of mass. This is true for all $$\theta,$$ including very small $$\theta.$$ For very small $$\theta, r(\theta) = \dfrac23 R.$$ Use this fact to find the magnitude of the force on the slice.

Return to a slice of angle $$\theta.$$ Considering the forces on it and its acceleration, find $$r(\theta).$$ Check that your answer agrees with parts (a) and (b) when $$\theta = \pi.$$

**d)** The center of mass of two objects of equal mass is the midpoint of the line segment between their centers of mass. Use this fact to relate $$r(\pi)$$ to $$r(\pi/2).$$

**e)** Following the general method of (d), find a relation between $$r(\theta)$$ and $$r(\theta/2).$$ Use this and your result from part (c) to find an alternative expression for $$ \cos\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\cos\left(\dfrac{\phi}{4}\right)\cos\left(\dfrac{\phi}{8}\right)\ldots.$$

label: PW202
name: This problem and the next one continue problem 8 from week 1 on a zero-length spring. You…
desc: This problem and the next one continue problem 8 from week 1 on a zero-length spring. You may wish to review that problem before working this one. A zero effective length spring (ZLS) is a spring for which the force is proportional to the spring's length, $$F = kL$$ for…
statement:
This problem and the next one continue problem 8 from week 1 on a zero-length spring. You may wish to review that problem before working this one.

A zero effective length spring (ZLS) is a spring for which the force is proportional to the spring's length, $$F = kL$$ for $$L>L_0,$$ where $$L_0$$ is the minimal length of the spring as well as its unstretched length. The figure shows the relation between the force $$F$$ and the spring length $$L$$ for a ZLS, where the slope of the line is the spring constant $$k.$$

A ZLS is useful in seismography and allows very accurate measurement of changes in the gravitational acceleration $$g.$$ Here, we shall consider a homogenous ZLS whose weight $$Mg$$ exceeds $$kL_0.$$ We define a corresponding dimensionless ratio, $$\alpha = kL_0/Mg < 1$$ to characterize the relative softness of the spring. The toy known as a "slinky" may be (but is not necessarily) such a ZLS.

Throughout this question, we will denote a point on the spring by its distance $$0 \le \ell \le L_0$$ from the bottom of the spring when it is unstretched. In particular, for every point on the spring, $$\ell$$ remains unchanged as the spring stretches.

Experiments show that when the spring is hung at rest and then released, it gradually contracts from the top, while the lower part remains stationary (see Figure 2 below).

As time advances, the contracting part moves as a solid chunk and accumulates additional turns of the spring, while the stationary part becomes shorter. Every point on the spring begins to move only when the moving part reaches it. The bottom end of the spring starts moving only when the spring is fully collapsed and reaches its unstretched length $$L_0.$$ After that, the contracted spring continues falling straight downwards, without tumbling, as a rigid body under the influence of gravity.

In the remaining parts of the question, you are asked to base your solution on this described model. You may neglect air resistance, but you are not allowed to neglect $$L_0.$$

**a)** The spring is held from its top and released. Calculate the time $$t_c$$ from the moment the spring is released to the moment it fully collapses back to its minimal length $$L_0.$$ Express your answer in terms of $$L_0, g,$$ and $$\alpha.$$

Compute the numerical value for $$t_c$$ for a spring with $$k = 1.02 \;\mathrm{N/m},$$ $$L_0 = 0.055 \;\mathrm{m},$$ and $$M = 0.201 \;\mathrm{kg},$$ while taking $$g$$ to be $$9.80 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

label: PW202
name: This problem continues the previous one.
desc: This problem continues the previous one. In this task, $$\ell$$ is used to denote the coordinate of the boundary between parts I (in figure 2, the moving part) and II (the stationary part). At a certain moment, while a stationary part still exists, its mass is $$m(\ell) =…
statement:
This problem continues the previous one.

In this task, $$\ell$$ is used to denote the coordinate of the boundary between parts I (in figure 2, the moving part) and II (the stationary part). At a certain moment, while a stationary part still exists, its mass is $$m(\ell) = \dfrac{\ell}{L_0} M.$$ The moving part moves with uniform instantaneous velocity $$v_I(\ell).$$At this moment (while there exists a stationary part), the velocity of the moving part is $$v_I(\ell) = \sqrt{A\ell + B}.$$ Express the constants $$A$$ and $$B$$ in terms of $$L_0, g,$$ and $$\alpha.$$

**note:** This problem is from IPhO 2019. The official solution uses the work-energy principle, and our official solution will use Newton's laws. You could try both approaches and compare them if you want extra practice. Also note that we expect this problem to take longer to solve than any USAPhO problem.

label: PW202
name: A Helium Balloon in an Accelerating Train — You are sitting in a stationary train, holding a helium balloon…
desc: You are sitting in a stationary train, holding a helium balloon by its string. The balloon floats above your hand with the string vertical. The train then begins to accelerate forward with constant acceleration $$a.$$ Which way does the balloon tilt — toward the front of the…
statement:
You are sitting in a stationary train, holding a helium balloon by its string. The balloon floats above your hand with the string vertical. The train then begins to accelerate forward with constant acceleration $$a.$$ Which way does the balloon tilt — toward the front of the train or toward the back?

__(a)__ Once the train is accelerating, the balloon accelerates forward along with it. What is the direction of the net force on the balloon?

__(b)__ One hypothesis is that this net forward force is supplied by the __tension__ in the string. If that were the case, which way would the balloon have to tilt — toward the front of the train or toward the back?

__(c)__ To settle which way the balloon actually tilts, switch to the reference frame accelerating along with the train; this turns the dynamics problem into a statics problem. In a frame accelerating at $$a,$$ Newton's laws hold provided every object of mass $$m$$ feels an extra __inertial force__ of magnitude $$ma$$ pointing opposite the frame's acceleration. An inertial force is indistinguishable from a uniform gravitational field, so in the train's frame there is an __effective gravity__ combining true gravity with the inertial field. Find the direction and magnitude of the effective gravity.

__(d)__ A helium balloon on a string floats in the direction __opposite__ gravity. Use the effective gravity to determine which way the balloon tilts, and find the angle the string makes with the vertical.

__(e)__ In the train's frame, the inertial force on the balloon points toward the back of the train, and you should have found that the string tension does too — yet the balloon tilts forward. What is pushing it forward?

label: PW202
name: Pressure and Wind in an Accelerating Train Car — A railroad car full of air moves along a straight track with…
desc: A railroad car full of air moves along a straight track with constant forward acceleration $$a.$$ Any initial sloshing has died down, so the air is at rest relative to the car. Analyze the air in the reference frame accelerating with the car. In such a frame Newton's laws hold…
statement:
A railroad car full of air moves along a straight track with constant forward acceleration $$a.$$ Any initial sloshing has died down, so the air is at rest relative to the car. Analyze the air in the reference frame accelerating with the car. In such a frame Newton's laws hold, provided every object of mass $$m$$ also feels an __inertial force__ of magnitude $$ma$$ pointing backward (opposite the car's acceleration).

__(a)__ Consider a small parcel of air of mass $$m$$ inside the car, as in the figure. In the car's frame the parcel is in equilibrium. Find the horizontal force that the surrounding air must exert on the parcel, and conclude in which horizontal direction the air pressure increases.

__(b)__ Now replace the parcel with a helium balloon occupying the same volume. The air the balloon displaces has mass $$m_{\rm air},$$ while the balloon itself (helium plus envelope) has the smaller mass $$m_b.$$ The surrounding air pushes on the balloon's surface exactly as it pushed on the parcel of air it replaced. Find the magnitude and direction of the net horizontal force on the balloon in the car's frame. What is the name for the force that the pressure differences in the air exert on the balloon?

__(c)__ Finally, consider the __transient__ — what happens between the first equilibrium (car at rest, still air) and the second (steady acceleration, pressure gradient established). The car, a very long one, suddenly begins accelerating at $$a$$; at that first instant the pressure inside is still uniform. What would a passenger feel in the air, and how does the air settle into its new equilibrium?

label: PW202
name: Coriolis Drift of a Baseball Pitch — A baseball pitcher has spent their entire career pitching at latitudes…
desc: A baseball pitcher has spent their entire career pitching at latitudes of around $$45^\circ\;\mathrm{N}.$$ The pitcher decides to play an exhibition match in Argentina, at a latitude of $$45^\circ\;\mathrm{S}.$$ A typical pitch has a speed of about $$40\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and…
statement:
A baseball pitcher has spent their entire career pitching at latitudes of around $$45^\circ\;\mathrm{N}.$$ The pitcher decides to play an exhibition match in Argentina, at a latitude of $$45^\circ\;\mathrm{S}.$$ A typical pitch has a speed of about $$40\;\mathrm{m/s}$$ and travels about $$18\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the pitcher to the batter. Should the pitcher worry that pitches will drift differently in the southern hemisphere?

If you aren't familiar with baseball: the player throwing the ball is the __pitcher__, the player catching it is the __catcher__, and the player holding the bat is the __batter__ (the animation shows a right-handed batter). A pitch that drifts toward the batter is called __inside__; one that drifts away from the batter is called __outside__.

On the rotating Earth, a moving object experiences the __Coriolis force__ $$\vec{F}_C = -2m\,\vec{\omega}\times\vec{v},$$ where $$\vec{\omega}$$ is Earth's angular velocity vector. It points along the rotation axis, out of the north pole, and since the Earth turns once per day its magnitude is $$|\vec{\omega}| = \dfrac{2\pi}{24\;\mathrm{h}} \approx 7.3\times 10^{-5}\;\mathrm{s^{-1}}.$$ Recall that a cross product has magnitude $$|\vec{u}\times\vec{w}| = uw\sin\theta,$$ where $$\theta$$ is the angle between the vectors, with direction given by the right-hand rule. For a pitch thrown horizontally due north at latitude $$45^\circ,$$ the angle between $$\vec{\omega}$$ and $$\vec{v}$$ is $$45^\circ.$$

__(a)__ Estimate the magnitude of the ball's acceleration due to the Coriolis force for a north-south pitch (the direction in which the effect is largest).

__(b)__ Estimate the sideways drift the Coriolis force produces over one pitch. Is the drift large enough that the pitcher needs to worry about it?

__(c)__ Which pitch experiences a greater Coriolis drift, measured in absolute distance — a slow one or a fast one? If the pitcher doubles the pitch speed, what happens to the drift?

__(d)__ Suppose the pitch travels due north toward a right-handed batter, and that for this arrangement a drift to the east is an __inside__ drift. In the northern hemisphere, does the Coriolis force push such a pitch inside or outside? What about in the southern hemisphere?

label: PW203
name: In tetherball, a ball is tied to the end of a rope, which wraps around a pole.
desc: In tetherball, a ball is tied to the end of a rope, which wraps around a pole. **a)** Model the pole as having radius $$R.$$ Model the rope as massless and the ball as a point of mass $$m.$$ At time $$t = 0,$$ the ball moves perpendicular to its displacement from its point of…
statement:
In tetherball, a ball is tied to the end of a rope, which wraps around a pole.

**a)** Model the pole as having radius $$R.$$ Model the rope as massless and the ball as a point of mass $$m.$$ At time $$t = 0,$$ the ball moves perpendicular to its displacement from its point of contact with the pole at speed $$v_0.$$ The length of rope from the pole to the ball is $$\ell_0.$$

What is the angular momentum of the ball about the center of the pole?

**b)** How long does it take the ball to collide with the pole?

label: PW203
name: The "Tennis Racket Theorem" describes a striking effect of rigid bodies rotating freely…
desc: The "Tennis Racket Theorem" describes a striking effect of rigid bodies rotating freely in space, illustrated below: Recall that in the handout, we briefly discussed the three principal axes for the rotation of a rigid body about its center. The "flipping" behavior seen in the…
statement:
The "Tennis Racket Theorem" describes a striking effect of rigid bodies rotating freely in space, illustrated below:

Recall that in the handout, we briefly discussed the three principal axes for the rotation of a rigid body about its center. The "flipping" behavior seen in the gif above occurs when rotating about the principal axis $$I_2$$ with a moment of inertia in between the other moments of inertia of the other two axes.

Although most explanations of this effect involve complicated analysis, in 2011 mathematician Terry Tao posted a simple explanation of the effect to the website MathOverflow. The YouTube channel "Veritasium" recently created a video illustrating this explanation.

The video is available (https://youtu.be/1VPfZ_XzisU); it may help to visualize the effects we'll analyze. The video is, however, incomplete; this problem will fill in some details.

Consider a cross made of two massless sticks of length $$2\ell.$$ The intersection between the sticks is located at the origin. One stick lies along the $$x$$ axis and the other lies along the $$y$$ axis.

The stick lying along the $$y$$ axis has two point masses attached to it; one at either end. The masses are each $$m.$$

The stick lying along the $$x$$ axis has two point masses attached to it as well; again one at each end. The masses are each $$M,$$ and we assume $$M \gg m.$$

**a)** Find the moments of inertia $$I_x, I_y,$$ and $$I_z$$ of the cross about each coordinate axis. Which axis is the intermediate axis?

**b)** We imagine the cross begins rotating about the $$y$$ axis with angular frequency $$\omega$$ in the direction such that the $$y$$ component of angular momentum is positive. (And the $$x$$ and $$z$$ components of angular momentum are zero.) Next, we transform into a frame rotating in the same sense, so that the cross is stationary. Find the forces on each mass in this frame.

**c)** The rotating frame can be described with coordinates $$x', y', z'$$ obeying \begin{aligned} y' & = y \\ x' & = x\cos\omega t + z \sin\omega t \\ z' & = z\cos\omega t - x \sin\omega t \\ \end{aligned}

If the cross is perfectly aligned with the $$y$$ axis, then in the rotating frame, we can have equilibrium, and no "flipping" motion occurs. Perfect alignment is never completely possible, though.

Suppose that the cross is very slightly misaligned, so that the stick along the $$y'$$ axis is actually inclined to the $$y'$$ axis by some angle $$\phi.$$

Find angular acceleration of the disk as a function of $$\phi,$$ and thereby find an equation of motion for $$\phi.$$ For this part of the problem, neglect Coriolis forces.

**d)** Suppose there were another T-shaped piece, like the one in the gif, but twice as big in all dimensions and the same density. How would the time between its flipping back and forth compare to the time between flipping back and forth for the piece in the gif? The video mentions a concern that Earth could flip upside down. If it were to do so based on the equation of motion you derived in part (c), estimate (to order of magnitude only) how long that would take.

**e)** The analysis above seems to explain why the cross would flip directions, then flip back, while spinning. But what if the cross were originally spinning around the $$x$$ axis? We could make exactly the same argument as before, imagining a slight rotation about the $$y$$ axis which, due to centrifugal forces, makes the cross flip back and forth. But this is not observed - it's only spinning around the $$y$$ axis that leads to instability. Why isn't spinning around the $$x$$ axis similarly unstable?

name: In this problem, we'll investigate the moment of inertia of a square slab with mass per…
desc: In this problem, we'll investigate the moment of inertia of a square slab with mass per unit area $$\sigma$$ and side length $$s.$$ You can calculate this directly, but we'll take this problem as an opportunity to investigate some properties of the moment of inertia. **a)**…
statement:
In this problem, we'll investigate the moment of inertia of a square slab with mass per unit area $$\sigma$$ and side length $$s.$$ You can calculate this directly, but we'll take this problem as an opportunity to investigate some properties of the moment of inertia.

**a)** Consider a square slab of mass per unit area $$\sigma$$ and side length $$s.$$ By dimensional analysis, what can you conclude about the slab's moment of inertia $$I$$ about its own center for an axis perpendicular to the plane of the slab? (Your answer will have an undetermined coefficient.)

**b)** Now consider a square slab with mass per unit area $$\sigma$$ and side length $$2s.$$ What is its moment of inertia, $$I_2,$$ in terms of $$I?$$

**c)** A square slab with side length $$2s$$ can be thought of as four square slabs, each with side length $$s,$$ arranged in a square. Use this fact to find the moment of inertia of a square slab of side length $$s$$ about its corner in terms of $$I.$$

**d)** Use the result from (c) to find the undetermined coefficient from part (a). You may want to consider

the parallel axis theorem

Next, we'll look at another way of finding the moment of inertia of the square slab about its center.

Consider an arbitrary two-dimensional shape in the $$x-y$$ plane. We'll consider rotations of the shape about its center of mass. We can rotate the shape about its center of mass with an axis in the $$\hat{x}, \hat{y},$$ or $$\hat{z}$$ direction. The first two of these are axis in the plane of the object itself; the last axis is perpendicular to the object. Call the moments of inertia for rotations about these axes $$I_x, I_y,$$ and $$I_z.$$

**e)** Prove that $$I_z = I_x + I_y.$$

**f)** Find $$I_x = I_y$$ for a square, defining them to be parallel to the sides of the square.

**g)** Hence, find $$I_z,$$ the moment of inertia for the square about its center on an axis perpendicular to the square.

Finally, we can confirm our answer with a direct calculation.

**h)** From the integral which defines the moment of inertia, calculate the moment of inertia of a square slab for an axis through the center of the square, perpendicular to the square.
