name: This problem continues a problem we studied in class during week 1 on statics. It's the…
desc: This problem continues a problem we studied in class during week 1 on statics. It's the problem about a heavy disk inside a cylinder. You may wish to review our previous work on the problem before working through this problem. Consider a solid wooden cylinder with radius $$R$$…
statement:
This problem continues a problem we studied in class during week 1 on statics. It's the problem about a heavy disk inside a cylinder. You may wish to review our previous work on the problem before working through this problem.

Consider a solid wooden cylinder with radius $$R$$ and thickness $$H.$$ A smaller cylindrical hole of radius $$r$$ and thickness $$h$$ is drilled out of the cylinder and replaced with a metal cylinder with higher density. The center of the metal cylinder is a distance $$d$$ from the center of the wooden cylinder.

Throughout the problem we assume the following quantities are known: \begin{aligned} R & = \text{radius of cylinder} \\ H & = \text{thickness of cylinder} \\ \rho_1 & = \text{density wood} \\ \rho_2 & = \text{density of metal}\\ M & = \text{total mass of cylinder} \end{aligned}

In class, we imagined placing this cylinder on an flat board and letting it come to rest. Then we imagined tilting the board up by an angle $$\theta$$ and noticing that the cylinder rolls downward, rotating through some angle $$\phi$$ about its own center. We determined that the distance $$b$$ from the center of the cylinder to the center of mass was $$b = R \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin\phi} .$$

Next we want to measure the moment of inertia $$I_{\mathcal{O}}$$ of the system with respect to an axis through the center of the disk $$\mathcal{O}$$ and perpendicular to the flat surfaces of the disk. To this end, we suspend the wooden cylinder at its symmetry axis from a rigid rod. We then turn it away from its equilibrium position by a small angle $$\phi$$ and let it go. We find that the disk oscillates with period $$T.$$

**a)** Find the equation of motion for $$\phi.$$ You may assume that we are only disturbing the equilibrium position by a small amount so that $$\phi$$ is always very small. Your equation may include $$I_{\mathcal{O}},$$ the moment of inertia about the center of the cylinder.

**b)** Express the moment of inertia $$I_{\mathcal{O}}$$ of the system around its symmetry axis $$\mathcal{O}$$ in terms of $$T, b,$$ and $$M.$$

**c)** From the measurements described in class and part (a), we now want to determine the geometry and position of the metal disk inside the wooden cylinder. Find an expression for the distance $$d$$ as a function of $$b$$ and the known quantities. You may also include $$r$$ and $$h,$$ the radius and thickness of the metal disk, as variables in your expression. (This means we haven't really determined $$d$$ yet, but by the end of the problem we'll determine $$r$$ and $$h,$$ and then $$d$$ can be considered determined.)

**d)** Find an expression for the moment of inertia $$I_{\mathcal{O}}$$ in terms of $$b$$ and the known quantities. You may also include $$r$$ and $$h$$ as variables in your expression.

**e)** Using all the above results, find an expression for $$h$$ and $$r$$ in terms of $$b, T,$$ and the known quantities. You may express $$h$$ as a function of $$r.$$

label: PW203
name: The Figure Skater's Scratch Spin — When a spinning figure skater pulls her arms in, she spins dramatically…
desc: When a spinning figure skater pulls her arms in, she spins dramatically faster — the "scratch spin." (The class clip came from "The Physics of Figure Skating," Science Friday.) Model the skater as follows: her torso, head, and legs form a rigid body of fixed moment of inertia…
statement:
When a spinning figure skater pulls her arms in, she spins dramatically faster — the "scratch spin." (The class clip came from "The Physics of Figure Skating," Science Friday.) Model the skater as follows: her torso, head, and legs form a rigid body of fixed moment of inertia $$I_0 = 0.8\;\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$$ about the vertical spin axis, and her two arms are point masses of $$m = 4\;\mathrm{kg}$$ each, held at perpendicular distance $$r_1 = 0.70\;\mathrm{m}$$ from the axis when extended and $$r_2 = 0.15\;\mathrm{m}$$ when pulled in. She starts spinning with arms extended at $$f_1 = 1.5$$ revolutions per second, and friction from the ice is negligible.

Useful facts: a point mass $$m$$ at perpendicular distance $$r$$ from an axis contributes $$mr^2$$ to the moment of inertia about that axis; a rigid body spinning at angular velocity $$\omega$$ has angular momentum $$L = I\omega$$ and rotational kinetic energy $$T = \frac12 I\omega^2$$ about its axis; and the rotational form of Newton's second law is $$\tau = \frac{dL}{dt}.$$

__(a)__ Explain why the skater's angular momentum about the vertical spin axis is conserved while she pulls her arms in, then compute her moments of inertia $$I_1$$ (arms out) and $$I_2$$ (arms in) and her angular momentum.

__(b)__ Find her spin rate $$f_2$$ after she pulls her arms in.

__(c)__ Compute her rotational kinetic energy before and after. Is mechanical energy conserved? If not, where does the difference come from?

__(d)__ Show that at fixed angular momentum the kinetic energy can be written $$T = \frac{L^2}{2I},$$ so that shrinking $$I$$ necessarily raises $$T.$$ Then explain, in terms of forces and displacements, why the skater must do positive work to pull her arms in.

label: PW203
name: Moments of Inertia from the Definition — The __moment of inertia__ of a body about an axis is defined by the…
desc: The __moment of inertia__ of a body about an axis is defined by the integral $$I = \iiint r_{\perp}^{2}\,\rho\,dV,$$ where $$r_{\perp}$$ is the perpendicular distance from each mass element to the axis and $$\rho$$ is the density. It plays the role of mass in rotational…
statement:
The __moment of inertia__ of a body about an axis is defined by the integral $$I = \iiint r_{\perp}^{2}\,\rho\,dV,$$ where $$r_{\perp}$$ is the perpendicular distance from each mass element to the axis and $$\rho$$ is the density. It plays the role of mass in rotational mechanics: $$L = I\omega$$ and $$T = \frac12 I\omega^2.$$ In this problem you will compute the most frequently used moments of inertia directly from the definition.

__(a)__ A thin uniform rod has mass $$M$$ and length $$L.$$ Take the axis perpendicular to the rod through its center, as shown. Writing the linear mass density as $$\lambda = M/L,$$ express $$I$$ as a single integral over the coordinate $$x$$ along the rod and evaluate it.

__(b)__ Now move the axis to one __end__ of the rod (still perpendicular to it). Compute the new moment of inertia by direct integration. Then verify your answer using the __parallel axis theorem__, which states that if a body of mass $$M$$ has moment of inertia $$I_{\rm cm}$$ about an axis through its center of mass, its moment of inertia about any parallel axis a distance $$d$$ away is $$I = I_{\rm cm} + Md^2.$$

__(c)__ A uniform disk has mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$; take the axis through its center, perpendicular to the disk. Slice the disk into thin rings of radius $$r$$ and width $$dr,$$ and evaluate the integral.

__(d)__ Without doing any new integrals, explain why a __solid cylinder__ of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ has the same moment of inertia about its long central axis as the disk in (c), no matter how long the cylinder is — and write down the moment of inertia of a thin __hoop__ of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ about its central perpendicular axis.

label: PW203
name: A Cylinder Rolls Downhill, Two Ways — A uniform solid cylinder of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ is released…
desc: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ is released from rest on a ramp inclined at angle $$\theta$$ and rolls down without slipping. Its moment of inertia about its central axis is $$I_{\rm cm} = \frac12 MR^2.$$ The motion of any rigid body can be analyzed as…
statement:
A uniform solid cylinder of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ is released from rest on a ramp inclined at angle $$\theta$$ and rolls down without slipping. Its moment of inertia about its central axis is $$I_{\rm cm} = \frac12 MR^2.$$ The motion of any rigid body can be analyzed as translation of the center of mass (obeying $$\vec F_{\rm net} = M\vec a_{\rm cm}$$) plus rotation about the center of mass (obeying $$\tau_{\rm cm} = I_{\rm cm}\alpha,$$ which remains valid even though the center of mass accelerates). Rolling without slipping means the contact point is momentarily at rest, which ties the two motions together: $$v_{\rm cm} = \omega R$$ and $$a_{\rm cm} = \alpha R.$$

__(a)__ Write Newton's second law for the center of mass along the incline and the torque equation about the center of mass (the friction force $$f$$ is the only force with a lever arm about the center). Solve for the acceleration $$a_{\rm cm}$$ and for $$f.$$

__(b)__ Redo the problem taking torques about the instantaneous contact point $$P$$: by the parallel axis theorem the moment of inertia about $$P$$ is $$I_P = I_{\rm cm} + MR^2 = \frac32 MR^2,$$ and both the normal force and friction act __at__ $$P,$$ so gravity supplies the only torque. Confirm that you get the same acceleration. (The class warned that torque equations about a moving or accelerating point are dangerous in general; the rolling contact point is one of the safe cases, because its acceleration points directly toward the center of mass.)

__(c)__ The friction here is static. Find the minimum coefficient of static friction $$\mu_s$$ required for the cylinder to roll without slipping.

__(d)__ The kinetic energy of a rigid body is $$T = \frac12 Mv_{\rm cm}^2 + \frac12 I_{\rm cm}\omega^2.$$ Use energy conservation to find the cylinder's speed after its center has descended a vertical height $$h,$$ and compare with the speed $$\sqrt{2gh}$$ of a block sliding down a frictionless ramp. Why doesn't the friction force spoil energy conservation here?

label: PW203
name: Velocities and Accelerations on a Rolling Wheel — A wheel of radius $$R$$ rolls without slipping to the right…
desc: A wheel of radius $$R$$ rolls without slipping to the right along level ground, its axle moving at constant speed $$v.$$ A point on the rim traces out the looping curve called a __cycloid__ (animation by Zorgit, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0): Analyze the rim's motion by…
statement:
A wheel of radius $$R$$ rolls without slipping to the right along level ground, its axle moving at constant speed $$v.$$ A point on the rim traces out the looping curve called a __cycloid__ (animation by Zorgit, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0):

Analyze the rim's motion by splitting it into translation plus rotation: each rim point's velocity is the velocity of the axle plus the velocity of the point's circular motion around the axle, $$\vec v_{\rm point} = \vec v_{\rm axle} + \vec v_{\rm rot},$$ where $$\vec v_{\rm rot}$$ is tangent to the wheel with magnitude $$\omega R.$$

__(a)__ Rolling without slipping means the rim point touching the ground is momentarily at rest. Use this to find the wheel's angular velocity $$\omega,$$ then find the velocity (magnitude and direction) of the __topmost__ point of the wheel and of the __leading__ point (the rim point at the same height as the axle, on the forward side).

__(b)__ Show that at this instant the entire wheel moves as if it were rigidly rotating about the contact point: every point's velocity is perpendicular to the line joining it to the contact point, with magnitude $$\omega$$ times its distance from the contact point. (This is the __instantaneous axis of rotation__.) Verify that this reproduces your answer for the topmost point.

__(c)__ The cycloid has sharp corners — __cusps__ — where the rim point meets the ground. Explain why the trajectory forms a cusp there.

__(d)__ Find the acceleration of the rim point that is instantaneously touching the ground. Is it zero? The class cautioned that treating a moving point as a rotation axis requires great care when computing accelerations and forces — explain how this result illustrates the danger.

label: PW203
name: The Rod That Falls Faster Than g — A uniform rod of mass $$M$$ and length $$L$$ is attached to a frictionless…
desc: A uniform rod of mass $$M$$ and length $$L$$ is attached to a frictionless hinge at one end. It is held horizontal and released from rest. The rod's moment of inertia about its end is $$I = \frac13 ML^2.$$ For a body rotating about an axle that is fixed in an inertial frame, the…
statement:
A uniform rod of mass $$M$$ and length $$L$$ is attached to a frictionless hinge at one end. It is held horizontal and released from rest. The rod's moment of inertia about its end is $$I = \frac13 ML^2.$$ For a body rotating about an axle that is fixed in an inertial frame, the rotational form of Newton's second law, $$\tau = \frac{dL}{dt},$$ becomes $$\tau = I\alpha,$$ with the torque and moment of inertia both taken about the axle. Gravity acts as if applied entirely at the rod's center of mass, the midpoint.

__(a)__ Find the rod's angular acceleration $$\alpha$$ at the instant of release.

__(b)__ Find the downward acceleration of the rod's free tip at that instant, and compare it with $$g.$$ A small coin rests on top of the rod right at the tip: what happens to it just after release? For which positions along the rod would a coin (momentarily) stay in contact?

__(c)__ Find the force the hinge exerts on the rod at the instant of release. (Hint: apply Newton's second law to the center of mass; note that at release $$\omega = 0,$$ so the center of mass has no centripetal acceleration yet.)

__(d)__ Computing torques about the hinge was legitimate here, while the class warned that torque equations about moving points need great care. What makes the hinge a safe choice?

Find the average pressure in the star.

desc: **a)** A planet has a radius $$R$$ and the gravitational field strength at its surface is $$g.$$ A satellite is placed in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around the planet. Obtain an expression for $$T,$$ the period of orbit of the satellite, in terms of $$R, g$$ and $$r.$$…
statement:
**a)** A planet has a radius $$R$$ and the gravitational field strength at its surface is $$g.$$ A satellite is placed in a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ around the planet. Obtain an expression for $$T,$$ the period of orbit of the satellite, in terms of $$R, g$$ and $$r.$$

**b)** Both the Earth and Jupiter can be assumed to have circular orbits about the Sun. Jupiter has an orbital period, $$T_{\mathrm{Jupiter}} = 11.9 \;\mathrm{years}.$$ What is the orbital radius of Jupiter in au?

**c)** The density of the Earth changes sharply between the core and the mantle. By taking just two suitable values of the density of the core and mantle of the Earth from the graph below, estimate a value of the mass of the Earth using this data.

**d)** A planet of mass $$M_p$$ has an orbiting moon of mass $$M_m.$$ The mass of the moon is about 1/8 the mass of the planet.

(i) Sketch a set of equipotential lines for the planet-moon system. Ignore the orbital motion of the moon. Without detailed calculation, indicate on your sketch the relative positions of the neutral point (a point of zero field strength) and the centre of mass of the planet-moon system.

A rocket of mass $$m$$ is launched from the planet. The rocket engine is used very briefly at take-off when it is close to the planet’s surface, and it almost immediately reaches speed $$v,$$ after which the fuel is exhausted and there is no further propulsion. It is then in free-fall and will have just enough energy to reach the moon. Assume that you can ignore relative motion of the planet and moon, and ignore air resistance.

Obtain expressions and calculate values for:

(ii) The distance, $$d,$$ from the planet’s centre, where the speed of the rocket is lowest.

(iii) The launch speed $$v$$ of the rocket from the planet.

For this question part, you may take \begin{aligned} M_p & = 6.00 \times 10^{24} \;\mathrm{kg} \\ M_m & = 7.50 \times 10^{23} \;\mathrm{kg} \\ D & = 3.84 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m}\\ R_p & = 6.4 \times 10^6 \;\mathrm{m}. \end{aligned}

**e)** The Earth can be considered to consist of concentric spheres of material, the outer sphere being the crust with a density of $$2500 \;\mathrm{kg m^{-3}}.$$ If the mass of the Earth is $$M_E = 6.0 \times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg}$$, what will be the fractional change in the gravitational field strength when descending to the bottom of a gold mine, a distance $$d = 3000 \;\mathrm{m}$$ below the surface of the Earth?

**f)** A planetary sized object similar to the Earth was formed from a very large spherical cloud of interstellar dust collapsing under gravity to form a spherical body of uniform density $$\rho$$ and radius $$R.$$

(i) Find an expression for the change in gravitational potential energy as the radius of the protoplanet increases from $$r$$ to $$r + \delta r$$ by the formation of a thin spherical shell of material of mass $$\delta m.$$

(ii) Now derive an expression for the total transfer of gravitational potential energy in the formation of the planet. Use the following terms: the gravitational constant $$G,$$ and the final radius and mass, $$R$$ and $$M$$ respectively.

(iii) If all of this energy was used to heat the planet formed at a very low initial temperature, estimate the temperature that the planet would have reached.

For this planet, take $$R = 6.4 \times 10^6 \;\mathrm{m}, M = 4.0 \times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg,}$$ and the average specific heat capacity of the material of the planet is $$700 \;\mathrm{J \cdot kg^{-1}\cdot K^{-1} }.$$

name: The critical density of the Universe is the density at which the gravitational attraction…
desc: The critical density of the Universe is the density at which the gravitational attraction of matter within the universe is balanced with its expansion in such a way that neither will ultimately prevail. If the density of the universe were lower than this critical density…
statement:
The critical density of the Universe is the density at which the gravitational attraction of matter within the universe is balanced with its expansion in such a way that neither will ultimately prevail. If the density of the universe were lower than this critical density, expansion will continue indefinitely. On the other hand, if the density of the universe were any higher, it would re-collapse upon itself.

**a)** The critical density of the universe is given by:

$$\rho_c = \dfrac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G}.$$

It is possible to arrive at this result through classical means. By modeling the universe as a sphere of uniform density, expanding linearly with velocity $$v = H_0r,$$ derive the above expression.

**b)** The density of ordinary (baryonic) matter in the universe is determined to be about $$3.8 \times 10^{-28} \;\mathrm{kg \cdot m^{-3}}.$$ Use this to provide a justification for the existence of dark matter.

Measurements of the universe curvature predict that the density of the universe should be close to the critical density. The latest estimates of the Hubble constant suggest a value of $$2.2 \times 10^{-18} \; \mathrm{s}^{-1}.$$

label: PW204
name: Galaxies are a large collection of stars and gas that are held together by their own…
desc: Galaxies are a large collection of stars and gas that are held together by their own gravity. One class of galaxies, spiral galaxies, are characterised by a spherical bulge and a flattened disk in which the stars form a spiral pattern. The stars and gas in a spiral galaxy trace…
statement:
Galaxies are a large collection of stars and gas that are held together by their own gravity. One class of galaxies, spiral galaxies, are characterised by a spherical bulge and a flattened disk in which the stars form a spiral pattern. The stars and gas in a spiral galaxy trace out circular orbits around the centre of the galaxy. A schematic of a spiral galaxy, the Milky Way, can be seen below.

**a)** Using the gravitational force acting on a star moving in a circular orbit and assuming spherical symmetry, determine the rotational velocity $$v_{\mathrm{rot}}$$ of a star as a function of the mass enclosed within a radius $$r.$$ Assume that only the mass of material contained within the orbital radius of the star contributes to the gravitational force of attraction, and that the force is the same as if all the mass were concentrated at the center of the galaxy.

**b)** Assuming that most of the mass of the galaxy is contained within the spherical bulge of radius $$r_0,$$ with uniform density $$\rho_0,$$ determine the shape of the rotation curve (the graph of $$v_{\mathrm{rot}}$$ against $$r)$$ inside and outside $$r_0.$$ Sketch the expected rotation curve of the galaxy.

**c)** Astronomers have observed the rotation curves of galaxies and found a significant discrepancy between what is measured and the theoretical prediction. They found that the rotation velocity curve was flat at $$r > r_0,$$ which cannot be explained by a centrally dominating mass. Another component was suggested to make up for the missing, invisible mass, called "dark matter". Assuming a more realistic density profile for the spherically distributed dark matter: $$\rho(r) = \rho_0 \left(\dfrac{r}{r_0}\right)^{-\alpha},$$ determine the exponent, $$\alpha,$$ needed such that the rotation curve is flat at $$r > r_0,$$ as seen from measurements.

**d)** At $$r = 2.8 \times 10^5$$ light years distant from the center of the Milky Way, our Sun has a measured velocity of $$v_{\mathrm{rot}} = 220 \;\mathrm{km \cdot s^{-1}}$$ and an expected velocity of $$v_{\mathrm{exp}} = 70 \;\mathrm{km \cdot s^{-1}}.$$ Calculate the visible as well as the true mass of the Milky Way. What is the percentage of dark matter in the galaxy? Express your answer in units of solar masses, $$M_{\odot}.$$

$$M_\odot = 1.99 \times 10^{30} \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

**e)** Although dark matter is now the widely accepted explanation for the rotation curve problem, an alternative has been suggested: modifying the laws of gravity. Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) postulates that Newton's second law can be re-written as $$F = m \mu\left(\dfrac{a}{a_0}\right)a,$$ where $$\mu$$ is a function with the property that $$\mu (x) = 1$$ for $$x \gg 1$$ and $$\mu(x) = x$$ for $$x \ll 1,$$ $$a$$ is the acceleration and $$a_0$$ is a constant that marks the transition between Newtonian physics and MOND. In the limits of small acceleration, $$a \ll a_0,$$ show that this formulation also leads to a flat rotation curve at large radii.

label: PW204
name: A star displays variation in radial velocity (the component of its velocity relative to…
desc: A star displays variation in radial velocity (the component of its velocity relative to Earth that points toward Earth) with a period of 297 days. The radial velocity curve has a maximum of $$1289 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ above baseline and a minimum of $$373 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ below…
statement:
A star displays variation in radial velocity (the component of its velocity relative to Earth that points toward Earth) with a period of 297 days. The radial velocity curve has a maximum of $$1289 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ above baseline and a minimum of $$373 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ below baseline. If the variation is due to the presence of a planet, determine the minimum eccentricity of the planet. (The baseline can be taken to be the radial velocity of the center of mass of the star-planet system.)

The eccentricity of an ellipse is

$$e = \dfrac{c}{a}$$ where $$c$$ is the distance from the center to a focus.

label: PW204
name: In this problem, we'll get more familiar with the **virial theorem**. The virial theorem…
desc: In this problem, we'll get more familiar with the **virial theorem**. The virial theorem is proved in the handout with an example problem, and here we'll take another perspective. We'll return to the virial theorem one more time when we study quantum mechanics in our final…
statement:
In this problem, we'll get more familiar with the **virial theorem**. The virial theorem is proved in the handout with an example problem, and here we'll take another perspective. We'll return to the virial theorem one more time when we study quantum mechanics in our final problem set.

The virial theorem for Newtonian gravity states that for any system of particles that is gravitationally bound (i.e. they interact via gravity, and the particles can't shoot off to infinity), $$\langle T \rangle = -\left\langle \dfrac{U}{2}\right\rangle $$ where $$T$$ is the total kinetic energy of the system and $$U$$ the total potential energy. The brackets $$(\langle \; \rangle)$$ indicate a time average over a very long time, e.g. $$ \langle T \rangle = \lim_{\tau\to\infty} \dfrac{1}{\tau} \int_0^\tau T(t)\mathrm{d}t.$$

**a)** Show that the virial theorem holds for a particle in a circular orbit around a star. You may ignore any effect of the particle on the star.

**b)** Now show it again, but this time, don't assume that the particle is much less massive than the star.

Next, we'll work through a proof of the virial theorem.

**c)** Define the following quantity $$G$$ as the "virial". $$ G = \sum_i \vec{p}_i \cdot \vec{r}_i.$$ Here, we are imagining a system of particles indexed by $$i.$$ $$\vec{p}_i$$ is the momentum of the $$i$$th particle and $$\vec{r}_i$$ is the position of the $$i$$th particle.

Express the time derivative $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}G}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ in terms of the total kinetic energy of the system and a sum over a term involving the net force on the $$i$$th particle, $$\vec{F}_i,$$ and $$\vec{r}_i.$$

**d)** Imagine watching the system for a very long time. What is the time-average of $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}G}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ in the limit where the time you spend watching the system goes to infinity? You should be able to answer this without doing any calculation.

**e)** In part (c), you derived an equation for $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}G}{\mathrm{d}t},$$ and you now know the value of the long-time average of quantity. Use this to find a relation between the long-time average of the system's kinetic energy and the long-time average of a quantity involving a sum over a function of $$\vec{F}_i$$ and $$\vec{r}_i.$$

To make sure you're on the right track, at this point you should have,

$$2 \langle T \rangle = \left\langle \sum_i \vec{F}_i \cdot \vec{r}_i \right\rangle.$$

You should now have something that's starting to look at bit like the virial theorem, but it involves a sum over particles involving forces and positions instead of simply the potential energy of the system. However, forces and positions, when combined, are related to potential energy, so our remaining job is to flesh out this relationship.

**f)** $$\vec{F}_i$$ is the net force on particle $$i.$$ Write this as a sum over all the particles $$j$$ not equal to $$i.$$ Rewrite your expression from part (e) using a double sum over $$i$$ and $$j eq i.$$

**g)** Consider two terms from the sum in part (f), one for $$i = 1, j = 2$$ and one for $$i = 2, j=1.$$ Then $$\vec{F}_{ij}$$ in the first case is the same as $$\vec{F}_{ji}$$ in the second. Use this fact to rewrite the sum to sum over $$i$$ and $$j < i$$ so that the sum evaluates to the same thing as before. Apply Newton's third law and simplify the result as much as possible.

An alternative way to communicate this instruction is: Split the sum into one for $$j < i$$ and one for $$j > i$$. Then reverse $$i$$ and $$j$$ in one of the sums to combine them back into a single sum for $$j < i$$."

You should find

$$ \langle T\rangle = -\dfrac12 \left\langle \sum_i\sum_{j < i} (\vec{F}_{ji}\cdot \left(\vec{r}_i -\vec{r}_j\right) \right\rangle.$$

**h)** Suppose the potential energy between any pair of particles is $$U_{ij} = k r_{ij}^n$$ where $$r_{ij}$$ is the distance between the particles. Find $$\vec{F}_{ij}$$ in terms of $$U_{ij}$$ and $$\hat{r}_{ij}$$ and use this to simplify your equation from part (g). You should now have a complete proof of the virial theorem.

label: PW204
name: **note:** This is a long problem. You don't have to do all of it to get the benefit of…
desc: **note:** This is a long problem. You don't have to do all of it to get the benefit of working on parts of it. **a)** A particle is a distance $$r$$ from the sun and moves at speed $$v.$$ Its velocity is perpendicular to the vector from the sun to the particle's position. On the…
statement:
**note:** This is a long problem. You don't have to do all of it to get the benefit of working on parts of it.

**a)** A particle is a distance $$r$$ from the sun and moves at speed $$v.$$ Its velocity is perpendicular to the vector from the sun to the particle's position. On the other side of the sun, the particle's distance from the sun is $$r'.$$ Find $$r'.$$

You should find that there are no allowed values of $$r'$$ for certain combinations of $$r$$ and $$v.$$ Find the condition on $$r$$ and $$v$$ such that $$r'$$ exists, and give an interpretation to your result.

---------------

In this problem, we'll explore the concept of an **effective potential**. This concept came up in the handout in the proof of Kepler's first law, but we didn't explicitly label it there. After you solve this problem, you might want to revisit the proof of Kepler's first law given in the handout to see how the effective potential was used.

Revisit the calculation in part (a).

If you try to make $$r'$$ smaller than the correct value and calculate $$v'$$ via conservation of energy, you'll find that the particle's angular momentum has decreased from the initial position of $$r$$ with speed $$v.$$ In other words, the particle can't get too close to the sun due to conservation of angular momentum. It's almost as if angular momentum creates a push that shoves particles out from the sun, countering the attractive force of gravity.

This is the idea that the effective potential formalizes.

**b)** In polar coordinates the velocity of a particle has two component, $$v_r$$ and $$v_\theta.$$ Find the energy of the particle in terms of these components and $$r, G,m,$$ and $$M.$$

**c)** Find the angular momentum of the particle using the variables as in part (b).

**d)** Use the result of part (c) to eliminate $$v_\theta$$ from part (b). You should find that the energy is the same as if the potential energy were $$V = U_{e} + U.$$ What is $$U_{e}?$$ The name for $$V$$ is the **effective potential**.

To check your answer, you should find

$$U_{e} = \dfrac{L^2}{2mr^2}.$$

**e)** A circular orbit is one where $$r$$ is constant. This means that $$V$$ is minimized at the correct $$r.$$ Use this fact to find the radius $$r_0$$ of a circular orbit under Newtonian gravity for a fixed $$L.$$ Verify that your result is correct by comparing it to a straightforward calculation based on Newton's laws.

**f)** Find the angular frequency of small oscillations about about $$r_0.$$ Is your answer what you expect based on Kepler's laws?

**g)** A masses $$m$$ is attached to the end of a string, which extends through a hole in a frictionless table. An external agent applies a constant tension $$T$$ to the end of the string hanging through the hole. The mass rotates around the table at an angular velocity $$\Omega$$ such that its distance from the hole is constant. Next, the mass is given a small radial velocity. Find the angular frequency $$\omega$$ of oscillations the mass's distance from the hole in terms of $$\Omega.$$ How does your result compare to what you found in the previous parts of this problem? What does this imply about whether the orbit is "closed" (I.E. the mass goes back to the same state after one orbit)?

**h)** Suppose that a particle is subjected to the central potential $$U = cr^n$$ With $$n$$ an integer. Throughout the rest of this problem, we will determine for which values of $$n$$ orbits are closed.

Our first step in this proof is: suppose the particle orbits with angular frequency $$\Omega,$$ then is given a small push in the radial direction. For what $$n$$ does the particle's distance from the center of its orbit oscillate?

For what $$n$$ does the particle return to its original state after one orbit, given these infinitesimal perturbations?

To check your progress, you should find the $$n$$ for which the particle returns to its original state after one orbit, given an infinitesimal push, are

\[ n = -1, 2, 7, 14, \ldots , k^2 - 2 , \ldots .\] for any integer $$k.$$

**i)** Our work in part (h) shows that for most potentials, orbits are not closed. It turns out, though, that even most of the potentials that survived our test in part (h) do not yield closed orbits when we allow the oscillations about a circular orbit to be any more than infinitesimal. Our goal in the rest of the problem is to determine which of the potentials that survived the test in part (h) truly give closed orbits. The result is called **Bertrand's Theorem**. (Although in reality, Bertrand's theorem is slightly stronger because it doesn't assume the potential is a power law where the exponent is an integer.)

In part (h), there should be both positive and negative $$n$$ among your answers. Why do we only need to focus on the positive $$n$$ for the rest of the problem? Among the positive $$n$$ values you found, are there any you know do yield closed orbits?

In order to evaluate positive $$n,$$ we'll do the following intermediate calculation:

For the small perturbations studied in part (h), find the angle between the position vector of the planet when it is furthest from the center of the orbit and when it is closest to the center of the orbit. This is called the **apsidal angle**.

In what follows, we'll assume that the apsidal angle does not vary depending on the orbital parameters. (This is true and can be shown via some manipulations of the equations of motion that we aren't going to bother with, but any online derivation of Bertrand's theorem will include them.)

In the final part of the problem, we'll use another line of reasoning to determine what the apsidal angle must be, assuming $$n>0$$ and the orbit is closed. Then only those $$n$$ with the correct apsidal angle can give closed orbits.

**j)** This final part of the problem is somewhat technical, but will allow us to determine the allowed apsidal angles in closed orbits with $$n > 0$$ using some tricks.

The main idea is that we want to turn our equations into something that looks like a system we understand: the harmonic oscillator. We have an understanding of the energy of our system based on the effective potential, and we will try to manipulate that energy to look like the energy in a harmonic oscillator.

The effective potential includes the angular momentum term $$\dfrac{L}{mr^2}.$$ This doesn't look like the potential energy of a harmonic oscillator, $$U = \dfrac12 kx^2.$$ But we can make it look like the harmonic oscillator by defining $$x = \dfrac{1}{r}$$ and turning the equation for energy in the orbit into an equation for $$x.$$

Write an equation for energy conservation in an orbit using $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t}, L, m, r, c,$$ and $$n.$$

Because we are interested in the apsidal angle, we want to study the variation in $$r$$ over $$\theta$$ instead of $$t,$$ so rewrite the equation using $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}\theta}, \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t}, L, m, r, c,n,$$ and $$E,$$ the total energy of the orbit. Then eliminate $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ using $$L, m,$$ and $$r.$$

Now switch to the variable $$x = \dfrac{1}{r}.$$ If all this went well, you should have

$$ \dfrac12 \dfrac{L^2}{m} \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 + \dfrac{L^2}{2m}x^2 + \dfrac{c}{x^n} = E.$$

This looks kinda of like a harmonic oscillator, but it has that extra term

$$\dfrac{c}{x^n}.$$

We need another trick to deal with the effect of this term. That trick will be to consider the limiting case where the energy of the orbit goes to infinity.

Let $$E \to \infty.$$ At typical $$x$$ values, what happens to that extra term, as compared to the rest of the potential? At what $$x$$ does the term still matter? Argue that the potential energy can be thought of, in this limit, as a harmonic oscillator potential energy with a key modification about where the particle is allowed to go inside the potential. What is that modification?

Based on that modification, what is the angular frequency of $$x(\theta)?$$ What does this imply about the apsidal angle? Finally, based on all the above, for what values of $$n$$ are orbits closed?

If you work through all of this, you'll have proved a simplified version of Bertrand's theorem! Enjoy working through the problem and share your progress on the message board.

label: PW204
name: Orbit Energy and the Vis-Viva Equation — A planet of mass $$m$$ orbits a star of mass $$M \gg m$$ along an…
desc: A planet of mass $$m$$ orbits a star of mass $$M \gg m$$ along an ellipse with semi-major axis $$a$$ and eccentricity $$e.$$ The star sits at one focus of the ellipse (Kepler's first law). The gravitational force on the planet is $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$$ directed toward the…
statement:
A planet of mass $$m$$ orbits a star of mass $$M \gg m$$ along an ellipse with semi-major axis $$a$$ and eccentricity $$e.$$ The star sits at one focus of the ellipse (Kepler's first law). The gravitational force on the planet is $$F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$$ directed toward the star, and the gravitational potential energy is $$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r},$$ taken to be zero at infinite separation. The closest point of the orbit (__perihelion__) is a distance $$r_p = a(1-e)$$ from the star, and the farthest point (__aphelion__) is $$r_a = a(1+e),$$ so that $$r_p + r_a = 2a.$$

__(a)__ At perihelion and aphelion — and only there — the planet's velocity is perpendicular to the line from the star to the planet. Use conservation of angular momentum to relate the speeds $$v_p$$ and $$v_a$$ at those two points.

__(b)__ Use conservation of energy between perihelion and aphelion, together with part (a), to show that the total energy of the orbit is $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a}.$$ Notice that the energy depends only on the semi-major axis, not on the eccentricity.

__(c)__ Combine part (b) with conservation of energy to derive the __vis-viva equation__: at any distance $$r$$ from the star, the planet's speed satisfies $$v^2 = GM\left(\dfrac{2}{r} - \dfrac{1}{a}\right).$$

__(d)__ Check the vis-viva equation in two limits. First, a circular orbit has $$r = a$$ everywhere; verify that the resulting speed agrees with what Newton's second law gives directly for a circular orbit. Second, a parabolic orbit is the marginal case of escape, obtained by letting $$a \to \infty.$$ Show that the resulting speed is the escape speed at distance $$r,$$ and that it exceeds the circular-orbit speed at the same $$r$$ by a factor of $$\sqrt{2}.$$

label: PW204
name: Mercury at Perihelion and Aphelion — Mercury orbits the Sun along an ellipse with semi-major axis $$a =…
desc: Mercury orbits the Sun along an ellipse with semi-major axis $$a = 5.79\times10^{10}\;\mathrm{m}$$ and eccentricity $$e = 0.206$$ — the most eccentric orbit of any planet. The Sun, of mass $$M = 1.99\times10^{30}\;\mathrm{kg},$$ sits at one focus (Kepler's first law), so…
statement:
Mercury orbits the Sun along an ellipse with semi-major axis $$a = 5.79\times10^{10}\;\mathrm{m}$$ and eccentricity $$e = 0.206$$ — the most eccentric orbit of any planet. The Sun, of mass $$M = 1.99\times10^{30}\;\mathrm{kg},$$ sits at one focus (Kepler's first law), so Mercury's perihelion (closest) and aphelion (farthest) distances are $$r_p = a(1-e)$$ and $$r_a = a(1+e).$$ The orbit conserves both energy and angular momentum about the Sun, the potential energy is $$U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r},$$ and the total energy of an elliptical orbit is $$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a}.$$ Take $$G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}.$$

__(a)__ At perihelion and aphelion, Mercury's velocity is perpendicular to the Sun-Mercury line. Show from conservation of angular momentum that $$\dfrac{v_p}{v_a} = \dfrac{1+e}{1-e},$$ independent of $$a.$$

__(b)__ Use energy conservation to find Mercury's speeds $$v_p$$ and $$v_a$$ numerically, and check that their ratio agrees with part (a).

__(c)__ Kepler's third law for an orbit around the Sun reads $$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 a^3}{GM}.$$ Compute Mercury's orbital period in days.

label: PW204
name: Binary Stars and the Barycenter — Two stars of masses $$M_1$$ and $$M_2$$ are gravitationally bound to each…
desc: Two stars of masses $$M_1$$ and $$M_2$$ are gravitationally bound to each other, far from any other bodies. Each star moves in a circle about the system's __barycenter__ (its center of mass), staying diametrically opposite the other star so that their separation keeps a constant…
statement:
Two stars of masses $$M_1$$ and $$M_2$$ are gravitationally bound to each other, far from any other bodies. Each star moves in a circle about the system's __barycenter__ (its center of mass), staying diametrically opposite the other star so that their separation keeps a constant value $$d.$$ The gravitational attraction between them has magnitude $$F = \dfrac{GM_1M_2}{d^2}.$$

__(a)__ Find the radii $$r_1$$ and $$r_2$$ of the two circular orbits in terms of $$M_1,$$ $$M_2,$$ and $$d.$$

__(b)__ Explain why the two stars must orbit with a common period, and show that this period satisfies $$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 d^3}{G(M_1 + M_2)}$$ — Kepler's third law with the __total__ mass of the system.

__(c)__ Take the limit $$M_2 \ll M_1$$ and show that the result reduces to the familiar one-body law $$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 d^3}{GM_1}$$ for a light planet circling a fixed star. When is it safe to ignore the distinction between the barycenter and the center of the heavier body?

__(d)__ Sirius A and Sirius B form a binary with an orbital period of $$T = 50.1$$ years; model their orbit as circular with separation $$d = 20.0\;\mathrm{AU}.$$ Using only the fact that the Earth orbits the Sun (mass $$M_\odot$$) at $$1\;\mathrm{AU}$$ with a period of $$1$$ year, find the total mass of the Sirius system in solar masses. No value of $$G$$ is required.

label: PW204
name: A Hohmann Transfer to Mars — A spacecraft is coasting around the Sun in Earth's orbit, which is circular with…
desc: A spacecraft is coasting around the Sun in Earth's orbit, which is circular with radius $$r_1 = 1.50\times10^{11}\;\mathrm{m},$$ and mission control wants to move it to Mars's circular orbit of radius $$r_2 = 2.28\times10^{11}\;\mathrm{m}.$$ The most fuel-efficient two-burn…
statement:
A spacecraft is coasting around the Sun in Earth's orbit, which is circular with radius $$r_1 = 1.50\times10^{11}\;\mathrm{m},$$ and mission control wants to move it to Mars's circular orbit of radius $$r_2 = 2.28\times10^{11}\;\mathrm{m}.$$ The most fuel-efficient two-burn route is the __Hohmann transfer__: fire the engine once to put the craft on an ellipse whose perihelion touches Earth's orbit and whose aphelion touches Mars's orbit, coast halfway around that ellipse, then fire again at aphelion to circularize. Each burn is brief, changing the craft's speed by $$\Delta v$$ without changing its position.

Useful facts: an orbit of semi-major axis $$a$$ around the Sun has total energy $$E = -\dfrac{GM_\odot m}{2a},$$ which combined with energy conservation gives the vis-viva relation $$v^2 = GM_\odot\left(\dfrac{2}{r} - \dfrac{1}{a}\right);$$ the orbital period satisfies $$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 a^3}{GM_\odot};$$ and $$GM_\odot = 1.327\times10^{20}\;\mathrm{m^3/s^2}.$$

__(a)__ Find the semi-major axis $$a$$ of the transfer ellipse, the speed the craft must have just after the first burn, and the burn's size $$\Delta v_1$$ (the speed of a circular orbit of radius $$r$$ is $$\sqrt{GM_\odot/r}$$).

__(b)__ Find the craft's speed when it arrives at aphelion. Is it then moving too slowly or too quickly to stay on Mars's circular orbit? Find the second burn's size $$\Delta v_2.$$

__(c)__ How long does the transfer take, in days?

label: PW204
name: The Gravitational Slingshot — Spacecraft bound for the outer solar system routinely steal energy from planets…
desc: Spacecraft bound for the outer solar system routinely steal energy from planets in __gravity assists__ (slingshots). Model the simplest version. A spacecraft of mass $$m$$ approaches Jupiter (mass $$M_J = 1.90\times10^{27}\;\mathrm{kg} \gg m$$) head-on: in the Sun's reference…
statement:
Spacecraft bound for the outer solar system routinely steal energy from planets in __gravity assists__ (slingshots). Model the simplest version. A spacecraft of mass $$m$$ approaches Jupiter (mass $$M_J = 1.90\times10^{27}\;\mathrm{kg} \gg m$$) head-on: in the Sun's reference frame the spacecraft moves at speed $$v = 10.0\;\mathrm{km/s}$$ directly opposite Jupiter's orbital velocity, while Jupiter moves at $$u = 13.1\;\mathrm{km/s}$$ along its orbit. The spacecraft swings around behind the planet in a tight hyperbolic hairpin and departs moving in the __same__ direction as Jupiter's velocity. The encounter is brief enough that the Sun's pull can be ignored during it, and Jupiter's velocity is essentially unchanged. The gravitational potential energy of the pair is $$U = -\dfrac{GM_Jm}{r},$$ which vanishes at large separation.

__(a)__ Work in Jupiter's reference frame. Use conservation of energy to explain why the spacecraft's speed long after the encounter, when it is again far from Jupiter, equals its speed long before — even though gravity has been acting on it the whole time.

__(b)__ Transform back to the Sun's frame to find the spacecraft's final speed. (You should recognize the result: it is exactly an elastic bounce off a massive, oncoming wall.)

__(c)__ The spacecraft's kinetic energy increased, yet gravity is conservative and the potential energy is the same (zero) before and after. Where did the energy come from? Take $$m = 720\;\mathrm{kg}$$ (roughly a Voyager probe) and use conservation of momentum to compute the change in Jupiter's speed.

__(d)__ Verify the energy bookkeeping: show that, to first order in Jupiter's tiny velocity change, the kinetic energy Jupiter loses equals the kinetic energy the spacecraft gains, and evaluate that energy in joules.

label: PW205
name: This problem consists of several short questions about friction.
desc: This problem consists of several short questions about friction. **a)** Suppose a book sits on an inclined plane. Assume $$\mu_s = \mu_k = \mu > \tan \theta,$$ so the book can sit stationary on the plane. Tie a string to the book and pull the book horizontally, in the direction…
statement:
This problem consists of several short questions about friction.

**a)** Suppose a book sits on an inclined plane. Assume $$\mu_s = \mu_k = \mu > \tan \theta,$$ so the book can sit stationary on the plane. Tie a string to the book and pull the book horizontally, in the direction perpendicular to the gradient of the plane. What is the book's motion and why?

**b)** A car may slip out of control, sliding out of its lane, when the driver slams on the brakes. Why is it when the driver slams on the brakes that this happens?

**c)** Balance a stick horizontally on your outstretched index fingers. Slowly move your right hand to the left. Why does the stick also move and why does it remain balanced?

**d)** Why does a badly lubricated door squeak? (You might want to try to answer this question now, then return to it after working the last two problems on this homework set.)

label: PW205
name: A satellite in low-Earth orbit experiences a small frictional force, the drag force…
desc: A satellite in low-Earth orbit experiences a small frictional force, the drag force, because although the air is very thin hundreds of kilometers up, it still exists. **a)** Does the drag force result in satellites speeding up or slowing down relative to the center of Earth?…
statement:
A satellite in low-Earth orbit experiences a small frictional force, the drag force, because although the air is very thin hundreds of kilometers up, it still exists.

**a)** Does the drag force result in satellites speeding up or slowing down relative to the center of Earth? Answer this question without performing any calculations.

We assume that the drag force may be written $$ \vec{F} = -k\vec{v}.$$

**b)** What are the dimensions of $$k?$$ If $$k$$ depends on the satellite's cross-sectional area $$A,$$ the air density $$\rho,$$ and the speed $$v,$$ what is a plausible formula for $$k?$$

**c)** A satellite orbits at altitude $$h = 160 \;\mathrm{km}.$$ The air density is $$\rho = 10^{-9} \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ The speed is $$v = 8 \;\mathrm{km/s}.$$ The satellite cross-sectional area is $$A = 1 \;\mathrm{m}^2.$$ Its mass is $$100 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ What is the ratio of the satellite's acceleration due to friction to the satellite's acceleration due to gravity?

**d)** Assume that the satellite's orbit is almost circular. Find the velocity of the satellite as a function of time over times short enough that the satellite's height about Earth does not vary significantly. Does your answer confirm what you found in part (a)? If not, you may wish to revise your answer to that part of the problem. You may give only a symbolic answer to this problem; plugging in the numbers is not necessary.

label: PW205
name: A box falls from a height $$h$$ onto a fast-moving horizontal conveyor belt. The…
desc: A box falls from a height $$h$$ onto a fast-moving horizontal conveyor belt. The coefficient of friction between the box and the belt is $$\mu.$$ The duration of the impact between the box and the belt is negligible. What is the highest angle $$\theta_m$$ above the horizontal to…
statement:
A box falls from a height $$h$$ onto a fast-moving horizontal conveyor belt. The coefficient of friction between the box and the belt is $$\mu.$$ The duration of the impact between the box and the belt is negligible.

What is the highest angle $$\theta_m$$ above the horizontal to which the box can bounce?

label: PW205
name: One end of a spring with spring constant $$k$$ is fixed at the top of a rough plane…
desc: One end of a spring with spring constant $$k$$ is fixed at the top of a rough plane inclined at an angle $$\theta$$ to the horizontal. The other end is attached to a block of mass $$m,$$ and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the slope is $$\mu_k.$$ The…
statement:
One end of a spring with spring constant $$k$$ is fixed at the top of a rough plane inclined at an angle $$\theta$$ to the horizontal. The other end is attached to a block of mass $$m,$$ and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the slope is $$\mu_k.$$ The coefficient of friction is small and the friction is a weak effect, but should be treated exactly.

**a)** Find the extension of the spring from its unstretched length at the position where the system is in equilibrium. You may neglect the influence of friction in this part only.

**b)** Find the potential energy of the system as a function of the displacement from the equilibrium position.

**c)** The spring is now displaced from its equilibrium position by a distance $$x_0$$ up the plane, and released. Sketch a graph of the displacement of the mass on the spring as a function of time.

**d)** Find the difference in position along the slope between successive points where the mass is stationary and about to move down the slope, and hence determine the maximum number of such points that can occur.

label: PW205
name: A round vertical cylinder of radius $$R$$ is fixed on a horizontal plane. An inextensible…
desc: A round vertical cylinder of radius $$R$$ is fixed on a horizontal plane. An inextensible thread of length $$L$$ is attached at the cylinder side near the bottom. Initially the thread is tangent to the side. A small puck (of negligible size) is attached to the other end of the…
statement:
A round vertical cylinder of radius $$R$$ is fixed on a horizontal plane. An inextensible thread of length $$L$$ is attached at the cylinder side near the bottom. Initially the thread is tangent to the side. A small puck (of negligible size) is attached to the other end of the thread. The puck is given an initial velocity $$v_0$$ perpendicular to the thread, so the puck starts sliding on the plane. How long will the puck motion last if there is a coefficient of kinetic friction $$\mu$$ between the puck and the plane?

(If the puck hits the cylinder, it stops immediately.)

label: PW205
name: Two small disks with frictionless lateral sides lie on a horizontal plane with a…
desc: Two small disks with frictionless lateral sides lie on a horizontal plane with a coefficient of kinetic friction $$\mu.$$ Initially, the first disk was at rest and the second one collided with it at a velocity $$\vec{v}.$$ Determine the distance between the disks when they stop…
statement:
Two small disks with frictionless lateral sides lie on a horizontal plane with a coefficient of kinetic friction $$\mu.$$ Initially, the first disk was at rest and the second one collided with it at a velocity $$\vec{v}.$$ Determine the distance between the disks when they stop moving in terms of $$\mu, g, v,$$ and $$x_1,$$ where $$x_1$$ is the distance the first disk moves after the collision.

What is the maximum and minimum distance between the disks for a given absolute value of velocity $$v$$ and the coefficient of kinetic friction $$\mu?$$

Assume the collision to be elastic but not necessarily central. Neglect the disk size.

label: PW205
name: A block is situated on a slope with angle $$\alpha.$$ The coefficient of friction between…
desc: A block is situated on a slope with angle $$\alpha.$$ The coefficient of friction between them is $$\mu > \tan \alpha$$. The slope is rapidly driven back and forth in such a way that its velocity vector $$\vec{u}$$ is parallel to both the slope and the horizontal and has…
statement: A block is situated on a slope with angle $$\alpha.$$ The coefficient of friction between them is $$\mu > \tan \alpha$$. The slope is rapidly driven back and forth in such a way that its velocity vector $$\vec{u}$$ is parallel to both the slope and the horizontal and has constant modulus $$v$$; the direction of $$\vec{u}$$ reverses abruptly after each time interval $$\tau$$. What will be the average velocity $$w$$ of the block's motion? Assume $$g\tau \ll v.$$

label: PW205
name: A uniform chain of mass $$m$$ and length $$\ell$$ is sliding off a rough table. At time…
desc: A uniform chain of mass $$m$$ and length $$\ell$$ is sliding off a rough table. At time $$t$$ length $$x$$ lies over the edge of the table. Assume that the rounded edge of the table is frictionless and of negligible extent compared to $$\ell,$$ but static and kinetic friction…
statement:
A uniform chain of mass $$m$$ and length $$\ell$$ is sliding off a rough table. At time $$t$$ length $$x$$ lies over the edge of the table. Assume that the rounded edge of the table is frictionless and of negligible extent compared to $$\ell,$$ but static and kinetic friction coefficients between the chain and table are both $$\mu.$$

**a)** Find the maximum $$x$$ such that the chain has no acceleration. Call this $$x_0.$$

**b)** Assuming that the chain accelerates in such a way that the picture above remains accurate (except that $$x$$ changes), find the equation of motion for the chain.

**c)** Find the solution to the equation of motion in (b) using the initial condition that the chain was placed at the maximum $$x$$ discovered in part (a), then given a small initial velocity $$v_0$$ in the direction towards the edge of the table.

**d)** The equation of motion found in (b) can only be discovered making certain assumptions which are true to a point, but cease to be true at a certain point of the chain falling off the table. Assuming the chain was released with $$x$$ just very slightly greater than the maximum $$x$$ discovered in part (a), find, approximately, the value of $$\dfrac{x}{\ell}$$ at which the equation of motion in (b) ceases to be an accurate description of the system. Give your answer in terms of $$\mu.$$ Is it possible to find an approximate value of $$\mu$$ such that the equation of motion found in (b) is a good model until the entire chain falls off the table?

label: PW205
name: The phenomenon of creaking is very common, and can be found in doors, closets, chalk…
desc: The phenomenon of creaking is very common, and can be found in doors, closets, chalk squeaking on a blackboard, playing a violin, new shoes, car brakes and other systems from everyday life. A similar phenomenon can cause violent earthquakes with a period of several decades. The…
statement:
The phenomenon of creaking is very common, and can be found in doors, closets, chalk squeaking on a blackboard, playing a violin, new shoes, car brakes and other systems from everyday life. A similar phenomenon can cause violent earthquakes with a period of several decades. The physical mechanism for creaking is based on elasticity combined with the difference between the static and the kinetic friction coefficients. In this question, we will study this mechanism and its application to the case of an opening door.

Consider the following system:

We would like to understand why this setup supports two different forms of motion:

1. The friction is always kinetic. This is known as the **pure slip** mode. 2. Kinetic and static friction alternate. This is known as a **stick-slip** mode. Stick-slip motion is the source of the creaking sound commonly encountered.

**a)** Consider the case where at the initial time $$t = 0,$$ the box slides on the floor with velocity $$v_0,$$ and the spring's tension exactly balances the kinetic friction. Assume $$0 < v_0 < u.$$ The **spring's elongation** $$x$$ will oscillate as a function of $$t.$$

Find the period $$T_0$$ and the amplitude $$A$$ of these oscillations.

Sketch a qualitative graph of the spring's elongation $$x(t)$$ for $$0 < t < 3T_0.$$

**b)** Now, consider the case where at $$t=0$$ the box is at rest, while the initial spring elongation $$x$$ is the same as in part (a). Sketch a qualitative graph of the velocity $$v(t)$$ of the box with respect to the floor for $$0 < t < 3T,$$ where $$T$$ is the (new) period of the oscillations $$x(t).$$ Motion to the right corresponds to a positive sign of $$v.$$ Indicate approximately on your graph the horizontal line $$v = u.$$

**c)** For the initial conditions of part (b), find the time-averaged value $$\bar{x}$$ of the spring's elongation after a sufficiently long time has passed.

**d)** For the conditions of part (b), find the period $$T$$ of the oscillations $$x(t).$$

label: PW205
name: This problem continues the previous one on creaking.
desc: This problem continues the previous one on creaking. A door hinge is a hollow, open-ended metal cylinder with radius $$r,$$ height $$h,$$ and thickness $$\Delta r.$$ The lower end of the cylinder lies on a metal base attached to the wall (the area of contact is a ring of radius…
statement:
This problem continues the previous one on creaking.

A door hinge is a hollow, open-ended metal cylinder with radius $$r,$$ height $$h,$$ and thickness $$\Delta r.$$ The lower end of the cylinder lies on a metal base attached to the wall (the area of contact is a ring of radius $$r.)$$ The static and kinetic friction coefficients between the cylinder and its base are $$\mu_s$$ and $$\mu_k$$ respectively, which $$\mu_k < \mu_s.$$ The upper end of the cylinder is attached to the door, which can be regarded as perfectly rigid. A typical door hangs on two or three such hinges, but its weight is concentrated on only one of them - this is the hinge that will creak. The cylinder of that hinge presses down on its metal base with the weight of the entire door, whose mass is $$M.$$

The cylinder is not a perfectly rigid body - it can twist tangentially without changing its overall form, so that vertical line segments become tilted with a small angle $$\alpha.$$ (Shown on the right.) the elastic force on a small area element $$\mathrm{d}S$$ of the base due to this deformation is given by $$\mathrm{d}F = G\alpha \mathrm{d}S,$$ where $$G$$ is a material property known as the shear modulus. Use the values \begin{aligned} r & = 5 \;\mathrm{mm} \\ h & = 3 \;\mathrm{cm} \\ \Delta r & = 1 \;\mathrm{mm}\\ \mu_s & = 0.75\\ \mu_k & = 0.55\\ G & = 8 \times 10^{10} \;\mathrm{Pa} \\ M & = 30 \;\mathrm{kg} \\ g & = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}. \end{aligned}

You may use the approximation $$\Delta r \ll r.$$

**a)** We start rotating the door very slowly from the equilibrium (zero torque). For small rotation angles, obtain an expression for the torsion coefficient $$\kappa = \dfrac{\tau}{\theta},$$ where $$\tau$$ is the torque which must be applied to rotate the door by an angle $$\theta.$$

**b)** At very low angular velocity, when a transition from stick to slip occurs, a sound pulse is emitted. Find the angular velocity $$\Omega$$ of the door for which the frequency of these pulses enters the audible range at $$f = 20 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ Assume the frequency $$f_0$$ of pure-slip oscillations in the hinge is much higher: $$f_0 \gg f.$$ Provide an expression and a numerical result.

label: PW205
name: A Bead Sliding on a Rough Circular Hoop — A small bead of mass $$m$$ is threaded onto a circular wire hoop of…
desc: A small bead of mass $$m$$ is threaded onto a circular wire hoop of radius $$R$$ that is held fixed in a __horizontal__ plane. The wire is the only thing supporting the bead, and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the bead and the wire is $$\mu.$$ The bead is given an…
statement:
A small bead of mass $$m$$ is threaded onto a circular wire hoop of radius $$R$$ that is held fixed in a __horizontal__ plane. The wire is the only thing supporting the bead, and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the bead and the wire is $$\mu.$$ The bead is given an initial speed $$v_0$$ along the hoop. How far does it slide before stopping? (Based on a problem from the British Physics Olympiad, 2018.)

__(a)__ The wire can push on the bead in any direction __perpendicular__ to the wire: vertically, to support the bead's weight, and horizontally, to turn its velocity around the circle. When the bead moves at speed $$v,$$ find these two perpendicular components of the normal force and show that its magnitude is $$N = m\sqrt{g^2 + v^4/R^2}.$$

__(b)__ Write Newton's second law along the direction of motion, with kinetic friction of magnitude $$\mu N$$ opposing the motion. The result is a differential equation for $$v(t)$$ with no elementary solution — but the problem asks for a __distance__, not a time. Eliminate time using the chain rule, $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = v\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}s},$$ where $$s$$ is the distance traveled along the hoop, to get a differential equation for $$v(s).$$

__(c)__ Integrate your equation to find the total distance $$s_{\rm stop}$$ the bead slides before stopping. (Useful antiderivative: $$\int \dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\sqrt{1+u^2}} = \operatorname{arcsinh}(u) + c = \ln\left(u + \sqrt{1+u^2}\right) + c.$$)

__(d)__ Check your answer in two extreme cases. For a slow launch, $$v_0^2 \ll gR,$$ compare with the skid distance of a puck on a flat rough floor. For a fast launch, $$v_0^2 \gg gR,$$ show that the speed decays as $$v \approx v_0 e^{-\mu\theta},$$ where $$\theta = s/R$$ is the angle swept around the hoop, so that the stopping distance grows only __logarithmically__ with $$v_0.$$

__(e)__ Generalize the fast regime. The bead now slides along a fixed horizontal wire bent into an arbitrary smooth curve. Near any point, the curve is locally approximated by its __osculating circle__, whose radius $$\rho(s)$$ is the local radius of curvature, so the centripetal acceleration is $$v^2/\rho(s).$$ Show that as long as $$v^2 \gg g\rho$$ everywhere, the speed depends only on the total angle $$\Delta\varphi$$ through which the direction of motion has turned: $$v = v_0\,e^{-\mu\,\Delta\varphi},$$ no matter what shape the curve has.

label: PW205
name: A Spinning Cylinder Wedged into a Corner — A uniform solid cylinder of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ is spun up…
desc: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ is spun up to angular speed $$\omega_0$$ about its axis and then gently placed into the corner between a rough vertical wall and a rough horizontal floor, with its axis horizontal and parallel to the wall. The coefficient…
statement:
A uniform solid cylinder of mass $$M$$ and radius $$R$$ is spun up to angular speed $$\omega_0$$ about its axis and then gently placed into the corner between a rough vertical wall and a rough horizontal floor, with its axis horizontal and parallel to the wall. The coefficient of kinetic friction at both contacts is $$\mu.$$ The spin direction is such that the cylinder's surface slides __downward__ against the wall. The cylinder stays in place, skidding against both surfaces, until friction brings it to rest. The moment of inertia of a uniform cylinder about its axis is $$I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2.$$ (MIT OpenCourseWare, 8.012 Classical Mechanics, Fall 2008.)

__(a)__ Draw the free-body diagram. The cylinder never translates, so the net force is zero — but be careful: the friction forces themselves enter the force balance, so the two normal forces are coupled to each other. Taking the wall friction to act upward and the floor friction to point toward the wall (check that these directions oppose the slipping of the surface!), find the normal forces $$N_{\rm floor}$$ and $$N_{\rm wall}.$$

__(b)__ Find the magnitude $$\alpha$$ of the cylinder's angular deceleration while it skids.

__(c)__ How long does the cylinder take to stop, and how many revolutions does it make before stopping?

__(d)__ Check the extreme cases $$\mu \to 0$$ and $$\mu \to \infty.$$ One of them is surprising: show that even __infinite__ friction stops the cylinder only after the finite time $$\dfrac{\omega_0 R}{2g},$$ and explain physically why an enormous $$\mu$$ does not produce enormous friction forces.

label: PW205
name: Holding a Heavy Weight with a Rope Around a Pole — A rope is wrapped through a total angle $$\theta_1$$…
desc: A rope is wrapped through a total angle $$\theta_1$$ around a fixed horizontal pole. The coefficient of static friction between the rope and the pole is $$\mu.$$ A weight of mass $$M$$ hangs from one end of the rope, and you hold the other end. In a classic lecture demonstration…
statement:
A rope is wrapped through a total angle $$\theta_1$$ around a fixed horizontal pole. The coefficient of static friction between the rope and the pole is $$\mu.$$ A weight of mass $$M$$ hangs from one end of the rope, and you hold the other end. In a classic lecture demonstration ("Rope Friction Around Pole," Harvard Natural Sciences lecture demonstrations), a couple of turns of rope around a post let a person support a very heavy hanging weight with a gentle pull. Your goal is to find the minimum holding force and see why the demonstration works.

Friction acts everywhere along the region of contact, so there is no single normal force and no single tension — both vary continuously along the rope. The standard technique for such __continuous systems__ is to analyze a small piece at an arbitrary location, find the differential equation it obeys, and integrate.

__(a)__ Consider a small piece of the rope (the rope's own weight is negligible compared with the tensions) subtending an angle $$\mathrm{d}\theta$$ at the pole's center, with tension $$T$$ on one side of the piece and $$T + \mathrm{d}T$$ on the other. Balance forces perpendicular to the rope, using $$\sin x \approx x$$ for small $$x$$ and discarding second-order products like $$\mathrm{d}T\,\mathrm{d}\theta,$$ to show that the normal force on the piece is $$\mathrm{d}N = T\,\mathrm{d}\theta.$$

__(b)__ Suppose the weight is on the verge of slipping downward, so the friction on every piece is at its maximum value $$\mu\,\mathrm{d}N,$$ directed so as to help your hand. Balance forces along the rope to get a differential equation relating $$\mathrm{d}T$$ and $$\mathrm{d}\theta,$$ then integrate it to find the minimum holding force $$F$$ in terms of $$Mg,$$ $$\mu,$$ and $$\theta_1.$$

__(c)__ Put in numbers for the demonstration: $$M = 50\;\mathrm{kg},$$ $$\mu = 0.4,$$ and you are willing to pull with only $$F = 10\;\mathrm{N}.$$ How many full turns of rope around the pole do you need? By what factor does each additional full turn multiply the weight you can hold?

__(d)__ The pole's radius appears nowhere in your answer. Explain physically why the wrap __angle__ matters but the radius does not.

label: PW205
name: A Washer Launched Sideways on an Inclined Plane — A small washer rests on a plane inclined at angle…
desc: A small washer rests on a plane inclined at angle $$\alpha$$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the washer and the plane is exactly $$\mu = \tan\alpha$$ — the critical value at which the washer could slide straight down the slope at constant velocity…
statement:
A small washer rests on a plane inclined at angle $$\alpha$$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the washer and the plane is exactly $$\mu = \tan\alpha$$ — the critical value at which the washer could slide straight down the slope at constant velocity. The washer is given an initial speed $$v_0$$ __horizontally__, that is, along the plane in the direction perpendicular to the slope's gradient. Find the washer's velocity after a very long time. (Irodov, __Problems in General Physics__, Problem 1.105.)

__(a)__ Work in the plane of the incline. Let the $$x$$-axis point straight down the slope, and let $$\varphi(t)$$ be the angle between the washer's velocity and the $$x$$-axis (so $$\varphi = 90^\circ$$ at launch). The component of gravity in the plane has magnitude $$g\sin\alpha,$$ pointing down-slope, and kinetic friction has magnitude $$\mu m g\cos\alpha,$$ directed opposite the velocity. Using $$\mu = \tan\alpha,$$ show that the speed $$v$$ and the down-slope velocity component $$v_x$$ obey $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = g\sin\alpha\,(\cos\varphi - 1)$$ and $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v_x}{\mathrm{d}t} = g\sin\alpha\,(1 - \cos\varphi),$$ and conclude that the combination $$v + v_x$$ is conserved.

__(b)__ Show that the washer can never come to rest — in fact, show its speed never drops below $$v_0/2$$ — and describe what the trajectory must do at late times.

__(c)__ Find the washer's velocity (magnitude and direction) as $$t \to \infty.$$

__(d)__ Sanity-check the conservation law on an easy case: a washer launched straight __down__ the slope at speed $$v_0.$$ What does the equation of motion predict, and is $$v + v_x$$ indeed constant?

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: The power $$P$$ dissipated in a resistance $$R$$ when there is a voltage $$V$$ applied…
desc: The power $$P$$ dissipated in a resistance $$R$$ when there is a voltage $$V$$ applied across it is given by $$P = \dfrac{V^2}{R} .$$ The resistance is \ and is known very precisely. The voltage is \ **a)** Find the value of $$P$$ and estimate its associated error $$\delta P$$…
statement:
The power $$P$$ dissipated in a resistance $$R$$ when there is a voltage $$V$$ applied across it is given by $$P = \dfrac{V^2}{R} .$$

The resistance is \ and is known very precisely. The voltage is \

**a)** Find the value of $$P$$ and estimate its associated error $$\delta P$$ using error propagation formulas.

**b)** Find the error in $$P$$ a second way. In this method, take the lowest estimated value of the voltage, $$10.4 \;\mathrm{V} - 0.4 \;\mathrm{V},$$ and use this voltage to estimate $$P.$$ Then repeat with the highest-estimated voltage. Use the range in $$P$$ obtained from these estimates to find the uncertainty in $$P.$$

How do your results from this method compare to those in part (a)?

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: Here are three short problems to use to practice error propagation.
desc: Here are three short problems to use to practice error propagation. **a)** A simple pendulum consists of a string of length $$\ell \pm \delta \ell$$ connected to a mass $$m \pm \delta m.$$ Estimate the accuracy to which local gravitational acceleration can be measured if the…
statement:
Here are three short problems to use to practice error propagation.

**a)** A simple pendulum consists of a string of length $$\ell \pm \delta \ell$$ connected to a mass $$m \pm \delta m.$$ Estimate the accuracy to which local gravitational acceleration can be measured if the period is known to very good accuracy.

Estimate the largest acceptable relative error in the period that will negligibly affect the results.

Estimate the maximum amplitude such that the formula for the small-amplitude period can be used while negligibly affecting the results. You may need to know $$\sin\theta \approx \theta - \dfrac{\theta^3}{6}.$$

Estimate the minimum mass of the string such that it needs to be accounted for in the calculations.

If the mass is a sphere connected to the string and $$\ell$$ the distance from the top of the string to the center of the sphere, estimate the minimum radius of the sphere such that it needs to be accounted for.

**b)**

In 1849, Fizeau devised the first accurate method for determining the speed of light.

Fizeau's experiment is illustrated below.

The experiment used a rotated wheel with square teeth. Light travelled from a gap between two adjacent teeth to a mirror $$8633 \;\mathrm{m}$$ away and was reflected back to the wheel.

Meanwhile, the adjacent tooth had replaced the gap and blocked out the returning beam.

Fizeau used a wheel with 720 teeth and a rotation rate of 12.6 revolutions per second. Determine the value of $$c$$ obtained.

If the rotation rate was accurate to $$4\%,$$ find the accuracy of his result.

**c)** Two students are asked to measure the rate of emission of alpha particles from a certain radioactive sample. Student A watches for 2 minutes and counts 32 particles. Student В watches for 1 hour and counts 786 particles. (The sample decays slowly enough that the expected rate of emission can be assumed to be constant during the measurements.) i. What is the uncertainty in Student A's result, 32, for the number of particles emitted in 2 minutes? ii. What is the uncertainty in Student B's result, 786, for the number of particles emitted in 1 hour? iii. Each student now divides their count by their number of minutes to find the rate of emission in particles per minute. Assuming the times, 2 min and 60 min, have negligible uncertainty, what are the two students' answers for the rate, with their uncertainties?

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: This problem has more practice with error propagation.
desc: This problem has more practice with error propagation. **a)** A block slides down an inclined plane with angle $$\theta.$$ The block slides a distance $$L,$$ starting from rest. The coefficient of friction between the block and plane is $$\mu < \tan\theta.$$ The time for the…
statement:
This problem has more practice with error propagation.

**a)** A block slides down an inclined plane with angle $$\theta.$$ The block slides a distance $$L,$$ starting from rest. The coefficient of friction between the block and plane is $$\mu < \tan\theta.$$ The time for the block to slide down the plane is $$T.$$

Measuring these values, an experimenter finds \begin{aligned} \theta & = 30 \pm 1^\circ \\ \mu & = .20 \pm 0.01 \\ T & = 1.1 \pm 0.1 \;\mathrm{s}\\ L & = 2.0 \pm 0.1 \;\mathrm{m} \\ \end{aligned}

Find uncertainty in local gravitational acceleration that can be deduced from the above information.

**b)** The normal average incidence of a certain kind of cancer has been established as 2 cases per 10,000 people per year. The suspicion has been aired that a certain town (population 20,000) suffers a high incidence of this cancer because of a nearby chemical dump. To test this claim, a reporter investigates the town's records for the past 4 years and finds 20 cases of the cancer. He calculates that the expected number and concludes that the observed rate is 25% more than expected. How did he arrive at this figure? Is he justified in claiming that this result proves that the town has a higher than normal rate for this cancer?

To answer this question, you may want to model occurrences of cancer in the same way we model other counting events.

**c)** If I have measured the radius of a sphere to be $$2.0 \pm 0.1 \;\mathrm{m},$$ what should I report for the sphere's volume? Repeat this question with your own made-up measurement of the volume, and find how the radius should be reported.

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: Here is some more practice with error propagation.
desc: Here is some more practice with error propagation. **a)** Suppose two independent measurements are made of some quantity, $$x.$$ The results are \begin{aligned} x_1 \pm \delta x_1 \\ x_2 \pm \delta x_2 \end{aligned} It is desired to get the best-possible estimate of $$x.$$ This…
statement:
Here is some more practice with error propagation.

**a)** Suppose two independent measurements are made of some quantity, $$x.$$ The results are \begin{aligned} x_1 \pm \delta x_1 \\ x_2 \pm \delta x_2 \end{aligned}

It is desired to get the best-possible estimate of $$x.$$ This will be done using a weighted average, $$x = \alpha x_1 + (1-\alpha) x_2.$$

Find the value of $$\alpha$$ that minimizes the uncertainty in $$x.$$

**b)** In his famous experiment with electrons, J.J. Thomson measured the "charge to mass ratio", $$r = e/m,$$ where $$e$$ is the electron's charge and $$m$$ its mass. A modern classroom version of this experiment finds the ratio $$r$$ by accelerating electrons through a voltage $$V$$ and then bending them in a magnetic field. The ratio $$r = e/m$$ is given by the formula $$r = \dfrac{125}{32 \mu_0^2 N^2} \dfrac{D^2 V}{d^2 I^2}.$$

In this equation, $$\mu_0$$ is the permeability constant of the vacuum (equal to $$4\pi \times 10^{-7} \;\mathrm{N/A^2}$$ exactly) and $$N$$ is the number of turns in the coil that produces the magnetic field. $$D$$ is the diameter of the field of coils. $$V$$ is the voltage that accelerates the electrons. $$d$$ is the diameter of the electrons' curved path. $$I$$ is the current in the field coils.

A student makes the following measurements: \begin{aligned} N & = 72 \\ D & = 661 \pm 2 \;\mathrm{mm} \\ V & = 45.0 \pm 0.2 \;\mathrm{V} \\ d & = 91.4 \pm 0.5 \;\mathrm{mm}\\ I & = 2.48 \pm 0.04 \;\mathrm{A} \end{aligned}

Find the student's answer for the charge to mass ratio of the electron, with its uncertainty. Assume all uncertainties are independent and random.

**c)** A student finds the refractive index n of a piece of glass by measuring the critical angle в for light passing from the glass into air as $$\theta = 41 \pm 1^\circ.$$ The relation between these is known to be $$n = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}.$$ Find the student's answer for $$n$$ and its uncertainty.

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: In radioactive decay, the number of isotopes present in a sample over time decreases…
desc: In radioactive decay, the number of isotopes present in a sample over time decreases exponentially: $$N(t) = N_0 (1/2)^{t/\tau}$$ where $$\tau$$ is the **half life** of the isotope. This formula is important in techniques such as radiocarbon dating, which allows scientists to…
statement:
In radioactive decay, the number of isotopes present in a sample over time decreases exponentially:
