$$N(t) = N_0 (1/2)^{t/\tau}$$ where $$\tau$$ is the **half life** of the isotope.

This formula is important in techniques such as radiocarbon dating, which allows scientists to determine the age of a sample by assuming what the original isotope concentration was, measuring the current isotope concentration, and using the known half-life to determine the sample's age.

The origin of the formula is that each atom, independently, has a small chance $$p$$ to decay in any given second.

**a)** Find $$\tau$$ in terms of $$p.$$

**b)** A sample of $$N$$ atoms of some isotope triggers decay events at some rate $$r$$ (with dimensions of inverse time) over a time short compared to the half life. What is the half life in terms of $$r$$ and $$N?$$

**c)** A nuclear physicist monitors the particles ejected by a radioactive sample for 2 hours. She counts the number of particles emitted in a 1-minute period and repeats the measurement at half-hour intervals, with the following results:

\begin{tabular}{cc} Time elapse (hours) & Number counted in 1 min \\ 0.0 & 214 \\ 0.5 & 134 \\ 1.0 & 101 \\ 1.5 & 61 \\ 2.0 & 54 \end{tabular}

Plot the data, including error bars. Find the half life and your uncertainty in it. The uncertainty in the elapsed time is zero. You may neglect the decay of the sample over the course of the 1-min collection intervals.

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: A hard steel ball, mass $$m,$$ falls vertically a distance $$h_1$$ onto the horizontal…
desc: A hard steel ball, mass $$m,$$ falls vertically a distance $$h_1$$ onto the horizontal surface of a soft steel anvil. It rebounds a distance $$h_2$$ after producing a small circular indentation of diameter $$d.$$ For small $$h_1,$$ theory predicts $$3mg h_2 = Pd^3$$ where $$P$$…
statement:
A hard steel ball, mass $$m,$$ falls vertically a distance $$h_1$$ onto the horizontal surface of a soft steel anvil. It rebounds a distance $$h_2$$ after producing a small circular indentation of diameter $$d.$$ For small $$h_1,$$ theory predicts $$3mg h_2 = Pd^3$$ where $$P$$ is a constant.

Experiments were performed with $$m = 4.00 \times 10^{-3} \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ The data obtained are given in Table 4.1. The accuracy of the measurements is correct to the last significant figure.

\begin{tabular}{ccc} $$h_1$$ (mm) & $$h_2$$ (mm) & $$d$$ (mm) \\ 1000 & 290 & 1.22 \\ 500 & 162 & 1.01 \\ 100 & 41 & 0.64 \\ 2.0 & 12.2 & {} 0.51 \end{tabular}

**a)** Graphically investigate the range of validity of the theory. State your conclusions.

**b)** What is the value and accuracy of $$P?$$

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: For a certain circuit element, the voltage $$U$$ and current $$I$$ are measured. The…
desc: For a certain circuit element, the voltage $$U$$ and current $$I$$ are measured. The results are shown below: \begin{tabular}{cc} U (volts) & I (amps) \\ 3.0 & 3.2 \\ 3.6 & 9.9 \\ 4.6 & 20.4 \\ 5.0 & 31.6 \\ 6.2 & 97 \\ 6.6 & 193 \end{tabular} It is conjectured that the voltage…
statement:
For a certain circuit element, the voltage $$U$$ and current $$I$$ are measured. The results are shown below:

\begin{tabular}{cc} U (volts) & I (amps) \\ 3.0 & 3.2 \\ 3.6 & 9.9 \\ 4.6 & 20.4 \\ 5.0 & 31.6 \\ 6.2 & 97 \\ 6.6 & 193 \end{tabular}

It is conjectured that the voltage and current obey the relation $$10^{U/ (1\;\mathrm{V})} = A \left(\dfrac{I}{1 \;\mathrm{A}}\right)^\alpha$$ for some constants $$A$$ and $$\alpha.$$

Determine $$A$$ and $$\alpha$$ and estimate their uncertainty.

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: In USAPhO and IPhO, there are two methods to find best fit lines, both of which are…
desc: In USAPhO and IPhO, there are two methods to find best fit lines, both of which are acceptable unless otherwise noted: 1) Simply draw the best-looking line you can through the data and estimating the slope by taking two points on that line. 2) Put the data into your calculator…
statement:
In USAPhO and IPhO, there are two methods to find best fit lines, both of which are acceptable unless otherwise noted:

1) Simply draw the best-looking line you can through the data and estimating the slope by taking two points on that line. 2) Put the data into your calculator and have it calculate the **least squares linear regression**.

The calculator finds the best fit line using a method called "least squares linear regression". In this problem, we'll see how this method works.

No line can go through all the data points. There will always be some vertical distance between the line and a given data point. These vertical distances are called "residuals". In least squares linear regression, we find the line such that the sum of the residuals is as small as possible.

A physical analogy is to think of the best fit line as a straight massless rod. The data points can be thought of as pegs to which we attach springs of zero rest length. Then the other side of the spring is attached to the rod. The springs are constrained to be vertical. The length of each spring is the residual. The rod is allowed to rotate and move up and down until it finds equilibrium.

**a)** Explain why the equilibrium position of the rod described above is the least-squares linear regression line.

**b)** Write down the equations for force and torque balance on the rod. You will need to expression your answer in terms of sums over the $$x$$ and $$y$$ values $$x_i$$ and $$y_i$$ of the $$i$$th data point.

**c)** Solve the equations from part (b) to find the slope and y-intercept of the rod. Express your answer in terms of $$\bar{x}$$ and $$\bar{y},$$ the average of these values, and $$\mathrm{var}(x) = \dfrac{1}{N}\left(\sum_i x_i^2 \right) - \bar{x}^2.$$ and $$\mathrm{cov}(x,y) = \dfrac{1}{N}\left(\sum_i x_iy_i \right) - \bar{x}\bar{y}.$$ where $$N$$ is the number of data points.

The first of these is the variance of $$x.$$ The second is the covariance of $$x$$ and $$y.$$ (Note that the variance of $$x$$ is the covariance of $$x$$ with itself.)

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: This problem examines the error in the slope and y-intercept of lines drawn through data…
desc: This problem examines the error in the slope and y-intercept of lines drawn through data points. **a)** One method for estimating the error in the slope of a line - generally accepted on the USAPhO and IPhO, is to draw the steepest-possible line that reasonably goes through the…
statement:
This problem examines the error in the slope and y-intercept of lines drawn through data points.

**a)** One method for estimating the error in the slope of a line - generally accepted on the USAPhO and IPhO, is to draw the steepest-possible line that reasonably goes through the your data and the shallowest-possible line (including error bars). The slope you report would be the slope half way between these two, and the error in the slope would be half the difference between these slopes.

Use this method to estimate the slope and error for the following data:

\begin{tabular}{cc} x & y \\ 1 & 3.92 \\ 2 & 5.68 \\ 3 & 9.12 \\ 4 & 11.33 \\ 5 & 13.76 \\ 6 & 16.05 \\ 7 & 19.05 \\ 8 & 22.16 \end{tabular}

**b)** Next, consider the formula for the slope using least-squares linear regression:

$$m = \dfrac{\sum x_iy_i - \dfrac{1}{N} \sum x_i \sum y_i}{\sum x_i^2 - \dfrac{1}{N} (\sum x_i)^2} .$$

Suppose that, for some regression, the $$x$$ values are known exactly. The $$y$$ values each have error $$\delta y.$$ What is the approximate error $$\delta m$$ in $$m$$ as a function of $$\bar{x}, \delta y, \sigma_x,$$ and $$N,$$ the number of data points? You do not need an exact approach (although a more precise formula can be looked up).

Recall $$\sigma_x^2 = \dfrac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i^2 - \bar{x}^2.$$

Use this method to estimate the slope and uncertainty in the slope using the data from part (a).

**c)** Consider the case where the number of data points collected is very large. Do you expect the results from (a) and (b) to agree? If not, which will be larger?

**d)** Give intuitive explanations for the following:

1) If all your data points are much larger than zero or much smaller than zero (compared to the range of data point), the $$y$$ intercept is very unreliable. 2) Increasing the range over which you take data points reduces the error in the slope, even if the number of data points stays the same.

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: This problem will introduce you to the Gaussian distribution. Contests often say to…
desc: This problem will introduce you to the Gaussian distribution. Contests often say to "assume Gaussian errors", which is not truly necessary for the error propagation formulas, but Gaussian distributions are very common in science. **a)** The Gaussian distribution is defined to be…
statement:
This problem will introduce you to the Gaussian distribution. Contests often say to "assume Gaussian errors", which is not truly necessary for the error propagation formulas, but Gaussian distributions are very common in science.

**a)** The Gaussian distribution is defined to be $$ p(x) = c \cdot \exp\left(\dfrac{-(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$

The meaning is that the probability for a measured value $$x$$ to be between $$x_1$$ and $$x_2$$ is $$P(x_1 < x < x_2) = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} p(x)\mathrm{d}x.$$

Find the constant $$c.$$ You may use the fact that $$\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}\mathrm{d}x = \sqrt{\pi}.$$

**b)** This part can be skipped, and simply shows one way to find the integral given at the end of part (a).

Consider the integral $$\iint_{x = -\infty, y=-\infty}^{x = \infty, y=\infty} e^{-x^2} e^{-y^2} \mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y.$$

Argue that this integral is the square of the one given at the end of part (a).

Evaluate the integral above by switching to polar coordinates, \begin{aligned} r^2 & = x^2 + y^2 \\ \tan\theta & = \frac{y}{x} \end{aligned}

You will need to make sure you integrate over the volume element in polar coordinates, which we discussed in the transcript of the class on friction.

From this, show \[\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}\mathrm{d}x = \sqrt{\pi}.\]

**c)** What is the mean of the Gaussian distribution?

The mean is defined by $$\langle x \rangle = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x p(x) \mathrm{d}x,$$ but you may be able to determine the mean without explicitly calculating the integral.

**d)** What is the standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution? This is defined by $$\sigma_x = \langle x^2 \rangle - \langle x \rangle^2.$$

And $$\langle x^2 \rangle = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^2 p(x) \mathrm{d}x.$$

To evaluate this, you may want to consider $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\alpha x^2}\mathrm{d}x.$$

**e)** Although some tricks can allow us to find the integral $$\int_{-\infty}^\infty p(x) \mathrm{d}x,$$ for other boundaries, the integral is evaluated numerically. The most-famous results are

\begin{aligned} \int_{-1}^1 e^{-x^2/2} \mathrm{d}x & \approx 0.683 \sqrt{2\pi}\\ \int_{-2}^2 e^{-x^2/2} \mathrm{d}x & \approx 0.955 \sqrt{2\pi}\\ \int_{-3}^3 e^{-x^2/2} \mathrm{d}x & \approx 0.997 \sqrt{2\pi} \end{aligned}

When sampling from a Gaussian distribution with mean $$\mu$$ and standard deviation $$\sigma,$$ what is the probability that the result will be between $$-\sigma$$ and $$2\sigma?$$

What is the probability that the result will be between $$\sigma$$ and $$3\sigma?$$

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: Uncertainty in a Measured Tangent — You measure an angle to be $$\theta = 72 \pm 1^\circ$$ and you need the…
desc: You measure an angle to be $$\theta = 72 \pm 1^\circ$$ and you need the quantity $$u = \tan\theta.$$ Your calculator gives $$\tan 71^\circ = 2.90,$$ $$\tan 72^\circ = 3.08,$$ and $$\tan 73^\circ = 3.27.$$ __(a)__ Without using any error-propagation formula, find the uncertainty…
statement:
You measure an angle to be $$\theta = 72 \pm 1^\circ$$ and you need the quantity $$u = \tan\theta.$$ Your calculator gives $$\tan 71^\circ = 2.90,$$ $$\tan 72^\circ = 3.08,$$ and $$\tan 73^\circ = 3.27.$$

__(a)__ Without using any error-propagation formula, find the uncertainty $$\delta u$$ in $$u.$$ (Hint: $$\tan\theta$$ is an increasing function of $$\theta,$$ so the largest plausible value of $$u$$ comes from the largest plausible value of $$\theta.$$) Report your result in the form $$u \pm \delta u.$$

__(b)__ Generalize the method: if a quantity $$x$$ is measured as $$x \pm \delta x$$ and you compute $$f(x),$$ write a formula for $$\delta f$$ that captures what you did in part (a).

__(c)__ Assuming $$\delta x$$ is small, apply the first-order Taylor approximation $$f(x + \delta x) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\,\delta x$$ to your formula from part (b) to derive the standard single-variable error-propagation rule. Then check it numerically against part (a), using $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\tan\theta = \sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta.$$ (Careful: the derivative rule needs $$\delta\theta$$ in radians.)

__(d)__ The figure below shows a wavy signal $$f(x).$$ You want to determine $$f$$ at some point, but your measurement of $$x$$ has uncertainty $$\delta x,$$ shown as the shaded vertical bands; the resulting range of $$f$$ values is the induced uncertainty $$\delta f.$$ At what kind of point on the curve should you measure if you want the error in $$f$$ caused by the error in $$x$$ to be almost zero? Explain using your formula from part (c).

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: Why Independent Uncertainties Add in Quadrature — You measure one length to be $$x = 5 \pm 1\;\mathrm{cm}$$…
desc: You measure one length to be $$x = 5 \pm 1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and another, independently measured, to be $$y = 3 \pm 1\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ ("Independent" means learning the value of one measurement tells you nothing about the error in the other.) For independent measurements…
statement:
You measure one length to be $$x = 5 \pm 1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and another, independently measured, to be $$y = 3 \pm 1\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ ("Independent" means learning the value of one measurement tells you nothing about the error in the other.) For independent measurements, uncertainties do not simply add; instead they __add in quadrature__: $$\delta(a+b) = \sqrt{(\delta a)^2 + (\delta b)^2}.$$

__(a)__ Should you report the sum as $$x + y = 8 \pm 2\;\mathrm{cm}?$$ Compute the correct uncertainty in $$x + y,$$ and give an intuitive reason why the uncertainty of a sum of independent measurements is always at least a little less than the sum of the uncertainties.

__(b)__ What is the uncertainty in the difference $$x - y?$$

__(c)__ The quadrature rule comes from the fact that reported uncertainties are __standard deviations__ (often written $$\sigma_x$$ instead of $$\delta x$$), whose squares are __variances__, $$\mathrm{var}(x) = \sigma_x^2.$$ For any two random variables, $$\mathrm{var}(x+y) = \mathrm{var}(x) + \mathrm{var}(y) + 2\,\mathrm{cov}(x,y),$$ where the __covariance__ $$\mathrm{cov}(x,y)$$ measures their joint variability; it is zero for independent variables, and $$\mathrm{cov}(x,x) = \mathrm{var}(x).$$ Use this to find the uncertainty $$\delta(2x)$$ in terms of $$\delta x.$$ Why does the quadrature rule __not__ apply to $$x + x?$$

__(d)__ Give an example of how two length measurements made in the same lab could fail to be independent.

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: Calipers and a Deck of Cards — A set of calipers can measure thicknesses of a few inches with an uncertainty…
desc: A set of calipers can measure thicknesses of a few inches with an uncertainty of $$\pm 0.005$$ inches. You measure the thickness of a full deck of 52 cards and get $$0.590\;\mathrm{in}.$$ (Adapted from Taylor, __Introduction to Error Analysis__.) __(a)__ What value do you…
statement:
A set of calipers can measure thicknesses of a few inches with an uncertainty of $$\pm 0.005$$ inches. You measure the thickness of a full deck of 52 cards and get $$0.590\;\mathrm{in}.$$ (Adapted from Taylor, __Introduction to Error Analysis__.)

__(a)__ What value do you calculate for the thickness of a single card?

__(b)__ What is the uncertainty in that single-card thickness? Note that the deck thickness is $$52t$$ where $$t$$ is one card's thickness, and the uncertainty in a scaled quantity obeys $$\delta(ct) = c\,\delta t$$ — this is __one__ measurement divided by 52, not 52 independent measurements, so no quadrature is involved. Write your final result with a reasonable number of significant figures.

__(c)__ You want to know the thickness of one card with an uncertainty of only $$0.00002\;\mathrm{in},$$ still using the same calipers. How many decks should you stack together and measure at once?

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: The Uncertainty of an Average — In some part of the world, the heights of six-year-old children average…
desc: In some part of the world, the heights of six-year-old children average $$45.0$$ inches with a standard deviation of $$3$$ inches. You measure the heights $$x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N$$ of $$N = 100$$ randomly selected six-year-olds and compute the sample average $$\bar{x} =…
statement:
In some part of the world, the heights of six-year-old children average $$45.0$$ inches with a standard deviation of $$3$$ inches. You measure the heights $$x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N$$ of $$N = 100$$ randomly selected six-year-olds and compute the sample average $$\bar{x} = \dfrac{1}{N}\sum_i x_i.$$ Treat each individual height as a measurement with uncertainty $$\delta x = 3\;\mathrm{in},$$ and recall that independent uncertainties add in quadrature: $$\delta(a+b) = \sqrt{(\delta a)^2 + (\delta b)^2}.$$

__(a)__ For a single six-year-old, a height of $$47.5$$ inches is unremarkable — less than one standard deviation above average. Is it likely that your __average__ of 100 children comes out as high as $$47.5$$ inches? Explain without calculating.

__(b)__ Warm up with three children: use quadrature to find the uncertainty in the sum $$x_1 + x_2 + x_3.$$ Then generalize to the uncertainty in the sum of $$N$$ heights.

__(c)__ Combine your result from (b) with the scaling rule $$\delta(cx) = c\,\delta x$$ to derive a formula for $$\delta\bar{x},$$ the uncertainty in the average of $$N$$ measurements that each have uncertainty $$\delta x.$$

__(d)__ Evaluate $$\delta\bar{x}$$ for your sample of 100 children. If you wanted to cut that uncertainty in half, how many children would you need to measure?

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: Counting Alpha Particles — When you count $$N$$ occurrences of a random, independent event in a fixed time…
desc: When you count $$N$$ occurrences of a random, independent event in a fixed time interval — such as decays of a radioactive sample — the statistical uncertainty in the count is $$\sqrt{N}.$$ That is, if you watch a sample for one hour and count $$N$$ decays, your estimate for the…
statement:
When you count $$N$$ occurrences of a random, independent event in a fixed time interval — such as decays of a radioactive sample — the statistical uncertainty in the count is $$\sqrt{N}.$$ That is, if you watch a sample for one hour and count $$N$$ decays, your estimate for the number of decays per hour is $$N \pm \sqrt{N}.$$ (The same rule applies to other random counts, like the number of collisions a gas molecule undergoes in a second.)

To measure the activity of a radioactive sample, two students count the alpha particles it emits. Student A watches for 3 minutes and counts 28 particles. Student B watches for 30 minutes and counts 310 particles. (Adapted from Taylor, __Introduction to Error Analysis__.)

__(a)__ Find each student's measured emission rate in particles per minute, with its uncertainty. (Careful with a common mistake: first attach the $$\sqrt{N}$$ uncertainty to the raw __count__, then divide both the count and its uncertainty by the observation time — the time does not go inside the square root.)

__(b)__ The two rates differ. Do the two measurements contradict one another?

__(c)__ Compute the __relative uncertainty__ (uncertainty divided by value) of each student's rate, and the ratio between the two relative uncertainties. Where does that ratio come from, and what does it say about how the precision of a counting measurement improves with observation time?

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: Power Delivered to a Resistor — A student studying a resistor measures the current through it and the voltage…
desc: A student studying a resistor measures the current through it and the voltage across it as $$I = 2.10 \pm 0.02\;\mathrm{A}$$ and $$V = 1.02 \pm 0.01\;\mathrm{V},$$ independently. They want the power $$P = IV$$ with its uncertainty. You already know two error rules: for a…
statement:
A student studying a resistor measures the current through it and the voltage across it as $$I = 2.10 \pm 0.02\;\mathrm{A}$$ and $$V = 1.02 \pm 0.01\;\mathrm{V},$$ independently. They want the power $$P = IV$$ with its uncertainty. You already know two error rules: for a function of a single variable, $$\delta f = f'(x)\,\delta x,$$ and for a sum of independent quantities, $$\delta(a+b) = \sqrt{(\delta a)^2 + (\delta b)^2}.$$ This problem builds the rule for __products__ from those two.

__(a)__ Find a function that converts the product into a sum, turning $$P = IV$$ into an equation those two rules can handle. There is a subtlety: it is not meaningful to apply your function directly to a dimensional quantity, as the expansion $$\ln(1+x) = x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} + \dfrac{x^3}{3} - \ldots$$ shows (if $$x$$ carried dimensions, the terms would all have different dimensions). Fix this by introducing arbitrary reference values $$I_0,$$ $$V_0,$$ and $$P_0 = I_0 V_0.$$

__(b)__ Show that if $$x$$ has uncertainty $$\delta x,$$ then $$\ln(x/x_0)$$ has uncertainty $$\dfrac{\delta x}{x}$$ — the __relative error__ of $$x$$ — independent of the reference value $$x_0.$$

__(c)__ Combine parts (a) and (b) with quadrature to derive the product rule for error propagation, expressing $$\dfrac{\delta P}{P}$$ in terms of $$\dfrac{\delta I}{I}$$ and $$\dfrac{\delta V}{V}.$$

__(d)__ Plug in the numbers and report $$P$$ with its uncertainty.

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: The Angle of a Frictionless Incline — A block, released from rest, slides down a frictionless plane of length…
desc: A block, released from rest, slides down a frictionless plane of length $$L \pm \delta L.$$ Local gravitational acceleration is $$g \pm \delta g.$$ The time for the block to slide the full length of the plane is measured to be $$t \pm \delta t.$$ Find the slope angle $$\theta$$…
statement:
A block, released from rest, slides down a frictionless plane of length $$L \pm \delta L.$$ Local gravitational acceleration is $$g \pm \delta g.$$ The time for the block to slide the full length of the plane is measured to be $$t \pm \delta t.$$ Find the slope angle $$\theta$$ of the plane and the uncertainty $$\delta\theta$$ in your result. Useful rules: $$\delta f = f'(x)\,\delta x$$ for a function of one variable; for products and quotients of independent quantities, relative errors add in quadrature; and for a power, $$\dfrac{\delta(x^n)}{x^n} = n\dfrac{\delta x}{x}.$$

__(a)__ Using the block's acceleration along the incline, derive a formula for $$\sin\theta$$ in terms of $$L,$$ $$g,$$ and $$t.$$

__(b)__ One route to $$\delta\theta$$ is to write $$\theta = \arcsin\!\left(\dfrac{2L}{gt^2}\right)$$ and differentiate, using $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\arcsin(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}.$$ Explain why this route is messy, and instead introduce the intermediate variable $$u = \sin\theta.$$ Write the relative error $$\dfrac{\delta u}{u}$$ in terms of the relative errors of $$L,$$ $$g,$$ and $$t.$$

__(c)__ Relate $$\delta u$$ to $$\delta\theta$$ using the single-variable rule, and combine with part (b) to obtain a closed formula for $$\delta\theta.$$

__(d)__ Now evaluate with $$L = 3.0 \pm 0.1\;\mathrm{m},$$ $$g = 9.8 \pm 0.03\;\mathrm{m/s^2},$$ and $$t = 1.0 \pm 0.01\;\mathrm{s}.$$ (To get $$\tan\theta$$ from $$\sin\theta,$$ it helps to draw a right triangle with hypotenuse 1 and use the Pythagorean theorem.) Express $$\delta\theta$$ in degrees — and be careful: the propagation formula naturally produces radians.

__(e)__ Compare the three relative uncertainties in part (d). Which one dominates? Show that keeping only the dominant one gives nearly the same $$\delta\theta$$ with much less work.

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: Drawing a Competition-Grade Plot — In experimental physics olympiad problems (USAPhO and IPhO), you draw…
desc: In experimental physics olympiad problems (USAPhO and IPhO), you draw graphs by hand on graph paper, and the graders use a rubric — the US IPhO team routinely loses points for plots that break the rules. Below is an official plot from the IPhO 2019 solutions to use as a model…
statement:
In experimental physics olympiad problems (USAPhO and IPhO), you draw graphs by hand on graph paper, and the graders use a rubric — the US IPhO team routinely loses points for plots that break the rules. Below is an official plot from the IPhO 2019 solutions to use as a model.

You have collected the data below: a length-like variable $$x$$ (in $$\mathrm{cm}$$) versus an energy $$y$$ (in $$\mathrm{J}$$), with uncertainties for each point. The $$x$$ values run from $$12.4\;\mathrm{cm}$$ to $$64.3\;\mathrm{cm}$$ with the same uncertainty $$\delta x$$ for every point; the $$y$$ values run from $$0.43\;\mathrm{J}$$ to $$2.13\;\mathrm{J},$$ and each $$\delta y$$ is approximately $$0.1\,y$$ — the __relative__ uncertainty in $$y$$ is the same for every point even though the absolute uncertainties differ.

__(a)__ List the features a competition-grade plot must (and need not) have. In particular: does it need a title? What must the axis labels include? How much of the graph paper should the data occupy? What besides the data points should appear?

__(b)__ Your graph paper has 28 squares vertically and 38 squares horizontally. Choose a good value per square for each axis. (A procedure: count the squares, find the range of the data, divide range by squares, then round __up__ to a convenient number; start labeling slightly below the bottom of the range.)

__(c)__ You draw a best-fit line through the data by eye, and it appears to pass nearly through the origin. What are the units of the slope? Estimate the slope quickly from a single data point — and explain why the __last__ data point is a better choice for this than the first, given that all points have the same absolute uncertainties.

__(d)__ When you add the error bars, the best-fit line passes comfortably through every single error bar. Is this reassuring, or a warning sign? Explain.

__(e)__ Describe the standard by-hand method for estimating the __uncertainty in the slope__ of a best-fit line, illustrated below.

lesson: PW206: Approximation Tools and Error Analysis
label: PW206
name: Linearizing Data and Log-Log Plots — Best-fit lines are easy to draw and read, but much of physics is not…
desc: Best-fit lines are easy to draw and read, but much of physics is not linear. __Linearizing__ data — plotting transformed variables so that the expected relationship becomes a straight line — is the main competition technique for extracting constants from nonlinear data. __(a)__…
statement:
Best-fit lines are easy to draw and read, but much of physics is not linear. __Linearizing__ data — plotting transformed variables so that the expected relationship becomes a straight line — is the main competition technique for extracting constants from nonlinear data.

__(a)__ You roll a ball from rest down an inclined plane and record its position $$x$$ at various times $$t$$ (each $$t$$ has uncertainty $$\delta t$$). Theory predicts $$x = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2.$$ Why is plotting $$x$$ versus $$t$$ and drawing a best-fit line useless here? What should you plot instead so the data forms a straight line, and what is the slope of that line in terms of $$a?$$

__(b)__ Plotting your transformed variable requires error bars for it. Find the uncertainty $$\delta(t^2)$$ in terms of $$t$$ and $$\delta t,$$ using the rule $$\delta f = f'(t)\,\delta t.$$

__(c)__ The plot below shows position data (in $$\mathrm{cm}$$) plotted against $$t^2$$ (in $$\mathrm{s^2}$$), with a best-fit line of slope about $$1\;\mathrm{cm/s^2}.$$ What is the acceleration $$a?$$ Name one alternative pair of variables you could have plotted instead to linearize the same law, and give the slope it would produce.

__(d)__ You collect the orbital period $$T$$ and semi-major axis $$a$$ for the planets of the solar system. The physics of orbits gives $$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3,$$ where $$G$$ is Newton's constant and $$M$$ the Sun's mass. What could you plot to get a straight line, and what physical quantity does the slope determine?

__(e)__ Now suppose you expect a __power law__ $$y = c\,x^a$$ but you do __not__ know the exponent $$a.$$ Trying exponents one at a time ($$y$$ vs $$x^2,$$ $$y$$ vs $$\sqrt{x},$$ ...) until something looks straight would take forever. Find a transformation of the data that turns the unknown __exponent__ into a __coefficient__, say what you would plot, and explain how to read both $$a$$ and $$c$$ off the resulting line.

__(f)__ You measure the moment of inertia $$I$$ of a series of solid spheres, all of the same density $$\rho$$ but varying radius $$r,$$ and plot $$\ln I$$ versus $$\ln r.$$ Using $$I = \dfrac{2}{5}Mr^2$$ for a solid sphere, what slope do you expect? What is awkward about interpreting the intercept, and how do people handle it in practice? (Recall that $$\ln(1+x) = x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} + \dfrac{x^3}{3} - \ldots$$ only makes sense for dimensionless $$x.$$)

label: PW207
name: A horizontal tube has a narrow central section of radius $$r$$ surrounded by two wider…
desc: A horizontal tube has a narrow central section of radius $$r$$ surrounded by two wider sections each of radius $$R.$$ Three small vertical tubes extend from the top of the horizontal tube, one in each section. Fluid moves from left to right through the tube. Qualitatively…
statement: A horizontal tube has a narrow central section of radius $$r$$ surrounded by two wider sections each of radius $$R.$$ Three small vertical tubes extend from the top of the horizontal tube, one in each section. Fluid moves from left to right through the tube. Qualitatively describe the height that fluid will rise in each of the small vertical tubes assuming no frictional losses in the flow, then again assuming there are frictional losses.

label: PW207
name: A bucket has a small hole in the bottom. When full, the bucket drains in 2 minutes.
desc: A bucket has a small hole in the bottom. When full, the bucket drains in 2 minutes. You have a faucet. With the hole plugged, the faucet fills the bucket in 1 minute. With the hole open, how long does it take the faucet to fill the bucket?
statement:
A bucket has a small hole in the bottom. When full, the bucket drains in 2 minutes.

You have a faucet. With the hole plugged, the faucet fills the bucket in 1 minute.

With the hole open, how long does it take the faucet to fill the bucket?

label: PW207
name: A tank with straight sides and mass $$M$$ is filled with water and sits on a frictionless…
desc: A tank with straight sides and mass $$M$$ is filled with water and sits on a frictionless surface. The total mass of the water is $$m$$. A small hole is placed in the bottom of the side of the tank, so that water shoots horizontally out of the hole. Find the fraction of water…
statement: A tank with straight sides and mass $$M$$ is filled with water and sits on a frictionless surface. The total mass of the water is $$m$$. A small hole is placed in the bottom of the side of the tank, so that water shoots horizontally out of the hole. Find the fraction of water that has drained when the tank's acceleration is maximum. You may assume the acceleration is small compared to $$g.$$

label: PW207
name: Suppose a soap bubble has radius $$R$$ and surface tension $$\sigma.$$ A small tube of…
desc: Suppose a soap bubble has radius $$R$$ and surface tension $$\sigma.$$ A small tube of radius $$r \ll R$$ is inserted into the soap bubble without breaking it, so that air begins rushing out of the soap bubble through the tube. The tube has negligible volume compared to the…
statement:
Suppose a soap bubble has radius $$R$$ and surface tension $$\sigma.$$ A small tube of radius $$r \ll R$$ is inserted into the soap bubble without breaking it, so that air begins rushing out of the soap bubble through the tube. The tube has negligible volume compared to the bubble. Find the radius of the bubble as a function of time. You may think of the air as an ideal incompressible fluid of density $$\rho.$$

Note: a soap bubble with surface area $$A$$ and surface tension $$\sigma$$ has an energy $$\sigma A$$ associated with the surface. You may use this fact to determine the pressure in the bubble.

label: PW207
name: A funnel is constructed to have a vertical symmetry axis with a radius $$r$$ that varies…
desc: A funnel is constructed to have a vertical symmetry axis with a radius $$r$$ that varies with height $$h$$ above the bottom of the funnel. At the bottom of the funnel is a short, straight tube of radius $$r_0$$ and length $$\ell.$$ ($$h$$ is measured from the top of the tube as…
statement:
A funnel is constructed to have a vertical symmetry axis with a radius $$r$$ that varies with height $$h$$ above the bottom of the funnel.

At the bottom of the funnel is a short, straight tube of radius $$r_0$$ and length $$\ell.$$ ($$h$$ is measured from the top of the tube as shown.)

$$r(h)$$ is chosen so that the level of water in the funnel decreases at a constant rate until the water level reaches $$h=0.$$ Find $$r(h).$$

label: PW207
name: A submarine of unknown nationality is travelling near the bottom of the Baltic sea at a…
desc: A submarine of unknown nationality is travelling near the bottom of the Baltic sea at a depth of $$h = 300 \;\mathrm{m}.$$ Its interior is one big room of volume $$V = 10 \;\mathrm{m}^3$$ filled with air ($$m = 29\;\mathrm{g/mol})$$ at pressure $$P = 10^5 \;\mathrm{Pa}$$ and…
statement:
A submarine of unknown nationality is travelling near the bottom of the Baltic sea at a depth of $$h = 300 \;\mathrm{m}.$$ Its interior is one big room of volume $$V = 10 \;\mathrm{m}^3$$ filled with air ($$m = 29\;\mathrm{g/mol})$$ at pressure $$P = 10^5 \;\mathrm{Pa}$$ and temperature $$T = 20^\circ C.$$

Suddenly, the submarine hits a rock and a large hole of area $$A = 20 \;\mathrm{cm}^2$$ is formed at the bottom of the submarine. As a result, the submarine sinks to the bottom and most of it is filled fast with water, leaving a bubble of air at increased pressure (no air escapes the submarine).

The density of water is $$\rho = 10^3 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}$$ and free fall acceleration is $$g = 10 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ The molar heat capacity of air as constant volume is $$c_V = \dfrac52 R,$$ where $$R = 8.31 \;\mathrm{J/(K \cdot mol)}$$ is the gas constant.

**a)** What is the volume rate ($$\mathrm{m^3/s})$$ at which the water flows into the submarine immediately after the formation of the hole?

**b)** The flow rate is so large that the submarine is filled with water so fast that the heat exchange between the gas and the water can be neglected (this also applies to the next question). What is the volume of the air bubble once water flow has stopped?

**c)** The water stream rushing into the submarine creates turbulent water inside the submarine; what is the total kinetic energy of this water turbulence (which later ends up being dissipated as heat), once the inflow has stopped due to equalized pressures?

label: PW207
name: In this problem, we'll study the shape of a vortex of the type you might see when…
desc: In this problem, we'll study the shape of a vortex of the type you might see when draining water from a bathtub. **a)** Choose the center of the vortex as the $$z$$ axis. Suppose that water a distance $$r$$ from the $$z$$ axis rotates in a circle as angular frequency…
statement:
In this problem, we'll study the shape of a vortex of the type you might see when draining water from a bathtub.

**a)** Choose the center of the vortex as the $$z$$ axis. Suppose that water a distance $$r$$ from the $$z$$ axis rotates in a circle as angular frequency $$\omega(r).$$ Find the centripetal force per unit volume of water as a function of $$\omega$$ and $$r.$$

**b)** Find $$\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial r},$$ the gradient in the pressure of the water.

**c)** One often assumes that the water has constant angular momentum per unit volume $$\ell.$$ Using this assumption, find the height of the water as a function of $$r.$$ This is the vortex shape. By "the height of the water", we mean the level of the surface of the water, relative to the level far away from the vortex.

The last part of this problem may help prepare you for some of the mathematics involved in Maxwell's equations, which we'll study next.

**d)** Read the definition of the (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulation_(fluid_dynamics)).

Show that the circulation of the flow in a vortex is zero for a path that does not include the center of the vortex, and is equal to some constant for any path that does encircle the center. Another way to say this is that the **vorticity** is zero everywhere but the center, where it is a "delta function" (infinitely-high peak with finite area).

It's a strange fact that vortices have no vorticity! In fact, for an ideal fluid, this is always true - the circulation of any path is zero. This is called **Kelvin's Theorem**.

label: PW207
name: In this problem you will analyze two simplified models of blood flow in vessels.
desc: In this problem you will analyze two simplified models of blood flow in vessels. Blood vessels are approximately cylindrical in shape, and it is known that for a steady, non turbulent flow of an incompressible fluid in a rigid cylinder, the difference in pressure of the fluid at…
statement:
In this problem you will analyze two simplified models of blood flow in vessels.

Blood vessels are approximately cylindrical in shape, and it is known that for a steady, non turbulent flow of an incompressible fluid in a rigid cylinder, the difference in pressure of the fluid at the two ends of the cylinder is given by $$ \Delta P = \dfrac{8\ell \eta}{\pi r^4}Q,$$ where \begin{aligned} \ell & = \text{length of cylinder} \\ r & = \text{radius of cylinder} \\ \eta & = \text{viscosity of fluid} \\ Q & = \text{volumetric flow rate, i.e. volume that passes the cylinder cross section per unit time} \end{aligned}

This expression is often able to provide the correct order of magnitude for the pressure difference in a vessel, even without taking into account the pulsatile flow, the vessel's compressibility and irregular shape, and the fact that blood is not a simple fluid but a mixture of cells and plasma. Also, this expression has the same form as Ohm's law, with the volumetric flow rate being interpreted as a current, the difference in pressure as a voltage, and the factor $$R = \dfrac{8\ell \eta}{\pi r^4}$$ as a resistance.

Consider the symmetrical network of arterioles (small arteries), depicted in the figure below. This network delivers blood to the capillary bed of a tissue. In this network, at each bifurcation a vessel is divided in two. We will call this moving to a higher level of the network.

The vessels of higher levels are thinner and shorter than those of lower levels. Assume that the radii and lengths of vessels in two consecutive levels, $$i$$ and $$i+1,$$ are related by $$r_{i+1} = \dfrac{r_i}{2^{1/3}}.$$ and by $$\ell_{i+1} = \dfrac{\ell_i}{2^{1/3}}.$$

**a)** Obtain an expression for the volumetric flow rate, $$Q_i,$$ in a vessel at any level $$i$$ as a function of the total number of levels $$N,$$ the viscosity $$\eta,$$ the radius $$r_0$$ and length $$\ell_0$$ of the first vessel, and the difference $$\Delta P = P_0 - P_{\mathrm{cap}}$$ between the pressure at the arteriole at level 0, $$P_0,$$ and the pressure at the capillary bed, $$P_{\mathrm{cap}}.$$

**b)** Calculate the numerical value of the volumetric flow rate $$Q_0$$ of the arteriole at level 0, if its radius is $$6.0 \times 10^{-5} \;\mathrm{m}$$ and its length is $$2.0 \times 10^{-3} \;\mathrm{m}.$$ Assume that the pressure at the arteriole inlet is $$7.3 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{Pa}$$ and the vessel network has $$N = 6$$ levels linking this arteriole to the capillary bed at the pressure $$4.0 \times 10^3 \;\mathrm{Pa}.$$ Assume that the blood viscosity is $$\eta = 3.5 \times 10^{-3} \;\mathrm{kg m^{-1} s^{-1}}.$$ Express your result in $$\mathrm{ml/h}.$$

label: PW207
name: This problem extends the previous one, making an analogy between fluid flow and an LRC…
desc: This problem extends the previous one, making an analogy between fluid flow and an LRC circuit. We'll study RLC circuits in class 10. You may want to work this problem now as a preview of that material, or wait and return to this material in several weeks. **A blood vessel as an…
statement:
This problem extends the previous one, making an analogy between fluid flow and an LRC circuit. We'll study RLC circuits in class 10. You may want to work this problem now as a preview of that material, or wait and return to this material in several weeks.

**A blood vessel as an RLC circuit**

The approximation of rigid cylindrical vessels falls short for several reasons. It is particularly important to include the time dependent flow and to take into account the change in vessel diameter that occurs when the pressure varies during a blood pumping cycle done by the heart. Also, it is observed that in the larger vessels the blood pressure varies significantly during a cycle, while in the smaller vessels the amplitude of the oscillations in pressure is much smaller, and the flow is almost time independent.

When the pressure increases in a single elastic vessel, there will be an increase in its diameter, thus permitting it to store more fluid in the vessel, and to deliver it when the pressure drops. For this reason, the elastic behaviour of the vessel can be simulated by adding a capacitor to our initial description. Moreover, when taking into account the time dependent blood flow rate, one has to consider the inertia of the fluid, proportional to its density $$\rho = 1.05\times 10^3 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ This inertia can be described by an inductance in our model. In the figure below we represent the equivalent circuit for a single vessel in this model. The equivalent capacitance and inductance are given by $$C = \dfrac{3\ell \pi r^3}{2Eh}.$$ $$L = \dfrac{9\ell \rho}{4\pi r^2}$$ respectively, where $$h$$ is the width of the vessel wall and $$E$$ is the artery Young's modulus, a coefficient that describes the alteration in size of the vessel tissue when a force is applied. The Young's modulus has units of pressure and is on the order of $$E = 0.06\;\mathrm{MPa}$$ for arterioles.

**c)** Obtain, in the stationary regime, the pressure amplitude at the vessel outlet, $$P_{\mathrm{out}},$$ as a function of the pressure amplitude at the inlet, $$P_{\mathrm{in}},$$ the equivalent resistance, $$R,$$ inductance, $$L,$$ and capacitance $$C$$ for a flow with angular frequency $$\omega.$$ Establish the condition between $$\eta, \rho, E, h, r,$$ and $$\ell$$ so that, for low frequencies, the pressure oscillation amplitude at the outlet is smaller than that of $$P_{\mathrm{in}}.$$

**d)** For the vessel network in part (b) of the previous problem, estimate the maximum arteriole wall thickness $$h$$ so that the condition established in (c) is satisfied. (Assume that $$h$$ is the same at all levels.)

label: PW207
name: This problem is an experiment in collaboration. It's got a lot of different pieces that…
desc: This problem is an experiment in collaboration. It's got a lot of different pieces that need to be put together to solve it. That makes it the sort of problem that a group of people, working together and trading ideas, can solve. So for this problem, feel free to post on the…
statement:
This problem is an experiment in collaboration. It's got a lot of different pieces that need to be put together to solve it. That makes it the sort of problem that a group of people, working together and trading ideas, can solve. So for this problem, feel free to post on the message board, without hiding your text, any little ideas you have. Check out the existing thread and reply to your classmates. Over time, we may collaborate our way to a solution.

This problem involves electric polarizability, which we will cover in future weeks, in addition to fluid dynamics. The relevant definition is given in the problem. You may wish to work the prior problem about a vortex first first, and recall its discussion of Kelvin's theorem, and to review the continuity equation and its relation to Gauss' law. This problem should help make the analogy between fluid flow and electromagnetism.

-------

When a body moves in liquid, the motion of the body puts the liquid into motion, too. The motion of liquid contributes to the total kinetic energy of the system, and hence, leads to an increased __effective mass__ of the body. The difference of the effective mass and the actual mass of the body is referred to as the added mass. The added mass depends on the size and shape of the body.

Consider a certain metallic body of volume $$V$$ and polarizability $$\alpha$$ along its symmetry axis $$x$$ (i.e. homogeneous externally applied electric field $$\vec{E}$$ induces total dipole moment $$\vec{p} = \alpha \vec{E}$$ on this body). Additionally, the body shape is such that if it were made from a homogeneous dielectric material and put into homogeneous electric field, the electric field inside the body would be also homogeneous. Find the added mass of this body when it starts moving translationally, parallel to the x-axis, in an incompressible initially motionless liquid of density ρ. The viscosity of the liquid is negligibly small. Express the answer in terms of $$V, \rho, \alpha,$$ and physical constants.

label: PW207
name: The Baltic Sprinkler — A sprinkler has the shape of a hemisphere of radius $$R$$ sitting on level ground with…
desc: A sprinkler has the shape of a hemisphere of radius $$R$$ sitting on level ground with its axis vertical. Small holes are drilled all over the spherical part of its surface, and water shoots out of every hole with the same speed $$v = 10\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ distributed evenly over…
statement:
A sprinkler has the shape of a hemisphere of radius $$R$$ sitting on level ground with its axis vertical. Small holes are drilled all over the spherical part of its surface, and water shoots out of every hole with the same speed $$v = 10\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ distributed evenly over all directions of the upper half-space. Assume $$R$$ is so much smaller than the range of the spray that it can be neglected, assume the water streams follow projectile parabolas without colliding or interfering, and take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$ (Estonian-Finnish Physics Olympiad, 2005.)

__(a)__ Find the distance $$r$$ from the sprinkler at which a stream launched at angle $$\theta$$ above the horizontal lands, the launch angle that maximizes $$r,$$ and the surface area of ground watered by the sprinkler.

__(b)__ Define the __watering intensity__ $$I$$ as the volume of water striking the ground per unit area per unit time. Find the dimensions of $$I,$$ and give a physical interpretation of a quantity with those dimensions.

__(c)__ At what distance from the sprinkler is the watering intensity highest? Two hints. First, sketch the landing distance $$r$$ as a function of $$\theta$$ and think about the water that lands between circles ("rings") of radius $$r$$ and $$r + \mathrm{d}r.$$ Second, the sprinkler emits equal amounts of water per unit area of the hemisphere's surface, so the water emitted between launch angles $$\theta$$ and $$\theta + \mathrm{d}\theta$$ is proportional to $$\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta;$$ spreading it over a ring of circumference proportional to $$r$$ gives $$I \propto \dfrac{\cos\theta}{r}\left|\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}r}\right|.$$

__(d)__ The factor $$\dfrac{\cos\theta}{r}$$ appears to blow up as $$r \to 0.$$ Why is the watering intensity not actually infinite right next to the sprinkler?

label: PW207
name: Net Force on a Curly Straw — The curly straws pictured below all have the same cross-sectional area $$A.$$…
desc: The curly straws pictured below all have the same cross-sectional area $$A.$$ You drink the same fluid, of density $$\rho,$$ through each one, always at the same rate, so the fluid moves through every straw at the same speed $$v.$$ __(a)__ For which straw is the net force from…
statement:
The curly straws pictured below all have the same cross-sectional area $$A.$$ You drink the same fluid, of density $$\rho,$$ through each one, always at the same rate, so the fluid moves through every straw at the same speed $$v.$$

__(a)__ For which straw is the net force from the fluid on the straw the greatest? A useful principle: in steady flow, the net force on the fluid inside the straw equals the rate of change of the fluid's momentum, $$F_{\mathrm{net}} = \dot{p},$$ and this depends only on the momentum flowing in at one end and out at the other — whatever loop-de-loops happen in between.

__(b)__ Suppose the direction the fluid exits a straw makes an angle $$\theta$$ with the direction it enters. Find the magnitude of the net force between the fluid and the straw in terms of $$A,$$ $$v,$$ $$\rho,$$ and $$\theta.$$

label: PW207
name: The Best Height for a Hole in a Bottle — __(a)__ Which drains faster out of a funnel: water or mercury?…
desc: __(a)__ Which drains faster out of a funnel: water or mercury? (Mercury is about $$13.6$$ times denser than water; ignore friction.) Justify your answer, and state what feature an equation for the draining time must have in order to confirm your conclusion. __(b)__ A bottle with…
statement:
__(a)__ Which drains faster out of a funnel: water or mercury? (Mercury is about $$13.6$$ times denser than water; ignore friction.) Justify your answer, and state what feature an equation for the draining time must have in order to confirm your conclusion.

__(b)__ A bottle with vertical sides is full of water and open to the air; the surface of the water is a height $$H$$ above the level ground the bottle sits on. You punch a small hole in the side of the bottle at a height $$h$$ above the ground, and water shoots out horizontally. The photograph below shows such a stream (a laser beam is trapped inside the stream by total internal reflection, lighting it up). The water inside the bottle moves negligibly slowly, so the pressure just inside the hole is the static pressure $$P = P_0 + \rho g(H-h),$$ where $$P_0$$ is atmospheric pressure and $$\rho$$ is the density of water; just outside the hole the pressure is $$P_0.$$ Use Bernoulli's equation, $$P_1 + \frac12\rho v_1^2 + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \frac12\rho v_2^2 + \rho g h_2,$$ to find the speed $$v$$ of the water leaving the hole. (Quantities like surface tension and viscosity could in principle matter, but on a competition, effects the problem doesn't mention should be ignored: use the simplest model consistent with the question.)

__(c)__ Find the horizontal distance from the bottle at which the stream lands, and the height $$h$$ that maximizes that distance. (Intuition check: a hole near the top has little pressure behind it; a hole near the bottom gives the water no height to fall through. The best hole is somewhere in between.)

__(d)__ The optimal $$h$$ involves neither $$g,$$ $$\rho,$$ nor $$P_0.$$ For each of these three quantities, give a reason — dimensional or physical — why it had to drop out.

label: PW207
name: A Pitot Tube in a Gas Pipeline — A Pitot tube is mounted along the axis of a gas pipeline whose…
desc: A Pitot tube is mounted along the axis of a gas pipeline whose cross-sectional area is $$S.$$ One opening of the tube faces directly into the flow, so the gas stagnates (comes to rest) at that opening. The other opening is parallel to the flow, which streams past it at the full…
statement:
A Pitot tube is mounted along the axis of a gas pipeline whose cross-sectional area is $$S.$$ One opening of the tube faces directly into the flow, so the gas stagnates (comes to rest) at that opening. The other opening is parallel to the flow, which streams past it at the full flow speed $$v.$$ The two openings connect to the two arms of a liquid-filled manometer (a U-shaped tube), and the liquid settles with a height difference $$\Delta h$$ between the arms. The densities of the liquid and the gas are $$\rho_\ell$$ and $$\rho_g$$ respectively. Assuming the viscosity is negligible, find the volume of gas flowing across a section of the pipe per unit time. (Pitot tubes are the standard airspeed sensors on aircraft; a faulty Pitot tube was suspected in the 2009 crash of a French commercial airliner.)

__(a)__ The opening that faces parallel to the flow samples the pressure of the moving gas; the opening that faces into the flow samples the pressure of stagnant gas. Explain why the liquid sits lower in the manometer arm connected to the stagnation opening.

__(b)__ Find the pressure difference between the two openings in terms of $$\rho_\ell,$$ $$g,$$ and $$\Delta h,$$ and use Bernoulli's equation to find the gas speed $$v$$ and the volumetric flow rate $$Q.$$ (Since $$\rho_g \ll \rho_\ell,$$ you may neglect the weight of the gas columns. For scale: water has density about $$1000\;\mathrm{kg/m^3},$$ while sea-level air has density about $$1.2\;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$)

__(c)__ Now do better: the gas above the liquid in the two arms also forms columns whose heights differ by $$\Delta h.$$ Show that accounting for this replaces $$\rho_\ell$$ by $$\rho_\ell - \rho_g$$ in your answer, and explain the minus sign physically.

label: PW207
name: Corrections to Torricelli's Law — By Bernoulli's equation, water emerges from a small hole a depth $$h$$…
desc: By Bernoulli's equation, water emerges from a small hole a depth $$h$$ below the free surface of a container at speed $$v_0 = \sqrt{2gh}$$ — this is __Torricelli's law__. It is not exactly correct, and in this problem you will compute two corrections to it and decide which…
statement:
By Bernoulli's equation, water emerges from a small hole a depth $$h$$ below the free surface of a container at speed $$v_0 = \sqrt{2gh}$$ — this is __Torricelli's law__. It is not exactly correct, and in this problem you will compute two corrections to it and decide which matters more. Take a bottle of radius $$5\;\mathrm{cm}$$ (cross-sectional area $$A$$) with a hole of radius $$r = 2\;\mathrm{mm}$$ (area $$a$$) in its side, a depth $$h = 10\;\mathrm{cm}$$ below the surface. Bernoulli's equation between a point at the surface (speed $$w,$$ pressure $$P_w,$$ a height $$h$$ above the hole) and a point in the emerging jet (speed $$v,$$ pressure $$P_v$$) reads $$P_w + \frac12\rho w^2 + \rho g h = P_v + \frac12\rho v^2.$$

__(a)__ Use the continuity equation — the volume of water the bottle loses per unit time equals the volume carried out through the hole per unit time — to find the speed $$w$$ at which the water surface descends, in terms of $$v,$$ $$a,$$ and $$A,$$ and numerically.

__(b)__ Torricelli's law assumes the water in the bottle is at rest ($$w = 0$$). Keeping the nonzero $$w$$ from part (a), solve Bernoulli's equation exactly for $$v.$$ Then, assuming $$a \ll A,$$ use the first-order binomial approximation $$(1+x)^n \approx 1 + nx$$ to find the correction $$\delta v = v - v_0.$$ Before calculating, predict the sign of $$\delta v$$ — checking signs against intuition is one of the best ways to catch algebra errors.

__(c)__ Creating an air-water interface of area $$A_s$$ costs energy $$\sigma A_s,$$ where $$\sigma = 7\times 10^{-2}\;\mathrm{N/m}$$ is the surface tension of water. The terms in Bernoulli's equation are energies per unit volume, so new forms of energy can be incorporated as new terms. Find the surface energy per unit volume of a cylindrical jet of radius $$r,$$ add it to Bernoulli's equation (this time ignore the motion of the surface in the bottle, and neglect the slowly-changing water-bottle interface), and find the resulting correction $$\delta v.$$ Again, predict the sign first.

__(d)__ Evaluate the ratio of the two corrections for the given numbers. Which effect is more important? The dimensionless quantity $$\dfrac{\sigma}{r\rho g h}$$ appearing in part (c) is the inverse of the __Bond number__ (named for Wilfrid Bond; also called the Eotvos number); is surface tension important at high or low Bond number?

__(e)__ The exact formula from part (c) predicts something strange for small holes. What happens to the flow as the hole's radius shrinks, and at what radius (for $$h = 10\;\mathrm{cm}$$) does it happen?

label: PW207
name: Flow Through a Venturi Meter — A Venturi meter in a water pipe consists of a slow taper from…
desc: A Venturi meter in a water pipe consists of a slow taper from $$100\;\mathrm{mm}$$ diameter down to $$80\;\mathrm{mm}$$ diameter. A pressure difference equivalent to a $$150\;\mathrm{mm}$$ __head__ of water is observed between the ends of the taper. ("Head" expresses a pressure…
statement:
A Venturi meter in a water pipe consists of a slow taper from $$100\;\mathrm{mm}$$ diameter down to $$80\;\mathrm{mm}$$ diameter. A pressure difference equivalent to a $$150\;\mathrm{mm}$$ __head__ of water is observed between the ends of the taper. ("Head" expresses a pressure as the height of a water column that would produce it: a head of $$\Delta h$$ means a pressure $$\rho g\,\Delta h,$$ with $$\rho$$ the density of water. For example, atmospheric pressure is a head of about $$10\;\mathrm{m}$$ of water — which is why even a perfect vacuum pump could not drink through a straw taller than about $$10\;\mathrm{m}.$$) Estimate the volumetric flow rate of the water in $$\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}.$$

The photograph below shows a simple Venturi meter, with gas flowing through the tapered horizontal tube and water in the small tube beneath it. A Venturi meter is similar in spirit to a Pitot tube, but works by narrowing the flow rather than stagnating it.

__(a)__ Write the two equations — continuity and Bernoulli — relating the speeds $$v_1$$ and $$v_2$$ in the wide and narrow sections, whose cross-sectional areas are $$A_1$$ and $$A_2.$$

__(b)__ Solve for the volumetric flow rate $$Q = A_2 v_2$$ in terms of $$A_1,$$ $$A_2,$$ $$g,$$ and the head $$\Delta h,$$ and put in the numbers.

label: PW207
name: Viscosity and the Reynolds Number — Hold two horizontal plates a small distance $$H$$ apart with fluid…
desc: Hold two horizontal plates a small distance $$H$$ apart with fluid between them (ignore gravity). Keep the bottom plate stationary and slide the top plate sideways at constant speed $$v_0.$$ If the fluid is thick, the plate moves slowly, and $$H$$ is small, the result is…
statement:
Hold two horizontal plates a small distance $$H$$ apart with fluid between them (ignore gravity). Keep the bottom plate stationary and slide the top plate sideways at constant speed $$v_0.$$ If the fluid is thick, the plate moves slowly, and $$H$$ is small, the result is __creeping flow__ (also called Stokes flow, and closely related to __laminar flow__): the fluid velocity grows steadily from $$0$$ at the bottom plate to $$v_0$$ at the top plate, $$v(y) = v_0\,\dfrac{y}{H}.$$ The fluid then drags backward on the top plate with a force per unit area $$\dfrac{F}{A} = \mu\,\dfrac{v_0}{H} = \mu\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}y},$$ where the constant $$\mu,$$ a property of the fluid, is its (dynamic) __viscosity__.

If instead the plate moves fast, the flow becomes __turbulent__, full of vortices and swirls, as in the photo below: dye injected into a flow stays in a neat line for a few centimeters (laminar flow), then erupts into a chaotic, expanding cloud.

__(a)__ Find the dimensions of viscosity and its SI units. (One $$\mathrm{g\,cm^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$$ is called a __Poise__; how many Poise is the SI unit?)

__(b)__ Viscous friction can be understood as a __momentum flux__: since $$F = \dot p,$$ a force per unit area is a rate of momentum flow per unit area. In the picture below, gas flows to the right with a bulk speed that increases with height, while the individual molecules also dart around randomly in all directions. Consider the imaginary horizontal plane shown. Explain microscopically why horizontal momentum flows __downward__ across this plane, and why the rate should be proportional to $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}y}.$$

__(c)__ A sphere of radius $$r$$ moves with speed $$v$$ through fluid of viscosity $$\mu$$ and density $$\rho.$$ Use dimensional analysis to constrain the drag force $$F.$$ With five variables built from three dimensions there are two independent dimensionless groups, so the most general answer has the form $$F = c\,\mu r v\,f(\mathbf{Re})$$ for a constant $$c,$$ an unknown function $$f,$$ and some dimensionless combination $$\mathbf{Re}$$ of the variables. Find $$\mathbf{Re}$$ (the __Reynolds number__).

__(d)__ Creeping flow corresponds to one extreme of the Reynolds number — which one? In that limit it turns out that $$c\,f \to 6\pi$$ (Stokes' law). You already know that in the opposite extreme, drag is proportional to $$v^2$$; show that this requires $$f(x)\sim x$$ there, and find the resulting form of $$F.$$

label: PW207
name: Draining a U-Tube Through a Capillary — For creeping (laminar) flow, the pressure drop across a uniform tube…
desc: For creeping (laminar) flow, the pressure drop across a uniform tube of radius $$R$$ and length $$L$$ carrying a volumetric flow rate $$Q$$ of fluid with viscosity $$\mu$$ is given by the __Hagen-Poiseuille equation__, $$\Delta P = \dfrac{8\mu L Q}{\pi R^4}.$$ The two arms of a…
statement:
For creeping (laminar) flow, the pressure drop across a uniform tube of radius $$R$$ and length $$L$$ carrying a volumetric flow rate $$Q$$ of fluid with viscosity $$\mu$$ is given by the __Hagen-Poiseuille equation__, $$\Delta P = \dfrac{8\mu L Q}{\pi R^4}.$$

The two arms of a U-tube, each of diameter $$10\;\mathrm{mm},$$ are connected at the bottom by a capillary of radius $$R = 0.5\;\mathrm{mm}$$ and length $$L = 0.1\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Initially, water stands in the two arms with a level difference of $$\Delta h_0 = 0.2\;\mathrm{m}.$$ How long does it take for the difference to fall to $$20\;\mathrm{mm}?$$ The viscosity of water at the temperature of the experiment is $$\mu = 1\;\mathrm{g\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}} = 10^{-3}\;\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}.$$

__(a)__ Let $$A$$ be the cross-sectional area of each arm, $$\rho$$ the density of water, and $$\Delta h$$ the instantaneous level difference. Find the differential equation satisfied by $$\Delta h.$$ (Watch the factor of two: as water flows, one level falls while the other rises.)

__(b)__ Solve the equation, and find the time constant $$\tau$$ in $$\Delta h = \Delta h_0\, e^{-t/\tau},$$ both symbolically and numerically.

__(c)__ Answer the question: how long until $$\Delta h = 20\;\mathrm{mm}?$$

label: PW207
name: An Equivalent Uniform Tube — A tube of circular bore and length $$L$$ has a slow conical taper, from radius…
desc: A tube of circular bore and length $$L$$ has a slow conical taper, from radius $$2r$$ at one end down to radius $$r$$ at the other. What would be the radius $$r'$$ of a __uniform__ tube of the same length that presents the same resistance to streamline (laminar) flow? Use the…
statement:
A tube of circular bore and length $$L$$ has a slow conical taper, from radius $$2r$$ at one end down to radius $$r$$ at the other. What would be the radius $$r'$$ of a __uniform__ tube of the same length that presents the same resistance to streamline (laminar) flow?

Use the Hagen-Poiseuille equation for laminar flow through a uniform tube of radius $$R$$ and length $$\ell$$: $$\Delta P = \dfrac{8\mu \ell\, Q}{\pi R^4},$$ where $$Q$$ is the volumetric flow rate and $$\mu$$ the viscosity. This has the same form as Ohm's law, with $$Q$$ playing the role of current, $$\Delta P$$ the role of voltage, and $$\mathcal{R} = \dfrac{8\mu\ell}{\pi R^4}$$ the role of resistance. Hint: treat the tapered tube as many thin tubes in series, each of length $$\mathrm{d}x$$ and resistance proportional to $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{R(x)^4},$$ and recall that series resistances add.

label: PW208
name: Suppose you knew only half of Gauss's law. You know that a charge inside an arbitrary…
desc: Suppose you knew only half of Gauss's law. You know that a charge inside an arbitrary closed surface causes a flux $$\Phi_E = \dfrac{q}{\epsilon_0}$$ through that surface. However, you don't know what a charge outside a charged surface does. Create an argument to determine the…
statement:
Suppose you knew only half of Gauss's law. You know that a charge inside an arbitrary closed surface causes a flux $$\Phi_E = \dfrac{q}{\epsilon_0}$$ through that surface. However, you don't know what a charge outside a charged surface does.

Create an argument to determine the net flux from a charge outside a closed surface.

name: What is the change in length of the spiral spring shown in the figure, which has $$N$$…
desc: What is the change in length of the spiral spring shown in the figure, which has $$N$$ turns, radius $$R,$$ length $$x_0,$$ and spring constant $$k,$$ when a current $$I_0$$ is made to flow through it? Assume the measurements are made with the spring in equilibrium, both with…
statement:
What is the change in length of the spiral spring shown in the figure, which has $$N$$ turns, radius $$R,$$ length $$x_0,$$ and spring constant $$k,$$ when a current $$I_0$$ is made to flow through it?

Assume the measurements are made with the spring in equilibrium, both with and without current running through.

You may assume the spring compresses a small amount.

Assume the solenoid is ideal and is very long compared to its radius.

Potentially useful: the energy density of a magnetic field is $$\dfrac{U}{V} = \dfrac12 \dfrac{B^2}{\mu_0}.$$

label: PW208
name: A conducting rod with resistance $$R$$ slides to the right on conducting rails of…
desc: A conducting rod with resistance $$R$$ slides to the right on conducting rails of negligible resistance, separated by a distance $$\ell.$$ There is a uniform $$B$$ field pointing into the page. The rod's initial speed is $$v_0.$$ The self-inductance of the setup is negligible…
statement:
A conducting rod with resistance $$R$$ slides to the right on conducting rails of negligible resistance, separated by a distance $$\ell.$$ There is a uniform $$B$$ field pointing into the page. The rod's initial speed is $$v_0.$$ The self-inductance of the setup is negligible.

**a)** Find $$\oint \vec{E} \cdot \mathrm{d}\vec{\ell}$$ around the loop consisting of the rails and the rod.

**b)** Find the emf around the loop consisting of the rails and the rod.

**c)** Find the power dissipated in the rod.

**d)** Suppose the rod has mass $$m$$. Find the distance it slides down the rails.

label: PW208
name: A parallel plate capacitor with circular plates of radius $$R$$ is being charged by a…
desc: A parallel plate capacitor with circular plates of radius $$R$$ is being charged by a current $$I.$$ This current flows onto the left plate and out from the right plate. **a)** Suppose we draw an Amperian loop in the shape of a circle of radius $$r$$ between the plates, with the…
statement:
A parallel plate capacitor with circular plates of radius $$R$$ is being charged by a current $$I.$$ This current flows onto the left plate and out from the right plate.

**a)** Suppose we draw an Amperian loop in the shape of a circle of radius $$r$$ between the plates, with the circle parallel to the planes of the plates and centered at the axis of the capacitor. Because no charge moves through the circle, the current piercing through the Amperian loop is zero. Does this imply that the line integral of the magnetic field around the loop is zero? Why or why not?

**b)** Find the magnetic field everywhere between the plates.

**c)** For $$r >R,$$ explain the relationship between the magnetic field and the field that would exist if, instead of charging a capacitor, the current simply continued past the same point in space as a straight wire.

label: PW208
name: Consider a rectangular loop of wire with dimensions $$a = 0.03 \;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$b =…
desc: Consider a rectangular loop of wire with dimensions $$a = 0.03 \;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$b = 1.0 \;\mathrm{m},$$ one side of which is parallel to another long straight wire carrying current $$I_0 = 1000 \;\mathrm{A},$$ at distance $$\ell = 0.01 \;\mathrm{m},$$ as shown in the figure…
statement:
Consider a rectangular loop of wire with dimensions $$a = 0.03 \;\mathrm{m}$$ and $$b = 1.0 \;\mathrm{m},$$ one side of which is parallel to another long straight wire carrying current $$I_0 = 1000 \;\mathrm{A},$$ at distance $$\ell = 0.01 \;\mathrm{m},$$ as shown in the figure (not to scale).

The resistance of the loop is $$R = 1.0 \;\mathrm{\Omega}.$$ The inductance of the loop is negligible.

**a)** Calculate the magnetic flux $$\Phi$$ through the loop.

**b)** At time $$t=0,$$ a switch is broken and the current in the long wire $$I$$ quickly drops to $$0.$$ What is the charge $$Q$$ that flows through a fixed cross-section of the loop of wire for $$t>0?$$

**c)** What is the net momentum $$p$$ given to the loop during $$t>0?$$

label: PW208
name: A long solenoid of radius $$r$$ produces a uniform magnetic field $$B_0$$ along its axis…
desc: A long solenoid of radius $$r$$ produces a uniform magnetic field $$B_0$$ along its axis $$O$$. A straight tube $$AM$$ made of a dielectric is fixed in a plane perpendicular to the axis at a distance $$R_0$$ from it. The angle $$AOM$$ equals $$\alpha = \pi/3.$$ The tube is much…
statement: A long solenoid of radius $$r$$ produces a uniform magnetic field $$B_0$$ along its axis $$O$$. A straight tube $$AM$$ made of a dielectric is fixed in a plane perpendicular to the axis at a distance $$R_0$$ from it. The angle $$AOM$$ equals $$\alpha = \pi/3.$$ The tube is much shorter than the solenoid. A small sphere of mass $$m$$ and carrying positive charge $$q$$ is placed inside the tube at $$A.$$ Determine the sphere velocity at the moment of departure from the tube. Do this assuming the magnetic field vanishes quickly, so the sphere travels a distance much less than $$R_0$$ while the field dies away. The friction and electromagnetic forces exerted by the tube on the sphere are negligible.

name: This problem should give you a bit more practice with circuit elements.
desc: This problem should give you a bit more practice with circuit elements. Consider an electric circuit consisting of a coil of negligibly small inductance, consisting of $$N = 10$$ turns and with surface area $$A = 10 \;\mathrm{cm}^2,$$ resistors $$R_1 = R_2 =…
statement:
This problem should give you a bit more practice with circuit elements.

Consider an electric circuit consisting of a coil of negligibly small inductance, consisting of $$N = 10$$ turns and with surface area $$A = 10 \;\mathrm{cm}^2,$$ resistors $$R_1 = R_2 = 3\;\mathrm{\Omega},$$ capacitor $$C = 0.2 \;\mathrm{F},$$ and an inductance $$L = 1\;\mathrm{H},$$ connected as shown in the figure.

At $$t = 0,$$ a magnetic field parallel to the axis of the coil is switched on. The strength of the magnetic field starts growing linearly, starting from $$B = 0$$ until the maximal value $$B = 1 \;\mathrm{T}$$ is achieved at $$t = 10 \;\mathrm{ms}.$$ After that, the strength of the magnetic field remains $$1 \;\mathrm{T}.$$

**a)**Find the approximate current through the resistors $$R_1$$ and $$R_2$$ at $$t = 5 \;\mathrm{ms}.$$

**b)**Find the approximate current through the resistors $$R_1$$ and $$R_2$$ at $$t = 15 \;\mathrm{ms}.$$

**c)** What is the net charge that passes through the resistor $$R_2?$$

label: PW208
name: A homogenous magnetic field $$\vec{B}$$ is perpendicular to a track which is inclined at…
desc: A homogenous magnetic field $$\vec{B}$$ is perpendicular to a track which is inclined at an angle $$\alpha$$ to the horizontal. A frictionless conducting rod of mass $$m$$ straddles the two rails of the track as shown in the figure. How does the rod move, after being released…
statement:
A homogenous magnetic field $$\vec{B}$$ is perpendicular to a track which is inclined at an angle $$\alpha$$ to the horizontal. A frictionless conducting rod of mass $$m$$ straddles the two rails of the track as shown in the figure.

How does the rod move, after being released from rest, if the circuit formed by the rod and the track is closed by:

**a)** a resistor of resistance $$R?$$ **b)** a capacitor of capacitance $$C?$$ **c)** a coil of inductance $$L?$$

label: PW208
name: Consider a loop of freely deformable conducting wire with insulation of length $$2\ell,$$…
desc: Consider a loop of freely deformable conducting wire with insulation of length $$2\ell,$$ the two ends of which are fixed (permanently) to the ceiling. A load of mass $$m$$ is fixed to the middle of the wire (the mass of the wire is negligible). There is also a horizontal…
statement:
Consider a loop of freely deformable conducting wire with insulation of length $$2\ell,$$ the two ends of which are fixed (permanently) to the ceiling. A load of mass $$m$$ is fixed to the middle of the wire (the mass of the wire is negligible). There is also a horizontal magnetic field of strength $$B.$$ Free fall acceleration is $$g.$$ A current $$I$$ flows through the wire. Neglect the field induced by the wires.

**a)** Sketch the shape of the wire.

**b)** What is the maximal height by which the load can be lifted in such a way (increasing the current, if necessary)?

**c)** How large a current $$I_0$$ is needed to lift the load by $$\Delta h_0 = \ell\left(1 - \dfrac{3}{\pi}\right)?$$

label: PW208
name: Flux Through a Square, No Integral Required — A point charge $$q$$ is located at $$(s/2,\,0,\,0).$$ A square…
desc: A point charge $$q$$ is located at $$(s/2,\,0,\,0).$$ A square with side length $$s$$ lies in the $$x=0$$ plane with its center at the origin and its sides parallel to the $$y$$ and $$z$$ axes. The goal is to find the electric flux through the square. Recall that the flux of the…
statement:
A point charge $$q$$ is located at $$(s/2,\,0,\,0).$$ A square with side length $$s$$ lies in the $$x=0$$ plane with its center at the origin and its sides parallel to the $$y$$ and $$z$$ axes. The goal is to find the electric flux through the square. Recall that the flux of the electric field through a surface $$\Sigma$$ is $$\Phi_E = \iint_{\Sigma} \vec{E}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{A} = \iint E\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z,$$ where $$\theta$$ is the angle between the electric field and the normal to the surface (here, the $$x$$ direction), and that Gauss's law says the total flux through any closed surface is $$\Phi_E = \dfrac{q_{\rm enc}}{\epsilon_0}.$$

__(a)__ A brute-force approach is to evaluate the flux integral directly. Without carrying it out, describe what such a calculation would involve — in particular, what two quantities you would have to express as functions of the point $$(y,z)$$ on the square before you could integrate.

__(b)__ Now find the flux through the square without doing any integral at all. (Hint: look for a closed surface, made up of identical copies of the square, with the charge at its center.)

label: PW208
name: Balancing Flux with a Tetrahedron — An equilateral triangle with side length $$s$$ sits in the $$xy$$ plane…
desc: An equilateral triangle with side length $$s$$ sits in the $$xy$$ plane with its center at the origin. A charge $$q$$ is located on the $$z$$ axis at a height $$z_0 \ll s$$ — essentially right next to the triangle. A second charge $$-2q$$ is also located on the $$z$$ axis, at a…
statement:
An equilateral triangle with side length $$s$$ sits in the $$xy$$ plane with its center at the origin. A charge $$q$$ is located on the $$z$$ axis at a height $$z_0 \ll s$$ — essentially right next to the triangle. A second charge $$-2q$$ is also located on the $$z$$ axis, at a height $$z_1.$$ The net electric flux through the triangle is zero. Find $$z_1.$$

Two geometry facts you may use: the height of a regular tetrahedron with side length $$s$$ is $$s\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3},$$ and the center of a regular tetrahedron lies $$\dfrac14$$ of the way from the base to the apex. (One way to see the second fact: by symmetry the center is the centroid of the four vertices, and three of the four lie in the base plane.)

__(a)__ Flux is a signed quantity, so the positive flux from $$q$$ can cancel the negative flux from $$-2q.$$ First find the flux through the triangle from the charge $$q$$ alone. (Hint: imagine closing up the surface with a second triangle just above the charge, forming a very thin prism.)

__(b)__ For the net flux to vanish, what fraction of the total flux of the charge $$-2q$$ must pass through the triangle?

__(c)__ Find a symmetric solid that produces exactly that fraction, and use it to determine $$z_1.$$

label: PW208
name: Charge Density of a Uniform Radial Field — Inside a sphere of radius $$R,$$ the electric field is $$\vec{E} =…
desc: Inside a sphere of radius $$R,$$ the electric field is $$\vec{E} = E_0\,\hat{r}$$ at all points $$r < R.$$ Here $$\hat{r}$$ is the unit vector pointing radially outward, so the field points away from the origin everywhere and its magnitude is the same constant $$E_0$$ at every…
statement:
Inside a sphere of radius $$R,$$ the electric field is $$\vec{E} = E_0\,\hat{r}$$ at all points $$r < R.$$ Here $$\hat{r}$$ is the unit vector pointing radially outward, so the field points away from the origin everywhere and its magnitude is the same constant $$E_0$$ at every point — it does not grow or shrink with $$r.$$

__(a)__ Use Gauss's law, $$\Phi_E = \dfrac{q_{\rm enc}}{\epsilon_0},$$ to find the total charge $$Q_e(r)$$ enclosed by a sphere of radius $$r < R$$ centered at the origin.

__(b)__ Find the charge density $$\rho(r),$$ which you may assume is spherically symmetric. Be careful: the derivative $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q_e}{\mathrm{d}r}$$ is a charge per unit __radius__, not a charge per unit volume. (Going from $$r$$ to $$r+\mathrm{d}r$$ adds a thin shell containing charge $$\rho(r)\cdot 4\pi r^2\,\mathrm{d}r.$$)

__(c)__ Your answer to (b) diverges as $$r \to 0.$$ Does that mean the total charge near the origin is infinite? Explain.

label: PW208
name: Could Gauss's Law Survive an Inverse-Cube World? — Suppose that Coulomb's law were an inverse-__cube__ law…
desc: Suppose that Coulomb's law were an inverse-__cube__ law, $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}\,\hat{r},$$ so that a point charge $$q$$ would create the radial electric field $$E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}.$$ In our universe, Gauss's law states that the flux of…
statement:
