Suppose that Coulomb's law were an inverse-__cube__ law, $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}\,\hat{r},$$ so that a point charge $$q$$ would create the radial electric field $$E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^3}.$$ In our universe, Gauss's law states that the flux of $$\vec{E}$$ through __any__ closed surface — any shape, any size — is $$\Phi_E = \dfrac{q_{\rm enc}}{\epsilon_0},$$ where $$q_{\rm enc}$$ is only the charge enclosed by the surface. Would some version of Gauss's law, relating the flux through a closed surface to the enclosed charge (perhaps with a different constant), still hold under the modified force law?

__(a)__ Compute the flux through a sphere of radius $$r$$ centered on a point charge $$q$$ under the modified law.

__(b)__ Explain why your answer to (a) already rules out a Gauss-style law, and why the situation is even worse for closed surfaces that are not spheres.

__(c)__ In real electrostatics, a charge __outside__ a closed surface contributes zero net flux through it. Test whether that survives: consider the closed surface shown below, built from two spherical caps centered on an external charge $$q$$ and joined by sides that run radially away from the charge. There is no flux through the radial sides. Compare the flux through the near cap and the far cap, both for the true $$1/r^2$$ field and for the modified $$1/r^3$$ field, and state the conclusion.

label: PW208
name: Magnetic Field of an Infinite Current Sheet — An infinite conducting sheet lies in the $$xz$$ plane and…
desc: An infinite conducting sheet lies in the $$xz$$ plane and carries a uniform current in the $$+x$$ direction with current per unit length $$\mathcal{J}$$: every strip of the sheet of width $$w$$ (measured along $$z$$) carries total current $$\mathcal{J}w.$$ Find the magnetic…
statement:
An infinite conducting sheet lies in the $$xz$$ plane and carries a uniform current in the $$+x$$ direction with current per unit length $$\mathcal{J}$$: every strip of the sheet of width $$w$$ (measured along $$z$$) carries total current $$\mathcal{J}w.$$ Find the magnetic field the sheet generates. Recall Ampere's law: the circulation of the magnetic field around a closed loop equals $$\mu_0$$ times the current passing through the loop, $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_{\rm enc}.$$

__(a)__ First establish the direction of the field. Using the right-hand rule for a single line of current along $$x,$$ argue that for $$y > 0$$ the sheet's field points in the $$+\hat{z}$$ direction and for $$y < 0$$ in the $$-\hat{z}$$ direction, and explain why the field can have no component pointing toward or away from the sheet.

__(b)__ Use Ampere's law with the rectangular Amperian loop shown below (from Purcell and Morin, __Electricity and Magnetism__): the rectangle is pierced by the sheet, with two sides of length $$\ell$$ parallel to the sheet — one on each side of it — running along the $$z$$ direction, perpendicular to the current. Find the magnitude $$B$$ of the field.

__(c)__ The electric field of an infinite sheet of charge with charge per unit area $$\sigma$$ is $$E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0},$$ pointing away from the sheet on both sides. Compare your magnetic-field answer to this result. What is similar?

label: PW208
name: The Falling Rod and the Fuse (USAPhO 2010) — This problem is from the 2010 USAPhO exam. Two long, parallel…
desc: This problem is from the 2010 USAPhO exam. Two long, parallel, vertical conducting wires are separated by $$\ell = 30\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ One pair of ends is connected through a resistor $$R = 0.25\;\mathrm{\Omega}$$ and a fuse that breaks instantaneously if $$5\;\mathrm{A}$$ of…
statement:
This problem is from the 2010 USAPhO exam. Two long, parallel, vertical conducting wires are separated by $$\ell = 30\;\mathrm{cm}.$$ One pair of ends is connected through a resistor $$R = 0.25\;\mathrm{\Omega}$$ and a fuse that breaks instantaneously if $$5\;\mathrm{A}$$ of current passes through it; the other pair of ends is unconnected. A conducting rod of mass $$m$$ is free to slide along the wires under the influence of gravity, never losing contact with them. The rod starts $$10\;\mathrm{cm}$$ from the resistor and fuse. The whole system is placed in a uniform, constant magnetic field $$B = 1.2\;\mathrm{T}$$ perpendicular to the plane of the wires, as shown. The resistance of the rod and wires is negligible. Take $$g = 10\;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

__(a)__ Trace the chain of physics when the rod is released: why does a current flow, and why does the rod's __mass__ matter for whether the fuse breaks, even though gravity accelerates all masses equally?

__(b)__ Suppose the fuse never broke. One might imagine the rod overshooting the speed at which the forces balance and then oscillating about it. Show that the rod's equation of motion has the form $$\dot{v} = g - \dfrac{1}{m}f(v)$$ with $$f(v) \propto v$$ — a __first-order__ differential equation — and explain why a first-order equation cannot oscillate, so the rod instead approaches its terminal velocity smoothly, as $$v = v_t\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right).$$ (Contrast with oscillators like $$\ddot{x} = -\omega^2 x,$$ which are second order.)

__(c)__ What is the smallest mass that breaks the fuse?

__(d)__ How fast is the rod moving at the moment the fuse breaks? Does this speed depend on the mass?

label: PW208
name: A Magnetic Monopole on a Track (USAPhO 2012) — This problem is from the 2012 USAPhO exam. Assume the…
desc: This problem is from the 2012 USAPhO exam. Assume the existence of a hypothetical particle known as a __magnetic monopole__. Such a particle has a "magnetic charge" $$q_m$$; in analogy with an electrically charged particle, it produces a radially directed magnetic field of…
statement:
This problem is from the 2012 USAPhO exam. Assume the existence of a hypothetical particle known as a __magnetic monopole__. Such a particle has a "magnetic charge" $$q_m$$; in analogy with an electrically charged particle, it produces a radially directed magnetic field of magnitude $$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{q_m}{r^2}$$ and, in the absence of electric fields, feels a force $$F = q_m B$$ in a magnetic field. (No conclusive evidence of magnetic monopoles exists, but physicists have not ruled them out.)

__(a)__ What is the magnetic version of Gauss's law in such a case? That is, find the constant $$c$$ in $$\Phi_B = c\cdot q_{m,\rm enc},$$ where $$\Phi_B$$ is the magnetic flux through a closed surface and $$q_{m,\rm enc}$$ is the enclosed magnetic charge.

A magnetic monopole of mass $$m$$ and magnetic charge $$q_m$$ is constrained to move on a vertical, nonmagnetic, insulating, frictionless U-shaped track. At the bottom of the track is a wire loop whose radius $$b$$ is much smaller than the width of the "U," so the section of track near the loop can be approximated as a long straight line through the loop's center, perpendicular to its plane. The wire that makes up the loop has radius $$a \ll b$$ and resistivity $$\rho.$$ The monopole is released from rest at a height $$H$$ above the bottom of the track. Ignore the self-inductance of the loop, and assume the monopole passes through the loop many times before coming to rest.

__(b)__ Suppose the monopole is a distance $$x$$ from the center of the loop. What is the magnetic flux $$\Phi_B$$ through the loop? (Hint: the flux through a surface is proportional to the __solid angle__ it subtends as seen from the monopole — Gauss's law gives the flux per solid angle. You may evaluate the flux through any surface bounded by the wire; a __spherical cap__ centered at the monopole, like the one pictured below, is easier than a flat disk. In spherical coordinates, a patch of a sphere of radius $$r$$ spanning $$\mathrm{d}\theta$$ and $$\mathrm{d}\phi$$ has area $$r^2\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}\phi.$$)

__(c)__ Suppose in addition that the monopole is traveling at velocity $$v.$$ What is the emf $$\varepsilon$$ induced in the loop?

__(d)__ Find the change in speed $$\Delta v$$ of the monopole in one trip through the loop, in terms of $$m,$$ $$q_m,$$ $$a,$$ $$b,$$ and $$\rho.$$ Treat $$v$$ as approximately constant during a single pass. You might want to make use of the integral $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(1+u^2)^3}\,\mathrm{d}u = \dfrac{3\pi}{8}.$$

__(e)__ How many times does the monopole pass through the loop before coming to rest?

label: PW208
name: Dimensional Analysis with Electromagnetic Quantities — In mechanics, dimensional analysis uses the three…
desc: In mechanics, dimensional analysis uses the three dimensions $$M$$ (mass), $$L$$ (length), and $$T$$ (time). Electromagnetism requires a fourth: charge $$Q.$$ (Current works just as well, since current is charge per time, $$|I| = QT^{-1}$$; in SI units the ampere is the official…
statement:
In mechanics, dimensional analysis uses the three dimensions $$M$$ (mass), $$L$$ (length), and $$T$$ (time). Electromagnetism requires a fourth: charge $$Q.$$ (Current works just as well, since current is charge per time, $$|I| = QT^{-1}$$; in SI units the ampere is the official base unit, but either choice is fine.) A useful strategy is to use familiar formulas to convert electromagnetic quantities into combinations with known dimensions. Take these as given: the magnetic force on a charge is $$F = qvB$$; Coulomb's law is $$F = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$$; the field of a long straight wire is $$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$; voltage is energy per charge; and the circuit-element laws are $$V = IR$$ (resistor), $$Q = CV$$ (capacitor), and $$V = L\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ (inductor).

__(a)__ Find the dimensions of the magnetic field $$B$$ in terms of $$M, L, T, Q.$$

__(b)__ Find the dimensions of $$\epsilon_0$$ and of $$\mu_0.$$

__(c)__ Find the dimensions of $$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}.$$ What famous physical quantity has these dimensions?

__(d)__ Show that $$RC,$$ $$\dfrac{L}{R},$$ and $$\sqrt{LC}$$ all have dimensions of time. (These are the natural time scales of circuits built from resistors, capacitors, and inductors.)

label: PW209
name: In the late 19th century the American student Edwin Hall was given the problem of…
desc: In the late 19th century the American student Edwin Hall was given the problem of observing the effect of a magnetic field on electrons traveling in a conductor. He was successful, and measured what is now known as the __Hall Effect__. The figure below illustrates Hall's…
statement:
In the late 19th century the American student Edwin Hall was given the problem of observing the effect of a magnetic field on electrons traveling in a conductor. He was successful, and measured what is now known as the __Hall Effect__.

The figure below illustrates Hall's experiment conceptually.

A current is passed through a strip of gold leaf and the current carriers (usually electrons) pass through the gold leaf. The current passes through the gold leaf in the direction shown.

There is a magnetic field as shown as well. The magnetic field acts on the moving current carriers and these carriers are pulled to the left.

One thin edge of the gold leaf becomes positively-charged (colored pink in the drawing), relative to the other side. This results in a potential difference across the gold leaf in the direction perpendicular to the current and the magnetic field. This potential difference is called the __Hall voltage__.

**a)** The number density of the carriers is $$n,$$ the cross sectional area of the strip is $$a,$$ the charge on the current carrier (electrons) is $$-e.$$ Derive an expression for the drift velocity $$v_d$$ in terms of $$I, n, a,$$ and $$e.$$

**b)** The Hall effect is used to create sensors that detect and measure magnetic fields. In semiconductors, there are fewer charge carriers per unit volume than in conductors. Would this result in sensors that are more sensitive to magnetic fields, or less sensitive?

**c)** In some materials, the Hall voltage goes in the opposite direction as that shown in the drawing. How could this occur?

**d)** The highest field available is $$0.1 \;\mathrm{T}.$$ The width of the gold leaf is $$40 \;\mathrm{mm},$$ the thickness is $$10 \;\mathrm{mm},$$ and the current is $$200 \;\mathrm{mA}.$$ What is the drift velocity of the free electrons? (There is one free electron per atom.) What would the Hall voltage be?

label: PW209
name: A small sphere carries charge Q. It is located at the center of a fixed, uncharged…
desc: A small sphere carries charge Q. It is located at the center of a fixed, uncharged conducting hollow sphere with outer radius $$R_2$$ and inner radius $$R_1.$$ The sphere is enclosed by a concentric dielectric layer of permittivity $$\epsilon$$ and the outer radius $$R_3.$$ What…
statement:
A small sphere carries charge Q. It is located at the center of a fixed, uncharged conducting hollow sphere with outer radius $$R_2$$ and inner radius $$R_1.$$ The sphere is enclosed by a concentric dielectric layer of permittivity $$\epsilon$$ and the outer radius $$R_3.$$

What is the minimum work required to move the small sphere to a distance much greater than $$R_3$$ through a narrow channel inside the conductor and the dielectric?

label: PW209
name: This problem describes the phenomenon of __magnetoresistance__, which is used, for…
desc: This problem describes the phenomenon of __magnetoresistance__, which is used, for example, to create hard disk read/write heads. Magnetic properties of electrons are intrinsically related to their spin. In ferromagnetic materials, unpaired electron spins line up with each other…
statement:
This problem describes the phenomenon of __magnetoresistance__, which is used, for example, to create hard disk read/write heads.

Magnetic properties of electrons are intrinsically related to their spin. In ferromagnetic materials, unpaired electron spins line up with each other within regions called domains. Within domains the magnetic field is therefore intense, though domains will generally be randomly orientated with respect to one another so that a bulk sample will usually be unmagnetized. However, an externally applied magnetic field can cause the magnetic domains to line up with each other; the material is said to be magnetized.

Electrons, although point particles, behave as if they were spinning and act like tiny magnets. Electrons in a ferromagnet whose spins are oriented in the direction of (parallel), or opposite to (antiparallel), the internal magnetization carry independent currents, leading to the material behaving as if it has different resistivities $$\rho_p$$ and $$\rho_a$$ for each of the two current components.

Two ferromagnetic layers with identical dimensions (length $$\ell,$$ cross-sectional area $$A)$$ but opposite magnetization are placed next to each other in parallel with a cell of e.m.f. $$\varepsilon$$ and internal resistance $$r.$$

The resistance of the rest of the external circuit is modeled by a resistance $$R$$ in series with the ferromagnetic layers.

**a)** Draw a diagram of the circuit described above.

**b)** Find the total resistance of the circuit.

**c)** An external magnetic field is now applied to the ferromagnetic layers, causing their magnetization to line up. Draw a new circuit diagram and find the total resistance in this case.

**d)** The current component parallel flows much more easily than that antiparallel, meaning that $$\rho_p \ll \rho_a.$$ Find an expression for the change in current between the two situations before and after the external field is applied.

**e)** For fixed resistances (and fixed resistivities $$\rho_p \ll \rho_a,)$$ under what conditions is the change in current maximized?

label: PW209
name: Certain magnetic toys are made up of ferromagnetic spheres and permanent magnets of…
desc: Certain magnetic toys are made up of ferromagnetic spheres and permanent magnets of cylindrical shape. These building blocks can be used to build, for instance, a tetrahedron, as shown below. (The letter "N" marks the northern side of the magnet.) Assume that all these permanent…
statement:
Certain magnetic toys are made up of ferromagnetic spheres and permanent magnets of cylindrical shape. These building blocks can be used to build, for instance, a tetrahedron, as shown below. (The letter "N" marks the northern side of the magnet.)

Assume that all these permanent magnets are identical and each of them alone can create a magnetic flux $$\Phi,$$ (assuming that both ends of the magnet are in contact with a U-shaped large piece of ferromagnetic material, so that a closed ferromagnetic contour is formed).

Assume also that due to high magnetic permeability of the material of the building blocks, all the magnetic field lines are constrained inside of them (i.e. in the surrounding medium, the magnetic field strength is zero).

**a)** Designate the fluxes in each permanent magnet (magnets A-F in the figure) by $$\Phi_A, \Phi_B, \ldots \Phi_F.$$ Find an equation relating $$\Phi_A, \Phi_B,$$ and $$\Phi_C$$ to each other (and possibly to $$\Phi.)$$

**b)** Find an equation relating $$\Phi_A, \Phi_B,$$ and $$\Phi_F$$ to each other (and possibly to $$\Phi.)$$

**c)** Find the ratio $$\dfrac{\Phi_F}{\Phi_C}.$$

**d)** Find the magnetic fluxes in each permanent magnet.

**e)** Which of the magnets is the most difficult one to remove? Why?

label: PW209
name: A dielectric cylinder of radius $$r$$ carries carries a charge of surface density…
desc: A dielectric cylinder of radius $$r$$ carries carries a charge of surface density $$\sigma$$ on its cylindrical surface and rotates with angular velocity $$\omega.$$ **a)** Determine the magnetic field strength inside the cylinder. If you wish, you can use the equation for the…
statement:
A dielectric cylinder of radius $$r$$ carries carries a charge of surface density $$\sigma$$ on its cylindrical surface and rotates with angular velocity $$\omega.$$

**a)** Determine the magnetic field strength inside the cylinder.

If you wish, you can use the equation for the inductance, $$L = \mu_0 N^2 S/\ell$$ of a solenoid of radius $$r,$$ length $$ \ell \gg r,$$ cross-sectional area $$S,$$ and $$N$$ loops.

**b)** A radial conducting wire connects the axis of the cylinder with the cylindrical surface (it rotates together with the cylinder). Find the electromotive force $$\varepsilon$$ between the ends of the wire.

**c)** Suppose that the wire connecting the axis of the cylinder with the cylindrical surface is not radial and has an arbitrary shape (still, there are no segments protruding outside the cylinder). Show that $$\varepsilon$$ does not depend on the shape of the wire.

label: PW209
name: Magnetic fields are everywhere around us. Some typical magnetic $$B$$-field values:
desc: Magnetic fields are everywhere around us. Some typical magnetic $$B$$-field values: Earth's magnetic field: $$25 - 60 \;\mathrm{\mu T}.$$ sunspots: $$0.3 \;\mathrm{T}.$$ strong permanent magnets: $$\sim 1\;\mathrm{T}.$$ continuously-maintained fields in laboratory: up to $$45…
statement:
Magnetic fields are everywhere around us. Some typical magnetic $$B$$-field values:

Earth's magnetic field: $$25 - 60 \;\mathrm{\mu T}.$$ sunspots: $$0.3 \;\mathrm{T}.$$ strong permanent magnets: $$\sim 1\;\mathrm{T}.$$ continuously-maintained fields in laboratory: up to $$45 \;\mathrm{T}.$$ neutron stars and magnetars: up to $$10^{11}\;\mathrm{T}.$$

The energy density of a magnetic field is $$w = B^2 \dfrac{1}{2\mu \mu_0},$$ where $$\mu_0 \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-6} \;\mathrm{N/A^2}$$ is the vacuum permeability, and $$\mu$$ the relative permeability of the medium.

Systems try to move toward lower-energy states, so ferromagnetic materials, which have $$\mu \gg 1,$$ are pulled towards regions with strong magnetic fields. Diamagnetic materials have $$\mu < 1$$ and are pushed out from magnetic fields. For diamagnetic materials, the magnetic susceptibility $$\chi = \mu - 1$$ is small, $$|\chi| \ll 1,$$ and so the effect is small unless the field is strong. Water is diamagnetic with $$\chi = -9 \times 10^{-6}$$ and animals are mostly made of water. So, a frog can levitate in a magnetic field if the field is strong enough, as shown below.

**a)** Let the frog height, $$h_f,$$ be not more than $$h_0 = 10 \;\mathrm{mm},$$ and let us assume that the squared magnetic field depends linearly on height $$z$$ as shown below.

Find the strength of magnetic field $$B_0$$ needed to levitate the frog.

Assume that the frog is made entirely of water with density $$\rho = 1000 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ Free fall acceleration is $$g = 9.8 \;\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

hint:

for $$|\chi| \ll 1,$$ we can write $$w \approx B^2 \dfrac{1-\chi}{2\mu_0}.$$ This means the energy density associated with the presence of water is $$\Delta w = B^2 \dfrac{1-\chi}{2\mu_0} - B^2 \dfrac{1}{2\mu_0} = -B^2 \dfrac{\chi}{2\mu_0}.$$

-------------------

Stars are made of a plasma which, is a good electrical conductor. Because of this, magnetic field lines behave as if they are "frozen" into the moving plasma. (This follows from Faraday's law and Kirchoff's voltage law: due to the absence of electric resistance, the voltage drop along a closed fictitious contour inside the plasma must be zero. This means the magnetic flux cannot change.)

If a star were to collapse into a neutron star, this effect would lead to an instantaneous increase of the magnetic field. See the sketch below of the magnetic field lines before and after the collapse (recall that magnetic field strength is proportional to the density of field lines).

**b)** Assuming that the polar magnetic field of a star is $$B_S = 100 \;\mathrm{\mu T}$$ and its average density is $$\rho_S = 1400 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3},$$ what would its polar magnetic field strength $$B_c$$ be after its collapse into a neutron star due to the compression of magnetic field lines depicted above? The neutron star has density $$\rho_n = 5\times 10^{17} \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$

label: PW209
name: This problem continues the previous one on magnetic levitation and stellar collapse.
desc: This problem continues the previous one on magnetic levitation and stellar collapse. **c)** In reality, magnetic fields of neutron stars are generated differently than we discussed in the previous problem. Let us consider a very simplified model. The interior part of the star…
statement:
This problem continues the previous one on magnetic levitation and stellar collapse.

**c)** In reality, magnetic fields of neutron stars are generated differently than we discussed in the previous problem. Let us consider a very simplified model. The interior part of the star has collapsed to a neutron star's size and density, but the exterior parts remain the same size. Assume that before the collapse, the star was rotating as a solid body with angular speed $$\omega_s.$$ Express the new angular speed of the interior part of the star $$\omega_n$$ in terms of $$\omega_s, \rho_s,$$ and $$\rho_n.$$

**d)** Rotation speeds of the inner and outer parts are different, hence the field lines will be stretched as shown below.

For the sake of simplicity,

- we use a 2-dimensional geometry. i.e. we think about stars as being cylindrical - the initial field was a dipole field. We assume that it was cylindrically symmetric as shown in the figure. - the endpoints of field lines are attached to the inner cylinder (the neutron star).

Let the initial magnetic field at the outer shell be $$B_0.$$ Express the magnetic field $$B$$ as a function of time $$t$$ in the region where field lines are being stretched for $$t \gg \dfrac{1}{\omega_n}$$ in terms of $$B_0$$ and $$\omega_n.$$

**e)** Energy is converted during the star collapse as follows: - gravitational energy is converted into kinetic energy (we neglect thermal energy) - kinetic energy is later converted to magnetic energy

Based on this scenario, estimate the maximum strength of the magnetic field $$B_{\mathrm{max}}$$ for a neutron star of mass $$M_n = 4\times 10^{30} \;\mathrm{kg}$$ and radius $$R = 13 \;\mathrm{km}.$$ Recall that $$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m^3 \, s^{-2} \, kg^{-2}}.$$

**f)** Very strong magnetic fields affect chemical properties of matter by changing the shape of electron orbits. This happens when the Lorentz force acting on an orbital electron becomes stronger than the Coulomb for ce due to the atomic nucleus. Estimate the strength of the magnetic field $$B_H$$ needed to distort the electron orbit of a hydrogen atom which has radius $$R_H = 5\times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{m}.$$ Note that $$\dfrac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \;\mathrm{m/F}, e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \;\mathrm{C},$$ and the electron mass is $$m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

label: PW209
name: A solenoid of length $$\ell = 20 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ is wound around a vertical, cylindrical…
desc: A solenoid of length $$\ell = 20 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ is wound around a vertical, cylindrical test tube made of glass, filled with water. The solenoid is thermally insulated from the water. The height of the water level is approximately $$20 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ above the upper end of the…
statement:
A solenoid of length $$\ell = 20 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ is wound around a vertical, cylindrical test tube made of glass, filled with water. The solenoid is thermally insulated from the water. The height of the water level is approximately $$20 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ above the upper end of the solenoid, the diameter of the test tube is $$1 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ the number of turns of the coil is $$N = 6000.$$ The atmospheric pressure is $$p_0 = 101 \;\mathrm{kPa},$$ the temperature of the water is $$293 \;\mathrm{K}.$$ The magnetic susceptibility of water is $$\chi = \mu - 1 = -9.04 \times 10^{-6}.$$ The vacuum permeability is $$\mu_0 = 12.57 \times 10^{-7} \;\mathrm{H/m}.$$

The current in the solenoid is slowly increased until the water starts boiling inside the coil. At which current strength would this happen? Make reasonable approximations when needed. Note that the required current strength might be slightly too large for the present technology.

label: PW209
name: All particles have a fundamental property called __spin__. Spin is an intrinsic form of…
desc: All particles have a fundamental property called __spin__. Spin is an intrinsic form of angular momentum. A full treatment of spin requires quantum mechanics, but we can still study spin using classical electromagnetism. In this problem, we investigate the influence of a…
statement:
All particles have a fundamental property called __spin__. Spin is an intrinsic form of angular momentum. A full treatment of spin requires quantum mechanics, but we can still study spin using classical electromagnetism. In this problem, we investigate the influence of a magnetic field on spin using classical physics.

The torque on a spin is given by $$\vec{\tau} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{L}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \vec{\mu}\times \vec{B}.$$

In this case, the angular momentum $$\vec{L}$$ represents the "instrinsic" spin of the particles, $$\vec{\mu}$$ is the magnetic moment of the particles, and $$\vec{B}$$ is the magnetic field. The spin of a particle is associated with a magnetic moment via the equation $$\vec{\mu} = -\gamma \vec{L}$$ where $$\gamma$$ is the __gyromagnetic ratio__.

**a)** Prove that the magnitude of magnetic moment $$\mu$$ is always constant under the influence of a magnetic field $$\vec{B}.$$ For the special case of a constant magnetic field, also show that the angle between $$\vec{\mu}$$ and $$\vec{B}$$ is constant.

**b)** A uniform magnetic field $$\vec{B}$$ exists and it makes an angle $$\phi$$ with a particle's magnetic moment $$\vec{\mu}.$$ Due to the torque by the magnetic field, the magnetic moment $$\vec{\mu}$$ rotates around the field $$\vec{B},$$ which is also known as Larmor precession. Determine the Larmor precession frequency $$\omega_0$$ of the magnetic moment with respect to $$\vec{B} = B_0 \hat{k}.$$

--------------

Next, we choose a rotating frame $$S'$$ as our frame of reference. The rotating frame $$S' = (x',y',z')$$ rotates with an angular velocity $$\omega \hat{k}$$ as seen by an observer in the laboratory frame $$S = (x,y,z).$$ The axes $$x',y',z'$$ intersect with $$x,y,z$$ at time $$t = 0.$$ Any vector $$\vec{A} = A_x \hat{i} + A_y \hat{j} + A_z \hat{k}$$ in a lab frame can be written as $$\vec{A} = A_x' \hat{i}' + A_y' \hat{j}' + A_z' \hat{k}'$$ in the rotating frame $$S'.$$ The time derivative of the vector becomes

$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}A_x'}{\mathrm{d}t} \hat{i}' + \dfrac{\mathrm{d}A_y'}{\mathrm{d}t} \hat{j}' + \dfrac{\mathrm{d}A_z'}{\mathrm{d}t}\hat{k}' \right) + \left(A_x' \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\hat{i}'}{\mathrm{d}t} + A_y' \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\hat{j}'}{\mathrm{d}t} + A_z' \dfrac{\mathrm{d}k'}{\mathrm{d}t}\right).$$

$$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)_{\mathrm{lab}} = \left( \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)_{\mathrm{rot}} + \left(\omega \hat{k} \times \vec{A}\right),$$

where $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}_{\mathrm{lab}}$$ is the time derivative of the vector $$\vec{A}$$ seen by an observer in the lab frame, and $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}_{\mathrm{rot}}$$ is the time derivative seen by an observer in the rotating frame. For all the following problems, the answers are referred to the rotating frame $$S'.$$

**c)** Show that the time evolution of the magnetic moment follows the equation $$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\vec{\mu}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)_{\mathrm{rot}} = -\gamma \vec{\mu}\times \vec{B}_{\mathrm{eff}},$$ where $$\vec{B}_{\mathrm{eff}} = \vec{B} - \dfrac{\omega}{\gamma} \hat{k}'$$ is the effective magnetic field.

**d)** For $$\vec{B} = B_0 \hat{k},$$ what is the new precession frequency $$\Delta$$ in terms of $$\omega_0$$ and $$\omega?$$

**e)** Now, let us consider the case of a time-varying magnetic field. Besides a constant magnetic field, we also apply a rotating magnetic field $$\vec{b}(t) = b(\cos \omega t \hat{i} + \sin \omega t \hat{j}),$$ so $$\vec{B} = B_0 \hat{k} + \vec{b}(t).$$

Show that the new Larmor precession frequency of the magnetic moment is $$\Omega = \gamma \sqrt{\left(B_0 - \dfrac{\omega}{\gamma}\right)^2 + b^2}.$$

**f)** Instead of applying the field $$\vec{b}(t) = b(\cos \omega t \hat{i} + \sin \omega t \hat{j}),$$ now we apply $$\vec{b}(t) = b(\cos \omega \hat{i} - \sin \omega t \hat{j}.$$ What is the effective magnetic field $$\vec{B}_{\mathrm{eff}}$$ for this case (in terms of the unit vectors $$\hat{i}', \hat{j}', \hat{k}')?$$ What is its time average, $$\overline{\vec{B}}_{\mathrm{eff}}?$$

label: PW209
name: This problem continues the previous one on spin.
desc: This problem continues the previous one on spin. For an ensemble of $$N$$ particles under the influence of a large magnetic field, the spin can have two quantum states: "up" and "down". Consequently, the total population of spin up $$N_{\uparrow}$$ and down $$N_{\downarrow}$$…
statement:
This problem continues the previous one on spin.

For an ensemble of $$N$$ particles under the influence of a large magnetic field, the spin can have two quantum states: "up" and "down". Consequently, the total population of spin up $$N_{\uparrow}$$ and down $$N_{\downarrow}$$ obeys the equation $$N_{\uparrow} + N_{\downarrow} = N.$$

The difference of spin up population and spin down population yields the macroscopic magnetization along the $$z$$ axis: $$ M = (N_{\uparrow} - N_{\downarrow}) \mu = N\mu_z.$$

In a real experiment, two magnetic field are usually applied, a large bias field $$B_0 \hat{k}$$ and an oscillating field with amplitude $$2b$$ perpendicular to the bias field $$(b \ll B_0).$$ Initially, only the large bias is applied, causing all the particles to lie in the spin up states ($$\vec{\mu}$$ is oriented in the $$z$$ direction at $$t=0).$$ Then, the oscillating field is turned on, where its frequency $$\omega$$ is chosen to be in resonance with the Larmor precession frequency $$\omega_0,$$ i.e. $$\omega = \omega_0.$$ In other words, the total field after time $$t=0$$ is given by $$\vec{B}(t) = B_0 \hat{k} + 2b \cos \omega_0 t \hat{i}.$$

**g)** In the totating frame $$S',$$ show that the effective field can be approximated by $$B_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx b \hat{i},$$ which is commonly known as the __rotating wave approximation__. What is the precession frequency $$\Omega$$ in frame $$S'?$$

**h)** Determine the angle $$\alpha$$ that $$\vec{\mu}$$ makes with $$\vec{B}_{\mathrm{eff}}.$$ Also, prove that the magnetization varies with time as $$M(t) = N \mu(\cos \Omega t).$$

**i)** Under the application of the magnetic field described above, determine the fractional population of each spin up $$P_{\uparrow} = N_{\uparrow}/N$$ and spin down $$P_{\downarrow} = N_{\downarrow}/N$$ as a function of time. Plot $$P_{\uparrow}(t)$$ and $$P_{\downarrow}(t)$$ on the same graph vs time $$t.$$ The alternating spin up and spin down population as a function of time is called __Rabi oscillation__.

label: PW209
name: Dipole Moment of a Conducting Slab — A region of space contains a uniform electric field of strength $$E_0$$…
desc: A region of space contains a uniform electric field of strength $$E_0$$ pointing in the $$\hat{z}$$ direction. A conducting slab of thickness $$t$$ is placed in the field with its two large faces perpendicular to the field. Each face has surface area $$A \gg t^2,$$ so edge…
statement:
A region of space contains a uniform electric field of strength $$E_0$$ pointing in the $$\hat{z}$$ direction. A conducting slab of thickness $$t$$ is placed in the field with its two large faces perpendicular to the field. Each face has surface area $$A \gg t^2,$$ so edge effects can be neglected. The slab carries no net charge. Assume that the electrons in the conductor are free to move while the positive charges stay fixed.

__(a)__ In which direction do the electrons shift relative to their equilibrium positions? Once the charges reach equilibrium, what is the electric field inside the slab, and where exactly does the displaced charge reside — spread through the interior, or on the surfaces? (Hint: relate the charge density inside the conductor to the divergence of the field via Gauss' law, $$\nabla \cdot \vec{E} = \rho/\epsilon_0.$$)

__(b)__ Find the surface charge density $$\sigma$$ on each face. You may use the fact (from Gauss' law) that a large flat sheet of charge with surface density $$\sigma$$ creates an electric field of strength $$E_\sigma = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$$ on each side of itself.

__(c)__ The __dipole moment__ of charges $$+q$$ and $$-q$$ separated by displacement $$\vec{d}$$ (pointing from the negative charge to the positive charge) is $$\vec{p} = q\vec{d}.$$ Find the dipole moment of the slab, and explain why the slab has no __monopole moment__ (net charge).

label: PW209
name: A Magnetic Dipole over a Superconducting Sheet — (European Physics Olympiad.) A large flat sheet is made of a…
desc: (European Physics Olympiad.) A large flat sheet is made of a material that can become superconducting; its linear size is much larger than every other length in the problem. Initially the sheet is in its normal (non-superconducting) state, and a magnetic dipole of moment $$m$$…
statement:
(European Physics Olympiad.) A large flat sheet is made of a material that can become superconducting; its linear size is much larger than every other length in the problem. Initially the sheet is in its normal (non-superconducting) state, and a magnetic dipole of moment $$m$$ and mass $$M$$ sits a distance $$a$$ from the sheet, pointing perpendicularly toward it. The sheet is then cooled until it becomes superconducting. The superconductor does not expel the existing magnetic flux, but from that moment on, the magnetic flux through every part of the sheet is locked at its current value. Finally, the dipole is moved perpendicular to the sheet to a new distance $$b.$$

Background you may use. In a superconductor there is never an electric field, so any attempt to change the flux through it induces persistent surface currents that hold the flux fixed (in an ordinary conductor such eddy currents die away because of resistance). The magnetic field of a dipole $$m$$ on its axis, a distance $$z$$ away, is $$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{m}{z^3}$$ — like all dipole fields it falls as $$1/z^3.$$ A __uniform__ field exerts no net force on a dipole; the force comes from the field's gradient. For a dipole $$\vec{m}$$ aligned with the $$z$$ axis, the force is $$F = m\,\dfrac{\partial B_z}{\partial z}.$$ Two coaxial dipoles pointing in the same direction attract each other; pointing in opposite directions, they repel.

Also recall the __method of images__ from electrostatics: a large grounded conducting plane near a point charge can be replaced by an opposite "image charge" mirrored behind the plane. The two setups have the same charges above the plane and produce the same potential on all boundaries (zero on the plane and at infinity), so by the __uniqueness theorem__ they produce the same field everywhere above the plane — and hence the same force on the real charge.

__(a)__ Explain physically why there is a force between the dipole and the superconducting sheet after the dipole is moved, and use Lenz's law to predict whether the force is attractive or repulsive in the cases $$b > a$$ and $$b < a.$$

__(b)__ Show that the frozen-flux boundary condition is reproduced by deleting the superconductor and adding __two image dipoles__ behind the sheet: one of moment $$m$$ pointing in the __same__ direction as the real dipole, mirrored at depth $$a,$$ and one of moment $$m$$ pointing in the __opposite__ direction, mirrored at depth $$b.$$ (Hint: first consider the special case $$b \to \infty,$$ where the real dipole is effectively removed; what single image keeps the flux through the sheet equal to its frozen value?)

__(c)__ Find the force between the sheet and the dipole, taking the positive direction to point away from the sheet, and check that its sign agrees with your answer to part (a).

__(d)__ Now suppose the dipole is displaced only slightly: $$b = a + \epsilon$$ with $$\epsilon \ll a.$$ Show that the dipole undergoes simple harmonic motion and find the angular frequency $$\omega$$ of the small oscillations.

label: PW209
name: A Capacitor Filled with Two Dielectrics — A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two conducting plates…
desc: A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two conducting plates separated by a distance $$d;$$ with vacuum between the plates, its capacitance is $$C.$$ A __dielectric__ (an insulating material) placed in an electric field becomes polarized: its positive and negative charges…
statement:
A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two conducting plates separated by a distance $$d;$$ with vacuum between the plates, its capacitance is $$C.$$ A __dielectric__ (an insulating material) placed in an electric field becomes polarized: its positive and negative charges separate slightly, which __weakens__ the field inside the material. If the applied field is $$E_0,$$ the field inside the dielectric is $$\dfrac{E_0}{\kappa},$$ where the constant $$\kappa > 1$$ is the material's __dielectric constant__ (the material's permittivity is $$\epsilon = \kappa\epsilon_0$$).

Facts you may use: completely filling a capacitor with a dielectric of constant $$\kappa$$ multiplies its capacitance by $$\kappa$$ (for fixed free charge on the plates, the field and hence the voltage drop by a factor $$\kappa,$$ so $$C = Q/V$$ rises by $$\kappa$$). The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is proportional to the plate area and inversely proportional to the plate separation. Capacitors in series combine as $$\dfrac{1}{C_{\mathrm{series}}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2},$$ and capacitors in parallel add: $$C_{\mathrm{parallel}} = C_1 + C_2.$$

__(a)__ The space within a distance $$a$$ of the left plate is filled with a dielectric of dielectric constant $$\kappa_a,$$ and the remaining thickness $$d - a$$ is filled with a dielectric of constant $$\kappa_b.$$ Find the new capacitance $$C'.$$ (Hint: imagine slipping a thin metal sheet between the two dielectrics — it changes nothing physically, but it turns the device into two recognizable circuit elements.)

__(b)__ Test your formula in three limits: $$a \to 0,$$ $$a \to d,$$ and $$\kappa_a = \kappa_b = \kappa.$$ In each case, say what the answer must be on physical grounds, and check that your formula delivers it.

__(c)__ Now solve the problem again with the dielectrics arranged the other way: the top half of the capacitor (half the plate area, but the full separation $$d$$) holds a dielectric of constant $$\kappa_\alpha,$$ and the bottom half holds a dielectric of constant $$\kappa_\beta.$$ Find the capacitance.

label: PW209
name: The Force on a Dielectric Slab in a Capacitor — A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two conducting square…
desc: A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two conducting square plates of side length $$s.$$ With vacuum between the plates, the capacitance is $$C.$$ The capacitor is charged to total charge $$Q$$ and then disconnected from any circuit, so the charge cannot change. A dielectric…
statement:
A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two conducting square plates of side length $$s.$$ With vacuum between the plates, the capacitance is $$C.$$ The capacitor is charged to total charge $$Q$$ and then disconnected from any circuit, so the charge cannot change. A dielectric slab of permittivity $$\epsilon$$ — that is, dielectric constant $$\kappa = \dfrac{\epsilon}{\epsilon_0}$$ — exactly the size of the gap is inserted halfway in between the plates, filling the gap up to a height $$\dfrac{s}{2}.$$ What force is needed to hold the slab in place? Ignore gravity. (This problem is a true classic.)

Useful facts: the energy stored in a capacitor of capacitance $$C$$ holding charge $$Q$$ is $$U = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C}.$$ A dielectric of constant $$\kappa$$ completely filling a capacitor multiplies its capacitance by $$\kappa.$$ Side-by-side regions between the same pair of plates act like capacitors in parallel (their capacitances add), and the capacitance of each region is proportional to its share of the plate area.

__(a)__ Before calculating anything: is the electric force on the slab pulling it further into the capacitor or pushing it out? Give an energy argument. Why does this argument suggest computing the force from the energy rather than directly from the fields?

__(b)__ Suppose the slab has been inserted a distance $$x$$ (so the setup in the problem is the special case $$x = \dfrac{s}{2}$$). Find the capacitance $$C'(x).$$ Why must we work with general $$x$$ rather than just $$x = \dfrac{s}{2}?$$

__(c)__ Find the stored energy $$U(x).$$

__(d)__ The force the capacitor exerts on the slab is $$F = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$ Compute it, evaluate it at $$x = \dfrac{s}{2},$$ and state the force needed to hold the slab in place.

__(e)__ Test your answer in the limit $$\kappa \to 1.$$ Then resolve a puzzle: in the idealized picture, the field lines between the plates run straight across, perpendicular to the slab's motion — so how can the field pull the slab __in__? The realistic field-line picture below is a hint.

label: PW209
name: The Magnetic Moment of an Orbiting Electron — (USAPhO 2007.) A model of the magnetic properties of materials…
desc: (USAPhO 2007.) A model of the magnetic properties of materials is based on the small magnetic moment generated by each atom, one source of which is the orbital motion of its electrons. Model an atom as a single electron of charge $$-e$$ and mass $$m_e$$ orbiting a single proton…
statement:
(USAPhO 2007.) A model of the magnetic properties of materials is based on the small magnetic moment generated by each atom, one source of which is the orbital motion of its electrons. Model an atom as a single electron of charge $$-e$$ and mass $$m_e$$ orbiting a single proton of charge $$e$$ and mass $$m_p \gg m_e,$$ in a circular orbit of radius $$R$$ lying in the $$x$$-$$y$$ plane. Coulomb's law gives the force between charges $$q_1$$ and $$q_2$$ separated by $$r$$ as $$F = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2},$$ where $$\epsilon_0 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi k}$$ is the permittivity of free space and $$k$$ is the Coulomb constant.

__(a)__ Calculate the net electrostatic force on the electron from the proton, in terms of any or all of $$e, m_e, m_p, R,$$ and $$\epsilon_0.$$

__(b)__ Determine the angular velocity $$\omega_0$$ of the electron around the proton, in terms of any or all of $$e, m_e, R,$$ and $$\epsilon_0.$$

__(c)__ The orbiting electron acts as a tiny current loop. Find the current $$I,$$ and then derive the magnitude of the magnetic field $$B_e$$ at a distance $$z \gg R$$ from the $$x$$-$$y$$ plane along the orbit's axis, in terms of any or all of $$e, m_e, R, \omega_0, z,$$ and $$\mu_0.$$ You may use the on-axis far field of a current loop of radius $$R$$ carrying current $$I$$: $$B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2z^3}.$$

__(d)__ A small bar magnet has a far field along its axis given by $$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 m}{2\pi z^3},$$ where $$z$$ is the distance from the magnet and $$m$$ is its magnetic dipole moment. Assuming the orbiting electron acts like a small bar magnet, find its dipole moment $$m$$ in terms of $$e, R,$$ and $$\omega_0.$$

label: PW209
name: A Microscopic Model of Diamagnetism — (USAPhO 2007, continued.) Model an atom as an electron of charge $$-e$$…
desc: (USAPhO 2007, continued.) Model an atom as an electron of charge $$-e$$ and mass $$m_e$$ in a circular orbit of radius $$R$$ in the $$x$$-$$y$$ plane with angular velocity $$\omega_0;$$ such an orbit is a current loop $$I = \dfrac{e\omega_0}{2\pi}$$ with magnetic dipole moment…
statement:
(USAPhO 2007, continued.) Model an atom as an electron of charge $$-e$$ and mass $$m_e$$ in a circular orbit of radius $$R$$ in the $$x$$-$$y$$ plane with angular velocity $$\omega_0;$$ such an orbit is a current loop $$I = \dfrac{e\omega_0}{2\pi}$$ with magnetic dipole moment of magnitude $$m = \dfrac{e\omega_0 R^2}{2}$$ directed along the orbit's axis. A __diamagnetic__ substance is modeled as $$N$$ such atoms, all with orbits in the $$x$$-$$y$$ plane, exactly half of them orbiting clockwise and half counterclockwise as viewed from the positive $$z$$ axis looking toward the origin.

__(a)__ With no external field applied, what is the total magnetic moment of the substance?

__(b)__ An external magnetic field $$\vec{B}_0 = B_0\hat{z}$$ is now applied. Assume the orbit radius $$R$$ does not change (parts (c) and (d) justify this), and that the resulting change in angular velocity satisfies $$\Delta\omega \ll \omega_0.$$ The centripetal force on each electron must now balance the Coulomb force __plus__ the magnetic force $$evB_0.$$ Determine $$\Delta\omega$$ for both the clockwise and the counterclockwise orbits, in terms of $$e, m_e,$$ and $$B_0$$ only. Which orbits speed up? (Remember that the electron's charge is negative when applying the right-hand rule.)

__(c)__ Suppose the external field is turned on at a constant rate during a time interval $$\Delta t$$ (zero at $$t = 0,$$ reaching $$B_0$$ at $$t = \Delta t$$). Determine the induced emf $$\varepsilon$$ __experienced by the electron__ — that is, the line integral of the induced electric field over the electron's entire path during the whole turn-on time, not just over one orbit. Faraday's law gives the integral around one loop: $$\oint \vec{E}\cdot\mathrm{d}\vec{\ell} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t},$$ where $$\Phi$$ is the magnetic flux through the orbit. Express $$\varepsilon$$ in terms of $$\omega_0, R,$$ and $$B_0.$$

__(d)__ Verify that the change in the electron's kinetic energy $$K = \dfrac{1}{2}m_e\omega^2 R^2$$ satisfies $$\Delta K = e\varepsilon.$$ (This consistency justifies the assumption that $$R$$ does not change.)

__(e)__ Determine the change $$\Delta m_{\mathrm{total}}$$ in the total magnetic moment of the $$N$$ atoms when the field is applied — both its magnitude and its direction relative to $$\vec{B}_0.$$ (Careful: before the field was applied, the total was your answer to part (a). Think about whether the clockwise and counterclockwise changes still cancel.)

__(f)__ If the uniform field is replaced by a bar magnet, is the diamagnetic substance attracted to the magnet or repelled by it? Justify with Lenz's law.

__(g)__ The __magnetization__ $$\vec{M}$$ of a material is its magnetic dipole moment per unit volume. For a weak magnetic response it is proportional to the applied field: $$\vec{M} = \chi\vec{H}$$ with $$\vec{H} \approx \dfrac{\vec{B}_0}{\mu_0},$$ where the dimensionless constant $$\chi$$ is the __magnetic susceptibility__; the material's permeability is then $$\mu = \mu_0(1 + \chi).$$ If the sample occupies volume $$V,$$ find $$\chi$$ and $$\mu$$ for this material.

label: PW210
name: A Wheatstone bridge circuit is used to determine the capacitance $$C_2$$ and leakage…
desc: A Wheatstone bridge circuit is used to determine the capacitance $$C_2$$ and leakage resistance $$R_2$$ of a certain capacitor. The bridge is balanced (meaning no current runs through the ammeter) when a harmonic alternating voltage is applied. It turns out that the balance…
statement: A Wheatstone bridge circuit is used to determine the capacitance $$C_2$$ and leakage resistance $$R_2$$ of a certain capacitor. The bridge is balanced (meaning no current runs through the ammeter) when a harmonic alternating voltage is applied. It turns out that the balance persists even under variations of the voltage frequency. Determine $$C_2$$ and $$R_2$$ in terms of $$R_1, R_3, R_4,$$ and $$L_3.$$

label: PW210
name: The edges of a tetrahedron form an RLC circuit as shown.
desc: The edges of a tetrahedron form an RLC circuit as shown. Two opposite edges are resistors $$R,$$ two opposite edges are capacitors $$C,$$ and two opposite edges are inductors $$L.$$ An alternating voltage with amplitude $$V_0$$ is connected to the circuit at the ends of one of…
statement:
The edges of a tetrahedron form an RLC circuit as shown.

Two opposite edges are resistors $$R,$$ two opposite edges are capacitors $$C,$$ and two opposite edges are inductors $$L.$$

An alternating voltage with amplitude $$V_0$$ is connected to the circuit at the ends of one of the resistors. If the frequency takes the form $$\omega = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},$$ and if additionally $$R = \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}},$$ find the amplitude of the total current through the circuit.

label: PW210
name: Three elements, which can be resistors, capacitors, and inductors, are connected in a…
desc: Three elements, which can be resistors, capacitors, and inductors, are connected in a $$Y$$ circuit as shown. If an AC source is connected to terminals 1 and 2, a voltmeter connected to terminals 1 and 3 displays 80 V. If connected to terminals 2 and 3, the voltmeter displays 45…
statement:
Three elements, which can be resistors, capacitors, and inductors, are connected in a $$Y$$ circuit as shown.

If an AC source is connected to terminals 1 and 2, a voltmeter connected to terminals 1 and 3 displays 80 V. If connected to terminals 2 and 3, the voltmeter displays 45 V.

If the same source is connected to terminals 1 and 3, the voltmeter measures 21 V across 2 and 3 and 28 V across 1 and 2.

If the source is connected to 2 and 3, the voltmeter readings are 21 V across 1 and 2 and 28 V across 1 and 3.

**a)** Determine the source output voltage.

**b)** Identify the elements corresponding to the legs of the $$Y$$ circuit. Is it possible to determine element types unambiguously?

**c)** Determine the ratio of curents $$I_{12}: I_{13} : I_{23}$$ through the AC source when it is connected to terminal 1 and 2, 1 and 3, and 2 and 3.

The source, the voltmeter, and all circuit elements are assumed to be ideal.

label: PW210
name: For the circuit shown in the figure, $$R_1 = 3R, R_2 = R, C_1 = C_2 = C,$$ and $$L_1 =…
desc: For the circuit shown in the figure, $$R_1 = 3R, R_2 = R, C_1 = C_2 = C,$$ and $$L_1 = L_2 = L.$$ The electromotive force of the battery is $$\varepsilon.$$ Initially the switch is closed and the system is operating in a stationary regime. **a)** Find the reading of the…
statement:
For the circuit shown in the figure, $$R_1 = 3R, R_2 = R, C_1 = C_2 = C,$$ and $$L_1 = L_2 = L.$$ The electromotive force of the battery is $$\varepsilon.$$ Initially the switch is closed and the system is operating in a stationary regime.

**a)** Find the reading of the voltmeter in the stationary regime.

**b)** Now, the switch is opened. Find the reading of the voltmeter immediately after the opening.

**c)** Find the total amount of heat which will be dissipated on each of the resistors after opening the switch, and until a new equilibrium state is achieved.

label: PW210
name: **a)** The diode in the above circuit is used to rectify an AC voltage supply. The AC…
desc: **a)** The diode in the above circuit is used to rectify an AC voltage supply. The AC voltage supply at time $$t$$ has the form $$V(t) = V_0 \cos(2\pi f t).$$ It has $$f = 50 \;\mathrm{Hz}$$ and $$V_0 = 20 \;\mathrm{V}.$$ The capacitor has capacitance $$C = 50 \;\mathrm{\mu F}$$…
statement:
**a)** The diode in the above circuit is used to rectify an AC voltage supply. The AC voltage supply at time $$t$$ has the form $$V(t) = V_0 \cos(2\pi f t).$$

It has $$f = 50 \;\mathrm{Hz}$$ and $$V_0 = 20 \;\mathrm{V}.$$ The capacitor has capacitance $$C = 50 \;\mathrm{\mu F}$$ and the resistance $$R,$$ can take the values $$10 \;\mathrm{k}\Omega, 1 \;\mathrm{k}\Omega,$$ and $$100 \;\Omega.$$

Determine the time constants for the discharge of the capacitor for all three values of the resistance.

**b)** Sketch a graph of the voltage form across the resistance for the three values of $$R,$$ superimposing the original AC source on each sketch.

**c)** For the case $$R = 10 \;\mathrm{k}\Omega,$$ deduce a relation for determining the time the diode conducts, $$T_D,$$ in terms of $$f$$ and $$T_1,$$ where $$T_1$$ is the time the capacitor discharge per cycle. Show that it is the solution of the equation $$e^{-T_1/RC} = \cos(2\pi f T_1)$$ and verify that $$T_1 = 0.019125 \;\mathrm{s}.$$

Determine the percentage of time that the diode is conducting.

**d)** Calculate the variation in voltage, from maximum to minimum, for $$R = 10\;\mathrm{k}\Omega.$$

label: PW210
name: Mechanical and electrical processes are sometimes strongly coupled. Very important…
desc: Mechanical and electrical processes are sometimes strongly coupled. Very important examples are systems containing piezoelectric materials, e.g. quartz resonators. Here we investigate a somewhat-simpler situation. There are two metal plates with area $$S$$ and mass $$m.$$ One…
statement:
Mechanical and electrical processes are sometimes strongly coupled. Very important examples are systems containing piezoelectric materials, e.g. quartz resonators. Here we investigate a somewhat-simpler situation.

There are two metal plates with area $$S$$ and mass $$m.$$ One plate is situated atop of the other one. Plates are connected to each other with springs, whose total spring constant is $$k.$$ The springs are made of an insulator. The lower plate is mounted on a steady base. The equilibrium distance between the plates is $$X_0.$$

**a)** Let us assume that there is a small vertical shift $$x$$ of the upper plate from its equilibrium position. Derive the acceleration $$\ddot{x}$$ of $$x$$ in terms of the system parameters. What is the angular frequency $$\omega_0$$ of the small vertical oscillations of the upper plate?

**b)** The plates are now connected to a constant high voltage source, so that they form a capacitor. Electrostatic forces between the plates cause an additional shift of the upper plate. The equilibrium distance between the plates is now $$X_1.$$ Derive expressions of the electrical attractive force $$F_e$$ and voltage applied to the plates $$U$$ in terms of $$X_0, X_1, S, m$$ and $$k.$$

**c)** The system is set to oscillate again, keeping the voltage $$U$$ constant. Let $$x$$ stand still for the shift from the equilibrium position. Derive an expression for the acceleration $$\ddot{x}$$ of $$x$$ in terms of $$X_0, X_1, S, m, k,$$ and $$x.$$ What is the angular frequency $$\omega_1$$ of the upper plate's small vertical oscillations?

label: PW210
name: A voltage rectifier is made according to the circuit depicted in the figure. The load $$R…
desc: A voltage rectifier is made according to the circuit depicted in the figure. The load $$R = 10 \;\mathrm{k}\Omega$$ is fed with DC, equal to $$I = 2 \;\mathrm{mA}.$$ In what follows we approximate the $$V-I$$ characteristic of the diode with the curve depicted in the figure. The…
statement:
A voltage rectifier is made according to the circuit depicted in the figure. The load $$R = 10 \;\mathrm{k}\Omega$$ is fed with DC, equal to $$I = 2 \;\mathrm{mA}.$$ In what follows we approximate the $$V-I$$ characteristic of the diode with the curve depicted in the figure. The relative variation of the current at the load has to satisfy the condition $$\Delta I/I < 1 \%.$$

**a)** Find the average power dissipation at the diode at the working regime of such a circuit.

**b)** Determine the amplitude of the AC voltage (with frequency $$f = 50 \;\mathrm{Hz})$$ which has to be applied at the input of the circuit.

**c)** Find the required capacitance $$C.$$

**d)** Find the average power dissipation at the diode during the first period (of AC input voltage) immediately following the application of AC voltage to the input of the circuit.

label: PW210
name: **a)** The figure below shows an ideal circuit with a battery, emf $$V,$$ a switch $$S,$$…
desc: **a)** The figure below shows an ideal circuit with a battery, emf $$V,$$ a switch $$S,$$ an ammeter $$A$$ of negligible resistance, and a capacitor with capacitance $$C.$$ The switch moves continuously from $$A$$ to $$B,$$ $$n$$ times per second, where $$n$$ is a large integer…
statement:
**a)** The figure below shows an ideal circuit with a battery, emf $$V,$$ a switch $$S,$$ an ammeter $$A$$ of negligible resistance, and a capacitor with capacitance $$C.$$ The switch moves continuously from $$A$$ to $$B,$$ $$n$$ times per second, where $$n$$ is a large integer. Obtain an expression for the average current $$I$$ registered by the ammeter.

**b)** How would this current change if a lead resistance $$R$$ were included with the battery? With the ammeter?

**c)** The expression $$F(t) = \dfrac{4}{\pi}\left( \cos(2\pi f t) - A \cos(6\pi ft) + B \cos(10 \pi f t)\right)$$ is an approximation to a unit square wave of frequency $$f$$ and time $$t,$$ as shown in the figure below.

Find $$A$$ and $$B.$$

label: PW210
name: **a)** Consider the circuit given in the figure below, where the diode can be assumed to…
desc: **a)** Consider the circuit given in the figure below, where the diode can be assumed to be ideal (i.e. have zero resistance for forward current and infinite resistance for reverse current.) The switch is turned on for a time $$\tau_C$$ and then switched off again. The input and…
statement:
**a)** Consider the circuit given in the figure below, where the diode can be assumed to be ideal (i.e. have zero resistance for forward current and infinite resistance for reverse current.)

The switch is turned on for a time $$\tau_C$$ and then switched off again. The input and output voltages are during the whole process constant and equal to $$U_i$$ and $$U_0,$$ respectively, $$(2U_i < U_0).$$

Plot the graphs of input and output currents as a function of time.

**b)** Now the switch is turned on and off periodically. Each time, the switch is kept closed for a time interval $$\tau_C$$ and open for $$\tau_C.$$ Find the average output current.

**c)** Now consider the new circuit shown below. The switch is turned on and off as in part (b). What will be the voltage on the load $$R$$ when a stationary working regime has been reached? You may assume that $$\tau_C \ll RC.$$ I.E. the voltage variation on the load (and capacitor) is negligible during the whole period (i.e. the charge on the capacitor has no time to change significantly.)

label: PW210
name: **a)** An AC power line cable transmits electrical power using a sinusoidal waveform with…
desc: **a)** An AC power line cable transmits electrical power using a sinusoidal waveform with frequency $$60 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ The load receives an RMS voltage of $$500 \;\mathrm{kV}$$ and requires $$1000 \;\mathrm{MW}$$ of average power. For this problem, consider only the cable…
statement:
**a)** An AC power line cable transmits electrical power using a sinusoidal waveform with frequency $$60 \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ The load receives an RMS voltage of $$500 \;\mathrm{kV}$$ and requires $$1000 \;\mathrm{MW}$$ of average power. For this problem, consider only the cable carrying current in one of the two directions, and ignore effects due to capacitance or inductance between the cable and with the ground.

Suppose that the load on the power line cable is a residential area that behaves like a pure resistor. What is the RMS current carried in the cable?

**b)** The cable has diameter $$3 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ is $$500 \;\mathrm{km}$$ long, and is made of aluminum with resistivity $$2.8 \times 10^{-8} \;\mathrm{\Omega \cdot m}.$$ How much power is lost in the wire?

**c)** A local rancher thinks he might be able to extract electrical power from the cable using electromagnetic induction. the rancher constructs a rectangular loop of length $$a$$ and width $$b < a,$$ consisting of $$N$$ turns of wire. One edge of the loop is to be placed on the ground; the wire is straight and runs parallel to the ground at a height $$h$$ much less than the length of the wire. Write the current in the wire as $$I = I_0 \sin\omega t,$$ and assume the return wire is far away. Determine an expression for the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance $$r$$ from the power line cable in terms if $$I, r,$$ and fundamental constants.

**d)** Where should the loop be placed, and how should it be oriented, to maximize the induced emf in the loop?

**e)** Assuming the loop is placed in this way, determine an expression for the emf induced in the loop as a function of time in terms of any or all of $$I_0, h, a, b, N, \omega, t,$$ and fundamental constants.

**f)** Suppose that $$a = 5 \;\mathrm{m}, b = 2 \;\mathrm{m},$$ and $$h = 100 \;\mathrm{m}.$$ How many turns of wire $$N$$ does the rancher need to generate an RMS emf of $$120 \;\mathrm{V}?$$

**g)** The load at the end of the power line cable changes to include a manufacturing plant with a large number of electric motors. While the average power consumed remains the same, it now behaves like a resistor in parallel with a $$0.25 \;\mathrm{H}$$ inductor. Does the power lost in the power line cable increase, decrease, or stay the same?

**h)** The power company wishes to make the load behave as it originally did by installing a capacitor in parallel with the load. What should be its capacitance?

label: PW210
name: Current and Resonance in a Driven RLC Circuit — A resistor $$R,$$ an inductor $$L,$$ and a capacitor $$C$$…
desc: A resistor $$R,$$ an inductor $$L,$$ and a capacitor $$C$$ are connected in series with an AC source whose voltage is $$V(t) = V_0 \cos\omega t,$$ as shown below. Use the method of __complex impedance__: represent the source by the complex voltage $$V_0 e^{i\omega t}$$ (the…
statement:
A resistor $$R,$$ an inductor $$L,$$ and a capacitor $$C$$ are connected in series with an AC source whose voltage is $$V(t) = V_0 \cos\omega t,$$ as shown below.

Use the method of __complex impedance__: represent the source by the complex voltage $$V_0 e^{i\omega t}$$ (the physical voltage is the real part), and represent each element by its impedance, $$Z_R = R,$$ $$Z_L = i\omega L,$$ $$Z_C = \dfrac{-i}{\omega C}.$$ Impedances combine in series and in parallel by the same rules as resistances, and the complex form of Ohm's law, $$V = IZ,$$ holds for each element and for the circuit as a whole.

__(a)__ Find the total impedance $$Z$$ of the circuit and its magnitude $$|Z|.$$ Use it to write the amplitude $$I_0$$ of the steady-state current in terms of $$V_0, R, L, C,$$ and $$\omega.$$

__(b)__ At what driving frequency $$\omega_0$$ is the current amplitude largest (the __resonance__ frequency), and what is the current amplitude there?

__(c)__ Write the steady-state current as $$I(t) = I_0\cos(\omega t - \phi)$$ and find $$\tan\phi.$$ For $$\omega < \omega_0,$$ does the current lead or lag the source voltage? For $$\omega > \omega_0?$$ Which element "dominates" the circuit in each regime?

__(d)__ Using the impedances evaluated at $$\omega_0,$$ show that an inductor and capacitor in __series__ act as a short circuit (zero impedance) at resonance, while an inductor and capacitor in __parallel__ act as an open circuit (infinite impedance). These two facts are worth memorizing.

label: PW210
name: The Q-Factor from Dimensional Analysis — A non-driven RLC circuit contains exactly three dimensional…
desc: A non-driven RLC circuit contains exactly three dimensional quantities: the resistance $$R,$$ the inductance $$L,$$ and the capacitance $$C.$$ Recall the complex impedances $$Z_R = R,$$ $$Z_L = i\omega L,$$ and $$Z_C = \dfrac{-i}{\omega C},$$ where $$\omega$$ is an angular…
statement:
A non-driven RLC circuit contains exactly three dimensional quantities: the resistance $$R,$$ the inductance $$L,$$ and the capacitance $$C.$$ Recall the complex impedances $$Z_R = R,$$ $$Z_L = i\omega L,$$ and $$Z_C = \dfrac{-i}{\omega C},$$ where $$\omega$$ is an angular frequency. Since impedances can be added to one another, all three expressions have the same dimensions (ohms).

__(a)__ Using only the impedance formulas, find a combination of $$L$$ and $$C$$ alone (no $$\omega,$$ no $$R$$) with the dimensions of resistance, and a combination of $$L$$ and $$C$$ alone with the dimensions of time.

__(b)__ Construct a dimensionless parameter of the circuit built from $$R, L,$$ and $$C$$ only. (Quantities like $$Z_R/Z_L$$ are dimensionless but involve $$\omega,$$ which is not a property of the circuit itself, so they do not count.) Is your parameter unique?

__(c)__ In circuit analysis one often hears statements like "when $$R$$ is small, the circuit rings for many cycles." Explain why a criterion like "$$R < 5\;\Omega$$ counts as small" cannot possibly be correct, and state what "$$R$$ is small" must actually mean for an RLC circuit.

label: PW210
name: Non-Dimensionalizing the RLC Circuit Equation — Dimensional analysis of an RLC circuit can be pushed further…
desc: Dimensional analysis of an RLC circuit can be pushed further: the circuit's full differential equation can be rewritten so that __every__ quantity in it is dimensionless. This technique, called __non-dimensionalizing__ the equation, shows exactly which parameters control the…
statement:
Dimensional analysis of an RLC circuit can be pushed further: the circuit's full differential equation can be rewritten so that __every__ quantity in it is dimensionless. This technique, called __non-dimensionalizing__ the equation, shows exactly which parameters control the physics. Consider the series RLC circuit below, driven by the voltage $$V_0\cos\omega t.$$

Let $$q$$ be the charge on the capacitor, so the current is $$I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}.$$ The voltage drops across the elements are $$IR$$ (resistor), $$L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}$$ (inductor), and $$\dfrac{q}{C}$$ (capacitor).

__(a)__ Apply Kirchhoff's loop rule to derive the differential equation $$V_0\cos\omega t = L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + R\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{q}{C}.$$

__(b)__ Define the characteristic time $$\tau = \sqrt{LC},$$ the dimensionless time $$t' = \dfrac{t}{\tau},$$ the characteristic charge $$q_0 = CV_0,$$ and the dimensionless charge $$\tilde{q} = \dfrac{q}{q_0}.$$ Show first that $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{1}{\tau}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t'},$$ then rewrite the entire equation in the dimensionless variables. Show that if the circuit is driven at its natural frequency $$\omega = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},$$ the result is $$\cos t' = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2\tilde{q}}{\mathrm{d}t'^2} + \dfrac{1}{Q}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{q}}{\mathrm{d}t'} + \tilde{q},$$ where $$Q = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}}$$ is the Q-factor.

__(c)__ Now remove the driving ($$V_0$$ appears only through the scale $$q_0,$$ so keep the scales and set the left side to zero): $$0 = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2\tilde{q}}{\mathrm{d}t'^2} + \dfrac{1}{Q}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{q}}{\mathrm{d}t'} + \tilde{q}.$$ A free RLC circuit can be __overdamped__, __critically damped__, or __underdamped__. Explain why which regime occurs can depend on nothing except $$Q,$$ and find the value of $$Q$$ separating the regimes.

__(d)__ Two RLC circuits have wildly different values of $$R, L,$$ and $$C,$$ but the same $$Q.$$ In what sense do the two circuits behave identically? In particular, how are plots of their free oscillations $$q(t)$$ related? What does this say about questions like "how many times does the circuit oscillate before its amplitude is cut in half"?

label: PW210
name: The Power Consumed by a Mystery Device — An electrical device $$D$$ is connected in series with a…
desc: An electrical device $$D$$ is connected in series with a $$100\;\Omega$$ resistor to a $$220\;\mathrm{V}$$ AC network, as shown below. An ideal ammeter in the loop reads $$I = 0.5\;\mathrm{A},$$ and an ideal voltmeter across the device reads $$V_D = 200\;\mathrm{V}.$$ All three…
statement:
An electrical device $$D$$ is connected in series with a $$100\;\Omega$$ resistor to a $$220\;\mathrm{V}$$ AC network, as shown below. An ideal ammeter in the loop reads $$I = 0.5\;\mathrm{A},$$ and an ideal voltmeter across the device reads $$V_D = 200\;\mathrm{V}.$$ All three values ($$220\;\mathrm{V},$$ $$0.5\;\mathrm{A},$$ $$200\;\mathrm{V}$$) are RMS values, as AC meters report. What is the device's power consumption? (Quantum Magazine, Vol. 3, No. 3.)

Useful fact: when a sinusoidal current and voltage differ in phase by $$\phi,$$ the average power delivered is $$P = V_{\mathrm{rms}} I_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos\phi.$$ Recall also that a circuit element with complex impedance $$Z$$ obeys $$V = IZ$$ with phasor voltages and currents, and that impedances in series add.

__(a)__ Warm-up: if the device were removed and replaced by a bare wire, what current would the ammeter show? What does the actual reading tell you about the device?

__(b)__ Suppose the device were a pure resistor $$R_D.$$ Find the value of $$R_D$$ required to produce the measured current, then compute the voltmeter reading that this hypothesis predicts. Conclude that the device cannot be a pure resistor.

__(c)__ Instead assume the device has a complex impedance $$Z_D = A + iB.$$ Use the two meter readings to find $$A$$ and $$|B|.$$ Can the sign of $$B$$ (inductive versus capacitive) be determined from these measurements?

__(d)__ Find the phase $$\phi$$ between the network voltage and the current, then compute the total average power drawn from the network, the power dissipated in the $$100\;\Omega$$ resistor, and finally the power consumed by the device.

__(e)__ Now re-solve the problem with almost no algebra. The resistor's voltage phasor (length $$IR,$$ in phase with the current) and the device's voltage phasor (length $$200\;\mathrm{V},$$ at some angle $$\phi_D$$ to the current) must add __as vectors__ to the network's $$220\;\mathrm{V}$$ phasor, as in the diagram below. Use the law of cosines to find $$\cos\phi_D,$$ and compute the device's power directly as $$P_D = I V_D \cos\phi_D.$$

label: PW211
name: **a)** The figure below shows an output pattern that was measured by a tiny microphone…
desc: **a)** The figure below shows an output pattern that was measured by a tiny microphone when two small piezo-loudspeakers separated by $$15 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ were pointed toward the microphone at a distance of $$1.5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ away. Given that the speed of sound was $$343…
statement:
**a)** The figure below shows an output pattern that was measured by a tiny microphone when two small piezo-loudspeakers separated by $$15 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ were pointed toward the microphone at a distance of $$1.5 \;\mathrm{m}$$ away. Given that the speed of sound was $$343 \;\mathrm{m/s}$$ in the room where the data were taken, estimate the frequency at which the speakers were driven.

**b)** Explain why the interference pattern has a central minimum.

label: PW211
name: A white light shines vertically down on a horizontal CD ROM disc. The disc is viewed by a…
desc: A white light shines vertically down on a horizontal CD ROM disc. The disc is viewed by a teacher whose eye is a horizontal distance $$0.50 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from the disc and $$0.35 \;\mathrm{m}$$ vertically above its horizontal plane, as shown below. A yellow light of wavelength…
statement:
A white light shines vertically down on a horizontal CD ROM disc. The disc is viewed by a teacher whose eye is a horizontal distance $$0.50 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from the disc and $$0.35 \;\mathrm{m}$$ vertically above its horizontal plane, as shown below.

A yellow light of wavelength $$590 \;\mathrm{nm}$$ is observed due to first order diffraction.

**a)** Deduce the spacing $$d$$ between adjacent tracks of the CD ROM.

**b)** The CD ROM is tilted clockwise, through an angle of $$5^\circ.$$ Determine the wavelength now observed.

label: PW211
name: A Newton's rings interference experiment uses a plano-convex lens resting on a glass…
desc: A Newton's rings interference experiment uses a plano-convex lens resting on a glass plate with light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ incident normally on the lens as shown below. The curvature of the lens is very slight, so you may ignore refraction. **a)** Derive the conditions for…
statement:
A Newton's rings interference experiment uses a plano-convex lens resting on a glass plate with light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ incident normally on the lens as shown below.

The curvature of the lens is very slight, so you may ignore refraction.

**a)** Derive the conditions for constructive and destructive interference resulting from a region where the air gap has thickness $$t.$$

**b)** A constructive interference ring, resulting from light passing through the air gap of thickness $$t,$$ has a radius $$r.$$ Show that the radius of curvature of the lens, $$a,$$ is given by the equation $$r^2 = 2at - t^2.$$

**c)** By neglecting $$t^2$$ in the above formula, derive a formula for $$a$$ in terms of $$r$$ and the order of interference, $$n,$$ that is independent of $$t$$ for the case in which the $$n$$th order destructive interference ring has radius $$r.$$

**d)** If, using sodium light of wavelength $$\lambda = 598 \;\mathrm{nm},$$ the diameter of the $$n$$ th order constructive interference ring is $$0.582 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ and that of the $$(n+20)$$th has diameter $$1.36 \;\mathrm{cm},$$ calculate the radius of curvature of the lens.

**e)** If, in $$5.0 \;\mathrm{s},$$ the air gap between the lens and the plate is filled with methyl alcohol of refractive index $$\mu = 1.33,$$ what are the average speeds at which the radii of the constructive interference rings increase in **(d)** in this time interval?

label: PW211
name: When light passes through a very narrow slit it diffracts. This means that the light…
desc: When light passes through a very narrow slit it diffracts. This means that the light spreads out and forms a pattern with bright and dark spots on a distant screen. Some examples of these patterns are shown below, with magnified images of the slits that generated them to the…
statement:
When light passes through a very narrow slit it diffracts. This means that the light spreads out and forms a pattern with bright and dark spots on a distant screen. Some examples of these patterns are shown below, with magnified images of the slits that generated them to the right.

The wavelength of the light and the distance from the slit to the screen were kept constant in these images.

The width of the central bright region is • proportional to the wavelength of the light • proportional to the distance from the slit to the screen • inversely proportional to the width of the slit.

**a)** Red light of wavelength $$650 \;\mathrm{nm}$$ is shone though a slit of width $$3.0 \times 10^{-4} \;\mathrm{m}$$ onto a screen $$1.20 \;\mathrm{m}$$ from the slit and produces the pattern labelled “(a)” below.

Exactly one of the slit width, wavelength, or distance to screen was changed to produce the pattern labelled “(b)” above. For each possible parameter below find its required value to make pattern “(b)”:

(i) slit width, (ii) wavelength, (iii) distance from the slit to the screen.

**b)** A diffraction pattern from a different single slit is shown below. Draw a possible single slit which could have produced this pattern.

**c)** When a narrow slit is replaced by a small rectangular aperture (hole) the light spreads out in all directions and forms a pattern such as the one below. This is shown in the first row of the table.

Draw diagrams to fill in the blanks of diffraction patterns or aperture shapes in the table.

**d)** Explain why the width of the central bright region is proportional to the distance from the slit to the screen.

label: PW211
name: A soap film has index of refraction $$n = 1.45.$$
desc: A soap film has index of refraction $$n = 1.45.$$ The film is contained in a vertical wire frame that has a wedged-shaped profile as seen from the side. The film drains under gravity, so it is thicker at the bottom than at the top. At the top, its thickness can be considered…
statement:
A soap film has index of refraction $$n = 1.45.$$

The film is contained in a vertical wire frame that has a wedged-shaped profile as seen from the side.

The film drains under gravity, so it is thicker at the bottom than at the top. At the top, its thickness can be considered zero.

The film is viewed, by reflection, with red and violet light at near normal incidence. Interference results from light reflected from the outer surface and that emerging after reflection at the inner surface of the film. The optical path difference between the two rays can be determined, to a good approximation, by assuming the film is of constant thickness, $$t,$$ in the region of these two reflections. This is illustrated below.

$$t$$ will increase with position down the film. The first violet (wavelength $$420 \;\mathrm{nm})$$ constructive interference band is observed at distance $$x_v = 3.0 \;\mathrm{cm}$$ from the top edge of the film. The wavelength of the red light is $$680\;\mathrm{nm}.$$

Determine:

**a)** the thickness of the film at the lowest order constructive violet interference band, $$t_v.$$

**b)** the film wedge angle $$\phi$$ in degrees.

**c)** for the red light, the lowest order constructive interference film thickness, $$t_R,$$ and distance $$x_R$$ from the top of the film.

**d)** The soap film drains so that $$\phi$$ decreases by $$8.3 \times 10^{-5}$$ degrees per minute. Determine the initial speed, $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x_v}{\mathrm{d}t},$$ in $$\;\mathrm{cm/min},$$ of the observed violet interference fringe by considering a small time interval $$\Delta t$$ in which $$\phi$$ changes by $$\Delta \phi$$ and $$x_v$$ change by $$\Delta x_v.$$

One possible approach is to first show $$x_v \Delta \phi + \phi \Delta x_v = 0.$$

label: PW211
name: **note:** This problem provides a review of geometric optics and Fermat's principle of…
