desc: **note:** This problem provides a review of geometric optics and Fermat's principle of least time, but not interference and diffraction. In 1838, Samuel Birley Rowbotham placed a series of poles of known height in the Old Bedford River in England. Rowbotham found that light rays…
statement:
**note:** This problem provides a review of geometric optics and Fermat's principle of least time, but not interference and diffraction.

In 1838, Samuel Birley Rowbotham placed a series of poles of known height in the Old Bedford River in England. Rowbotham found that light rays traveled at a constant distance above the surface of the lake over the course of six miles, and concluded that the Earth is flat.

**a)** Qualitatively explain why light may travel a long distance across the surface of the Earth remaining at approximately the same elevation, when traveling in a straight line would result in gaining elevation due to the Earth curving away underneath the path of the light.

**b)** Estimate the temperature gradient in air, in degrees $$K$$ per meter, needed for light to follow a path with the same radius of curvature as Earth. You can take the index of refraction of air to be $$1.0003$$ at one atmosphere and $$300\;\mathrm{K},$$ and to vary linearly with the density of air. You may assume that difference in the density of air due to temperature are much larger than those due to differences in pressure. The radius of Earth is $$R \approx 6.4 \times 10^6 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

When driving on a hot road, one often sees a mirage.

We will assume you are driving on a perfectly flat road.

**c)** Suppose your eye is at point $$E.$$ There is some point $$B$$ which is the furthest point along the road at which light from the road still reaches your eye.

Suppose the index of refraction at the air just above the road is $$n_B.$$ What is the index of refraction of the air at your eye, $$n_E?$$ Give your answer in terms of the the angle $$\theta_E$$ that light makes with the vertical as it enters your eye.

**d)** Suppose that, due to the atmosphere, the speed of light decreases linearly with height above the road. What is the trajectory of a light ray?

label: PW211
name: Consider an opaque barrier in the $$x-y$$ plane at $$z = 0,$$ with a single slit along…
desc: Consider an opaque barrier in the $$x-y$$ plane at $$z = 0,$$ with a single slit along the $$x$$ axis of width $$2a,$$ but with regions on either side of the slit each with width $$2a$$ which are partially transparent, designed to reduce the intensity by a factor of $$2.$$ When…
statement:
Consider an opaque barrier in the $$x-y$$ plane at $$z = 0,$$ with a single slit along the $$x$$ axis of width $$2a,$$ but with regions on either side of the slit each with width $$2a$$ which are partially transparent, designed to reduce the intensity by a factor of $$2.$$ When this barrier is illuminated by a plane wave in the $$z$$ direction, the amplitude of the oscillating field at $$z = 0$$ is $$f(x,y)e^{i\omega t}$$ for \begin{aligned} f(x,y) & = 1 ;& |y| < a \\ f(x,y) & = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ;& a < |y| < 3a \\ f(x,y) & = 0 ; & 3a < |y| \end{aligned}

Near the slit, this just produces a beam which is less intense by a factor of two on the edges. Far away, however, the diffraction pattern is quite different from that of the single slit. At a fixed large distance $$R = \sqrt{y^2 + z^2}$$ away from the slit, the intensity as a function of $$\xi = k_y a = \dfrac{\omega y a}{cR}$$ is shown in the figure below for positive $$\xi.$$

The value of the peak of $$\xi = 0$$ is normalized to $$1,$$ but has been suppressed in the graph to show the details of the secondary maxima.

**a)** Find the smallest positive value of $$\xi$$ for which the intensity vanishes.

**b)** Find the ratio of the intensity at $$\xi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$$ to that at $$\xi = 0.$$

**note**: This problem will be continued in class 13 on polarization.

label: PW211
name: **note** Portions of this problem concern diffraction, while other portions preview…
desc: **note** Portions of this problem concern diffraction, while other portions preview concepts of electromagnetic radiation we will study in more detail next class. It has been proposed that tiny probes could be sent to other stars by accelerating them away from Earth using a…
statement:
**note** Portions of this problem concern diffraction, while other portions preview concepts of electromagnetic radiation we will study in more detail next class.

It has been proposed that tiny probes could be sent to other stars by accelerating them away from Earth using a powerful laser.

**a)** To push the probe hard enough for it to reach other solar systems will require a large laser focused on the sail of a small probe. One way of focusing the laser is to make use of existing optics by using a telescope in reverse. Given a telescope of diameter $$D$$ emitting a laser beam of wavelength $$\lambda$$ and a probe sail of diameter $$d,$$ what is the distance $$R$$ the probe can get before less the 90% of the light hits the sail? How far is this for a sail of size $$1 \;\mathrm{m},$$ a telescope diameter of $$10 \;\mathrm{m},$$ and a laser wavelength of $$600 \;\mathrm{nm}?$$ (You may give an estimate; a precise calculation is not needed.)

**b)** Assume that when the monochromatic laser light hits the sail of the probe at right angles it has power $$W.$$ What is the force $$F$$ exerted on a black (perfectly absorbing) sail and a silvered (perfectly reflective) sail?

**c)** Using your previous expression, find the time it would take a probe of mass $$m$$ to travel a distance $$L.$$ For simplification, you may assume that the probe feels the full force of the laser beam up to a distance $$R,$$ and nothing after that, and that it has a perfectly reflective sail. The proposal calls for the probe to have mass $$10^{-3} \;\mathrm{kg},$$ the laser power to be $$100 \;\mathrm{GW},$$ and for the probe to go to Alpha Centauri, which is $$4.2$$ light years away. Using the optics described in the first part, how long will this take?

**d)** One way of reducing this time considerably is to increase $$R$$ by using a different optical set up. Rather than using one telescope, several telescopes could on different bits of land could be used together in order to create an interference pattern. What is the maximum possible effective diameter of such a setup? What would be the travel time to Alpha Centauri under this setup? (Only an approximate answer is desired.)

label: PW211
name: A point source $$S$$ emits coherent light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ isotropically in all…
desc: A point source $$S$$ emits coherent light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ isotropically in all directions. This means the wavefronts are concentric spheres. The waves reflect from a dielectric surface placed at a distance $$l = N\lambda$$ (where $$N$$ is a large integer) from the…
statement:
A point source $$S$$ emits coherent light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ isotropically in all directions. This means the wavefronts are concentric spheres.

The waves reflect from a dielectric surface placed at a distance $$l = N\lambda$$ (where $$N$$ is a large integer) from the point source, and the interference pattern is observed on a screen which is placed a distance $$L \gg l$$ from the point source, as shown below.

In what follows we use the $$x, y,$$ and $$z$$ coordinates as defined in the figure. The screen is parallel to the mirror and lies in the $$y-z$$ plane.

**a)** At which values of the $$y$$ coordinate (for $$z=0)$$ are the interference maxima observed on the screen? You may assume that $$y \ll L.$$

**b)** Sketch the shape of the few smallest-sized interference maxima on the screen (in the $$y-z$$ plane).

**c)** Now imagine that the flat screen is replaced with a spherical screen of radius $$L,$$ centered around the point source. How many interference maxima can be observed?

label: PW211
name: Monochromatic light can be focused into a point using a holographic lens (better known as…
desc: Monochromatic light can be focused into a point using a holographic lens (better known as a __Fresnel zone plate__). This is a thin film which has a system of opaque and transparent concentric rings: the opaque rings obstruct those light waves which would arrive at the focus in…
statement:
Monochromatic light can be focused into a point using a holographic lens (better known as a __Fresnel zone plate__). This is a thin film which has a system of opaque and transparent concentric rings: the opaque rings obstruct those light waves which would arrive at the focus in the opposite phase (as compared with the light from the transparent rings). In what follows, let us assume that the diameter and focal length of such a lens are $$d = f = 10 \;\mathrm{cm}.$$ The wavelength of the monochromatic incident light radiation is $$\lambda = 5\times 10^{-7} \;\mathrm{m}.$$

**a)** Starting enumeration from the opaque center of the lens, what is the radius of the $$m$$th transparent ring (more precisely, the circle at the middle of the ring)?

**b)** Let us consider also a glass lens of the same focal length $$f$$ and diameter $$d$$, such that a parallel incident beam is collected perfectly into the focus. (The lens has aspherical surfaces.) What is the minimal possible thickness of such a lens if the coefficient of refraction of the glass is $$n = 1.5?$$

**c)** If a short light pulse falls onto a lens, the behavior of the holographic lens is very different from that of the glass lens. Indeed, if we ignore the dispersion of the glass (the dependence of $$n$$ on the wavelength,) the pulse duration at the focus of the glass lens is the same as that of the incident beam. Meanwhile, in the case of a short pulse ($$\tau = 3\times 10^{-14} \;\mathrm{s}),$$ the pulse durations at the focus of the holographic lens become significantly dilated. Sketch qualitatively the light intensity $$I$$ at the focus of the holographic lens as a function of time. A scale is required for time $$t,$$ but not for $$i.$$ The speed of light is $$c = 3 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

label: PW211
name: Adding Two Waves Out of Phase — Two waves are given by $$\Psi_1(x,t) = A \sin(kx - \omega t)$$ and…
desc: Two waves are given by $$\Psi_1(x,t) = A \sin(kx - \omega t)$$ and $$\Psi_2(x,t) = A \sin(kx - \omega t + \phi).$$ The __intensity__ of a wave is the power it delivers per unit area. For essentially every kind of wave, the intensity is proportional to the __square of the…
statement:
Two waves are given by $$\Psi_1(x,t) = A \sin(kx - \omega t)$$ and $$\Psi_2(x,t) = A \sin(kx - \omega t + \phi).$$ The __intensity__ of a wave is the power it delivers per unit area. For essentially every kind of wave, the intensity is proportional to the __square of the amplitude__. (For an electromagnetic wave this follows from energy densities: the energy density of an electric field is proportional to the square of the field strength — as in the capacitor energy $$\frac12 CV^2$$ — and likewise the energy density of a magnetic field is proportional to the square of the field strength, as in the inductor energy $$\frac12 LI^2.$$)

__(a)__ When the two waves are superimposed, the intensity is twice as great as either wave's intensity individually. What is $$\phi?$$

__(b)__ A __phasor diagram__ represents each wave as a vector whose length is the amplitude, with the angle between the vectors equal to the phase difference. The diagram below shows the first wave along the horizontal axis and the second wave at angle $$\phi$$ to it; the resultant amplitude $$A'$$ is the length of the vector sum. Use the law of cosines on this diagram to find $$A'^2$$ in terms of $$A$$ and $$\phi,$$ and then write the intensity $$I(\phi)$$ of the superposed wave in terms of the intensity $$I_0$$ of a single wave.

__(c)__ Describe the plot of $$I$$ as a function of $$\phi.$$ What is the maximum height of the plot, in units of $$I_0,$$ and at which values of $$\phi$$ does the intensity vanish?

label: PW211
name: The Colors of a Soap Film — The photograph below shows __thin-film interference__ in a soap film illuminated…
desc: The photograph below shows __thin-film interference__ in a soap film illuminated by white light (a mix of all visible colors). Some light reflects off the front surface of the film and some reflects off the back surface; the two reflections interfere, and the colors come from…
statement:
The photograph below shows __thin-film interference__ in a soap film illuminated by white light (a mix of all visible colors). Some light reflects off the front surface of the film and some reflects off the back surface; the two reflections interfere, and the colors come from the wavelengths that interfere constructively. The film drains downward under gravity, so it is thinnest at the top.

Take the film to have thickness $$t$$ and index of refraction $$n,$$ illuminated at normal incidence by light of vacuum wavelength $$\lambda.$$ You will need one fact about reflections: when light reflects off a medium with a __higher__ index of refraction, its phase shifts by $$\pi$$; when it reflects off a medium with a __lower__ index of refraction, there is no phase shift.

__(a)__ The index of refraction is defined so that the wave speed inside the film is $$c/n.$$ Show that the wavelength inside the film is $$\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{n}.$$

__(b)__ Which of the two reflections (front surface, back surface) undergoes a $$\pi$$ phase shift? If the film is much thinner than a wavelength, what does the reflected light look like, and what happens to the incident light instead? Use this to explain why the film in the photograph is black at the very top — and to determine whether the light source is on the camera's side of the film or behind it.

__(c)__ Combine three effects — the round trip through the film, the shortened wavelength inside the film, and the reflection phase shift — to find the condition on $$t$$ for constructive interference of the reflected light. What is the smallest film thickness that gives constructive interference?

__(d)__ Explain briefly why different horizontal bands of the film show different colors.

label: PW211
name: Oil on a Wet Road: Interference at an Angle — After a rain, a thin layer of oil floating on water in a…
desc: After a rain, a thin layer of oil floating on water in a parking lot shows colorful interference bands: Light reflects off the top surface of the oil and off the oil-water surface beneath, and the two reflections interfere. Assume the index of refraction of the oil is between…
statement:
After a rain, a thin layer of oil floating on water in a parking lot shows colorful interference bands:

Light reflects off the top surface of the oil and off the oil-water surface beneath, and the two reflections interfere. Assume the index of refraction of the oil is between that of air and that of water, so __both__ reflections are off a medium of higher index; both then suffer the same $$\pi$$ phase flip, and the reflections introduce no relative phase difference. Unlike a soap film viewed face-on, here the light arrives at an __angle__, which lengthens the path through the film. The diagram below shows the geometry: light hits the top surface at $$A$$ at angle of incidence $$\theta_1$$ (measured from the normal); part reflects, and part refracts to angle $$\theta_2,$$ crosses the film of thickness $$d$$ and index $$n,$$ reflects off the bottom at $$B,$$ and exits at $$C$$ parallel to the first reflected ray. Point $$D$$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $$C$$ to the ray reflected at $$A.$$ Take the index of air to be $$1,$$ so Snell's law reads $$\sin\theta_1 = n\sin\theta_2.$$

Because the destination of the light (your eye, meters away) is enormously far compared to the film thickness (microns), the two parallel outgoing rays can be treated as meeting at the same faraway point, with $$D$$ and $$C$$ equidistant from it. So the phase difference at your eye is set by comparing the path $$ABC$$ (through the oil) with the path $$AD$$ (through the air).

__(a)__ The quantity to compare is not geometric length but __optical path length__: the physical length of a path multiplied by the index of refraction of the medium it passes through. Explain why multiplying by $$n$$ (rather than, say, dividing) gives the quantity that controls the phase.

__(b)__ Find the length $$|ABC|$$ in terms of $$d$$ and $$\theta_2,$$ and the length $$|AD|$$ in terms of $$d,$$ $$\theta_1,$$ and $$\theta_2.$$

__(c)__ Show that the optical path difference between the two routes simplifies to $$\mathrm{OPD} = 2nd\cos\theta_2,$$ and write the condition for constructive interference.

__(d)__ If you walk past the oil splotch, or crouch down next to it, you sweep your viewing angle $$\theta_1$$ through a wide range — yet the colors barely shift. Taking $$n = 1.5,$$ find the full range of possible values of $$\cos\theta_2$$ as $$\theta_1$$ ranges from $$0$$ to $$\pi/2,$$ and use it to explain why.

label: PW211
name: Two Radio Receivers Watch the Sun — (British Physics Olympiad, 2003.) A radio telescope has two receivers…
desc: (British Physics Olympiad, 2003.) A radio telescope has two receivers $$50\;\mathrm{m}$$ apart on an East-West line on the equator. On March 21st at noon, it records the radio signals from the Sun at a wavelength of $$0.75\;\mathrm{m}.$$ The amplitudes of the signals received…
statement:
(British Physics Olympiad, 2003.) A radio telescope has two receivers $$50\;\mathrm{m}$$ apart on an East-West line on the equator. On March 21st at noon, it records the radio signals from the Sun at a wavelength of $$0.75\;\mathrm{m}.$$ The amplitudes of the signals received are fed through equal lengths of cable, added together, and amplified, with coherence of the signals maintained. The figure shows the resultant intensity $$I$$ as a function of the time $$t$$ elapsed after 12 noon. Determine the time interval between adjacent maxima around noon.

(Background: pairing distant receivers like this is the principle behind telescope arrays such as the Very Large Array — two receivers a distance $$d$$ apart act like pieces of one giant telescope of size $$d.$$)

__(a)__ The problem says "coherence of the signals being maintained." Two sources are __coherent__ when their relative phase stays fixed rather than drifting randomly. Explain why coherence between the two receivers' signals is essential here, and why the cables being exactly equal in length matters less than their lengths being stable.

__(b)__ Why does the problem specify March 21st at noon, and why is the intensity a maximum at that moment?

__(c)__ Later, the Sun's direction makes a small angle $$\theta$$ with the vertical. Using the diagram below, find the difference in the path lengths from the Sun to the two receivers in terms of the separation $$d$$ and $$\theta,$$ and write the condition on $$\theta$$ for the next intensity maximum.

__(d)__ The Earth rotates through $$2\pi$$ radians in $$24$$ hours. Find the time interval between adjacent maxima.

label: PW211
name: Coherence: Sunlight, Slits, and DVDs — Two sources are __coherent__ when their relative phase stays fixed in…
desc: Two sources are __coherent__ when their relative phase stays fixed in time; interference fringes can only be observed between coherent sources. Every light source has a __coherence length__: the maximum separation over which the light still maintains a fixed phase relationship…
statement:
Two sources are __coherent__ when their relative phase stays fixed in time; interference fringes can only be observed between coherent sources. Every light source has a __coherence length__: the maximum separation over which the light still maintains a fixed phase relationship with itself. A typical laser has a coherence length of roughly $$20\;\mathrm{cm},$$ while sunlight has a coherence length of only about $$30\;\mathrm{\mu m}.$$

__(a)__ You cut two slits, a few millimeters apart, in a piece of paper and shine direct sunlight on them. You see no interference fringes on a screen behind the paper. Explain precisely what goes wrong. In particular, explain why a __constant__ phase lag between the light at the two slits would not destroy the fringes, but what sunlight actually does at this slit separation does destroy them.

__(b)__ Yet interference effects from sunlight are common: oil films on parking lots show colored fringes, and tilting a CD or DVD in sunlight shows a rainbow (an interference effect between adjacent data tracks, which act like slits about a micron apart). Why does sunlight produce visible interference in these cases but not in case (a)?

__(c)__ Thomas Young's original double-slit experiment used sunlight and slits much farther apart than the coherence length of sunlight — and it worked. The trick appears in sketches of his setup as an extra initial slit, $$S_0,$$ placed before the double slit:

Explain why passing the sunlight through a single narrow slit first makes the light at the two slits $$S_1$$ and $$S_2$$ coherent.

label: PW211
name: The Bright Spot in the Shadow — __Diffraction__ is interference in which the sources form a continuous region…
desc: __Diffraction__ is interference in which the sources form a continuous region rather than one or two points. The fundamental tool is __Huygens' principle__: every point along a wavefront can be considered the source of a new outgoing spherical wave; the wave farther on is the…
statement:
__Diffraction__ is interference in which the sources form a continuous region rather than one or two points. The fundamental tool is __Huygens' principle__: every point along a wavefront can be considered the source of a new outgoing spherical wave; the wave farther on is the superposition of all these wavelets.

__(a)__ A coherent light source (a laser) shines on a small opaque round disk, with the light arriving as a plane wave traveling along the disk's symmetry axis. The light continues to a screen, where the disk casts a shadow. According to Huygens' principle, the sources to sum over are all the illuminated points around the disk — in particular, the points just outside the disk's rim. What does this predict at the exact center of the shadow, and why? (This question has a famous history: Poisson, an opponent of the wave theory of light, derived this prediction from Fresnel's wave theory believing it absurd — and then Arago did the experiment.) A real photograph of the result:

__(b)__ Below is a series of theoretically calculated diffraction patterns of disks of different sizes, with everything else held fixed. By direct observation, the central spot gets larger from left to right. Are the disks that generated these patterns arranged from larger to smaller, or smaller to larger? State the general rule relating the size of a diffracting object to the size of its diffraction pattern, and give one other example of the rule.

__(c)__ A typical laboratory setup for observing the spot is shown below. If the laser is moved off to the side so the light comes in at a slight angle, the spot moves across the screen — so the disk acts as a crude telescope, reporting the direction of the incoming light. You can locate the spot's center only to about the spot's own size. Explain why a __small__ disk makes a poor telescope, and state the resulting rule of thumb (the __resolution limit__) for the smallest angle $$\Delta\theta$$ that a device of size $$d$$ can resolve using waves of wavelength $$\lambda.$$

label: PW211
name: How Many Pixels Can You See? — How far away do you have to hold an iPhone before it is physically impossible…
desc: How far away do you have to hold an iPhone before it is physically impossible for adding more pixels to improve the image? This is an estimation problem built on the __resolution limit__: any optical system of aperture size $$d$$ using light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ can…
statement:
How far away do you have to hold an iPhone before it is physically impossible for adding more pixels to improve the image?

This is an estimation problem built on the __resolution limit__: any optical system of aperture size $$d$$ using light of wavelength $$\lambda$$ can distinguish directions only to about $$\Delta\theta \approx \dfrac{\lambda}{d}.$$ Your eye is such a system — no matter how well-shaped your cornea and lens are, the eye is diffraction-limited like any telescope. Useful numbers: all light entering the eye passes through the pupil (the eye's __aperture__), which is about $$5\;\mathrm{mm}$$ across; visible light has wavelengths down to about $$\lambda = 500\;\mathrm{nm}$$; and an iPhone display has a pixel density of about $$200$$ pixels per centimeter.

__(a)__ Estimate the smallest angle your eye can possibly resolve.

__(b)__ Find the angle subtended by one pixel at a distance $$L$$ from your eye, and hence the distance beyond which your eye cannot resolve individual pixels — the distance past which more pixels cannot help.

label: PW212
name: Graham has gone fishing, and is sitting quietly waiting for a fish to bite, but nothing…
desc: Graham has gone fishing, and is sitting quietly waiting for a fish to bite, but nothing is happening. So Graham turns on the radio to try to find some music to encourage the fish. The first piece of music Graham finds is a bass guitar solo, which has a very low frequency. Graham…
statement:
Graham has gone fishing, and is sitting quietly waiting for a fish to bite, but nothing is happening. So Graham turns on the radio to try to find some music to encourage the fish. The first piece of music Graham finds is a bass guitar solo, which has a very low frequency. Graham doesn’t like the sound of that, so he finds another station which is playing a selection of soprano duets, which are much higher frequency.

**a)** Which music, if any, will travel from the radio to the fish faster by a significant amount?

**b)** The path of the sound bends when it reaches the surface of the water as shown below:

Describe what happens to the frequency, the wavelength, and the speed of the sound when it moves from the air to the water.

label: PW212
name: In class, we derived the equation for the speed of sound in terms of universal constants…
desc: In class, we derived the equation for the speed of sound in terms of universal constants, the molecular mass of air, and the adiabatic index of air. We assumed that sound waves compress air adiabatically. Isaac Newton attempted the same calculation, but made the assumption that…
statement: In class, we derived the equation for the speed of sound in terms of universal constants, the molecular mass of air, and the adiabatic index of air. We assumed that sound waves compress air adiabatically. Isaac Newton attempted the same calculation, but made the assumption that sound wave compress air isothermally. By what factor was Newton's calculation incorrect?

label: PW212
name: Newton's cradle is a famous experiment in which a row of steel balls (let's assume five…
desc: Newton's cradle is a famous experiment in which a row of steel balls (let's assume five of them) are suspended by strings. When the leftmost ball is pulled to the left and released, it falls down under gravity's pull and collides with the four remaining stationary balls. The…

label: PW212
name: The figure below shows a long, heavy, flexible (but unstretchable) rope with mass per…
desc: The figure below shows a long, heavy, flexible (but unstretchable) rope with mass per unit length $$\rho$$ that is kept tight by a tension $$T.$$ A sudden movement causes a circular loop of radius $$R$$ to form. This loop moves along the rope in a horizontal plane at transverse…
statement:
The figure below shows a long, heavy, flexible (but unstretchable) rope with mass per unit length $$\rho$$ that is kept tight by a tension $$T.$$ A sudden movement causes a circular loop of radius $$R$$ to form. This loop moves along the rope in a horizontal plane at transverse speed $$v.$$

**a)** Calculate the speed $$v$$ of the loop in terms of the given variables.

**b)** Determine the energy, momentum, and angular momentum (about its own center) of the loop.

label: PW212
name: In the handout, we saw that the dispersion relation for gravity-driven water waves in…
desc: In the handout, we saw that the dispersion relation for gravity-driven water waves in deep water is $$\omega_{\rm deep \, water} = \sqrt{gk}.$$ In this problem, we look at what happens when the water is not deep compared to $$\dfrac{1}{k}.$$ **a)** Explain why, in this case, we…
statement:
In the handout, we saw that the dispersion relation for gravity-driven water waves in deep water is $$\omega_{\rm deep \, water} = \sqrt{gk}.$$ In this problem, we look at what happens when the water is not deep compared to $$\dfrac{1}{k}.$$

**a)** Explain why, in this case, we cannot determine the dispersion relationship via dimensional analysis alone.

**b)** The basic theory of these waves, assuming the amplitude of the waves is small compared to $$h,$$ states that $$\omega^2 = gk {\rm tanh}(kh)$$ where $$h$$ is the depth of the water. Show that this recovers the deep water dispersion relation in the appropriate limit.

**c)** In the limit of shallow water, how does the speed of a wave depend on its wavelength?

**d)** Suppose the amplitude of the wave is not small compared to $$h.$$ Which moves faster - the crest of a wave or the trough?

**e)** Qualitatively explain why waves break as they approach the shore of the ocean.

label: PW212
name: In this problem, we investigate the group velocity…
desc: In this problem, we investigate the group velocity, $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}k}$$ for waves in a dispersive medium (one in which the phase velocity $$\dfrac{\omega}{k}$$ depends on $$\omega$$.) **a)** Briefly explain why a simple harmonic wave does not transmit…
statement:
In this problem, we investigate the group velocity, $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}k}$$ for waves in a dispersive medium (one in which the phase velocity $$\dfrac{\omega}{k}$$ depends on $$\omega$$.)

**a)** Briefly explain why a simple harmonic wave does not transmit information from place to place. For example, explain why a radio station cannot truly broadcast on a single frequency.

**b)** Instead, for a wave to transmit information, there will need to be at least two frequencies involved. We will study the simplest case. Imagine a wave traveling through some medium along the $$x$$ axis. At $$x = 0,$$ the displacement is $$\Psi = A \cos \omega_1 t + A \cos\omega_2 t$$

This wave can be written $$\Psi(0,t) = 2A \cos \omega_{\rm mod}t \cos \omega_{\rm av} t. $$

Find $$\omega_{\rm mod}$$ and $$\omega_{\rm av}.$$

**c)** Suppose $$|\omega_1 - \omega_2| \ll \omega_1.$$ How do $$\omega_{\rm mod}$$ and $$\omega_{\rm av}$$ compare?

Explain why this sort of wave is called an __amplitude-modulated__ wave. (Like AM radio.)

**d)** Find $$\Psi(x,t)$$ using $$k_1$$ and $$k_2,$$ the wavenumbers associated with $$\omega_1$$ and $$\omega_2.$$ Do not assume a non-dispersive wave. Rewrite the result in terms of $$\omega_{\rm mod}, \omega_{\rm av}, k_{\rm mod},$$ and $$k_{\rm av}.$$ Give the definitions of $$k_{\rm mod}$$ and $$k_{\rm av}.$$ Draw a sketch of the wave.

**e)** Your sketch from part (d) should show \emph{modulations}, places where the amplitude of the wave is large and places where the amplitude is small. What is the speed of propagation of the modulations? Write your answer first in terms of $$\omega_{\rm mod}$$ and $$k_{\rm mod},$$ then in terms of $$\omega_1, \omega_2, k_1,$$ and $$k_2.$$

**f)** Again assuming $$|\omega_1 - \omega_2|$$ is small, rewrite your result, to first order, as a derivative.

**g)** Reviewing your work, explain the interpretation of the group velocity.

label: PW212
name: A theory for the origin of the index of refraction of electromagnetic waves through a…
desc: A theory for the origin of the index of refraction of electromagnetic waves through a dilute gas gives the result $$n^2 = 1 + N\alpha$$ where $$n$$ is the index of refraction, $$N$$ is the number density of the atoms (number of atoms per unit volume), and $$\alpha$$ is the…
statement:
A theory for the origin of the index of refraction of electromagnetic waves through a dilute gas gives the result $$n^2 = 1 + N\alpha$$ where $$n$$ is the index of refraction, $$N$$ is the number density of the atoms (number of atoms per unit volume), and $$\alpha$$ is the atomic polarizability, defined by $$\vec{p} = \epsilon_0 \alpha \vec{E}$$ where $$\vec{p}$$ is the electric dipole moment of an individual atom and $$\vec{E}$$ is an applied electric field.

In this problem, we will not examine the full theory of the origin of the index of refraction, but will attempt to understand some of the results.

**a)** Given the result above, find the dispersion relation for the material.

**b)** The above result is derived from a model in which an electron is considered a tiny charged ball with mass $$m$$ and charge $$e$$ attached to the immovable nucleus via a spring with some spring constant $$\kappa.$$ (We use $$\kappa$$ for the spring constant so that $$k$$ is reserved for the wavenumber.)The forces on the electron are those from the spring, a damping force $$F_d = m\gamma \dot{x}$$ for some coefficient $$\gamma$$ (where $$x$$ is the displacement of the electron from equilibrium), and an electric force from the passing electromagnetic wave.

For what frequency of light do you expect the largest polarizability of the atom?

**c)** Estimate this frequency as a function of $$h, e, \epsilon_0,$$ and $$m,$$ where $$h$$ is Planck's constant, $$h \approx 6.6\times 10^{-34} \;\mathrm{J\cdot s}.$$ Find the resonant frequency to order of magnitude. What sort of electromagnetic wave is this? Is the index of refraction particularly low or particularly high at this frequency? For visible light, is the index of refraction increasing or decreasing with wavelength?

**d)** Based on this model, give a qualitative explanation of why the index of refraction varies depending on wavelength. That is, explain the origin of dispersion.

**e)** In such a model, what happens to the amplitude of an electromagnetic wave as it travels through a thick pane of glass? How do you know?

label: PW212
name: In this problem, we study how electromagnetic waves relate to Maxwell's equations.
desc: In this problem, we study how electromagnetic waves relate to Maxwell's equations. Consider an electromagnetic wave of the form \begin{aligned} \vec{E} = E_0 \sin(kz - \omega t) \hat{x} \\ \vec{B} = B_0 \sin(kz - \omega t + \phi) \hat{y} \end{aligned} Assume such a wave is…
statement:
In this problem, we study how electromagnetic waves relate to Maxwell's equations.

Consider an electromagnetic wave of the form \begin{aligned} \vec{E} = E_0 \sin(kz - \omega t) \hat{x} \\ \vec{B} = B_0 \sin(kz - \omega t + \phi) \hat{y} \end{aligned}

Assume such a wave is traveling through a vacuum.

**a)** Show that such a wave obey's Gauss' law for electric fields and for magnetic fields.

**b)** Consider a loop which begins at $$(x_0, y_0, z_0),$$ then extends to $$(x_0, y_0, z_0 + \mathrm{d}z),$$ then to $$(x_0 + h, y_0, z_0 + \mathrm{d}z),$$ then to $$(x_0 + h, y_0, z_0),$$ and then closes, returning to $$(x_0, y_0, z_0).$$ Apply the Maxwell-Faraday equation to such a loop and summarize the result.

**c)** Construct a similar loop to which you can fruitfully apply Ampere's law. Apply it and summarize the result.

**d)** Show that the wave can obey Maxwell's equations. In order to obey Maxwell's equation, what must be $$\phi, \dfrac{E_0}{B_0},$$ and $$\dfrac{\omega}{k}?$$

label: PW212
name: This problem continues the previous one.
desc: This problem continues the previous one. **e)** Show that the direction of propagation of the wave is the same as the direction of $$\vec{E} \times \vec{B}.$$ **f)** Take a volume of space shaped like a thin slice, with the thin side along the $$z$$ axis. Let the thickness be…
statement:
This problem continues the previous one.

**e)** Show that the direction of propagation of the wave is the same as the direction of $$\vec{E} \times \vec{B}.$$

**f)** Take a volume of space shaped like a thin slice, with the thin side along the $$z$$ axis. Let the thickness be $$\mathrm{d}z.$$ This is like a pancake parallel to the $$xy$$ plane. Let the cross-sectional area of the pancake be $$A.$$ Find the energy inside the pancake. You will need the expressions for the energy density of the electric and magnetic fields, \begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{electric}} & = \dfrac12 \epsilon_0 E^2 \\ u_{\rm magnetic} & = \dfrac12 \dfrac{1}{\mu_0} B^2 \end{aligned}

**g)** Suppose that flux of energy carried by the electromagnetic wave is some vector $$\vec{S}.$$ Find both the rate that energy enters the volume considered in part (f) in terms of $$S$$ and the rate that energy leaves. Find the net rate that energy enters the volume.

**h)** You now have two expressions for the rate that energy enters the volume. Equate them. Use your results from part (d) to simplify the result.

**i)** Show that the result of part (h) is satisfied by the Poynting vector, $$\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0} \vec{E}\times\vec{B}.$$

label: PW212
name: We have studied electromagnetic waves in various contexts, but so far they have all be…
desc: We have studied electromagnetic waves in various contexts, but so far they have all be plane waves. Another important case is a spherical wave. This is a wave in which all the wavefronts are spheres. Try to find a solution to the wave equation in three dimensions representing a…
statement:
We have studied electromagnetic waves in various contexts, but so far they have all be plane waves.

Another important case is a spherical wave. This is a wave in which all the wavefronts are spheres.

Try to find a solution to the wave equation in three dimensions representing a spherical wave.

The wave equation in three dimensions is $$ \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial y^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial z^2} = \dfrac{1}{c^2} \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial t^2}.$$

In spherical coordinates, assuming the wave has no dependence on $$\theta$$ or $$\phi,$$ the equation becomes $$ \dfrac{1}{r^2} \dfrac{\partial}{\partial r} \left( r^2 \dfrac{\partial \Psi}{\partial r}\right) = \dfrac{1}{c^2} \dfrac{\partial^2 \Psi}{\partial t^2}.$$

You may want to guess at the form of the solution on physical grounds, then verify that the solution is correct.

label: PW212
name: Energy Carried by a Plane Electromagnetic Wave — A plane electromagnetic wave travels through vacuum. Its…
desc: A plane electromagnetic wave travels through vacuum. Its electric field oscillates sinusoidally with amplitude $$E_0 = 12.0\;\mathrm{V/m}.$$ Find the average rate at which the wave transports energy per unit area, in $$\mathrm{W/m^2}.$$ Useful facts: the energy density (energy…
statement:
A plane electromagnetic wave travels through vacuum. Its electric field oscillates sinusoidally with amplitude $$E_0 = 12.0\;\mathrm{V/m}.$$ Find the average rate at which the wave transports energy per unit area, in $$\mathrm{W/m^2}.$$

Useful facts: the energy density (energy per unit volume) stored in an electric field of strength $$E$$ is $$u_E = \dfrac12 \epsilon_0 E^2,$$ where $$\epsilon_0 = 8.85\times 10^{-12}\;\mathrm{F/m}.$$ In an electromagnetic wave, the magnetic field carries an energy density exactly equal to that of the electric field at every instant. The wave travels at $$c = 3.00\times 10^8\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

__(a)__ Suppose for a moment that the electric field has some fixed instantaneous strength $$E.$$ The wave carries all of its field energy forward at speed $$c.$$ Find the instantaneous rate of energy transport per unit area in terms of $$\epsilon_0,$$ $$E,$$ and $$c.$$

__(b)__ The field is not constant: it varies sinusoidally with amplitude $$E_0.$$ Find the __time-averaged__ rate of energy transport per unit area. (Helpful fact: the average value of $$\sin^2 x$$ or $$\cos^2 x$$ is $$\dfrac12$$ — they sum to $$1$$ everywhere and have the same shape, so each must average to $$\dfrac12.$$)

__(c)__ Evaluate numerically for $$E_0 = 12.0\;\mathrm{V/m},$$ and compare the result to the intensity of direct sunlight at Earth, about $$1.4\times 10^3\;\mathrm{W/m^2}.$$

label: PW212
name: Poynting Vector I: A Moving Charged Rod (USAPhO 2013) — This problem and the two that follow are adapted from…
desc: This problem and the two that follow are adapted from USAPhO 2013. They concern the transfer of energy into a region of space by electromagnetic fields. Whenever an electric and a magnetic field are at an angle to each other, energy is transferred; the power transferred per unit…
statement:
This problem and the two that follow are adapted from USAPhO 2013. They concern the transfer of energy into a region of space by electromagnetic fields. Whenever an electric and a magnetic field are at an angle to each other, energy is transferred; the power transferred per unit area is given by the __Poynting vector__ $$\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0} \vec{E} \times \vec{B}.$$ The last part of each problem asks you to verify that the rate of energy transfer agrees with the Poynting vector, so do __not__ use the Poynting vector formula before the last part.

A long, insulating cylindrical rod has radius $$R$$ and carries a uniform volume charge density $$\rho.$$ A uniform external electric field $$E$$ exists in the direction of the rod's axis. The rod moves in the direction of its axis at speed $$v.$$

__(a)__ Find the power per unit length $$\mathcal{P}$$ delivered to the rod by the external field.

__(b)__ Find the magnetic field $$B$$ at the surface of the rod, and describe its direction. (The moving charged rod constitutes a current; use Ampere's law, $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot \mathrm{d}\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_{\rm enclosed}.$$)

__(c)__ Now compute the Poynting vector at the surface of the rod, give its direction, and verify that it accounts for the rate of energy transfer you found in part (a).

label: PW212
name: Poynting Vector II: A Charging Capacitor (USAPhO 2013) — (Adapted from USAPhO 2013; see the previous problem…
desc: (Adapted from USAPhO 2013; see the previous problem for the series.) The power transferred per unit area by crossed electric and magnetic fields is the __Poynting vector__ $$\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0} \vec{E} \times \vec{B}.$$ Do not use this formula before the last part. A…
statement:
(Adapted from USAPhO 2013; see the previous problem for the series.) The power transferred per unit area by crossed electric and magnetic fields is the __Poynting vector__ $$\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0} \vec{E} \times \vec{B}.$$ Do not use this formula before the last part.

A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two discs of radius $$R$$ separated by a distance $$d \ll R.$$ The capacitor carries charge $$Q$$ and is being charged by a small, constant current $$I.$$

Useful facts: the energy stored in a capacitor is $$U = \dfrac12 QV,$$ and for parallel discs the capacitance is $$C = \dfrac{\epsilon_0 \pi R^2}{d}.$$ Although no charge flows across the gap, a changing electric flux acts in Ampere's law exactly like a current — the __displacement current__ — via the Ampere-Maxwell equation $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot \mathrm{d}\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_{\rm enclosed} + \mu_0 \epsilon_0 \dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_E}{\mathrm{d}t}.$$

__(a)__ Find the power $$P$$ delivered to the capacitor.

__(b)__ Find the magnetic field $$B$$ just inside the edge of the capacitor, and describe its direction. (Ignore fringing effects in the electric field.)

__(c)__ Compute the Poynting vector just inside the rim of the capacitor, give its direction, and verify that it agrees with the rate of energy transfer from part (a).

label: PW212
name: Poynting Vector III: A Solenoid with Increasing Current (USAPhO 2013) — (Adapted from USAPhO 2013; see the…
desc: (Adapted from USAPhO 2013; see the previous two problems for the series.) The power transferred per unit area by crossed electric and magnetic fields is the __Poynting vector__ $$\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0} \vec{E} \times \vec{B}.$$ Do not use this formula before the last part. A…
statement:
(Adapted from USAPhO 2013; see the previous two problems for the series.) The power transferred per unit area by crossed electric and magnetic fields is the __Poynting vector__ $$\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0} \vec{E} \times \vec{B}.$$ Do not use this formula before the last part.

A long solenoid of radius $$R$$ has $$N$$ turns of wire per unit length. The solenoid carries current $$I,$$ and this current is increased at a small, constant rate $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.$$

Useful facts: the energy density stored in a magnetic field of strength $$B$$ is $$u_B = \dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.$$ Ampere's law is $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot \mathrm{d}\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_{\rm enclosed},$$ and the Maxwell-Faraday equation is $$\oint \vec{E}\cdot \mathrm{d}\vec{\ell} = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t}.$$

__(a)__ Find the magnetic field inside the solenoid using Ampere's law, then find the power per unit length $$\mathcal{P}$$ delivered to the solenoid.

__(b)__ Find the electric field $$E$$ just inside the surface of the solenoid, and describe its direction.

__(c)__ Compute the Poynting vector just inside the surface, give its direction, and verify that it agrees with the rate of energy transfer from part (a).

label: PW212
name: Is a Gaussian Pulse an Electromagnetic Wave? — Consider the electric field $$\vec{E} = E_0 \…
desc: Consider the electric field $$\vec{E} = E_0 \, e^{-(x-ct)^2/(2\sigma)} \, \hat{z},$$ where $$c$$ is the speed of light and $$\sigma$$ is a constant. This is a __Gaussian wave packet__ — a single localized bump shaped like the normal distribution from statistics, rather than an…
statement:
Consider the electric field $$\vec{E} = E_0 \, e^{-(x-ct)^2/(2\sigma)} \, \hat{z},$$ where $$c$$ is the speed of light and $$\sigma$$ is a constant. This is a __Gaussian wave packet__ — a single localized bump shaped like the normal distribution from statistics, rather than an endless sinusoid.

Useful facts: any function of the form $$f(x - vt)$$ solves the one-dimensional wave equation with propagation speed $$v.$$ In a vacuum electromagnetic wave, the magnetic field is perpendicular to the electric field, the Poynting vector $$\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0}\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$$ points in the direction of propagation, and the field magnitudes are related by $$B = \dfrac{E}{c}.$$

__(a)__ Can this be the electric field of a traveling electromagnetic wave in vacuum, even though it is not a sine function? Explain.

__(b)__ If so, describe the accompanying magnetic field: its shape, its magnitude, and its direction.

__(c)__ A sinusoid stretches out forever, yet this packet decays to zero on both sides. Explain qualitatively how a localized pulse like this can be built out of sinusoidal waves.

label: PW212
name: Chasing a Beam of Light — A light wave moves at speed $$c$$ in the $$\hat{z}$$ direction. A spaceship moves…
desc: A light wave moves at speed $$c$$ in the $$\hat{z}$$ direction. A spaceship moves at speed $$\dfrac{c}{2}$$ in the same direction. From the point of view of the ship, what is the speed of the light wave? __(a)__ What answer does everyday (Galilean) velocity addition predict?…
statement:
A light wave moves at speed $$c$$ in the $$\hat{z}$$ direction. A spaceship moves at speed $$\dfrac{c}{2}$$ in the same direction. From the point of view of the ship, what is the speed of the light wave?

__(a)__ What answer does everyday (Galilean) velocity addition predict?

__(b)__ What is the actual answer? Justify it using Maxwell's equations. (Helpful facts: light in vacuum is a solution of Maxwell's equations in free space; as a consequence of those equations, light in vacuum is __non-dispersive__ — there is only one possible propagation speed, $$c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \epsilon_0}} \approx 3\times 10^8\;\mathrm{m/s},$$ fixed entirely by the constants appearing in the equations.)

__(c)__ If the speed of the wave is the same for the ship as for an observer at rest, what properties of the wave __do__ differ between the two reference frames?

label: PW213
name: At a particular beach on a particular day near sundown, the horizontal component of the…
desc: At a particular beach on a particular day near sundown, the horizontal component of the electric field vector is $$2.3$$ times the vertical component. A standing sunbather puts on polarizing sunglasses. The glasses suppress the horizontal field component. **a)** What fraction of…
statement:
At a particular beach on a particular day near sundown, the horizontal component of the electric field vector is $$2.3$$ times the vertical component. A standing sunbather puts on polarizing sunglasses. The glasses suppress the horizontal field component.

**a)** What fraction of the light energy received before the glasses were put on now reaches the eyes?

**b)** The sunbather, still wearing the glasses, lies on his side. What fraction of the light energy received before the glasses were put on reaches the eyes now?

label: PW213
name: An ideal polarizer is rotated at a rate $$\omega$$ between a similar pair of stationary…
desc: An ideal polarizer is rotated at a rate $$\omega$$ between a similar pair of stationary crossed polarizers. If the first polarized has light emerging from it of intensity $$I_1,$$ find the intensity of light emerging from the third polarizer as a function of time. What is the…
statement:
An ideal polarizer is rotated at a rate $$\omega$$ between a similar pair of stationary crossed polarizers.

If the first polarized has light emerging from it of intensity $$I_1,$$ find the intensity of light emerging from the third polarizer as a function of time. What is the frequency of oscillations of the intensity of the light emitted from the last polarizer?

label: PW213
name: In addition to linear and circular polarization, light can have __elliptical__…
desc: In addition to linear and circular polarization, light can have __elliptical__ polarization. That is, at any fixed point in space, the electric field vector traces out an ellipse. Find a linear superposition of two plane-polarized waves with the same amplitude so that the result…
statement:
In addition to linear and circular polarization, light can have __elliptical__ polarization. That is, at any fixed point in space, the electric field vector traces out an ellipse.

Find a linear superposition of two plane-polarized waves with the same amplitude so that the result is elliptically-polarized light, where the major axis of the ellipse is twice the minor axis.

label: PW213
name: This problem continues a problem on interference from class 11.
desc: This problem continues a problem on interference from class 11. Consider an opaque barrier in the $$x-y$$ plane at $$z = 0,$$ with a single slit along the $$x$$ axis of width $$2a,$$ but with regions on either side of the slit each with width $$2a$$ which are partially…
statement:
This problem continues a problem on interference from class 11.

Consider an opaque barrier in the $$x-y$$ plane at $$z = 0,$$ with a single slit along the $$x$$ axis of width $$2a,$$ but with regions on either side of the slit each with width $$2a$$ which are partially transparent, designed to reduce the intensity by a factor of $$2.$$ When this barrier is illuminated by a plane wave in the $$z$$ direction, the amplitude of the oscillating field at $$z = 0$$ is $$f(x,y)e^{i\omega t}$$ for \begin{aligned} f(x,y) & = 1 ;& |y| < a \\ f(x,y) & = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} ;& a < |y| < 3a \\ f(x,y) & = 0 ; & 3a < |y| \end{aligned}

Near the slit, this just produces a beam which is less intense by a factor of two on the edges. Far away, however, the diffraction pattern is quite different from that of the single slit. At a fixed large distance $$R = \sqrt{y^2 + z^2}$$ away from the slit, the intensity as a function of $$\xi = k_y a = \dfrac{\omega y a}{cR}$$ is shown in the figure below for positive $$\xi.$$

The value of the peak of $$\xi = 0$$ is normalized to $$1,$$ but has been suppressed in the graph to show the details of the secondary maxima.

**a)** (done in week 11, re-presented as a reminder) Find the smallest positive value of $$\xi$$ for which the intensity vanishes.

**b)** (done in week 11, re-presented as a reminder) Find the ratio of the intensity at $$\xi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$$ to that at $$\xi = 0.$$

**c)** (new for this week) So far, we have not mentioned the polarization of the light, assuming that it is irrelevant. In fact, we get the pattern shown above for any polarization, so long as the shading doesn't affect the polarization (and $$\xi$$ is small). However, if the light is initially polarized in the direction $$45^\circ$$ from the $$x$$ axis, we could reduce the intensity by two by passing it through a perfect polarizer aligned with the $$y$$ axis. Suppose that our slit between $$-a$$ and $$a$$ is completely empty, but between $$-3a$$ and $$-a$$ and between $$a$$ and $$3a,$$ we put such a polarizer. Now, as before, the beam close to the slit just has the intensity on the edges reduced by a factor of $$2.$$ However, the diffraction pattern is quite different. As a function of $$\xi,$$ the intensity at large fixed $$R$$ is $$\propto \dfrac{1}{10} \left[ \left( \dfrac{\sin 3\xi}{\xi}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\sin \xi}{\xi}\right)^2 \right],$$ which looks nothing like the pattern above. Explain the difference.

label: PW213
name: A beam of plane polarized monochromatic light is passed through a quarter wave plate…
desc: A beam of plane polarized monochromatic light is passed through a quarter wave plate, which converts it to circularly-polarized light, then through a half-wave plate and a second quarter wave plate. The half wave plate is now rotated about an axis normal to its plane at a speed…
statement:
A beam of plane polarized monochromatic light is passed through a quarter wave plate, which converts it to circularly-polarized light, then through a half-wave plate and a second quarter wave plate.

The half wave plate is now rotated about an axis normal to its plane at a speed of $$6000$$ revolutions per minute.

Show that what emerges from the second quarter wave plate is plane polarized light having a different frequency from the light entering the system, and determine by how much the frequency is altered.

label: PW213
name: A cosmic object travels at a constant speed along a straight line and transmits periodic…
desc: A cosmic object travels at a constant speed along a straight line and transmits periodic radio pulses. An astronomer has determined that during an observation period $$t$$, the direction to the object changed by a small angle $$\Delta \phi$$ while a period of the radio pulses'…
statement:
A cosmic object travels at a constant speed along a straight line and transmits periodic radio pulses. An astronomer has determined that during an observation period $$t$$, the direction to the object changed by a small angle $$\Delta \phi$$ while a period of the radio pulses' arrival changed from $$T$$ to $$T + \Delta T$$. You can assume $$\Delta T \ll T.$$ Determine the distance between the astronomer and the object.

You can assume the speed $$v$$ of the object is constant, but this speed should not be cited in your final answer.

label: PW213
name: The __Lyman alpha line__ in the spectrum of hydrogen is the absorption / emission line…
desc: The __Lyman alpha line__ in the spectrum of hydrogen is the absorption / emission line associated with electrons transitioning from the $$n=1$$ to $$n=2$$ orbital. Its frequency is $$2.47 \times 10^{15} \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ Estimate the broadening of this line due to the thermal…
statement:
The __Lyman alpha line__ in the spectrum of hydrogen is the absorption / emission line associated with electrons transitioning from the $$n=1$$ to $$n=2$$ orbital. Its frequency is $$2.47 \times 10^{15} \;\mathrm{Hz}.$$

Estimate the broadening of this line due to the thermal motion hydrogen at temperature $$T.$$ Evaluate for $$T \approx 6000 \;\mathrm{K},$$ the approximate temperature of the sun.

Boltzmann's constant is $$k_B \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \;\mathrm{J/K}.$$

label: PW213
name: Lieutenant-experimenter Glitch did some research with new flare rockets on a military…
desc: Lieutenant-experimenter Glitch did some research with new flare rockets on a military range. The rocket flew at a constant speed $$v$$ and emitted a sound at a constant frequency $$f_0.$$ Glitch used frequency sensors to register the sound. The speed of sound on the range is $$c…
statement:
Lieutenant-experimenter Glitch did some research with new flare rockets on a military range. The rocket flew at a constant speed $$v$$ and emitted a sound at a constant frequency $$f_0.$$ Glitch used frequency sensors to register the sound. The speed of sound on the range is $$c = 330 \;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

**a)** What frequency will be registered by a sensor if a rocket is coming directly towards it?

**b)** What frequency will be registered by a sensor located far away from a flying rocket if there is an angle $$\phi$$ between the rocket velocity and the direction to the sensor?

**c)** When doing his research, Glitch accidentally fired a faulty rocket which began flying in a circle of radius $$r$$ at low height above the ground. The rocket flew with constant speed $$v.$$ The time dependence of the frequency received by sensor 1 and sensor 2 was recorded and is plotted below. Determine the distance between the sensors.

name: In this problem, we analyze the working principle of a radar gun (used by police to…
desc: In this problem, we analyze the working principle of a radar gun (used by police to determine drivers' speeds, for example). A radar gun has a transmitter which emits an electromagnetic wave of frequency $$f_0 = 24 \;\mathrm{GHz}.$$ The wave gets reflected from an approaching…
statement:
In this problem, we analyze the working principle of a radar gun (used by police to determine drivers' speeds, for example).

A radar gun has a transmitter which emits an electromagnetic wave of frequency $$f_0 = 24 \;\mathrm{GHz}.$$ The wave gets reflected from an approaching car moving with speed $$v.$$ The reflected wave is recorded by the receiver of the speed camera.

**a)** Find the frequency $$f_1$$ of the reflected wave.

**b)** In the radar gun, the received waveform is multiplied with the original emitted waveform. Find all frequency components present in the multiplied signal.

**c)** Given the lowest frequency component $$f_{\rm low} = 4.8 \;\mathrm{kHz}$$ present in the signal, calculate the speed of the car $$v.$$

name: Crossed Polarizers and Malus' Law — An __ideal linear polarizer__ transmits, without any loss, the component…
desc: An __ideal linear polarizer__ transmits, without any loss, the component of a light wave's electric field along the polarizer's __axis__, and completely blocks the perpendicular component. Whatever light goes in, the light that emerges is linearly polarized along the polarizer's…
statement:
An __ideal linear polarizer__ transmits, without any loss, the component of a light wave's electric field along the polarizer's __axis__, and completely blocks the perpendicular component. Whatever light goes in, the light that emerges is linearly polarized along the polarizer's axis.

__(a)__ Derive __Malus' law__: if linearly-polarized light whose polarization direction makes an angle $$\theta$$ with a polarizer's axis is sent through the polarizer, what fraction of the light's __intensity__ is transmitted? (The intensity of light is proportional to the square of its electric field amplitude.)

The animation above demonstrates the law with two real polarizers: when their axes point in the same direction, the second polarizer blocks almost no extra light, but when the second is rotated a quarter turn from the first, it blocks nearly all of the light.

__(b)__ Light passes through a polarizer with its axis in the $$\hat{y}$$ direction, then continues on to a second polarizer with its axis in the $$\hat{x}$$ direction. What fraction of the light that passes through the first polarizer also passes through the second?

__(c)__ A third polarizer, with its axis in the $$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\hat{x} + \hat{y}\right)$$ direction, is inserted between the $$\hat{y}$$ polarizer and the $$\hat{x}$$ polarizer. Now what fraction of the light passing through the $$\hat{y}$$ polarizer makes it through the final $$\hat{x}$$ polarizer? Comment on the result: how can inserting an element that itself blocks half the light __increase__ the total light transmitted?

label: PW213
name: Rotating Polarization with N Polarizers — You have $$N$$ ideal linear polarizers. (An ideal polarizer…
desc: You have $$N$$ ideal linear polarizers. (An ideal polarizer transmits the electric-field component along its axis without loss and blocks the perpendicular component; by __Malus' law__, linearly-polarized light meeting a polarizer at angle $$\theta$$ to its axis is transmitted…
statement:
You have $$N$$ ideal linear polarizers. (An ideal polarizer transmits the electric-field component along its axis without loss and blocks the perpendicular component; by __Malus' law__, linearly-polarized light meeting a polarizer at angle $$\theta$$ to its axis is transmitted with intensity fraction $$\cos^2\theta,$$ emerging polarized along the axis.) You are given light polarized in the $$\hat{y}$$ direction, and you must output light polarized in the $$\hat{x}$$ direction. What is the greatest fraction of the light's intensity that can be passed through into the $$\hat{x}$$ polarization?

__(a)__ If any one polarizer sits at $$\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$ to the one before it, no light gets through at all, so the arrangement matters. Take as given that the optimal arrangement spaces the axes at __equal__ angles, starting from the incoming $$\hat{y}$$ polarization and ending with the last polarizer along $$\hat{x}.$$ Find the angle between adjacent polarizers and the fraction of the light that passes through all $$N$$ polarizers.

__(b)__ Evaluate the limit $$N \to \infty$$: given enough ideal polarizers, can you rotate the polarization by $$\dfrac{\pi}{2}$$ while letting arbitrarily close to all the light through? Useful tools: the small-angle approximation $$\cos x \approx 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2},$$ and the binomial approximation $$(1+x)^n \approx 1 + nx,$$ valid when $$x \ll 1$$ __and__ $$n \ll \dfrac{1}{x}.$$ Show that for large $$N$$ the fraction of light __lost__ is approximately $$\dfrac{\pi^2}{4N}.$$

__(c)__ The binomial approximation carries the condition $$n \ll \dfrac{1}{x}$$ — it is not enough for $$x$$ alone to be small. To see why, consider $$\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{100}\right)^{100}.$$ What does the binomial approximation predict, and what is the true value close to?

label: PW213
name: Circular Polarization and the Polarization Vector — If light is linearly polarized, the electric field at a…
desc: If light is linearly polarized, the electric field at a fixed point in space oscillates along a fixed line — for example $$\vec{E}_1 = E_0\sin(\omega t)\,\hat{x}.$$ Now superpose a second linear polarization, rotated $$90^\circ$$ and given a quarter-cycle phase lag, $$\vec{E}_2…
statement:
If light is linearly polarized, the electric field at a fixed point in space oscillates along a fixed line — for example $$\vec{E}_1 = E_0\sin(\omega t)\,\hat{x}.$$ Now superpose a second linear polarization, rotated $$90^\circ$$ and given a quarter-cycle phase lag, $$\vec{E}_2 = E_0\cos(\omega t)\,\hat{y},$$ to get $$\vec{E} = E_0\left(\sin(\omega t)\,\hat{x} + \cos(\omega t)\,\hat{y}\right).$$

__(a)__ Find the magnitude $$|\vec{E}|$$ of the superposed field as a function of time, and explain why this light is called __circularly polarized__.

__(b)__ The intensity of light is proportional to the time average of the square of its electric field. Find the time-averaged intensity $$I$$ of the circularly-polarized wave relative to the intensity $$I_1$$ of the single linear wave $$\vec{E}_1$$ alone. What does the result say about whether two perpendicularly-polarized waves can interfere?

It is convenient to describe polarization states with a complex __polarization vector__ $$\vec{e}.$$ For light $$\vec{E} = E_0\left(\cos(kz - \omega t)\,\hat{x} + \cos(kz - \omega t - \phi)\,\hat{y}\right),$$ in which the $$y$$ component lags the $$x$$ component by phase $$\phi,$$ we write $$\vec{e} = \hat{x} + e^{-i\phi}\,\hat{y}.$$ (Overall normalization factors only fiddle with the amplitude and may be dropped.)

__(c)__ The animation above shows __right circularly polarized__ light traveling in the $$+\hat{z}$$ direction: point your right thumb along the propagation direction, and the electric field rotates the way your fingers curl. Write the polarization vectors $$\vec{e}_R$$ and $$\vec{e}_L$$ for right and left circularly polarized light.

__(d)__ Express $$\hat{x}$$-polarized and $$\hat{y}$$-polarized light as combinations of $$\vec{e}_R$$ and $$\vec{e}_L,$$ then find a combination of $$\vec{e}_R$$ and $$\vec{e}_L$$ describing light linearly polarized along $$\hat{x} + \hat{y}.$$ Along the way, explain why a __global phase factor__ — a factor such as $$-1,$$ $$i,$$ or $$e^{-i\phi}$$ multiplying an entire $$\vec{e}$$ vector — can always be ignored.

label: PW213
name: Optical Activity in a Sugar Solution — A sugar solution has one index of refraction, $$n_R,$$ for light with…
desc: A sugar solution has one index of refraction, $$n_R,$$ for light with right circular polarization, and a different index, $$n_L,$$ for light with left circular polarization. A beam of plane (linearly) polarized light of wavelength $$\lambda = 0.5\;\mathrm{\mu m}$$ (measured…
statement:
A sugar solution has one index of refraction, $$n_R,$$ for light with right circular polarization, and a different index, $$n_L,$$ for light with left circular polarization. A beam of plane (linearly) polarized light of wavelength $$\lambda = 0.5\;\mathrm{\mu m}$$ (measured outside the solution) is passed through the solution. (From Pippard, __Cavendish Problems in Classical Physics__.)

Useful facts. Linearly-polarized light is a superposition of the two circular polarizations: with polarization vectors $$\vec{e}_R = \hat{x} - i\hat{y}$$ and $$\vec{e}_L = \hat{x} + i\hat{y}$$ (where a coefficient $$e^{-i\phi}$$ on a component denotes a phase lag $$\phi$$), we have $$\hat{x} \propto \vec{e}_R + \vec{e}_L$$ and $$\hat{y} \propto \vec{e}_R - \vec{e}_L,$$ and more generally the __direction__ of the linear polarization is set by the relative phase between the two circular components. Also, inside a medium with index of refraction $$n,$$ the wavelength of the light is $$\dfrac{\lambda}{n},$$ so a thickness $$d$$ of the medium contains $$\dfrac{dn}{\lambda}$$ wavelengths.

__(a)__ Describe qualitatively what happens to the linearly-polarized beam as it propagates through the solution.

__(b)__ Measurements show that the solution rotates the polarization of linearly-polarized light by $$9^\circ$$ per millimeter. How thick a layer of solution turns $$\hat{x}$$-polarized light into $$\hat{y}$$-polarized light, and what phase lag between the right- and left-circular components does that rotation require?

__(c)__ Find the difference $$|n_R - n_L|$$ between the two refractive indices.

__(d)__ Now stretch the idea, as practice in working out something new on the fly: suppose an index of refraction is a __complex__ number, $$n = a + ib.$$ A wave in the medium can be written $$e^{i(nkx - \omega t)}$$ (the physical field is the real part), where $$k$$ is the vacuum wavenumber. What does the imaginary part of $$n$$ do to the light, and what physical phenomenon could a complex index describe?

__(e)__ Finally, suppose the sugar solution has complex indices for both senses of circular polarization, absorbing one sense more quickly than the other. Linearly-polarized light enters. Is the light that comes out linearly polarized? Circularly polarized? Describe its polarization.

label: PW213
name: Circularly Polarized Light Reflecting from a Mirror — Right circularly polarized light travels in the…
desc: Right circularly polarized light travels in the $$+\hat{z}$$ direction and strikes a mirror head-on, reflecting straight back. Treat the mirror as a dielectric with a higher index of refraction than the medium the light arrives through; reflection from such a surface gives the…
statement:
Right circularly polarized light travels in the $$+\hat{z}$$ direction and strikes a mirror head-on, reflecting straight back. Treat the mirror as a dielectric with a higher index of refraction than the medium the light arrives through; reflection from such a surface gives the electric field a phase shift of $$\pi.$$

The animation shows the incoming right circularly polarized light: pointing the right thumb along the propagation direction, the electric field rotates the way the fingers curl. In polarization-vector notation the incoming light is $$\vec{e} = \hat{x} - i\hat{y},$$ where a complex coefficient $$e^{-i\phi}$$ on a component denotes a phase lag $$\phi$$ of that component.

__(a)__ Apply the reflection phase shift to both components of $$\vec{e}.$$ Write the polarization vector of the reflected light, and show that it can be rewritten as the original $$\hat{x} - i\hat{y}$$ — explain why that rewriting is allowed.

__(b)__ Does part (a) mean the reflected light is still right circularly polarized? Determine the handedness of the reflected light.

__(c)__ The direction of energy flow of light is given by the Poynting vector $$\vec{S} = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0}\vec{E}\times\vec{B}.$$ At the reflection, the electric field reverses (the phase shift of $$\pi$$) and the energy flow reverses (the light now travels in $$-\hat{z}$$). What happens to the light's magnetic field?

label: PW213
name: A Galaxy's Rotation from Its Redshift — The image below, based on NASA data, shows a galaxy together with…
desc: The image below, based on NASA data, shows a galaxy together with measurements of the __redshift__ of light from several slices across it, reported as a recession velocity for each slice. (The colors in the picture are not the color of the light — they only match slices of the…
statement:
The image below, based on NASA data, shows a galaxy together with measurements of the __redshift__ of light from several slices across it, reported as a recession velocity for each slice. (The colors in the picture are not the color of the light — they only match slices of the photo to points on the graph.)

Background: redshift and blueshift are results of the __Doppler effect__. When a light source recedes from us at speed $$v \ll c,$$ the wavelengths we receive are stretched (redshifted) by the fraction $$\dfrac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \dfrac{v}{c}$$; an approaching source is blueshifted by the same fraction. A galaxy's redshift is measured using __spectral lines__: starlight has a smooth black-body spectrum interrupted by sharp lines at frequencies set by the atoms emitting or absorbing the light, as in the sample stellar spectrum below. Comparing received line frequencies with their known rest-frame values gives the redshift. The speed of light is $$c \approx 3\times 10^5\;\mathrm{km/s}.$$

__(a)__ Light from the entire galaxy is redshifted, but the left side is redshifted more than the right side. Which direction does the galaxy rotate, as viewed from above: clockwise or counterclockwise?

__(b)__ About how fast is the galaxy receding from us, and by what fraction is its light redshifted? Decide whether you need a relativistic formula.

__(c)__ Suppose the galaxy's image is blurry, so light from the left and right halves overlaps on the spectrometer's sensor. Besides being shifted by the overall recession, what happens to the shape of a spectral line? Name at least one other physical situation that affects a spectral line in the same way.

label: PW213
name: Reflection from a Receding Mirror — A mirror is receding from you at speed $$v \ll c.$$ You shine a beam of…
desc: A mirror is receding from you at speed $$v \ll c.$$ You shine a beam of light with frequency $$f$$ at the mirror. What is the frequency of the reflected light that returns to you, to first order in $$\dfrac{v}{c}?$$ Useful fact: for $$v \ll c,$$ light received across a gap that…
statement:
A mirror is receding from you at speed $$v \ll c.$$ You shine a beam of light with frequency $$f$$ at the mirror. What is the frequency of the reflected light that returns to you, to first order in $$\dfrac{v}{c}?$$

Useful fact: for $$v \ll c,$$ light received across a gap that is opening at speed $$v$$ — a receding source, or an observer receding from the source — is shifted down in frequency by the fraction $$\dfrac{v}{c},$$ that is, $$\delta f = -f\dfrac{v}{c}$$ to first order. Suggested technique: break the reflection into two steps using reference frames. First find the light's frequency in the mirror's frame; the reflection itself does not change the frequency in that frame; then transform the reflected light back into your frame.

label: PW213
name: The Falling Tape Recorder (USAPhO 2008) — A tape recorder playing a single tone of frequency $$f_0$$ is…
desc: A tape recorder playing a single tone of frequency $$f_0$$ is dropped from rest at a height $$h_0$$ at time $$t = 0.$$ You stand directly underneath the tape recorder and measure the frequency you hear as a function of time: $$\begin{array}{c|c} t\;(\mathrm{s}) &…
statement:
A tape recorder playing a single tone of frequency $$f_0$$ is dropped from rest at a height $$h_0$$ at time $$t = 0.$$ You stand directly underneath the tape recorder and measure the frequency you hear as a function of time: $$\begin{array}{c|c} t\;(\mathrm{s}) & f\;(\mathrm{Hz}) \\ \hline 2.0 & 581 \\ 4.0 & 619 \\ 6.0 & 665 \\ 8.0 & 723 \\ 10.0 & 801 \end{array}$$

The acceleration due to gravity is $$g = 9.80\;\mathrm{m/s^2}$$ and the speed of sound in air is $$v_{\mathrm{snd}} = 340\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$ Ignore air resistance, and consider only times before the recorder reaches the ground (its speed never exceeds the speed of sound). (USAPhO 2008.)

Useful facts. The Doppler formula for sound, for source and observer moving along the same line, is $$f = f_0\,\dfrac{v_{\mathrm{snd}} \pm v_{\mathrm{obs}}}{v_{\mathrm{snd}} \pm v_{\mathrm{src}}},$$ with signs chosen by the directions of motion: a source moving __toward__ a stationary observer takes the minus sign in the denominator, raising the pitch. One warning: the sound you hear at time $$t$$ was emitted at an __earlier__ time $$t' < t,$$ when the recorder was higher up and moving more slowly — the sound took time to travel down to you.

__(a)__ Determine the frequency heard on the ground at time $$t,$$ in terms of $$f_0,$$ $$g,$$ $$h_0,$$ and $$v_{\mathrm{snd}}.$$

__(b)__ Verify graphically that your result is consistent with the data. (Choose what to plot so that the predicted relationship is a __straight line__ — a straight line is easy to recognize by eye, unlike the difference between, say, a square and a cube law.)

__(c)__ From your graph, find numerically the frequency $$f_0$$ played by the tape recorder.

__(d)__ From your graph, find the height $$h_0$$ from which the tape recorder was dropped.
