desc: A tall vertical vessel contains a gas composed of two kinds of molecules of mass $$m_1$$ and $$m_2,$$ with $$m_2 > m_1.$$ The concentrations of these molecules at the bottom of the vessel are equal to $$n_1$$ and $$n_2$$ respectively, with $$n_2 > n_1.$$ Assuming the temperature…
statement: A tall vertical vessel contains a gas composed of two kinds of molecules of mass $$m_1$$ and $$m_2,$$ with $$m_2 > m_1.$$ The concentrations of these molecules at the bottom of the vessel are equal to $$n_1$$ and $$n_2$$ respectively, with $$n_2 > n_1.$$ Assuming the temperature $$T$$ and the free fall acceleration $$g$$ to be independent of height, find the height $$h$$ at which the concentrations of those kinds of molecules are equal.

label: PW214
name: A cubic vessel whose volume is $$V = 1 \;\mathrm{L}$$ contains $$m = 0.01 \;\mathrm{g}$$…
desc: A cubic vessel whose volume is $$V = 1 \;\mathrm{L}$$ contains $$m = 0.01 \;\mathrm{g}$$ of Helium at a temperature $$T = 300 \;\mathrm{K}.$$ If we follow the motion of a particular molecule, how many times will it hit the top of the vessel during $$t = 1 \;\mathrm{min}?$$ The…
statement:
A cubic vessel whose volume is $$V = 1 \;\mathrm{L}$$ contains $$m = 0.01 \;\mathrm{g}$$ of Helium at a temperature $$T = 300 \;\mathrm{K}.$$ If we follow the motion of a particular molecule, how many times will it hit the top of the vessel during $$t = 1 \;\mathrm{min}?$$

The atomic mass of Helium is $$4 \;\mathrm{amu}$$ and $$1 \;\mathrm{amu} \approx 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Boltzmann's constant is $$k_B \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \;\mathrm{J/K}.$$

label: PW214
name: At the 2004 International Physics Olympiad in Korea, a demonstration showed how a table…
desc: At the 2004 International Physics Olympiad in Korea, a demonstration showed how a table tennis ball could make a hole in ceramic plates. Photos from the demonstration are below. The ceramic plates were placed between two glass tubes. The tubes were then evacuated so that there…
statement:
At the 2004 International Physics Olympiad in Korea, a demonstration showed how a table tennis ball could make a hole in ceramic plates. Photos from the demonstration are below.

The ceramic plates were placed between two glass tubes. The tubes were then evacuated so that there was a vacuum on each side of the plates. Suddenly, the tube was opened on the side of the ball adjacent to the end of the tube, as shown in figure 2.1. The atmospheric pressure on that side shot the ball into the plates, making a hole in the plates. We can assume that the ball made an airtight fit with the tube, and neglect any friction between the ball and the tube.

**a)** Find the maximum speed at which the ball could conceivably hit the plates, assuming the temperature in the air was $$300 \;\mathrm{K}$$ and that air is made of nitrogen molecules.

**b)** The ball has a mass of $$0.01 \;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Calculate its maximum conceivable kinetic energy.

**c)** Consider a cubic box of side length $$L$$ and volume $$V$$ containing $$n$$ molecules, each of mass $$m,$$ and all moving in random directions at constant speed $$v.$$ All collisions are assumed to be perfectly elastic, and the total volume of the molecules is much less than $$V.$$

What is the change in momentum when a molecule, moving in an arbitrary direction, hits a face of the box with speed $$u$$ normal to the face of the box?

**d)** Calculate the average time it takes this molecule to traverse the box.

**e)** Using the results from (c) and (d), find the pressure in the box as a function of $$V, n, m,$$ and $$v.$$

**f)** Below is a diagrammatic sketch of the tennis ball experiment, with a piston replacing the tennis ball.

You may assume that the speed of the piston is small compared to the speed of sound, and therefore that the number density and speed of the molecules near the piston is the same as in the atmosphere in general.

If the piston's speed is $$u_x,$$ find the force on the piston from the air. This force should be somewhat lower than $$P_0A,$$ where $$P_0$$ is atmospheric pressure and $$A$$ is the cross-sectional area of the piston.

label: PW214
name: An important quantity in the kinetic theory is the __mean free path__ of a molecule.
desc: An important quantity in the kinetic theory is the __mean free path__ of a molecule. Suppose we follow an individual molecule in a gas. It travels some distance, then has a collision with another molecule, changing its direction of motion. If we watch the molecule until it has…
statement:
An important quantity in the kinetic theory is the __mean free path__ of a molecule.

Suppose we follow an individual molecule in a gas. It travels some distance, then has a collision with another molecule, changing its direction of motion. If we watch the molecule until it has undergone a very large number of collisions, then the total distance traveled divided by the number of collisions is called the mean free path of the molecule, and is denoted $$\lambda.$$

**a)** Via dimensional analysis and some intuition, estimate $$\lambda$$ for a dilute gas of hard spheres with radius $$r$$ and number density $$n.$$

**b)** A surprising experimental result is that the viscosity of a gas does not depend on its density. Explain how this can be the case, given that viscosity does depend linearly on both number density and mean free path.

**c)** Suppose the mean free path in some gas is $$\lambda.$$ Suppose we are watching a molecule, at it has already traveled a distance $$\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$$ without any collisions. What is the mean distance it will travel before its next collision?

label: PW214
name: A molecule of oxygen near the surface of the Earth has a velocity vertically upwards…
desc: A molecule of oxygen near the surface of the Earth has a velocity vertically upwards equal in magnitude to the root mean square value. If it does not encounter another molecule, calculate: **a)** The height $$h$$ reached if the surface temperature is $$283 \;\mathrm{K}.$$ **b)**…
statement:
A molecule of oxygen near the surface of the Earth has a velocity vertically upwards equal in magnitude to the root mean square value. If it does not encounter another molecule, calculate:

**a)** The height $$h$$ reached if the surface temperature is $$283 \;\mathrm{K}.$$

**b)** The surface temperature $$T_s$$ required for the molecule to escape from the Earth's gravitational field.

\begin{aligned} G & = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \;\mathrm{N \cdot kg^{-2} \cdot m^2} \\ M_{\oplus} & = 5.97 \times 10^{24} \;\mathrm{kg} \\ R_{\oplus} & = 6.4 \times 10^6 \;\mathrm{m}\\ m_{\rm oxygen \; molecule} & = 5.3 \times 10^{-26} \;\mathrm{kg}\\ k_B & = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \;\mathrm{J/K} \end{aligned}

label: PW214
name: When we study quantum mechanics, we will use the Bohr model to discover that the energy…
desc: When we study quantum mechanics, we will use the Bohr model to discover that the energy levels of a hydrogen atom obey $$E_n = -\dfrac{E_0}{n^2},$$ where $$E_0 \approx 13.6 \;\mathrm{eV}$$ is the ionization energy of the hydrogen atom and $$n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots.$$ The number of…
statement:
When we study quantum mechanics, we will use the Bohr model to discover that the energy levels of a hydrogen atom obey $$E_n = -\dfrac{E_0}{n^2},$$ where $$E_0 \approx 13.6 \;\mathrm{eV}$$ is the ionization energy of the hydrogen atom and $$n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots.$$

The number of different states for an electron with energy $$E_n$$ is $$2n^2.$$ So there are two different ground states ($$n=1$$) for the electron (because it is in the ground state, but its spin can be either up or down). Then there are 8 different states all with the energy $$E_2.$$ If you have studied chemistry, you know these as the $$2s$$ and $$2p$$ states (which have the same energy for a hydrogen atom). There are 18 states with energy $$E_3,$$ etc.

Suppose a hydrogen atom is in thermal contact with a reservoir of temperature $$T = 300 \;\mathrm{K},$$ about room temperature.

**a)** Estimate the probability that the Hydrogen atom is not at its ground state energy. For this estimate, assume that the only two possible states are the ground state and the first excited state; ignore the higher-$$n$$ states on the ground that when $$n$$ is very large, the mathematical solution is no longer reasonable; the orbital radius would also be very large, and small influences from surroundings would ionize the atom.

**b)** Find the temperature at which the electron electron is equally likely to have energy $$E_1$$ or $$E_2.$$

**c)** We might expect hydrogen atoms to begin ionizing at a temperature where $$k_b T \approx E_0,$$ but in fact significant ionization occurs at much lower temperatures, especially if the hydrogen is in a gas or plasma of very low density. Briefly explain why.

label: PW214
name: This problem has further discussion of the hydrogen atoms, begun in the previous problem.
desc: This problem has further discussion of the hydrogen atoms, begun in the previous problem. **a)** What is the entropy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state? **b)** What is the entropy of a hydrogen atom in its first excited state? **c)** For what temperatures is the Helmholtz…
statement:
This problem has further discussion of the hydrogen atoms, begun in the previous problem.

**a)** What is the entropy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state?

**b)** What is the entropy of a hydrogen atom in its first excited state?

**c)** For what temperatures is the Helmholtz free energy $$F = U-TS$$ of a hydrogen atom lower in its first excited state than in its ground state?

**d)** Interpret the answer to part (c) in terms under what conditions the atom will spontaneously tend to go to its ground state.

label: PW214
name: Consider a thin flat disk of mass $$M$$ and surface area on one face $$S$$ at initial…
desc: Consider a thin flat disk of mass $$M$$ and surface area on one face $$S$$ at initial temperature $$T_1,$$ resting initially in weightlessness in a gas of density $$\rho$$ at temperature $$T_0.$$ Assume $$T_1 = 1000 T_0.$$ Once of the faces of the disk is covered with a…
statement:
Consider a thin flat disk of mass $$M$$ and surface area on one face $$S$$ at initial temperature $$T_1,$$ resting initially in weightlessness in a gas of density $$\rho$$ at temperature $$T_0.$$ Assume $$T_1 = 1000 T_0.$$ Once of the faces of the disk is covered with a thermally-insulating layer. The other face has a very good thermal contact with the surrounding gas: gas molecules of mass $$m$$ obtain the temperature of the disk during a single collision with the surface.

Estimate the initial acceleration $$a_0$$ and maximal speed $$v_{\rm max}$$ of the disk during its subsequent motion.

Assume the hat capacity of the disk to be on the order of $$N k_B,$$ where $$N$$ is the number of atoms in it, and $$k_B$$ is the Boltzmann constant. Also assume that the molar mass of the gas and disk's materials are the same. The mean free path length of the gas molecules is much larger than the size of the disk. Neglect any edge effects occurring at the edge of the disk.

label: PW214
name: This problem introduces the __partition function__, a useful tool for calculations…
desc: This problem introduces the __partition function__, a useful tool for calculations involving the Boltzmann factor and degeneracy of energy levels. **a)** Suppose that a system is in thermal contact with a reservoir at temperature $$T,$$ so that the probability of the system…
statement:
This problem introduces the __partition function__, a useful tool for calculations involving the Boltzmann factor and degeneracy of energy levels.

**a)** Suppose that a system is in thermal contact with a reservoir at temperature $$T,$$ so that the probability of the system being in any given state of energy $$E_i$$ is proportional to $$e^{-E_i/k_B T}.$$

That is, the probability to be in state $$i$$ is $$P_i = \dfrac{1}{Z} e^{-E_i/k_B T}$$ for some $$Z.$$

Write $$Z$$ as a sum over $$i$$.

**b)** $$Z$$ is called the __partition function__. For any given system, $$Z$$ is a function of $$T.$$

Often, it is useful to define $$\beta = \dfrac{1}{k_B T},$$ in which case $$Z$$ is a function of $$\beta.$$

Show that the mean energy of the system is given by $$ \langle E\rangle = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \beta} \ln Z.$$

**c)** In physics, it shouldn't matter where we set the zero of potential energy. Suppose we add some energy $$E_0$$ to all the energy levels of a system. Show that the probabilities of individual energy levels do not change according to our formalism, and find the new mean energy.

**d)** It is sometimes useful to know the spread in energies of a system. One measure of this spread is the standard deviation, $$\sigma_E = \sqrt{\langle E^2\rangle - \langle E \rangle^2}.$$

Show that $$\langle E^2 \rangle = \dfrac{1}{Z} \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 Z}{\mathrm{d}\beta^2}.$$

**e)** Now use the results above to show $$\sigma_E = k_B T \sqrt{C/k_B}$$ where $$C$$ is the system's heat capacity, $$C = \dfrac{\partial \langle E \rangle }{\partial T}.$$

label: PW214
name: Consider two liquids, A and B, which are insoluble (they do not mix). The pressures…
desc: Consider two liquids, A and B, which are insoluble (they do not mix). The pressures $$p_i$$ ($$i = A$$ or $$B$$) of their saturated vapors obey, to a good approximation, the formula $$\ln(p_i/p_0) = \dfrac{\alpha_i}{T} + \beta_i$$ where $$p_0$$ denotes the normal atmospheric…
statement:
Consider two liquids, A and B, which are insoluble (they do not mix). The pressures $$p_i$$ ($$i = A$$ or $$B$$) of their saturated vapors obey, to a good approximation, the formula $$\ln(p_i/p_0) = \dfrac{\alpha_i}{T} + \beta_i$$ where $$p_0$$ denotes the normal atmospheric pressure, $$T$$ the absolute temperature of the vapor, and $$\alpha_i$$ and $$\beta_i$$ certain constants depending on the liquid.

The values of the ratio $$p_i/p_0$$ for the liquids A and B at the temperature $$40^\circ C$$ and $$90^\circ C$$ are given in the table below.

**a)** Determine the boiling temperatures of the liquids A and B under the pressure $$p_0.$$

**b)** The liquids A and B were poured into a vessel in which the layers shown in the figure below were formed. The surface of the liquid B has been covered with a thin layer of a non-volatile liquid C, which is insoluble in the liquids A and B and vice versa, thereby preventing any free evaporation from the upper surface of the liquid B. The ratio of molecular masses of the liquids A and B (in the gaseous phase) is $$\gamma = \dfrac{\mu_A}{\mu_B} = 8.$$

The masses of the liquids A and B were initially the same, each equal to $$m = 100 \;\mathrm{g}.$$ The heights of the layers of the liquids in the vessel and the densities of the liquids are small enough to make the assumption that the pressure in any point in the vessel is practically equal ot the normal atmospheric pressure $$p_0.$$

The system of liquids in the vessel is slowly, but continuously and uniformly heated. It was established that the temperature $$t$$ of the liquids changed with time $$\tau$$ as shown schematically in the figure on the right above.

Determine the temperatures $$t_1$$ and $$t_2$$ corresponding to the horizontal parts of the diagram and the masses of the liquids A and B at the time $$\tau_1.$$ The temperatures should be rounded to the nearest degree and the masses of the liquids should be determined to one tenth of a gram.

Assume that the vapors of the liquids, to a good approximation, obey the rule that the pressure of a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the gases forming the mixture, and that the gases can be treated as ideal.

label: PW214
name: The Boltzmann Factor and the Height of the Atmosphere — Perhaps the single most important result in…
desc: Perhaps the single most important result in statistical mechanics is the __Boltzmann factor__: if a system in thermal contact with a large reservoir at fixed absolute temperature $$T$$ can occupy states $$i$$ with energies $$E_i,$$ then the probability of finding it in state…
statement:
Perhaps the single most important result in statistical mechanics is the __Boltzmann factor__: if a system in thermal contact with a large reservoir at fixed absolute temperature $$T$$ can occupy states $$i$$ with energies $$E_i,$$ then the probability of finding it in state $$i$$ is proportional to $$e^{-E_i/k_B T},$$ where $$k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\;\mathrm{J/K}$$ is __Boltzmann's constant__ and $$T$$ must be measured on an absolute scale such as Kelvin. As a first application, consider a single air molecule of mass $$m$$ bouncing around inside a room of height $$h.$$ The walls of the room act as the heat bath: energy passes back and forth between the molecule and the jiggling atoms of the walls.

__(a)__ Model the molecule with just two states: "low," near the floor, with energy $$E_0,$$ and "high," near the ceiling, with energy $$E_0 + mgh.$$ Show that $$\dfrac{P_{\rm high}}{P_{\rm low}} = e^{-mgh/k_B T},$$ and explain why the value of $$E_0$$ never matters — only the energy __gap__ between the two states does.

__(b)__ Using your formula from part (a), write a condition on $$k_B T$$ compared to $$mgh$$ under which the molecule is nearly equally likely to be found near the floor or near the ceiling. Is the room you are sitting in "very hot" in this sense? (Hint: does breathing feel any different lying on the floor versus standing on your desk?)

__(c)__ How tall would a room have to be for the density of air to fall by a factor of two between the floor and the ceiling, assuming the air is nitrogen at $$T = 300\;\mathrm{K}?$$ Nitrogen has atomic mass $$14$$ and is diatomic (the molecules are $$\mathrm{N_2}$$), and $$1\;\mathrm{amu} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\;\mathrm{kg}.$$

__(d)__ The height of Mt. Everest is a bit under $$9\;\mathrm{km}.$$ Is your answer to part (c) reasonable, given what you know about how the air thins as you climb?

label: PW214
name: The Average Gravitational Energy of an Air Molecule — A single molecule of mass $$m$$ moves in a very tall…
desc: A single molecule of mass $$m$$ moves in a very tall column of air held at uniform temperature $$T.$$ Because the molecule's height $$h$$ above the ground can be any nonnegative real number, the Boltzmann factor now gives a continuous probability distribution: the probability…
statement:
A single molecule of mass $$m$$ moves in a very tall column of air held at uniform temperature $$T.$$ Because the molecule's height $$h$$ above the ground can be any nonnegative real number, the Boltzmann factor now gives a continuous probability distribution: the probability density for the molecule to be at height $$h$$ is $$P(h) = \alpha\, e^{-mgh/k_B T}$$ for some constant $$\alpha.$$

__(a)__ Probabilities must add up to one: $$\int_0^\infty P(h)\,\mathrm{d}h = 1.$$ Use this normalization condition to find $$\alpha.$$ (The quantity $$Z = \dfrac{1}{\alpha}$$ turns out to be an important object called the __partition function__.)

__(b)__ The average of a quantity is its probability-weighted sum; for a continuous variable, $$\langle h \rangle = \int_0^\infty h\, P(h)\, \mathrm{d}h.$$ Find the average gravitational potential energy $$\langle mgh \rangle$$ of the molecule. You may use the fact $$\int_0^\infty x e^{-x}\,\mathrm{d}x = 1.$$

__(c)__ The __equipartition theorem__ is usually quoted as "the mean energy per degree of freedom is $$\tfrac{1}{2} k_B T$$" — for instance, an ideal gas molecule has three translational degrees of freedom and mean kinetic energy $$\tfrac{3}{2} k_B T.$$ Your answer to part (b) should not match $$\tfrac{1}{2} k_B T.$$ The full version of the theorem says that a coordinate entering the energy through a power $$n,$$ as $$E \propto q^n,$$ contributes mean energy $$\dfrac{1}{n} k_B T.$$ Check that this full version agrees with your answer to (b), and check that it reproduces the familiar $$\tfrac{1}{2} k_B T$$ for a mass on a spring with $$E = \tfrac{1}{2} k x^2.$$

label: PW214
name: The Most Likely Speed of a Gas Molecule — A gas of molecules of mass $$m$$ is at temperature $$T.$$ The…
desc: A gas of molecules of mass $$m$$ is at temperature $$T.$$ The Boltzmann factor says the probability for a molecule to be in an individual state of energy $$E$$ is proportional to $$e^{-E/k_B T}$$ — a function that strictly __decreases__ with energy, so each individual low-energy…
statement:
A gas of molecules of mass $$m$$ is at temperature $$T.$$ The Boltzmann factor says the probability for a molecule to be in an individual state of energy $$E$$ is proportional to $$e^{-E/k_B T}$$ — a function that strictly __decreases__ with energy, so each individual low-energy state is more probable than each individual high-energy state. Nevertheless, the most likely __speed__ of a gas molecule is not zero: it is a medium speed, with kinetic energy comparable to $$k_B T.$$

__(a)__ The Boltzmann factor gives the probability per __state__, but many different states can share the same speed. Explain why the probability for the molecule to have energy $$E$$ is $$P(E) \propto \Omega(E)\, e^{-E/k_B T},$$ where $$\Omega(E)$$ is the number of states with energy $$E$$ (called the __degeneracy__). As a warm-up example: if a room is very wide at the top and very narrow at the bottom, where might a molecule most likely be found, even though states at the bottom have lower energy?

__(b)__ The state of a molecule is its position and momentum, and for the speed distribution the position is irrelevant. Show that the number of momentum states corresponding to speed $$v$$ scales as $$v^2,$$ and conclude that the probability of finding the molecule at speed $$v$$ obeys $$P(v) \propto v^2 e^{-mv^2/(2 k_B T)}.$$ This is the __Maxwell-Boltzmann probability distribution__.

__(c)__ By maximizing $$P(v),$$ find the most probable speed $$v_p$$ in terms of $$m,$$ $$T,$$ and $$k_B,$$ and confirm that the corresponding kinetic energy is comparable to $$k_B T.$$

__(d)__ The figure below shows the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distributions of several noble gases at room temperature. The helium curve and the xenon curve have exactly the same shape. Explain why helium's curve is so much more spread out.

label: PW214
name: Counting States: Entropy and Why Gases Spread Out — If a system at fixed energy has access to $$\Omega$$…
desc: If a system at fixed energy has access to $$\Omega$$ different states, its __entropy__ is defined as $$S = k_B \ln \Omega.$$ (The number $$\Omega$$ is usually astronomically huge, which is why we track its logarithm; the factor $$k_B$$ is pure convention.) __(a)__ Suppose system…
statement:
If a system at fixed energy has access to $$\Omega$$ different states, its __entropy__ is defined as $$S = k_B \ln \Omega.$$ (The number $$\Omega$$ is usually astronomically huge, which is why we track its logarithm; the factor $$k_B$$ is pure convention.)

__(a)__ Suppose system $$A$$ can be in any of $$\Omega_A$$ states and system $$B$$ in any of $$\Omega_B$$ states, independently. How many states does the combined system have? Use your answer to show that the entropy of the combined system is $$S_A + S_B.$$ A quantity that scales up with system size like this is called __extensive__ (energy and mass are other examples); quantities like temperature and pressure that do not change when you scale up the system are called __intensive__.

__(b)__ For a single gas molecule in a container, the number of available states is proportional to the volume: $$\Omega \sim V.$$ A student argues: "So if we double the volume of any ideal gas, the entropy changes by $$\Delta S = k_B \ln(2V) - k_B \ln(V) = k_B \ln 2$$ — a fixed amount, no matter how much gas there is." That conclusion is wrong. Find the correct entropy change for a gas of $$N$$ molecules whose volume is doubled, and identify the student's error.

__(c)__ The second law of thermodynamics — isolated systems maximize their entropy — rests on the idea that at fixed total energy, every individual state is equally likely. A state with all $$N$$ gas molecules on the right half of a container is exactly as likely as any one particular spread-out state. So why does gas released on the right side of a container always expand to fill it? Estimate the ratio of the number of states with the molecules spread between both halves to the number with all molecules on the right, and evaluate the implications using Avogadro's number, $$6 \times 10^{23}.$$

label: PW214
name: Temperature Defined by Entropy — For a monatomic ideal gas of $$N$$ molecules with total energy $$E,$$ define…
desc: For a monatomic ideal gas of $$N$$ molecules with total energy $$E,$$ define the average energy per molecule $$\bar{E} = E/N.$$ A state count shows that the entropy of the gas is $$S = S_0 + \tfrac{3}{2} N k_B \ln \bar{E},$$ where $$S_0$$ is a constant that absorbs the volume…
statement:
For a monatomic ideal gas of $$N$$ molecules with total energy $$E,$$ define the average energy per molecule $$\bar{E} = E/N.$$ A state count shows that the entropy of the gas is $$S = S_0 + \tfrac{3}{2} N k_B \ln \bar{E},$$ where $$S_0$$ is a constant that absorbs the volume dependence and other details.

__(a)__ Explain physically why heating the gas (increasing $$\bar{E}$$) increases its entropy. (Recall that the number of momentum vectors available at speed $$v$$ grows like $$v^2.$$)

__(b)__ Compute $$\dfrac{\partial S}{\partial E},$$ holding $$N$$ fixed.

__(c)__ In statistical physics, temperature is __defined__ by $$T \equiv \dfrac{\partial E}{\partial S}.$$ Use this definition together with part (b) to find $$\bar{E}$$ in terms of $$T,$$ and check the result against the equipartition theorem.

__(d)__ Two systems are placed in thermal contact and isolated from everything else, so energy passes between them but the total energy is fixed. The second law says the total entropy is maximized at equilibrium. Using $$\mathrm{d}S = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{T}$$ for each system, show that equilibrium — the point where transferring a little energy no longer changes the total entropy — occurs exactly when the two temperatures are equal.

label: PW214
name: Where the Boltzmann Factor Comes From — Earlier we simply assumed the Boltzmann factor; this problem derives…
desc: Earlier we simply assumed the Boltzmann factor; this problem derives it from counting states. A small system can be in one of two states, with energies $$E_1$$ and $$E_2 > E_1.$$ It is in thermal contact with an environment that is very large and has temperature $$T.$$ The total…
statement:
Earlier we simply assumed the Boltzmann factor; this problem derives it from counting states. A small system can be in one of two states, with energies $$E_1$$ and $$E_2 > E_1.$$ It is in thermal contact with an environment that is very large and has temperature $$T.$$ The total energy of system plus environment is fixed, and the fundamental postulate of statistical mechanics says that at fixed total energy, every individual state of the combined universe (system plus environment) is equally likely.

__(a)__ Let $$\Omega_1$$ be the number of states of the universe in which the system has energy $$E_1,$$ and $$\Omega_2$$ the number in which it has energy $$E_2.$$ The system contributes exactly one state in each case — so why is $$\Omega_1 \neq \Omega_2?$$ Which is larger?

__(b)__ The statistical definition of temperature, $$T \equiv \dfrac{\partial E}{\partial S},$$ can be rewritten as $$\mathrm{d}S = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{T}.$$ When the system jumps from energy $$E_1$$ to $$E_2,$$ the environment loses energy $$\Delta E = E_2 - E_1.$$ Find the resulting change in the environment's entropy. (Why is it legitimate to treat $$T$$ as constant during this change?)

__(c)__ Invert the definition of entropy, $$S = k_B \ln \Omega,$$ to write $$\Omega$$ in terms of $$S,$$ and combine with part (b) to compute the ratio $$\dfrac{\Omega_2}{\Omega_1}.$$ Conclude that the probability for the system to occupy a state of energy $$E$$ is proportional to $$e^{-E/k_B T}.$$

label: PW214
name: Hot Water, Cold Water, and Dissolving Salt — When salt is dropped into water, the salt molecules break apart…
desc: When salt is dropped into water, the salt molecules break apart into ions that float freely through the water — but only up to a point. Add enough salt and the water __saturates__: it holds the maximum amount of dissolved ions, and the remaining salt sits in clumps. Two…
statement:
When salt is dropped into water, the salt molecules break apart into ions that float freely through the water — but only up to a point. Add enough salt and the water __saturates__: it holds the maximum amount of dissolved ions, and the remaining salt sits in clumps. Two thermodynamic facts about this process: first, the entropy per dissolved ion behaves like an ideal gas's, scaling as $$\dfrac{S}{N} \sim \ln\dfrac{V}{N},$$ where $$V$$ is the volume of water and $$N$$ the number of dissolved ions. Second, dissolving is __endothermic__: separating the ions requires breaking ionic bonds, and that energy is drawn from the thermal energy of the salt and water, which cool slightly as salt dissolves. Recall also that removing heat $$\mathrm{d}Q$$ from matter at temperature $$T$$ lowers its entropy by $$\mathrm{d}S = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{T}.$$

__(a)__ Which state has higher entropy (counting only the positional entropy of the ions) — salt dissolved in the water, or salt sitting in clumps? And which creates more entropy: dissolving a pinch of salt into nearly fresh water, or into water that is already very salty?

__(b)__ Dissolving salt increases the positional entropy of the ions. What __other__ entropy change must be weighed against it, and what is its sign?

__(c)__ The universe maximizes total entropy. Use parts (a) and (b) to explain why salt dissolves but eventually saturates, and then to answer the main question: does __more__ salt dissolve in hot water or in cold water?

__(d)__ Predict what happens if very salty water is cooled and frozen extremely slowly. (Bonus: a popsicle that partially thaws and refreezes sometimes ends up with sugary gunk on its surface. Why?)

label: PW214
name: A Gas, a Spring, and the Helmholtz Free Energy — A horizontal cylinder of cross-sectional area $$A$$ and…
desc: A horizontal cylinder of cross-sectional area $$A$$ and length $$L$$ contains a movable divider at distance $$x$$ from the left end. To the left of the divider is an ideal gas of $$N$$ molecules; to the right is a spring of spring constant $$k$$ whose relaxed length equals the…
statement:
A horizontal cylinder of cross-sectional area $$A$$ and length $$L$$ contains a movable divider at distance $$x$$ from the left end. To the left of the divider is an ideal gas of $$N$$ molecules; to the right is a spring of spring constant $$k$$ whose relaxed length equals the full cylinder length $$L,$$ so $$x$$ is also the spring's compression. Ignore gravity and friction. The gas stays in thermal contact with a reservoir at temperature $$T,$$ and the divider moves slowly enough that the gas is always at temperature $$T.$$ The gas pushes the divider right; the spring pushes it left; the divider settles at an equilibrium position $$x_{\rm eq}.$$ Two facts you may use: the entropy of an ideal gas at fixed temperature obeys $$S_{\rm gas} = S_0 + N k_B \ln V,$$ and the energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature and the number of molecules.

__(a)__ Using $$V = A x,$$ show that moving the divider from $$x$$ to $$x + \mathrm{d}x$$ changes the entropy of the gas by $$\mathrm{d}S_{\rm gas} = \dfrac{N k_B}{x}\,\mathrm{d}x.$$

__(b)__ As the divider moves right by $$\mathrm{d}x,$$ the spring's energy $$\tfrac{1}{2} k x^2$$ increases. Track where that energy comes from, keeping in mind that the gas's energy stays constant, and show that the entropy of the environment (the reservoir) changes by $$\mathrm{d}S_{\rm env} = -\dfrac{k x}{T}\,\mathrm{d}x.$$

__(c)__ The second law says equilibrium maximizes the total entropy, so $$\mathrm{d}S_{\rm gas} + \mathrm{d}S_{\rm env} = 0$$ at $$x_{\rm eq}.$$ Find $$x_{\rm eq}.$$

__(d)__ Show that your equilibrium condition is identical to the ordinary mechanical force balance: the spring force $$k x$$ equals the gas pressure force $$P A.$$ (The ideal gas law $$P V = N k_B T$$ will help.)

__(e)__ In mechanics, force is a derivative of energy, $$f = -\dfrac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}x}$$ — but that fails for the gas here, whose energy never changes. Show instead that the gas's force can be written $$f_{\rm gas} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(T S_{\rm gas}\right),$$ and conclude that the equilibrium condition is $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(U - T S\right) = 0.$$ The quantity $$F = U - TS$$ is called the __Helmholtz free energy__; explain in a sentence why minimizing $$F$$ captures the energy-entropy competition.

__(f)__ Without recomputing anything, say which way $$x_{\rm eq}$$ moves if $$k$$ is increased, and which way it moves if $$T$$ is increased — and interpret each shift as the energy-entropy competition tipping one way or the other.

label: PW215
name: Supernova 1987A occurred approximately $$1.7 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{ly}$$ from Earth. The…
desc: Supernova 1987A occurred approximately $$1.7 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{ly}$$ from Earth. The supernova emitted a burst of neutrinos, some of which could be detected at Earth. Assume that the supernova emitted an extremely short burst of electron neutrinos and that neutrinos with an…
statement: Supernova 1987A occurred approximately $$1.7 \times 10^5 \;\mathrm{ly}$$ from Earth. The supernova emitted a burst of neutrinos, some of which could be detected at Earth. Assume that the supernova emitted an extremely short burst of electron neutrinos and that neutrinos with an energy of $$15 \;\mathrm{MeV}$$ arrived our detectors $$15 \;\mathrm{s}$$ before the arrival of $$7.5 \;\mathrm{MeV}$$ neutrinos. What mass must the neutrinos have to account for the time delay in their arrival?

label: PW215
name: In this problem, we examine the __Pound-Rebka__ experiment, conducted in 1960 by Robert…
desc: In this problem, we examine the __Pound-Rebka__ experiment, conducted in 1960 by Robert Pound and Glen Rebka Jr. This experiment was the first experimental confirmation of the __equivalence principle__, which states that holding stationary in a gravitational field is equivalent…
statement:
In this problem, we examine the __Pound-Rebka__ experiment, conducted in 1960 by Robert Pound and Glen Rebka Jr. This experiment was the first experimental confirmation of the __equivalence principle__, which states that holding stationary in a gravitational field is equivalent to accelerating at $$g$$ when there is no gravitational field.

Pound and Rebka had an iron-57 source, which they placed at the top of the Jefferson Laboratory at Harvard. They placed a second iron-57 source at the bottom of the laboratory. Gamma rays were emitted from the source at the top of the lab and absorbed by the source at the bottom of the lab. The vertical distance between the two sources was $$d = 22.5 \;\mathrm{m}.$$

When the source at the top of the lab emitted a gamma ray, it traveled down the lab to the other source at the bottom. During this time, we can think of the effect of gravity as equivalent to what would happen if the entire lab were accelerating upward at $$g.$$ Thus, it is as if the source at the bottom of the lab picked up some small speed $$v$$ moving towards the gamma ray as it fell.

(Note that gamma rays are light; they move at speed $$c.$$)

**a)** Find a simplified formula, correct to first order in $$d,$$ for the fractional shift in the wavelength $$\dfrac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda}$$ of the gamma ray as detected at the lower source when $$v/c\ll 1.$$ Your answer should be in terms of $$g, d,$$ and $$c.$$

**b)** What would be the fractional shift in wavelength in a lab on the earth's surface?

**c)** In the experiment, it was important that the sample at the bottom be able to absorb gamma rays emitted by the sample at the top. To that end, the choice of iron-57 was deliberate, as it is a useful isotope for M$$\text{\"{o}}$$ssbauer spectroscopy. When a gamma ray is emitted from an atomic nucleus, it carries momentum. To conserve momentum, the entire nucleus is kicked back in the opposite direction. However, in the M$$\text{\"{o}}$$ssbauer effect, the "kickback" momentum does not go to just the nucleus of the atom that emitted the gamma rays, but to the entire crystal in which that nucleus lies. Briefly explain why Pound and Rebka needed to use a sample that exhibits the M$$\text{\"{o}}$$ssbauer effect in their experiment.

**d)** Up until now, we have assumed that the source and target samples of iron-57 were at rest with respect to each other, as viewed from the lab frame with gravitational acceleration. In fact, in the experiment this was not the case. Instead, Pound and Rebka mounted the source on a speaker, which oscillated sinusoidally. They found that the absorption of the gamma rays oscillated as well (although not sinusoidally; the oscillation peaked once per cycle of the speaker). The peak of the absorption plot did not line up with the peak of the displacement of the speaker. Instead, they were different by some phase $$\phi.$$ Find $$\phi$$ in terms of $$A,$$ the amplitude of speaker oscillations, $$f,$$ the frequency of the speaker oscillations, and $$g, d,$$ and $$c.$$

label: PW215
name: This problem continues discussion of the equivalence principle, which we began in the…
desc: This problem continues discussion of the equivalence principle, which we began in the previous problem on the Pound-Rebka experiment. Another consequence of the equivalence principle is that light will be bent in a gravitational field. This has never been measured on the surface…
statement:
This problem continues discussion of the equivalence principle, which we began in the previous problem on the Pound-Rebka experiment.

Another consequence of the equivalence principle is that light will be bent in a gravitational field. This has never been measured on the surface of the Earth, but was verified qualitatively by Arthur Eddington by observing starlight passing near the sun's edge during a total eclipse in 1919. (Eddington needed to wait for a solar eclipse because this was the only time it was possible to observe the position in the sky of stars whose light passed close by the sun.)

In this problem, we ask why the observation can't practically be done on earth's surface.

Let's predict how much bending we should see in a laboratory at rest on the earth's surface. What one would observe in such a laboratory should be the same as what one would observe in a laboratory accelerating in deep space with a uniform acceleration of $$\vec{a} = -\vec{g},$$ where $$\vec{g}$$ is the acceleration due to gravity on Earth's surface.

Imagine that a laser at one end of the laboratory emits a beam of light that originally travels parallel to the laboratory floor. This light shines on the opposite wall of the laboratory a horizontal distance $$d = 30.0 \;\mathrm{m}$$ away from the laser.

**a)** Find the magnitude of this deflection in a laboratory on the surface of the earth.

**b)** Find the magnitude of this deflection if the laboratory sits on the surface of a neutron star with mass $$M = 3.0 \times 10^{30} \;\mathrm{kg}$$ and a radius of $$R = 12 \;\mathrm{km}.$$

label: PW215
name: **a)** When an electron annihilates with a positron (the antiparticle of an electron…
desc: **a)** When an electron annihilates with a positron (the antiparticle of an electron, having all the same properties as an electron, but with opposite charge), photons are produced. Explain why it is not possible for this process to produce a single photon only. **b)** A…
statement:
**a)** When an electron annihilates with a positron (the antiparticle of an electron, having all the same properties as an electron, but with opposite charge), photons are produced. Explain why it is not possible for this process to produce a single photon only.

**b)** A positron moving with velocity $$v$$ in the positive $$x$$ direction annihilates with a stationary electron, producing two identical photons. Find the angle between the emitted photons in terms of $$\gamma_v = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}.$$

**c)** Fluorine-18 undergoes beta-plus decay and is commonly used in positron emission tomography. Positrons are emitted with a range of kinetic energies up to a maximum of $$635 \;\mathrm{keV}.$$ If a positron were to immediately annihilate with an electron, producing two photons, what would be the minimum angle between them?

The rest mass of an electron or positron is $$511 \;\mathrm{keV}.$$

label: PW215
name: Below is a spacetime diagram showing two worldlines. Also shown in dots are hyperbolas…
desc: Below is a spacetime diagram showing two worldlines. Also shown in dots are hyperbolas which connect spacetime points that all have the same invariant interval, $$\Delta s^2 = \Delta x^2 - c \Delta t^2,$$ from the origin (labeled $$0).$$ One worldline is the vertical line…
statement:
Below is a spacetime diagram showing two worldlines. Also shown in dots are hyperbolas which connect spacetime points that all have the same invariant interval, $$\Delta s^2 = \Delta x^2 - c \Delta t^2,$$ from the origin (labeled $$0).$$

One worldline is the vertical line, labeled $$B.$$ It is at rest in this frame.

The other worldline is a segmented line that connects events $$0,1,2$$ and $$3.$$ It moves at different speeds between the events. The proper time experienced along each segment of this worldline is written next to the wordline.

**a)** Trace the axes and hyperbolas onto a blank piece of paper. Sketch a qualitatively-correct spacetime diagram for the same pair of worldlines observed in a frame in which the particle on the segmented worldline has zero velocity between event 1 and event 2.

**b)** What is the velocity, in this new frame, of the particle moving along worldline $$B?$$

**c)** On each straight portion of the segmented worldline for this new frame, write the numerical value of the interval between the two connected events.

label: PW215
name: In 1851, well before Einstein introduced special relativity, Hippolyte Fizeau conducted…
desc: In 1851, well before Einstein introduced special relativity, Hippolyte Fizeau conducted experiments to measure the speed of light through moving water. A schematic sketch of Fizeau's experiment is shown below. (This is only a schematic, not a true representation of Fizeau's…
statement:
In 1851, well before Einstein introduced special relativity, Hippolyte Fizeau conducted experiments to measure the speed of light through moving water. A schematic sketch of Fizeau's experiment is shown below. (This is only a schematic, not a true representation of Fizeau's actual apparatus; more details on the experiment can be found on the Wikipedia page.)

**a)** If the index of refraction of water is $$n$$ and the water moves at speed $$v_w,$$ find the speed of light through the water, as observed in the lab frame.

**b)** Suppose light traveled $$2 \;\mathrm{m}$$ through each arm of the interferometer shown above. Suppose the water speed began at $$v_w = 0$$ and the wavelength of light was $$600 \;\mathrm{nm}$$ outside the water. You can assume $$n = 1.3.$$ How fast would the water have to travel for the dark and light fringes in Fizeau's experiment to exchange places?

label: PW215
name: **a)** Suppose a rocket moves at speed $$v$$ in the $$x$$ direction in the rest frame of…
desc: **a)** Suppose a rocket moves at speed $$v$$ in the $$x$$ direction in the rest frame of a laboratory. A meter stick lies at rest in the rocket frame and makes an angle $$\phi'$$ with the $$x'$$ axis. Laboratory observers measured the $$x$$ and $$y$$ projections of the stick as…
statement:
**a)** Suppose a rocket moves at speed $$v$$ in the $$x$$ direction in the rest frame of a laboratory.

A meter stick lies at rest in the rocket frame and makes an angle $$\phi'$$ with the $$x'$$ axis. Laboratory observers measured the $$x$$ and $$y$$ projections of the stick as it streaks past. What values do they measure for these projections, compared with the $$x'$$ and $$y'$$ projections measured by rocket observers?

**b)** What angle $$\phi$$ does the stick make with the $$x$$ axis in the laboratory frame?

**c)** What is the length of the meter stick in the laboratory frame?

**d)** Assume (without proof for now) that the directions of electric field lines transform in the same way as the direction of meter sticks. Qualitatively sketch the electric field lines near a charge moving at relativistic speed.

label: PW215
name: The results of this problem should be compared and contrasted with those of the previous…
desc: The results of this problem should be compared and contrasted with those of the previous problem on a meter stick. **a)** A rocket moves at speed $$v$$ in the $$x$$ direction in the rest frame of a laboratory. A particle moves with uniform speed $$v_y'$$ along the $$y'$$ axis of…
statement:
The results of this problem should be compared and contrasted with those of the previous problem on a meter stick.

**a)** A rocket moves at speed $$v$$ in the $$x$$ direction in the rest frame of a laboratory.

A particle moves with uniform speed $$v_y'$$ along the $$y'$$ axis of the rocket frame. Find the velocity of the particle in the unprimed laboratory frame.

**b)** Now suppose that the particle, in the rocket frame, moves in a direction at an angle $$\phi'$$ with the $$x'$$ axis. Find the angle $$\phi$$ that the velocity vector of the particle makes with the $$x$$ axis of the laboratory frame. Is your answer the same as for the tilted meter stick in the previous problem? Why or why not?

**c)** A flash of light is emitted at an angle $$\phi'$$ with respect to the $$x'$$ axis of the rocket frame. Find the angle $$\phi$$ of the direction of motion of the flash with respect to the $$x$$ axis of the laboratory frame.

**d)** A particle at rest in the rocket frame emits light uniformly in all directions. Consider the 50 percent of this light that goes into the forward hemisphere in the rocket frame. Show that in the laboratory frame, this light is concentrated in a narrow forward cone of half angle $$\phi_0$$ whose axis lies along the direction of motion of the particle. Find $$\phi_0.$$

(This result is called the __headlight effect__.)

label: PW215
name: This is one more problem on sticks and the lab and rocket frames.
desc: This is one more problem on sticks and the lab and rocket frames. A meter stick lying parallel to the $$x$$ axis moves in the $$y$$ direction in the laboratory frame at speed $$v_y.$$ A rocket moves in the $$x$$ direction in the laboratory frame. In the rocket frame, the meter…
statement:
This is one more problem on sticks and the lab and rocket frames.

A meter stick lying parallel to the $$x$$ axis moves in the $$y$$ direction in the laboratory frame at speed $$v_y.$$

A rocket moves in the $$x$$ direction in the laboratory frame. In the rocket frame, the meter stick appears tilted compared to the $$x'$$ axis by an angle $$\phi'.$$

Explain the origin of this effect and find $$\phi'.$$

label: PW215
name: A spaceship travels with constant acceleration $$g$$ as perceived by the passengers along…
desc: A spaceship travels with constant acceleration $$g$$ as perceived by the passengers along a straight line. At a certain moment, it launches two missiles in the direction of its motion, one with speed $$v$$ and another with speed $$2v.$$ (These are the speeds in the spaceship's…
statement: A spaceship travels with constant acceleration $$g$$ as perceived by the passengers along a straight line. At a certain moment, it launches two missiles in the direction of its motion, one with speed $$v$$ and another with speed $$2v.$$ (These are the speeds in the spaceship's frame.) Find the proper time interval in the space ship between catching the first missile and catching the second missile.

label: PW215
name: How Fast Is Relativistic? Approximating the Lorentz Factor — A phenomenon is called __non-relativistic__ when…
desc: A phenomenon is called __non-relativistic__ when corrections to Newtonian physics from special relativity are too small to matter. The size of relativistic effects is governed by the __Lorentz factor__, $$\gamma(v) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}},$$ which equals $$1$$ for an…
statement:
A phenomenon is called __non-relativistic__ when corrections to Newtonian physics from special relativity are too small to matter. The size of relativistic effects is governed by the __Lorentz factor__, $$\gamma(v) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}},$$ which equals $$1$$ for an object at rest and grows without bound as the speed $$v$$ approaches the speed of light $$c.$$

__(a)__ Find, exactly, the speed $$v$$ at which the Lorentz factor reaches $$\gamma = 1.01$$ — roughly meaning that relativistic corrections are a $$1\%$$ effect. Express $$v$$ as a fraction of $$c.$$ Is the speed larger or smaller than you expected?

__(b)__ Now redo the calculation generically: find an approximate expression for the speed $$v$$ at which $$\gamma = 1 + z,$$ where $$z \ll 1.$$ (The number $$z$$ is called the __redshift__ in astronomy and cosmology.) Use the __binomial approximation__, $$(1+\epsilon)^n \approx 1 + n\epsilon$$ for $$|n\epsilon| \ll 1,$$ keeping only the __leading-order__ correction — drop terms like $$z^2,$$ but never drop the $$z$$ term itself, since that would erase the very effect you are computing. Check that your formula approximately reproduces your answer to part (a).

__(c)__ Finally, consider the opposite extreme: a speed very close to $$c.$$ Suppose $$v = c(1 - x)$$ with $$x \ll 1.$$ Find an approximate expression for $$\gamma$$ in this regime. (When $$\gamma \gg 1,$$ the phenomenon is called __ultra-relativistic__.)

label: PW215
name: Energy and Momentum in the Two Extreme Regimes — In special relativity, a particle of mass $$m$$ moving at…
desc: In special relativity, a particle of mass $$m$$ moving at speed $$v$$ has energy $$E = \gamma m c^2$$ and momentum $$p = \gamma m v,$$ where $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}.$$ __(a)__ Show that in the non-relativistic regime ($$v \ll c$$), the relativistic momentum…
statement:
In special relativity, a particle of mass $$m$$ moving at speed $$v$$ has energy $$E = \gamma m c^2$$ and momentum $$p = \gamma m v,$$ where $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}.$$

__(a)__ Show that in the non-relativistic regime ($$v \ll c$$), the relativistic momentum reduces to the Newtonian formula.

__(b)__ Setting $$\gamma = 1$$ in the energy formula gives only the rest energy $$E = mc^2,$$ with no trace of Newtonian kinetic energy. Expand $$\gamma$$ one order further using the binomial approximation $$(1+\epsilon)^n \approx 1 + n\epsilon,$$ and show that the Newtonian kinetic energy emerges. Why does the extra constant term not affect Newtonian dynamics?

__(c)__ Now consider the __ultra-relativistic__ regime, $$\gamma \gg 1,$$ where $$v \approx c.$$ Find the relationship between $$E$$ and $$p$$ in this regime. What familiar particle does an ultra-relativistic electron closely resemble, and why?

label: PW215
name: When Does a Gas Become Relativistic? — Consider a gas of particles of mass $$m$$ at temperature $$T.$$ By the…
desc: Consider a gas of particles of mass $$m$$ at temperature $$T.$$ By the __equipartition theorem__, the average kinetic energy of each particle is $$E = \dfrac32 k_B T,$$ where $$k_B \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\;\mathrm{J/K}$$ is Boltzmann's constant. We will say the gas "becomes…
statement:
Consider a gas of particles of mass $$m$$ at temperature $$T.$$ By the __equipartition theorem__, the average kinetic energy of each particle is $$E = \dfrac32 k_B T,$$ where $$k_B \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\;\mathrm{J/K}$$ is Boltzmann's constant. We will say the gas "becomes relativistic" at the temperature where the Lorentz factor of a typical particle reaches $$\gamma \approx 1.02.$$ Since this is barely above $$1,$$ you may use the non-relativistic expansion $$\gamma \approx 1 + \dfrac12\dfrac{v^2}{c^2}$$ and the Newtonian kinetic energy $$\dfrac12 mv^2.$$

__(a)__ Find a formula for the temperature at which the gas becomes relativistic, in terms of $$\gamma - 1,$$ $$m,$$ $$c,$$ and $$k_B.$$

__(b)__ Evaluate this temperature for electrons, which have mass $$m \approx 10^{-30}\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ (At such temperatures, atoms are smashed apart into nuclei and free electrons — a plasma. The electrons are the relevant particles because they are far lighter than nuclei, so they move faster and become relativistic at a lower temperature.)

__(c)__ Compare your answer to some astronomical temperatures: the sun's core is about $$10^7\;\mathrm{K},$$ the core of a red giant about $$10^8\;\mathrm{K},$$ and a supernova about $$10^9\;\mathrm{K}.$$ In which of these environments are the electrons relativistic?

label: PW215
name: Simultaneity on a Moving Train — A train has length $$L'$$ in its own reference frame (the __primed frame__)…
desc: A train has length $$L'$$ in its own reference frame (the __primed frame__) and moves in the $$+x$$ direction at speed $$v$$ through a laboratory (the __unprimed frame__). Two events occur: event $$B$$ at the back of the train and event $$F$$ at the front. In the train's frame…
statement:
A train has length $$L'$$ in its own reference frame (the __primed frame__) and moves in the $$+x$$ direction at speed $$v$$ through a laboratory (the __unprimed frame__). Two events occur: event $$B$$ at the back of the train and event $$F$$ at the front. In the train's frame, $$B$$ and $$F$$ are simultaneous.

For the parts that use them, here are the __Lorentz transformations__ in the standard configuration (primed frame moving at $$+v$$ along $$x$$ in the unprimed frame, origins coinciding): $$x' = \gamma(x - vt)$$ and $$t' = \gamma\left(t - \dfrac{v}{c^2}x\right),$$ with $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}.$$ To invert them, swap primed and unprimed coordinates and replace $$v$$ with $$-v.$$

__(a)__ What is the length $$L$$ of the train in the laboratory frame, in terms of $$L'$$ and $$\gamma?$$

__(b)__ Imagine that when events $$B$$ and $$F$$ occur, a flash of light is emitted from each, and both flashes travel toward an observer standing at the middle of the train. Use this thought experiment to determine which event occurs first in the laboratory frame. (Hint: the arrival of the two flashes at the observer is a single event, so all frames agree the flashes arrive together.)

__(c)__ Still reasoning in the laboratory frame, compute the time $$\Delta t$$ by which the earlier event precedes the later one. You may use closing speeds like $$c + v$$ and $$c - v$$ for the rate at which the distance between a light flash and the moving observer shrinks — a closing speed may exceed $$c$$ because it is not the speed of any object.

__(d)__ Now confirm your answer with the Lorentz transformations. Assign coordinates in the train frame: $$x'_B = 0,$$ $$t'_B = 0,$$ $$x'_F = L',$$ $$t'_F = 0.$$ Find $$t_B$$ and $$t_F$$ in the laboratory frame.

__(e)__ The same transformation gives the laboratory positions $$x_B = 0$$ and $$x_F = \gamma L'.$$ Since $$B$$ happened at the back of the train and $$F$$ at the front, it seems the train's length in the lab frame is $$x_F - x_B = \gamma L'$$ — contradicting part (a). Resolve the contradiction.

__(f)__ Suppose two clocks ride on the train, one at the back and one at the front, synchronized with each other in the train's frame. To observers in the laboratory frame, which clock reads a later time, and by how much? (Careful: there is a second relativistic effect to account for besides the simultaneity shift.)

label: PW215
name: Velocity Transformation in Two Dimensions — Adopt the standard configuration: a train (the __primed frame__)…
desc: Adopt the standard configuration: a train (the __primed frame__) moves in the $$+x$$ direction at speed $$v$$ in the frame of a laboratory (the __unprimed frame__), with the origins of the two frames coinciding. The Lorentz transformations are $$x' = \gamma(x - vt),$$ $$y' =…
statement:
Adopt the standard configuration: a train (the __primed frame__) moves in the $$+x$$ direction at speed $$v$$ in the frame of a laboratory (the __unprimed frame__), with the origins of the two frames coinciding. The Lorentz transformations are $$x' = \gamma(x - vt),$$ $$y' = y,$$ and $$t' = \gamma\left(t - \dfrac{v}{c^2}x\right),$$ where $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}.$$

In the laboratory frame, a particle moves with constant velocity components $$u_x$$ and $$u_y.$$ Find $$u_x'$$ and $$u_y',$$ the velocity components of the particle in the train frame.

Hint: to apply Lorentz transformations, first identify events and assign them coordinates. Nothing special happens to this particle, so invent your own events: let event $$A$$ be the particle passing through the origin, with coordinates $$(x_A, y_A, t_A) = (0,0,0)$$ in the lab frame, and let event $$B$$ be the particle's position at a later lab time $$t.$$ (Because the Lorentz transformation is __linear__, it maps the origin to the origin, so $$A$$ has coordinates $$(0,0,0)$$ in the train frame too.)

label: PW215
name: Two Invariants: the Spacetime Interval and the Mass — An __invariant__ is a quantity that has the same value…
desc: An __invariant__ is a quantity that has the same value in every inertial reference frame. This problem establishes the two most important ones. __(a)__ The __spacetime interval__ between two events $$A$$ and $$B$$ is defined as $$\Delta s^2 = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2…
statement:
An __invariant__ is a quantity that has the same value in every inertial reference frame. This problem establishes the two most important ones.

__(a)__ The __spacetime interval__ between two events $$A$$ and $$B$$ is defined as $$\Delta s^2 = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2 - c^2\Delta t^2,$$ where $$\Delta x = x_A - x_B$$ and so on. Show that the Lorentz transformations $$x' = \gamma(x - vt),$$ $$y' = y,$$ $$z' = z,$$ $$t' = \gamma\left(t - \dfrac{v}{c^2}x\right)$$ preserve the interval: $$\Delta s'^2 = \Delta s^2$$ for any pair of events. (Helpful facts: $$y$$ and $$z$$ transform trivially, so you may ignore them; and because the Lorentz transformation is linear, coordinate __differences__ transform exactly the same way as coordinates themselves.)

__(b)__ A particle of mass $$m$$ moving at speed $$v$$ has energy $$E = \gamma mc^2$$ and momentum $$p = \gamma mv.$$ Energy and momentum are each different in different frames — neither is invariant. Show, however, that the combination $$E^2 - c^2p^2$$ depends only on the mass, and find the mass in terms of $$E$$ and $$p.$$ Why does this prove $$E^2 - c^2 p^2$$ is invariant?

label: PW215
name: Decay of the S Meson (USAPhO 2012, Problem A1) — Suppose a newly-discovered subatomic particle, the __S…
desc: Suppose a newly-discovered subatomic particle, the __S meson__, has mass $$M.$$ When at rest, it lives for exactly $$\tau = 3\times 10^{-8}\;\mathrm{s}$$ before decaying into two identical particles called __P mesons__, each of mass $$\alpha M$$ (with $$\alpha < \tfrac12$$)…
statement:
Suppose a newly-discovered subatomic particle, the __S meson__, has mass $$M.$$ When at rest, it lives for exactly $$\tau = 3\times 10^{-8}\;\mathrm{s}$$ before decaying into two identical particles called __P mesons__, each of mass $$\alpha M$$ (with $$\alpha < \tfrac12$$). Recall that a particle of mass $$m$$ moving at speed $$v$$ has total energy $$E = \gamma mc^2$$ (including rest energy $$mc^2$$), kinetic energy $$K = (\gamma - 1)mc^2,$$ and momentum $$p = \gamma m v,$$ where $$\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}.$$ (This problem appeared as USAPhO 2012, Problem A1.)

__(a)__ In the reference frame where the S meson is at rest, find the kinetic energy, the momentum, and the speed of each P meson, in terms of $$M,$$ $$\alpha,$$ and the speed of light $$c.$$ (Why must the two P mesons have equal kinetic energies?)

__(b)__ Now work in a reference frame where the S meson travels a distance $$d = 9\;\mathrm{m}$$ between its creation and its decay. Find the velocity and the kinetic energy of the S meson in this frame, in terms of $$c$$ and $$M.$$ Warning: the naive answer $$v = d/\tau$$ ignores time dilation. A slick approach: the creation and decay of the meson are two events, and the __invariant interval__ $$\Delta s^2 = \Delta x^2 - c^2\Delta t^2$$ between them is the same in every frame — evaluate it in the meson's own frame, then in the lab frame.

label: PW215
name: Compactness and the Equivalence Principle — General relativity is a theory of gravity that incorporates…
desc: General relativity is a theory of gravity that incorporates special relativity; its corrections to Newtonian gravity are negligible for most systems but dominant for others. This problem builds the dimensionless number that tells you which regime you are in — playing the role…
statement:
General relativity is a theory of gravity that incorporates special relativity; its corrections to Newtonian gravity are negligible for most systems but dominant for others. This problem builds the dimensionless number that tells you which regime you are in — playing the role for gravity that $$\gamma$$ plays in special relativity.

__(a)__ Using Newton's gravitational constant $$G,$$ the speed of light $$c,$$ and a system's mass $$M$$ and size $$R,$$ construct a dimensionless constant that grows larger the more important general relativity is, using a single power of $$G.$$ (Hint: you needn't memorize the dimensions of $$G$$ — instead, recall that $$\dfrac{GM^2}{R}$$ is an energy, namely the scale of the system's gravitational potential energy, and compare it to another natural energy of the system.)

__(b)__ Evaluate your constant, to order of magnitude, for the Earth ($$M \approx 6\times 10^{24}\;\mathrm{kg},$$ $$R \approx 6.4\times 10^6\;\mathrm{m}$$) and for the sun ($$M \approx 2\times 10^{30}\;\mathrm{kg},$$ $$R \approx 7\times 10^8\;\mathrm{m}$$). Then evaluate it exactly for a black hole, taking $$R$$ to be the __Schwarzschild radius__ $$R_s = \dfrac{2GM}{c^2}.$$ Use $$G \approx 6.7\times 10^{-11}\;\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}.$$

__(c)__ The most important idea in general relativity is the __equivalence principle__: on small scales of space and time, there is no physical difference between a gravitational field and an acceleration of your reference frame. As a concrete example: you stand on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at $$0.25\,g,$$ and your mass is $$m.$$ What does the scale read? If you drop your phone, how does its fall compare to a fall in ordinary gravity? Use the equivalence principle to explain why astronauts on the space station feel weightless even though Earth's gravity at their altitude is nearly as strong as on the ground.

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: An inulin molecule has a molecular weight of $$4000$$ daltons, meaning that one mole has…
desc: An inulin molecule has a molecular weight of $$4000$$ daltons, meaning that one mole has a weight of $$4000 \;\mathrm{g}.$$ Assume that it is spherical with a radius of $$1.2 \;\mathrm{nm}.$$ What is the angular frequency $$\omega$$ of a photon absorbed when an inulin molecule…
statement:
An inulin molecule has a molecular weight of $$4000$$ daltons, meaning that one mole has a weight of $$4000 \;\mathrm{g}.$$ Assume that it is spherical with a radius of $$1.2 \;\mathrm{nm}.$$

What is the angular frequency $$\omega$$ of a photon absorbed when an inulin molecule increases its rotational quantum number from 10 to 11?

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Some elements have radioactive isotopes (radioisotopes) which can be used for medical…
desc: Some elements have radioactive isotopes (radioisotopes) which can be used for medical imaging. A radioisotope is injected into the bloodstream, whence it is taken up by organs in the body. Areas of extremely high cell growth or repair such as tumors take up and retain this…
statement:
Some elements have radioactive isotopes (radioisotopes) which can be used for medical imaging. A radioisotope is injected into the bloodstream, whence it is taken up by organs in the body. Areas of extremely high cell growth or repair such as tumors take up and retain this isotope much more efficiently than any other tissue. Thus, imaging using radioisotopes can be used to indicate malignant tissue growth.

Technetium--99m ($${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$) is one such radioisotope. It is used for imaging organs such as the thyroid, liver, kidneys, and brain. The half life of this isotope is $$\tau_{1/2} = 6.01 \;\mathrm{h}.$$

Rates of radioactivity can be measured in Curies (Ci), equivalent to $$3.7 \times 10^{10}$$ decays per second.

In this question, we examine a model of the process of $${}^{99mc}\mathrm{Tc}$$ uptake in a patient's cancerous thyroid glands. The patient is an otherwise healthy adult. In this model, $$A = 10.0 \;\mathrm{mCi}$$ of $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$ is injected into a vein in the patient's arm. The radius of the vein is $$1.00 \;\mathrm{mm}.$$ The radioisotope enters the bloodstream, then enters each thyroid gland through an artery in the patient's neck. The radius of this artery is $$1.70 \;\mathrm{mm}.$$

Let the velocities of blood flow in the partient's arm and neck be $$v_a = 3.00 \;\mathrm{mm/s}$$ and $$v_n = 40.0 \;\mathrm{cm/s}.$$ Let the total blood volume of the patient be $$V = 5 \;\mathrm{L},$$ and let each thyroid gland (there are two) have volume $$V_t = 9 \;\mathrm{mL}.$$

The $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$ emits gamma rays of energy $$E = 2.24 \times 10^{-14} \;\mathrm{J}.$$

**a)** What is the concentration (in number of atoms per liter) of $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$ in the bloodstream after the injection?

**b)** Qualitatively, sketch the amount of $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}$$ in the thyroid as a function of time, starting from the time of injection.

**c)** The continuity equation in fluid mechanics states that the volume flow rate of fluid flowing through a pipe is constant. Consider the blood flow in the arm and neck of the patient. Does the continuity equation hold in this model? Explain why or why not.

**d)** What is the initial rate of energy release due to gamma radiation emitted from a thyroid gland? In this and subsequent parts you may neglect the time taken for the thyroid glands to saturate with $${}^{99m}\mathrm{Tc}.$$

**e)** A scan is taken over $$t_s = 10.0 \;\mathrm{min}.$$ If the total energy detected by the scanner exceeds $$E_{\rm min} = 5\times 10^{-4} \;\mathrm{J},$$ an image appears due to radioactivity in the thyroid gland. Approximately how much time will elapse before radioactivity is no longer detected in a scan?

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: At very high temperatures (as in the early universe), the proton and the neutron can be…
desc: At very high temperatures (as in the early universe), the proton and the neutron can be thought of as two different states of the same particle, called the __nucleon__. (The reactions that convert a proton to a neutron or vice versa require the absorption of an electron or a…
statement:
At very high temperatures (as in the early universe), the proton and the neutron can be thought of as two different states of the same particle, called the __nucleon__. (The reactions that convert a proton to a neutron or vice versa require the absorption of an electron or a positron or a neutrino, but all of these particles tend to very abundant at sufficiently high temperatures.)

Since the neutron's mass is higher than the proton's by $$2.3 \times 10^{-30} \;\mathrm{kg},$$ its energy is higher by this amount times $$c^2.$$ Suppose, that at some very early time, the nucleons were in thermal equilibrium with the rest of the universe at $$10^{11} \;\mathrm{K}.$$ What fraction of the nucleons at that time were protons, and what fraction were neutrons?
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: The mass of an electron is $$m_e$$ and its charge is $$-e.$$ Consider the nucleus of a…
desc: The mass of an electron is $$m_e$$ and its charge is $$-e.$$ Consider the nucleus of a hydrogen atom to be infinitely massive and have charge $$e.$$ Imagine the electron to be confined to a ball centered on the nucleus with radius $$r.$$ **a)** Estimate the kinetic energy of the…
statement:
The mass of an electron is $$m_e$$ and its charge is $$-e.$$ Consider the nucleus of a hydrogen atom to be infinitely massive and have charge $$e.$$ Imagine the electron to be confined to a ball centered on the nucleus with radius $$r.$$

**a)** Estimate the kinetic energy of the electron from the uncertainty principle.

**b)** Find $$r$$ that minimizes the sum of the electrostatic potential energy of the system and the kinetic energy of the electron. Compare your result to the Bohr radius.

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Use dimensional analysis to estimate the speed of sound in diamond from fundamental…
desc: Use dimensional analysis to estimate the speed of sound in diamond from fundamental constants and $$m_n,$$ the mass of a carbon nucleus, and $$m_e,$$ the mass of an electron. Is dimensional analysis alone enough to determine this speed? If not, use our equations for the binding…
statement: Use dimensional analysis to estimate the speed of sound in diamond from fundamental constants and $$m_n,$$ the mass of a carbon nucleus, and $$m_e,$$ the mass of an electron. Is dimensional analysis alone enough to determine this speed? If not, use our equations for the binding energy and radius of atoms, combined with your understanding of the theory of waves, to conjecture the correct equation up to a constant. Compare your result to the true speed of sound in diamond, about $$10^4\;\mathrm{m/s}.$$

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Think of the nucleus of an atom as a liquid of protons and neutrons; the nucleus itself…
desc: Think of the nucleus of an atom as a liquid of protons and neutrons; the nucleus itself is like a drop of liquid. The binding energy of a nucleus is $$\epsilon \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-14} \;\mathrm{J}$$ per nucleon. The radius of a nucleus is about $$r \approx 10^{-14}…
statement:
Think of the nucleus of an atom as a liquid of protons and neutrons; the nucleus itself is like a drop of liquid.

The binding energy of a nucleus is $$\epsilon \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-14} \;\mathrm{J}$$ per nucleon.

The radius of a nucleus is about $$r \approx 10^{-14} \;\mathrm{m}.$$

The mass of a nucleon is about $$m \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-27} \;\mathrm{kg}.$$

Let the number of nucleons be $$A.$$

Suppose that the surface tension $$\sigma$$ of the drop is such that the surface energy is similar to the binding energy.

Use these figures and assumptions to estimate the frequency of oscillations of the nucleus.
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: A nucleus contains $$N$$ neutrons and $$Z$$ protons. It therefore contains $$A = N+Z$$…
desc: A nucleus contains $$N$$ neutrons and $$Z$$ protons. It therefore contains $$A = N+Z$$ nucleons. The mass, $$M(A,N,Z)$$ can be approximated using the __semi-empirical mass formula__: $$M(A,Z) \approx N m_n + Z m_p - a_a A + a_2 A^{2/3} + a_3 Z^2 A^{-1/3} + a_4(A - 2Z)^2 A^{-1} +…
statement:
A nucleus contains $$N$$ neutrons and $$Z$$ protons. It therefore contains $$A = N+Z$$ nucleons.

The mass, $$M(A,N,Z)$$ can be approximated using the __semi-empirical mass formula__: $$M(A,Z) \approx N m_n + Z m_p - a_a A + a_2 A^{2/3} + a_3 Z^2 A^{-1/3} + a_4(A - 2Z)^2 A^{-1} + a_5 \delta(A,Z)$$ where \begin{aligned} a_1 & = 15.8 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \\ a_2 & = 18.3 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \\ a_3 & = 0.714 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \\ a_4 & = 23.2 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \\ a_5 & = 12 \;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2 \end{aligned} and $$ \delta(A,Z) = \begin{cases} -A^{-1/2}; \;\; \text{ Z and N are odd} \\ A^{1/2}; \;\; \text{ Z and N are even} \\ 0; \;\; \text{A is odd} \end{cases} $$

The model is partly based on theory and partly based on experiment. $$A$$ and $$Z$$ are taken to vary continuously in this model.

**a)** Find an expression for the binding energy of the nucleus. The $$\delta(A,Z)$$ terms captures the tendency of nucleons to form pairs in the nucleus, so is often referred to as the "pairing" term. Give a brief explanation of the origin of the other terms in the equation. Your goal is not to look these up, but to your understanding of the functional forms and the places that energy might come from to conjecture what each term means.

**b)** The term in equation which has a constant $$a_3$$ in front is often written as $$a_3 Z(Z-1) A^{-1/3}.$$ Suggest why this might be.

**c)** Represent the binding energy graphically as a function of $$Z$$ for a given mass number, justifying your reasoning.
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Planck's blackbody radiation law says that the power per unit surface radiated by a…
desc: Planck's blackbody radiation law says that the power per unit surface radiated by a convex black body at temperature $$T$$ between the wavelengths $$\lambda$$ and $$\lambda + \mathrm{d}\lambda$$ is $$W(\lambda, T) = \dfrac{2\pi c^2 h}{\lambda^5\left(e^{hc/(\lambda k_B T)} -…
statement:
Planck's blackbody radiation law says that the power per unit surface radiated by a convex black body at temperature $$T$$ between the wavelengths $$\lambda$$ and $$\lambda + \mathrm{d}\lambda$$ is $$W(\lambda, T) = \dfrac{2\pi c^2 h}{\lambda^5\left(e^{hc/(\lambda k_B T)} - 1\right)}.$$

In this problem we do a couple of basic calculations with this law; in the next two problems we see where it comes from.

**a)** Find the total power emitted per unit surface area. The result is called the __Stefan-Boltzmann law__, and often written $$\sigma T^4,$$ where $$\sigma$$ is the __Stefan-Boltzmann constant__. Express $$\sigma$$ in terms of other fundamental constants.

You may use the result $$\int_0^\infty \dfrac{x^3}{e^x - 1}\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{\pi^4}{15}.$$

**b)** Wien's displacement law says that the wavelength where the spectrum peaks is given by $$\lambda_{\rm peak} = \dfrac{b}{T}.$$ Find $$b,$$ finding the value of any constants involved to three significant figures.
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: In this problem and the next, we derive Planck's blackbody radiation law, combining…
desc: In this problem and the next, we derive Planck's blackbody radiation law, combining results from quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics. You may want to review the problems on the partition function from our statistical mechanics class before working this problem. **a)**…
statement:
In this problem and the next, we derive Planck's blackbody radiation law, combining results from quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics. You may want to review the problems on the partition function from our statistical mechanics class before working this problem.

**a)** Consider a one-dimensional box of length $$L.$$ Inside the box are photons. These behave as quantum particles in a box. What are the allowed wavelengths, momenta, and energies of the photons? Give your answer in terms of fundamental constants and $$n,$$ the quantum number of the photon. ($$n=1$$ in the lowest allowed mode.)

**b)** Find the partition function for the box at temperature $$T.$$

**c)** Find the average energy $$\bar{E}$$ of the box at temperature $$T.$$

**d)** Next we consider a three-dimensional box. A photon in this box has three quantum numbers: $$n_x, n_y,$$ and $$n_z.$$ You can think of its wavefunction as multiplying three wavefunctions together - one for each dimension of the box. Find the energy of a photon in terms of $$n_x, n_y,$$ and $$n_z.$$

**e)** Suppose we wanted to find the total energy inside the box. To do this, we take the average energy in each mode and integrate over all the modes. Although the modes are discrete, we can approximate them as continuous with the integral $$U = 2\int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \bar{E}(n_x,n_y,n_z) \mathrm{d}n_x \mathrm{d}n_x \mathrm{d}n_z.$$

We have included an extra factor of $$2$$ to account for the two independent polarization states of a photon.

To actually carry out this integral, we convert to spherical coordinates, obtaining $$U = \int_0^\infty \mathrm{d}n \int_0^{\pi/2} \mathrm{d}\theta \int_0^{\pi/2} \mathrm{d}\phi n^2 \sin \theta \bar{E}(n).$$

Find $$U/V,$$ the energy per unit volume in the box.

**f)** Find the entropy of this "photon gas".

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: This problem continues the previous one on a derivation of the black body spectrum.
desc: This problem continues the previous one on a derivation of the black body spectrum. **g)** For the integral in part (e), perform just the integrals over $$\theta$$ and $$\phi$$ to obtain a one-dimensional integral over $$n.$$ Change variables to $$\epsilon,$$ the energy of a…
statement:
This problem continues the previous one on a derivation of the black body spectrum.

**g)** For the integral in part (e), perform just the integrals over $$\theta$$ and $$\phi$$ to obtain a one-dimensional integral over $$n.$$ Change variables to $$\epsilon,$$ the energy of a photon.

The resulting integrand is denoted $$u(\epsilon),$$ it is the energy density per unit photon energy inside the box. Find $$u(\epsilon).$$

**h)** Suppose a small hole of area $$a$$ is poked in the box. What is the power per unit wavelength, $$\lambda,$$ that comes out of the hole? (This involves two parts - studying the kinematics of the photons to see how many escape the hole per unit time, and switching variables from photon energy to wavelength.) Your result black body radiation law.

**i)** Give an argument from thermodynamics that an ideal black body must radiate in the same way as the hole in the box full of photons.
