lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Matter Waves and the Energy of a Photon — In 1924, Louis de Broglie proposed that particles of matter can be…
desc: In 1924, Louis de Broglie proposed that particles of matter can be modeled as waves, with the wavelength of a particle of momentum $$p$$ given by $$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p},$$ where $$h \approx 6.626\times 10^{-34}\;\mathrm{J\cdot s}$$ is __Planck's constant__. Light also comes in…
statement:
In 1924, Louis de Broglie proposed that particles of matter can be modeled as waves, with the wavelength of a particle of momentum $$p$$ given by $$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p},$$ where $$h \approx 6.626\times 10^{-34}\;\mathrm{J\cdot s}$$ is __Planck's constant__. Light also comes in individual bundles, called __photons__, and the same wavelength formula applies to them. From relativity, recall that the energy and momentum of light are related by $$E = pc.$$

__(a)__ Two particles of the same mass travel at different (non-relativistic) speeds. Which has the smaller de Broglie wavelength — the faster particle or the slower one? A microscope can only resolve details comparable to the wavelength of the particles it uses; use your answer to explain why an __electron microscope__ can see much finer detail than a light microscope.

__(b)__ Combine $$E = pc,$$ $$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p},$$ and the wave relation $$c = f\lambda$$ to find the energy of a photon in terms of its frequency $$f.$$ Then rewrite the energy in terms of the angular frequency $$\omega = 2\pi f$$ and the __reduced Planck's constant__ $$\hbar = \dfrac{h}{2\pi} \approx 1.054\times 10^{-34}\;\mathrm{J\cdot s}.$$

__(c)__ Name a quantity from classical mechanics with the same dimensions as Planck's constant.

__(d)__ A radio transmitter with power $$P = 50\;\mathrm{kW}$$ broadcasts at frequency $$f = 1\;\mathrm{MHz}.$$ How many photons does it emit per period of the wave?

__(e)__ An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of $$100\;\mathrm{V}.$$ What is its kinetic energy, in electron-volts and in joules? (One __electron-volt__ is the charge of an electron times one volt: $$1\;\mathrm{eV} = 1.602\times 10^{-19}\;\mathrm{J}.$$) The rest mass energy of an electron is $$m_e c^2 \approx 0.5\;\mathrm{MeV},$$ i.e. $$m_e \approx 9.11\times 10^{-31}\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Explain why the electron is non-relativistic, and find its de Broglie wavelength.

__(f)__ The __Compton wavelength__ of a particle is the wavelength of a photon whose energy equals the particle's rest mass energy $$mc^2.$$ Find the Compton wavelength $$\lambda_c$$ of a particle of mass $$m$$ in terms of $$h,$$ $$m,$$ and $$c.$$
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Gamma Rays Identified by Compton Scattering — A sample of a certain element is irradiated with high-energy…
desc: A sample of a certain element is irradiated with high-energy gamma-ray photons. The gamma radiation scatters off electrons in the sample, transferring a large amount of kinetic energy to them; some electrons gain enough energy to be ejected from their atoms and hit a detector…
statement:
A sample of a certain element is irradiated with high-energy gamma-ray photons. The gamma radiation scatters off electrons in the sample, transferring a large amount of kinetic energy to them; some electrons gain enough energy to be ejected from their atoms and hit a detector screen. The electrons can be considered free and at rest before each scattering event. The measured spectrum of the scattered electrons shows that the incoming gamma radiation is almost perfectly monochromatic, and the __maximum__ measured kinetic energy of the ejected electrons is $$E_c = 170\;\mathrm{keV}.$$ What is the wavelength of the incoming gamma radiation?

Useful facts: the mass of an electron is $$m_e = 9.1094\times 10^{-31}\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Compton derived that when a photon of initial wavelength $$\lambda_0$$ scatters off a single free electron through a __scattering angle__ $$\theta$$ (the angle between the photon's incoming and outgoing paths, so $$\theta = 0$$ means the photon continues straight ahead), the scattered photon's wavelength is $$\lambda' = \lambda_0 + \lambda_c(1 - \cos\theta),$$ where $$\lambda_c = \dfrac{h}{m_e c} \approx 2.43\times 10^{-12}\;\mathrm{m}$$ is the electron's __Compton wavelength__. A photon of wavelength $$\lambda$$ has energy $$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}.$$

__(a)__ Which scattering angle $$\theta$$ gives the ejected electron its maximum kinetic energy? Justify your answer both intuitively and from Compton's formula.

__(b)__ Use conservation of energy to set up an equation for $$\lambda_0,$$ and solve it to find the wavelength of the incoming gamma rays.
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Bosons and Fermions in a Harmonic Oscillator — A one-dimensional __quantum harmonic oscillator__ — the…
desc: A one-dimensional __quantum harmonic oscillator__ — the quantum version of a mass on a spring, with classical angular frequency $$\omega$$ — has __discrete__ energy levels: its energy can only take certain fixed values. The lowest possible energy (the __ground state__ energy) is…
statement:
A one-dimensional __quantum harmonic oscillator__ — the quantum version of a mass on a spring, with classical angular frequency $$\omega$$ — has __discrete__ energy levels: its energy can only take certain fixed values. The lowest possible energy (the __ground state__ energy) is $$E_0 = \dfrac{\hbar\omega}{2},$$ and adjacent levels are separated by equal steps of $$\hbar\omega.$$ (This uniform spacing is special to the harmonic oscillator; most quantum systems have unevenly spaced levels.) The figure shows the wavefunctions of the lowest levels, each drawn at the height of its energy in the potential well. The __square__ of the wavefunction gives the probability density for finding the particle at each position.

__(a)__ Write the energy $$E_n$$ of the $$n$$th level, for $$n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

__(b)__ For the ground state ($$n = 0$$), where is the particle most likely to be found? For a highly excited state such as $$n = 7,$$ is the particle more likely to be found near the center of the well or out near the edges? Explain why the highly excited case makes sense from the point of view of a __classical__ oscillator. (The matching of quantum behavior to classical behavior at large quantum numbers is called the __correspondence principle__.)

Now place three identical, non-interacting particles of mass $$m$$ in this oscillator. ("Non-interacting" means we ignore any forces between the particles, such as electrostatic repulsion, and focus purely on __quantum statistics__.) __Bosons__ are particles that are allowed to occupy the same quantum state. __Fermions__ are not: no two fermions may be in exactly the same quantum state — this is the __Pauli exclusion principle__. An electron is a fermion, and in addition to its position wavefunction it carries a property called __spin__ with exactly two possible states, up and down; two electrons in the same oscillator level with opposite spins are in different quantum states.

Find the minimum total energy of the system if __(c)__ the particles are bosons; __(d)__ the particles are electrons; __(e)__ the particles are electrons whose spins are all polarized in the same direction.
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: A Quantum Bouncing Ball — Consider a particle of mass $$m$$ that elastically bounces off of an infinitely…
desc: Consider a particle of mass $$m$$ that elastically bounces off of an infinitely hard horizontal surface under the influence of gravity. The total mechanical energy of the particle is $$E$$ and the acceleration of free fall is $$g.$$ Treat the particle as a point mass and assume…
statement:
Consider a particle of mass $$m$$ that elastically bounces off of an infinitely hard horizontal surface under the influence of gravity. The total mechanical energy of the particle is $$E$$ and the acceleration of free fall is $$g.$$ Treat the particle as a point mass and assume the motion is non-relativistic. (From the USA Physics Olympiad.)

__(a)__ An estimate for the regime where quantum effects become important can be found by considering when the de Broglie wavelength of the particle, $$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p},$$ is on the same order as the height of a bounce. Assuming that the de Broglie wavelength is defined by the __maximum__ momentum of the bouncing particle, determine the value of the energy $$E_q$$ where quantum effects become important. Write your answer in terms of some or all of $$g,$$ $$m,$$ and Planck's constant $$h.$$

__(b)__ A second approach gives an estimate for the actual allowed energy levels of the bouncing particle. Assuming the particle rises to a height $$H,$$ impose the __Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization condition__ $$2\int_0^H p\,\mathrm{d}x = \left(n + \dfrac12\right)h,$$ where $$p$$ is the momentum as a function of the height $$x$$ above the ground and $$n$$ is a non-negative integer. Determine the allowed energies $$E_n$$ as a function of the integer $$n$$ and some or all of $$g,$$ $$m,$$ and $$h.$$

__(c)__ Numerically determine the minimum energy of a bouncing __neutron__. The mass of a neutron is $$m_n = 1.675\times 10^{-27}\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ Give your answer in joules or electron-volts.

__(d)__ Determine the bounce height of one of these minimum-energy neutrons.
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Energy Levels from the Bohr Model — In the __Bohr model__, the negatively charged electron orbits a small…
desc: In the __Bohr model__, the negatively charged electron orbits a small, positively charged nucleus, much as a planet orbits the sun. Derive the possible energy levels of the hydrogen atom (one proton, one electron) from these assumptions: the electron of mass $$m_e$$ and charge…
statement:
In the __Bohr model__, the negatively charged electron orbits a small, positively charged nucleus, much as a planet orbits the sun. Derive the possible energy levels of the hydrogen atom (one proton, one electron) from these assumptions: the electron of mass $$m_e$$ and charge $$-e$$ moves in a circle of radius $$r$$ around the proton (charge $$+e$$); matter has the de Broglie wavelength $$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p};$$ and an __integer number of matter waves fits around one orbit__. The attractive Coulomb force between proton and electron has magnitude $$F = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}.$$

__(a)__ Turn the "integer number of waves in one orbit" condition, $$n\lambda = 2\pi r,$$ into a statement about the electron's angular momentum $$L = pr.$$ Show that you get the same statement from the __Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization condition__ $$\oint p\,\mathrm{d}s = nh$$ integrated around the circular orbit.

__(b)__ Find the electron's speed $$v$$ in terms of $$n,$$ $$\hbar,$$ $$m_e,$$ and $$r.$$

__(c)__ The Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force, $$\dfrac{m_e v^2}{r}.$$ Combine this with part (b) to find the allowed orbit radii $$r_n$$ in terms of $$\epsilon_0,$$ $$h,$$ $$e,$$ $$m_e,$$ and $$n.$$ Evaluate $$r_1$$ numerically.

__(d)__ The total energy of the $$n$$th orbit is $$E_n = \dfrac{m_e v^2}{2} - \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r_n}.$$ Show that $$E_n = -\left(\dfrac{m_e e^4}{8h^2\epsilon_0^2}\right)\dfrac{1}{n^2}.$$ The constant in parentheses evaluates to $$13.6\;\mathrm{eV}$$ — the __ionization energy__ of hydrogen, the minimum energy required to remove its electron.

__(e)__ Now let the nucleus have charge $$+Ze$$ (with still just one electron). How do the orbit radii and the energy levels change? Express the new energies $$E_{n;Z}$$ in terms of the hydrogen energies $$E_n.$$

__(f)__ Find the ionization energy of the lithium ion $$\mathrm{Li}^{2+},$$ which has $$Z = 3$$ protons and a single remaining electron.
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Estimates from the Uncertainty Principle — The __Heisenberg uncertainty principle__ says there is a…
desc: The __Heisenberg uncertainty principle__ says there is a fundamental limit on how precisely a particle's position and momentum can simultaneously be determined: $$\Delta p\,\Delta x \ge \dfrac{\hbar}{2}.$$ A similar relation connects the uncertainty in a state's energy to the…
statement:
The __Heisenberg uncertainty principle__ says there is a fundamental limit on how precisely a particle's position and momentum can simultaneously be determined: $$\Delta p\,\Delta x \ge \dfrac{\hbar}{2}.$$ A similar relation connects the uncertainty in a state's energy to the uncertainty in its lifetime: $$\Delta E\,\Delta t \ge \dfrac{\hbar}{2}.$$

__(a)__ An unstable quantum state has a very short lifetime. What does the uncertainty principle say about how precisely the energy of that state is determined?

__(b)__ Estimate, to order of magnitude, the kinetic energy (in electron-volts) of an electron trapped inside a volume the size of a hydrogen atom, $$\Delta x \approx 10^{-10}\;\mathrm{m}.$$ Take the electron's momentum to be of the same order as its momentum uncertainty, $$p \approx \Delta p \approx \dfrac{\hbar}{\Delta x},$$ and use $$m_e \approx 9\times 10^{-31}\;\mathrm{kg}$$ and $$1\;\mathrm{eV} = 1.602\times 10^{-19}\;\mathrm{J}.$$

__(c)__ In the Bohr model, a nucleus of charge $$Ze$$ binds its innermost electron at an orbit radius proportional to $$\dfrac{1}{Z}.$$ Use the uncertainty principle to explain quantitatively why a simple non-relativistic model of the atom must break down for very heavy nuclei (large $$Z$$).
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: The Proton-Proton Chain in the Sun — The energy radiated by the Sun is generated primarily by the fusion of…
desc: The energy radiated by the Sun is generated primarily by the fusion of hydrogen into helium-4. In stars the size of the Sun, the primary mechanism is the __proton-proton chain__. (From the USA Physics Olympiad.) In each reaction below, the amount listed in parentheses is the…
statement:
The energy radiated by the Sun is generated primarily by the fusion of hydrogen into helium-4. In stars the size of the Sun, the primary mechanism is the __proton-proton chain__. (From the USA Physics Olympiad.) In each reaction below, the amount listed in parentheses is the total kinetic energy carried by the products, including gamma rays; $$p$$ is a proton, $$e^+$$ a positron, $$e^-$$ an electron, $$\gamma$$ a gamma ray, and $$X_1, \ldots, X_7$$ are particles for you to identify.

The chain begins with: reaction 1, $$2p \rightarrow X_1 + e^+ + X_2 \quad (0.42\;\mathrm{MeV});$$ and reaction 2, $$p + X_1 \rightarrow X_3 + \gamma \quad (5.49\;\mathrm{MeV}).$$ The density of electrons in the Sun's core is high enough that the positron is annihilated almost immediately, releasing an energy $$x$$: reaction 3, $$e^+ + e^- \rightarrow 2\gamma \quad (x).$$

Subsequently, two major processes occur simultaneously. The "pp I branch" is the single reaction 4, $$2X_3 \rightarrow {}^4\mathrm{He} + 2X_4 \quad (y),$$ which releases an energy $$y.$$ The "pp II branch" consists of three reactions: reaction 5, $$X_3 + {}^4\mathrm{He} \rightarrow X_5 + \gamma;$$ reaction 6, $$X_5 + e^- \rightarrow X_6 + X_7 \quad (z),$$ where $$z$$ is the energy released in that reaction; and reaction 7, $$X_6 + X_4 \rightarrow 2\,{}^4\mathrm{He}.$$

__(a)__ Identify $$X_1$$ through $$X_7.$$ $$X_2$$ and $$X_7$$ are neutral particles of negligible mass. Useful conservation laws: electric charge; __baryon number__ (the number of particles made of quarks — each proton or neutron counts $$+1$$); and __lepton number__ (electrons and neutrinos count $$+1,$$ positrons and antineutrinos $$-1$$). It is useful to know that the first few elements, in order of atomic number, are H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O.

__(b)__ The mass of the electron is $$0.51\;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2,$$ the mass of the proton is $$938.27\;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2,$$ and the mass of the helium-4 nucleus is $$3727.38\;\mathrm{MeV}/c^2.$$ Find the energy released during the production of one helium-4 nucleus, including the kinetic energy of all products and all energy carried by gamma rays.

__(c)__ Find the unknown energies $$x$$ and $$y$$ above.

__(d)__ Reaction 6 could be rewritten as $$X_5 \rightarrow X_6 + e^+ + X_7$$ without breaking any conservation laws. However, this alternative reaction does not proceed, because there is insufficient energy. What constraint does this fact place on $$z?$$

__(e)__ In which of the reaction steps is the energy carried by any given product the same every time the step occurs? Assume that the kinetic energy carried in by the reactants in each step is negligible, and that the products are in their ground states.
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Dating a Supernova with a Decay Chain — Element $$A$$ is an alpha emitter with a half-life of $$1.0\times…
desc: Element $$A$$ is an alpha emitter with a half-life of $$1.0\times 10^8$$ years. Its decay product $$B$$ has a half-life of $$60\;\mathrm{s}$$; it decays by beta decay to element $$C,$$ which is stable. It is thought that element $$A$$ was formed in the supernova that produced…
statement:
Element $$A$$ is an alpha emitter with a half-life of $$1.0\times 10^8$$ years. Its decay product $$B$$ has a half-life of $$60\;\mathrm{s}$$; it decays by beta decay to element $$C,$$ which is stable. It is thought that element $$A$$ was formed in the supernova that produced the material of the solar system. A sample of rock on Earth contains all three elements. (From the British Physics Olympiad.)

Recall that a radioactive substance with __decay constant__ $$\lambda$$ obeys $$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t},$$ where $$N$$ is the number of undecayed nuclei, and that the __half-life__ is $$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}.$$

__(a)__ What will happen to the proportions of $$A,$$ $$B,$$ and $$C$$ in the rock during one year? (You should not need to calculate anything.)

__(b)__ The ratio of the number of atoms of $$C$$ to those of $$A$$ in the rock is $$1.0\times 10^{11}.$$ When did the supernova occur?

__(c)__ What assumptions did you make in determining the date of the supernova?
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei

lesson: PW216: Quantum Mechanics: Probability, Uncertainty, Atoms, and Nuclei
label: PW216
name: Half-Lives from Activity Measurements — The __activity__ of a radioactive sample is its decay rate. Each…
desc: The __activity__ of a radioactive sample is its decay rate. Each nucleus decays independently, so the activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei: for a single radioactive species with decay constant $$\lambda,$$ the activity is $$A = \lambda N,$$ and it decreases…
statement:
The __activity__ of a radioactive sample is its decay rate. Each nucleus decays independently, so the activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei: for a single radioactive species with decay constant $$\lambda,$$ the activity is $$A = \lambda N,$$ and it decreases exponentially, $$A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t},$$ with half-life $$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\lambda}.$$

__(a)__ The activity of a certain substance is observed to decrease by $$1.00\%$$ over $$10^8\;\mathrm{s}$$ (approximately $$3$$ years). Determine the half-life $$t_{1/2}$$ of the substance.

__(b)__ Next, suppose we receive a sample of an unknown radioactive material. We bring it to the lab, measure the decay rate over time, and collect the data below, where $$N$$ is the measured activity in decays per second.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} t\;(\mathrm{s}) & N\;(\mathrm{decays/s}) & \ln N \\ \hline 0 & 42065 & 10.649 \\ 5 & 21262 & 9.9645 \\ 10 & 10851 & 9.2920 \\ 20 & 3023 & 8.0139 \\ 30 & 1044 & 6.9511 \\ 40 & 530.3 & 6.2734 \\ 50 & 383.7 & 5.9500 \\ 60 & 330.2 & 5.8000 \\ 80 & 279.3 & 5.6322 \\ 100 & 242.6 & 5.4915 \\ 120 & 211.2 & 5.3528 \\ 140 & 183.9 & 5.2142 \\ 160 & 160.1 & 5.0756 \\ 180 & 139.3 & 4.9370 \\ 200 & 121.3 & 4.7983 \end{array}$$

How many different radioactive nuclei does the sample __at least__ contain? (Hint: think about what a graph of $$\ln N$$ versus $$t$$ looks like for a single radioactive species, then plot the data.)

__(c)__ Estimate the two half-lives that can be found from the data.

__(d)__ Estimate how many nuclei of each species existed at $$t = 0.$$
tags: quantum mechanics: probability, uncertainty, atoms, and nuclei
